articles.title: More than 80 reported abducted in Nigeria as police find human remains
articles.excerpt: More than 80 people have been reported missing in Nigeria after being abducted by armed gangs, a media report said, as authorities announced the discovery of human remains suspected to belong to victi...
articles.body_text:
More than 80 people have been reported missing in Nigeria after being abducted by armed gangs, a media report said, as authorities announced the discovery of human remains suspected to belong to victims of kidnapping in the southeastern state of Abia.

The AFP news agency reported on Monday that at least 87 people, mostly women, were missing after two separate weekend attacks.

At least 47 farmers were abducted by armed men while harvesting peanuts in the northern Niger State on Saturday, while 40 women were kidnapped in the neighbouring state of Zamfara on Sunday, the agency reported, citing two security reports and a local source.

The kidnappings in the Mariga area of Niger and Yargada in Zamfara are the latest attacks by criminal gangs who specialise in ransom kidnappings and cattle rustling. Locally known as “bandits”, they regularly carry out bloody raids on villages, killing residents and torching homes after looting them.

Separately, police in Abia announced in a statement on Sunday that they found 28 human skulls and bones ”suspected to be [of kidnapped] victims”, after raiding camps linked to criminal groups in the forests.

In a statement on X, the police said suspects at the scene had fled and added that “efforts are intensified to apprehend the fleeing suspects”.

Mass abductions for ransom have become common in parts of northwestern and north-central Nigeria, with armed gangs frequently holding abductees until they are paid large sums of money.

In August, gunmen abducted as many as 600 worshippers during Friday prayers at a mosque in Dekera village in the north-central Niger State.

According to research from SBM Intelligence, a Lagos-based consultancy, armed groups raised some 7.8 billion naira (nearly $6m) in ransom payments between July 2025 and June 2026, more than triple the 2.6 billion naira paid during the same period last year.

The latest wave of kidnappings comes a few months ahead of the January presidential elections, in which security, along with the rising cost of living, is set to be a major issue.

President Bola Tinubu has faced growing criticism over lax security.

Residents of Niger State protested last Monday over the abduction of hundreds of people who, they said, remained in captivity a month after gunmen attacked several communities in one of the country’s largest mass kidnappings.

articles.title: OpenAI scraps rollout of new model over safety concerns
articles.excerpt:
OpenAI will not release its next-generation model - GPT-6.1 Astra - due to safety concerns, the ChatGPT-maker confirmed on Tuesday.

The AI system - which performs tasks like browsing the web and usin...
articles.body_text:
OpenAI will not release its next-generation model - GPT-6.1 Astra - due to safety concerns, the ChatGPT-maker confirmed on Tuesday.

The AI system - which performs tasks like browsing the web and using apps by itself - "didn't quite meet the bar" of the company's standards, Saachi Jain, head of safety systems at OpenAI, said.

In recent weeks, top AI leaders including OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic boss Dario Amodei have urged the industry to slow the pace of development due to concerns about risks associated with the technology.

The debate around those risks has intensified in recent weeks after models developed by top AI firms were involved in a number of incidents.

OpenAI's decision, first reported by the Wall Street Journal, is a rare instance of a major AI developer pulling a new release over safety concerns.

The latest model fell short in terms of "staying within scope and authorisation, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it's done," Jain said.

"We want to make sure our model development is safe no matter whether that's in the company, or when we ship it to users. But when we ship it to users, we have an extremely high bar in terms of safety and alignment," she added.

The flagship GPT-6 Astra agentic model was released in September and specialises in complex reasoning and executing tasks autonomously. OpenAI said it was the result of "years of research and big bets".

The company's security controls have come under intense scrutiny after several high-profile incidents involving its technology.

Last week, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that a rogue OpenAI agent had hacked into a government website in June and accessed private data in what experts said was the first known case of its kind in the world.

In July, OpenAI said its AI systems had accessed the internet and hacked into open-source developer hub Hugging Face, prompting researchers and officials to call for tighter controls over the technology.

On Monday, AI chip giant Nvidia released a set of software safety tools for autonomous AI platforms - called agents - that it said could have prevented the Hugging Face hack.

One of the new tools uses hardware features in Nvidia's chips to contain agents.

Nvidia boss Jensen Huang has largely dismissed calls for tighter AI regulations, arguing that rogue agents are an engineering problem that can be solved.

Nvidia agreed to buy Hugging Face for $12.9bn (£9.74bn) earlier this month.

articles.title: Reparations activist does not expect compensation from New York officials as action is delayed for years
articles.excerpt:
President of the U.S. Freedmen Project Devine Prince explained to Fox News Digital why monetary compensation is necessary for reparations.

A reparations activist with a grassroots organization called...
articles.body_text:
President of the U.S. Freedmen Project Devine Prince explained to Fox News Digital why monetary compensation is necessary for reparations.

A reparations activist with a grassroots organization called the U.S. Freedmen Project told Fox News Digital that their group expects no financial compensation from New York state officials after lawmakers quietly delayed a high-profile study into historic remedies.

"What the mainstream reparations movement is really about ... is spinning your wheels until [those] to whom the debt is owed tire out, give up, and give in," U.S. Freedmen Project President Devine Prince told Fox News Digital. "That's the only reason why you would pursue race-based policies within a system and within a country that has the 14th Amendment, which bans and prohibits race-based policies."

The U.S. Freedmen Project — a group of self-identified "Foundational Black Americans" — aims to educate the public on the legal and historical distinctions between African Americans who are direct descendants of enslaved people in the U.S. and immigrants from Africa or the Caribbean who arrived voluntarily in recent decades.

CHAOS ERUPTS AT NY REPARATIONS HEARING AS ‘FOUNDATIONAL’ BLACK AMERICANS CLASH WITH LEFT-LEANING GROUPS

The U.S. Freedmen Project called out delays from New York's reparations commission.  (Getty Images)

Prince’s comments follow sharp backlash after state leaders extended the timeline for the New York State Community Commission on Reparations Remedies to issue its final report. A provision embedded in the recently passed state budget pushed the commission's deadline back two years — from 2027 to 2029 — nearly four years beyond its original 2025 deadline.

The New York Civil Liberties Union (NYCLU) publicly criticized the delay in June.

"The state’s decision to spend an additional three years before it takes any action to address these harms raises a lot of questions about when Black New Yorkers will receive reparations," said Chantelle Williams, assistant director of the NYCLU’s Racial Justice Center.

"Meanwhile, the impact of discrimination continues to harm Black individuals and communities across the state. This delay is not just a bureaucratic inconvenience. It is a disservice to those who have suffered the profound and lasting consequences of inequality," Williams added.

NEW YORK FAR-LEFT GROUP CLAIMS REPARATIONS 'OWED' AS BLACKS' MEDIAN WEALTH 'NEARLY 15 TIMES LESS' THAN WHITES

The New York Civil Liberties Union (NYCLU) publicly criticized state leaders' delay of a reparations remedy report. (Carolyn Cole / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

The nine-member state commission, established by legislation signed by Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul in late 2023, was tasked with examining the Empire State's historical ties to slavery, Jim Crow-era discrimination, and economic disparities like redlining. The panel was charged with delivering recommendations for potential state-level financial compensation and policy reforms.

The commission recently concluded a series of statewide public hearings, culminating in a May 30 forum in Harlem titled "From Extraction to Repair: Closing the Racial Wealth Gap."

However, state lawmakers opted to move back the commission's deadline. Assemblymember Michaelle C. Solages, D-N.Y., who sponsored the original legislation, acknowledged the extension was requested to navigate a shifting national legal environment. Solages cited conservative legal challenges targeting diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) initiatives and the broader erosion of race-conscious policies.

The budget measure also included a provision shielding commissioners from personal legal liability if targeted by lawsuits over their findings.

Lineage advocates with the U.S. Freedmen Project, who attended the Harlem hearing, pushed back strongly against both the delay and the commission's framework. They argue that reparations should be strictly limited to direct descendants of individuals enslaved within the United States rather than broader race-based categories.

Activists with the group contend that progressive organizations like the NYCLU fail to represent the distinct legal and historical claims of descendant Black Americans by attempting to include recent Black immigrants under the same umbrella.

Prince claimed that members of the New York commission were appointed to preserve the status quo rather than deliver tangible results.

"These are individuals that have been put in place to keep the status quo intact while pretending they're working to undo it," Prince said. "There's a bunch of things moving around in the background that tie them to this ideology that benefits them if we keep the status quo of race-based advocacy alive."

"What we are focused on is true repair — and, unfortunately, true repair means repairing those who were truly harmed. Not everyone who comes in and says, 'Hey, I'm included in that, too,'" he added.

Supporters of the Freedmen Project maintain that any state-level reparations bill based on race rather than direct lineage would violate the U.S. Constitution's Equal Protection Clause. They urged state officials to adopt strict lineage-based criteria to reduce the program's exposure to legal challenges.

New York is part of a broader wave of blue states and municipalities attempting to construct local reparative frameworks. In Illinois, the Chicago suburb of Evanston, Illinois made headlines as the first U.S. city to distribute reparations, offering $25,000 housing grants to eligible Black residents.

Despite public hearings and ongoing research, Prince expressed skepticism that New York state will ever deliver payments to descendants.

TRUMP ADMIN VOWS TO STOP REPARATIONS PROGRAMS, ACCUSES OFFICIALS OF 'VIRTUE SIGNALING' TO GET 'VOTES'

The Freedmen Project supporters argued that the reparations bill includes language that violates the Constitution. Therefore, state officials should instead base the reparations' eligibility criteria on "lineage." (Fox News Digital)

"Realistically, I'm expecting the same thing that I expected going into this: nothing," Prince said. "Based on all the advocacy we did before this was even signed into law — all the recommendations we suggested and experts we brought to the New York Legislature to inform them on how to get this right — once all those things were ignored, I knew it would end up right where it is now. Realistically, I'm expecting them to find a way to distance themselves from this."

New York officials did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Joshua Q. Nelson is a reporter for Fox News Digital.

Joshua focuses on cultural trends, education, and public policy. He extensively covered reparations developments across the U.S., the Department of Education, and immigration issues.

Joining Fox News Digital in 2019, he previously graduated from Syracuse University's Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs and received the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton Public Policy Certificate.

Story tips can be sent to joshua.nelson@fox.com and Joshua can be followed on Instagram, Twitter and LinkedIn.

articles.title: Vietnamese government accused of abducting Melbourne human rights activist
articles.excerpt:
Tran Hiep, a 50-year-old Vietnamese Australian anti-human trafficking campaigner, not heard from since 18 September

Vietnamese authorities have detained three activists, including an Australian, on w...
articles.body_text:
Tran Hiep, a 50-year-old Vietnamese Australian anti-human trafficking campaigner, not heard from since 18 September

Vietnamese authorities have detained three activists, including an Australian, on what have been described as “fabricated” charges.

The Vietnamese government said the three confessed to being members of Viet Tan – a pro-democracy organisation – which it describes as a terrorist organisation.

In a statement, Viet Tan said it “strongly condemns the abduction of two of its members in Cambodia and the fabricated charges issued by the Vietnamese communist authorities to cover up an act of transnational repression”.

It is not clear if the third person is a Viet Tan member as well.

Tran Hiep, a 50-year-old Vietnamese Australian democracy campaigner, was due to return to Bangkok, Thailand, to reunite with his wife, Chloe Dang, after a short trip to Phnom Penh, Cambodia, to meet with human rights defenders.

Earlier, his wife implored the federal government to find him and bring him home after he failed to board his flight.

He had not communicated with his wife since 18 September, leaving her worried for his safety.

“My family and I are really worried about his safety, and we just only want to know where he is and what happened to him,” Dang said from Bangkok airport before boarding a flight to Melbourne.

“My husband deserves protection, and I really hope the Australian government will continue to put pressure on Cambodia to do an investigation to find out where he is right now.”

Hiep, a freelance IT professional who founded the Australian Alliance to Combat Human Trafficking, was travelling with another human rights activist Nguyen Duc Thuan, who is also Vietnamese and holds a Norwegian passport.

The pair travelled to Cambodia to meet with dissident Vietnamese activists for training.

Viet Tan says it aims to “overcome dictatorship and build the foundation for a sustainable democracy”, and that it was “committed to peaceful, nonviolent struggle”.

“We are convinced that nonviolent means are most effective for generating maximum civic participation,” the organisation said on its website.

Human Rights Watch has previously described Viet Tan as “an opposition political party … which operates openly and lawfully in many countries including Australia, but which Hanoi arbitrarily labels ‘terrorist’.”

Vietnam in recent years has ramped up its crackdown on dissidents, with more than 55 activists arrested under broad criminal laws in 2025.

On 18 September, Human Rights Watch said more than 160 political prisoners were currently locked up in Vietnam, and that activists faced “police harassment, intimidation, surveillance, and interrogation on a daily basis”.

Viet Tan urged the Norwegian and Australian authorities to ask for access to the Hiep and Thuan, to “ensure their wellbeing and access to needed medication”.

It said the pair had “no intention” of entering Vietnam and the claim they had done so illegally was a “blatant fabrication” to cover up their abduction.

“Viet Tan is particularly concerned that To Lam’s police state is using its security apparatus to pursue and repress activists and foreign nationals even beyond Vietnam’s borders,” it said.

“Meeting with, exchanging ideas with, and supporting human rights defenders, democracy activists, and civil society is a peaceful form of advocacy to advance freedom, democracy, and human rights in Vietnam.”

Civil society groups and United Nations human rights experts have repeatedly warned of growing cooperation between Vietnamese authorities and neighbouring governments targeting advocates.

Viet Tan, a pro-democracy diaspora political party, had earlier described the pair’s disappearance as concerning given previous cases involving Vietnamese dissidents vanishing in neighbouring countries and subsequently appearing in custody in Vietnam.

“Their disappearance is not an ordinary ‘missing person’ incident. Both men are longtime human rights advocates and Viet Tan members,” the organisation said.

Dang, 36, said fretting over her husband’s whereabouts had taken a psychological toll.

“It’s been 11 days and I’m really in the dark,” she said, choking back tears.

“I don’t know where he is and how he’s doing – it’s driving me crazy.

The Australian government confirmed consular officials were in contact with Dang but declined to comment further.

“The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is providing consular assistance to the family of an Australian reported missing in Cambodia,” a department spokesperson said on Monday.

The families of the missing men have filed an appeal with the UN working group on enforced or involuntary disappearances.

articles.title: Hungary lifts immunity of Prime Minister Magyar, two Orban-era ministers
articles.excerpt: Hungary’s Parliament has stripped Prime Minister Peter Magyar and two ministers in former leader Viktor Orban’s nationalist government of their immunity, clearing the way for prosecutors to pursue sep...
articles.body_text:
Hungary’s Parliament has stripped Prime Minister Peter Magyar and two ministers in former leader Viktor Orban’s nationalist government of their immunity, clearing the way for prosecutors to pursue separate criminal investigations into each of them.

The vote on Monday came after Magyar, who is being investigated for theft, specifically asked for his immunity to be lifted so he could clear himself of “character assassination”. The probes against the Orban-era ministers – who are suspected of embezzlement and bribery – are the first corruption investigations against top government figures from Orban’s 16 years in power.

Legislators voted overwhelmingly in favour of lifting their immunity.

Orban’s Fidesz party and its ally KDNP boycotted the session.

The vote was in response to a request last week from prosecutors seeking to investigate Magyar, as well as former Minister of Culture Balazs Hanko and former Minister of National Development Miklos Sesztak.

Magyar is being investigated over an incident at a Budapest nightclub in June 2024, when prosecutors allege he took a mobile phone from a man filming him and threw it into the Danube River.

Magyar has called the case a “sham” and last week accused prosecutors of trying “to conflate” the ex-ministers’ cases “with the attempt at political character assassination… which has already failed several times”.

Hanko, a legislator from Orban’s Fidesz party, is accused of embezzling more than 40 million euros ($46m) in public funds. Prosecutors allege the money was used to help finance the 2026 parliamentary election campaign and for the personal benefit of others.

Sesztak, a lawmaker from KDNP, is under investigation over allegedly accepting more than $37.2m in bribes and kickbacks connected to vehicle procurements under Hungary’s state bus company, as well as to state construction projects.

The cases come less than six months after Magyar’s Tisza party ended Orban’s 16 years in power with a landslide election victory. Magyar campaigned on pledges to tackle corruption, restore rule-of-law safeguards, and rebuild Hungary’s strained relationship with the European Union.

His government has since made fighting alleged corruption and overpriced public procurement a central part of its programme, including plans for a new asset-recovery office focused on wrongdoing linked to the Orban era.

articles.title: Tennessee to execute a woman for first time in 200 years after governor denies clemency
articles.excerpt:
Lawyers for Christa Pike, 50, convicted of killing classmate in Knoxville in 1995, ask supreme court to grant stay

Christa Pike, a woman who was convicted of murder 30 years ago, is set to be put to ...
articles.body_text:
Lawyers for Christa Pike, 50, convicted of killing classmate in Knoxville in 1995, ask supreme court to grant stay

Christa Pike, a woman who was convicted of murder 30 years ago, is set to be put to death on Wednesday after her request for clemency was denied by Tennessee governor Bill Lee on Monday. If the execution goes through, she will be the first woman executed in the state in 200 years.

Pike, who is now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend, who was 17 at the time, killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmate at Knoxville Job Corps in 1995.

The case received widespread attention because of the brutality of the killing, the ages of the people involved, and because a satanic symbol was carved into the victim’s body.

Pike was convicted of first-degree murder the following year and sentenced to death, making her the youngest woman to be put on death row in modern US history. Since her sentence, her history as a victim of sexual abuse and mental health challenges has come to light.

As her execution date approached, civil rights groups like the ACLU and Amnesty International have called on the public to reach out to the governor’s office to ask that he take Pike off of death row.

“After deliberate consideration of Christa Gail Pike’s request for clemency and after a thorough review of the case, I am upholding the sentence of the State of Tennessee and do not plan to intervene,” he said in a statement.

In response to Lee’s decision, Pike’s attorneys said that they were “deeply saddened and heartbroken” by the governor’s decision and that through this choice the state is dismissing decades of research about the amount of responsibility an 18-year-old – especially one with severe trauma – should bear for their criminal actions.

“Throughout her childhood, Christa was failed by people and institutions that should have shown her care and meaningful intervention,” Pike’s attorneys said in a statement. “The 18-year-old girl suffering from severe mental illness and near-debilitating trauma no longer exists. Christa is a 50-year-old remorseful woman who understands her actions, receives proper treatment for her mental illness, and provides for and guides fellow incarcerated women.”

Pike’s attorneys have also asked the supreme court to stay the execution.

Assistant federal defender Stephen Ferrell said Pike was sexually abused starting from when she was a toddler and that she was raped at 11 and 17. He said Pike’s lawyers at the penalty phase of her trial did not present the jury with what he said was critical information about her past or argue that her age should be a consideration.

Pike, who has never denied her role in Slemmer’s killing, was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.

“I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime,” Pike said in a statement included in her clemency petition.

Ferrell said more is known today about adolescent brain development and that Pike’s death sentence is an outlier. He noted that Pike’s boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, who was 17 at the time, was sentenced to life with the possibility of parole because of his age. He was denied parole last year. A third teen admitted to being an accessory and received probation.

May Martinez, Slemmer’s mother, told the Associated press that her daughter volunteered with the Special Olympics, loved roller skating and wanted to pursue a career in computers.

“She was easygoing. She was a computer geek to begin with. She and my husband would build and tear apart the computers constantly,” Martinez told the outlet. “She trusted everybody, and that was her downfall.”

Most recently, Missouri in 2023 executed Amber McLaughlin, a transgender woman, for a 2003 killing, in what is believed to be the first execution of a transgender woman in the US.

In 2021, the federal government executed Lisa Montgomery, marking the first time in nearly seven decades that the US government has put a female inmate to death. Georgia executed a woman in 2015.

articles.title: Sign before praying: A new conversion law is affecting churchgoers in Indian state
articles.excerpt:
A new anti-conversion law in Maharashtra has sparked fears among Christians

Some churches in and around India's financial capital Mumbai have begun asking worshippers to give a declaration in writing...
articles.body_text:
A new anti-conversion law in Maharashtra has sparked fears among Christians

Some churches in and around India's financial capital Mumbai have begun asking worshippers to give a declaration in writing - "I came here to pray of my own free will."

Visitors write down their names, sometimes add an ID card number, and sign to say that nobody forced or enticed them to attend church. The forms, a copy of which the BBC has seen, have no official standing. Churches keep them in case a prayer meeting is challenged and its organisers are accused of trying to convert those inside.

The practice began at some churches in late August, just before a new law against religious conversion took effect in Maharashtra state, of which Mumbai is the capital.

The law prohibits religious conversions brought about by force, fraud, coercion or inducement. It also requires people who want to convert voluntarily to notify authorities in advance. An unlawful conversion can lead to a prison sentence of up to seven years, rising to 10 for a repeat offence.

Maharashtra's government says the law protects people, particularly those who are socially or economically vulnerable, from being forced or deceived into changing their religion.

But critics say its broad definitions, severe penalties and scrutiny of even voluntary conversions risk drawing the state and the police into one of the most private decisions a person can make. The state government did not respond to the BBC's repeated requests for comment.

While the law applies to all religions, the anxiety is being felt most deeply at places where minorities, especially Christians, worship. At the heart of the debate is a long-running tension over allegations, usually made by right-wing groups, about people being coerced or induced to change their religion for benefits.

Devdan Tribhuvan has seen some of that anxiety up close.

A fourth-generation Christian in Vasai, a suburb of Mumbai, he is part of an organisation that provides legal aid to Christians in and around the city. In recent months, he says, people have increasingly approached him not about court cases, but with accounts of disrupted prayer meetings and questions about what they are still free to do.

Some have described strangers walking into churches and questioning those inside: "What is your name? Why are you here? Has anyone offered you something?"

People from all religions visit the famous Mount Mary Church in Mumbai

The questions can become more pointed, Tribhuvan said, when a worshipper has a name that does not sound Christian: "Has anyone forced you to come? Has anyone offered you an inducement?"

Many who contact him are not looking to take legal action. They want to know whether simply gathering to pray could leave them vulnerable to an accusation of conversion.

In July, an investigation by The Indian Express, external documented five disruptions of Christian prayer meetings around Mumbai between April and July. Nine police cases followed - seven against worshippers or prayer organisers, and two against members of the Hindu nationalist group Bajrang Dal. Police did not respond to detailed questions about the cases or the action taken.

"Is gathering for prayer itself conversion?" Tribhuvan asks.

In Mumbai, Tribhuvan's question carries particular weight. The city grew by drawing people from across India and beyond, bringing their gods and rituals with them. A church bell can sound within earshot of a mosque's call to prayer; a shrine belonging to one faith can draw followers of another.

People of many faiths make their way to the Muslim shrine Haji Ali. Hindus light candles at Mount Mary, a Catholic basilica overlooking the city. Crowds fill the streets around Lalbaug during the Hindu festival of Ganesh Chaturthi and stream to Siddhivinayak temple throughout the year.

Maharashtra is the latest of more than a dozen states to restrict religious conversion. The laws differ, but their reach has expanded in recent years, particularly in states governed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party. Several are being challenged before the Supreme Court.

Behind that expansion lie claims long made by Hindu nationalist groups, that Christians use money, schooling or medical care to draw poor and tribal communities away from Hinduism, and that Muslim men court Hindu women to convert them - an alleged conspiracy they call "love jihad."

A bunch of anti-conversion laws in Indian states have made interfaith marriages more challenging

Critics say such accusations have fuelled harassment of Christian prayer meetings and interfaith couples, and that the laws give those making them a way to draw the police into questions of prayer, marriage and belief.

Maharashtra's government says the new law leaves people free to convert by choice, while addressing what it says is a rise in forced conversions that existing laws have failed to curb.

Critics question where it draws the line between force and choice.

"We do not support forceful conversions, if any," said Samsuddin Tamboli, president of the Muslim Satyashodhak Mandal (Muslim Truth-seeking Society), a reformist organisation. His concern is what the law counts as inducement.

Its definition of "allurement" includes employment, free education at a religious institution, a promise of marriage, a "better lifestyle" and "divine healing". Even glorifying one religion over another can fall within it.

"The definition has been kept so vague that almost any benefit accruing to a person can be considered or argued to be an allurement," said Abhay Thipsay, a retired Bombay High Court judge.

"If a person receives some benefit and consciously chooses to convert for that reason, why should it be considered wrong?"

The law also allows parents, siblings and other relatives to complain to police about an allegedly unlawful conversion, leaving the person accused of causing or assisting it to prove that it was lawful.

Critics say for interfaith couples, that provision adds another potential obstacle to marriages that can already face family opposition.

Indian law allows people of different faiths to marry without converting, but requires a month's notice. Lara Jesani, a lawyer who has helped interfaith couples obtain court protection, said details of planned weddings have sometimes reached relatives and Hindu nationalist groups opposed to them within that notice period.

Critics fear the new law may give families or right-wing organisations a new way to target interfaith couples

In cases she has handled, she said, families have taken women away, even from the marriage registrar's office.

Now, she fears the new law may give the families or right-wing organisations a new way to target such couples.

"Even when neither intend to convert, [the couples] fear a relative could accuse one partner of trying to convert the other."

The Maharashtra government did not respond to detailed questions from the BBC about these concerns. But when the law was passed, state minister Pankaj Bhoyar said it did not infringe upon the right to change religion. The notification requirement, he said, was intended to establish whether a conversion was voluntary, while allowing the state to act against those brought about by fraud, coercion or inducement.

But Tribhuvan is still worried, an anxiety, he says, which reaches even the small prayer gatherings held closer to home when a church is too far away.

Fifty people might attend, he said, sometimes 100 - and someone who is not Christian might join too.

"If someone else wishes to come and pray, we cannot stop them," he said. "That is what we call the right to choose."

To Thipsay, the retired judge, the precaution points to a larger question.

"If an adult has the power to make major decisions - such as whom to marry - and has been given the right to vote," he said, "why should they not have the power to make this decision too?"

articles.title: ABC's 'The View' co-host Ana Navarro urges viewers to vote for Dem in key Florida congressional race
articles.excerpt:
"The View" co-host Ana Navarro urged viewers in Florida to vote for Democratic hopeful Elliott Rodriguez in a key congressional race.

ABC is facing blowback Monday after "The View" co-host Ana Navarr...
articles.body_text:
"The View" co-host Ana Navarro urged viewers in Florida to vote for Democratic hopeful Elliott Rodriguez in a key congressional race.

ABC is facing blowback Monday after "The View" co-host Ana Navarro urged viewers to vote for a Democrat in a key Florida congressional race.

Navarro marveled at the tightening race between incumbent Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, R-Fla., and her Democratic opponent Elliott Rodriguez in the Sunshine State's 27th district. Salazar recently made headlines for releasing an ad critical of President Donald Trump's immigration policies.

The host noted to viewers she lives in that district.

ABC FIRES BACK AT FCC PROBE OF 'THE VIEW,' CALLS OUT AGENCY'S 'CHILLING EFFECT ON FIRST AMENDMENT'

"The View" co-host Ana Navarro urged viewers to vote for the Democratic candidate in a key congressional race in Florida. (Patrick McMullan via Getty Images)

"I had taken for granted this race because she won two years ago by 20 points. And this is a district Donald Trump won by 15 points ... but polls have her dead even," Navarro said.

"So, anybody who lives in Coral Gables, in Miami, in Key Biscayne, in downtown Miami, pay attention to that race and go vote because it's going to matter," she continued. "And we can actually knock this woman out. There's a great guy running. His name is Elliott Rodriguez. Give him a look!"

ABC HAS NO BUSINESS ON PUBLIC AIRWAVES BECAUSE IT OPERATES 'LIKE A PARTISAN CABLE NETWORK,’ WATCHDOG TELLS FCC

Rep. María Elvira Salazar, R-Fla., is running in a tight race in the Sunshine State's 27th district. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Critics have accused ABC of "electioneering" and questioned whether Navarro's comments violate broadcast licensing rules.

"How is this not electioneering? She's literally telling them who to vote for," Daily Wire opinion editor Ben Domenech reacted on X.

"Wannabe ‘bona fide’ news," Media Research Center President David Bozell wrote.

"This should be the absolute end of ABC’s license," Heritage Foundation media fellow Tim Young posted.

DISNEY SUES FCC OVER ‘RETALIATORY CAMPAIGN AGAINST ABC,’ SEEKS TO BLOCK EARLY RENEWAL PROCEEDINGS

"The View" has been under intense scrutiny by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), which has had a bitter legal battle with ABC and whether programs like "The View" are considered "bona fide news," allowing it to be exempt from equal time rules for political candidates.

'VIEW' HOST ANA NAVARRO REJECTS HUNTER BIDEN'S ASSERTION THAT TRUMP IS 'ALREADY' A 'DICTATOR'

Federal Communications Commission Chairman Brendan Carr previously launched an investigation into ABC's "The View" over the equal opportunities requirement. (John McDonnell/Getty Images)

Navarro has never been shy about her politics. She has been a vocal Trump critic and served as a host at the 2024 Democratic National Convention.

Neither ABC News nor the FCC responded to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

Joseph A. Wulfsohn is a media reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to joseph.wulfsohn@fox.com and on Twitter: @JosephWulfsohn.

articles.title: OpenAI scraps release of latest AI model over safety concerns
articles.excerpt:
OpenAI has cancelled the release of its latest AI model over safety concerns, the latest move by the industry to slow the development of the frontier technology.

The AI giant’s announcement on Monday...
articles.body_text:
OpenAI has cancelled the release of its latest AI model over safety concerns, the latest move by the industry to slow the development of the frontier technology.

The AI giant’s announcement on Monday comes amid heightened fears about the potential for AI to do catastrophic harm following a slew of incidents involving AI agents going rogue.

Saachi Jain, OpenAI’s head of safety systems, said the upcoming model, GPT-6.1 Astra, had failed to meet its standards for acting in accordance with human wishes during testing.

“For anything regarding safety and alignment, there’s a trade off. You really do need to find what’s the right line between staying within scope, but also avoiding laziness in terms of how the model actually pursues tasks even when it hits friction,” Jain said in a statement provided to Al Jazeera.

While GPT-6.1 Astra improved in comparison with its predecessor in some areas, the model did not meet the bar for “scope and authorization, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it’s done”, Jain said.

“Of course we want to make sure our model development is safe no matter whether that’s in the company, or when we ship it to users,” Jain said.

“But when we ship it to users, we have an extremely high bar in terms of safety and alignment.”

articles.title: Africa’s space ambitions are moving from policy to practice
articles.excerpt: Accra, Ghana – The Africa Space Expo (ASPEX), which closed in Abidjan, Ivory Coast, last week, was not designed as a showcase for rockets and astronauts. Organisers presented it instead as a marketpla...
articles.body_text:
Accra, Ghana – The Africa Space Expo (ASPEX), which closed in Abidjan, Ivory Coast, last week, was not designed as a showcase for rockets and astronauts. Organisers presented it instead as a marketplace for space applications in food security, climate resilience, territorial monitoring, connectivity and maritime security, bringing start-ups, project labs and investors together to move ideas from demonstration to deployment.

The event also produced several concrete agreements. The Ivory Coast signed the Artemis Accords, becoming the 75th signatory of the agreement on space exploration and development, while Angola signed a letter of intent on space cooperation with the United Arab Emirates.

But beyond the agreements, the expo highlighted a question that is becoming harder to avoid: Can Africa move from using space technology to building more of it itself?

Ghana offers a clear illustration of both the progress and the gap.

Ghana’s ambitions in space and nuclear science date back to its early years of independence. In 1961, President Kwame Nkrumah’s government initiated a nuclear reactor project in Accra. Two years later, the government established the Ghana Atomic Energy Commission through an act of Parliament with a mandate covering the peaceful applications of nuclear energy.

The reactor project was shelved after Nkrumah was overthrown in 1966, but the institution he helped establish remains the parent body of the Ghana Space Science and Technology Institute (GSSTI).

Joseph Tandoh, director of the GSSTI, traces Ghana’s more recent space programme to a partnership with South Africa.

“Ghana became a partner through South Africa,” he told Al Jazeera. “Through that project, we were able to reconstruct the old satellite antenna at Kuntunse into a radio telescope.”

Through its partnership with South Africa on radio astronomy, Ghana converted a redundant 32-metre (105ft) antenna at Kuntunse into a functioning radio telescope. Ghana became the first of South Africa’s eight African Square Kilometre Array partner countries to complete the conversion, and the telescope was launched in August 2017.

Ghana’s National Space Policy was approved by the cabinet in 2022 and launched in 2024. The government approved the establishment of a Ghana Space Agency in 2025, beginning the process of creating a dedicated national institution for the sector.

The institutional framework is taking shape. The harder question is how Ghana moves from using space technology to developing and building more of it itself.

At the GSSTI, that transition is already under way.

Tandoh told Al Jazeera GEOMAIZE, a partnership between the GSSTI and VITO, the Flemish Institute for Technological Research in Belgium, has demonstrated how satellite data can be applied to Ghanaian agriculture.

The project monitored crop health and developed algorithms to classify crops. Ghana is also expanding its use of Earth observation data and artificial intelligence for crop monitoring and yield prediction.

But predicting yields has proved more difficult. Tandoh said the model’s accuracy fell short of expectations, largely because many Ghanaian farmers practise smallholder mixed cropping and satellite soil-moisture data are too coarse to capture differences between small farms.

A follow-up project supported by the French embassy and international research partners, is now working to improve the estimates.

The GSSTI has also used satellite data to track forest loss linked to mining and is working with partners in Nigeria on a digital twin to simulate coastal erosion at Keta and Agavedzi. Japanese cooperation has provided technical training while the French government supported work on space legislation that produced a draft now being reviewed by the attorney general.

“We always say that Ghana Space Science and Technology Institute becoming an agency is to position Ghana in a way that we will not only be users of the technology but we will also contribute to designing, developing and building our own tools,” Tandoh said.

Victor Tagborloh founded Galaxy Aerospace Ghana in 2020. Two years later, his team launched a high-altitude balloon into near space, capturing images of Ghana’s geography with clearance from national security and airport authorities.

The company has since designed mini-rockets for the GSSTI, trained young people in space robotics and artificial intelligence and pushed for the introduction of Starlink in Ghana in 2024.

But Tagborloh said the company has yet to secure an investor, six years after it was founded.

Galaxy’s longer-term plans include a space university on 33,000 hectares (82,000 acres) that it has secured at Apam in Ghana’s Central Region as well as a ground station that would give the country greater capacity to monitor floods, mining activity and coastal erosion.

The company is seeking investors for the ground station and a geospatial intelligence platform. Tagborloh said the curriculum is ready and the land is available. What is missing is the capital to turn those plans into infrastructure.

He also argued that Ghana’s position near the equator could provide an advantage for launching spacecraft, potentially reducing the fuel required to reach orbit. Several other African countries share similar geography.

But Tagborloh’s ambition goes beyond launching rockets. He wants Ghana to develop more of the infrastructure and expertise needed to build its own space capabilities.

Bright Atsu Sogbey, president of the Africa Development Council and a senior research engineer at the Ghana Atomic Energy Commission, argued that the private sector cannot build the industry alone.

“Borrowed technology cannot be sustainable,” Sogbey told Al Jazeera. “The state must be in the driver’s seat, using the natural resources we have to ensure that, in partnership with the private sector, we can have laboratories and manufacturing hubs for the space industry.”

He pointed to South Africa, Egypt and Nigeria, which have established space laboratories and manufactured test satellites. Ghana, he said, still lacks the state-backed laboratories and manufacturing hubs needed to produce more of its own components rather than importing them.

“Enough of the talk shop,” Sogbey said. “The next expo should see African satellites assembled on this continent and launching capability for African satellites.”

Engineer Daniel Aboagye, CEO of African Progressive Research and Innovations, said the change must also begin in education.

“With how technology is advancing, Africa must introduce space science into its education systems,” Aboagye told Al Jazeera. “We cannot continue to be consumers of technology we do not understand.”

Kwadwo Dwomo II, CEO of COMCENT Ghana, works on agritech systems that depend on satellite data. He also called for greater government investment in the sector.

Ghana is home to a small cluster of companies, including Galaxy Aerospace, Xavier Space Solutions and Ayeji Aerospace, working in areas such as satellite technology, Earth observation and geospatial services.

Galaxy Aerospace confirmed to Al Jazeera that it was unable to participate in this year’s expo. The company said it hopes to participate in the next expo.

The challenge facing Ghana is shared across much of Africa: moving from using space technology to developing and building more of it locally while overcoming limited investment, infrastructure and manufacturing capacity.

ASPEX was designed in part to address that gap.

The African Space Agency, headquartered in Egypt, is intended to provide a continental framework for cooperation while the expo aims to connect investors with African start-ups, researchers and space projects.

But the distance between the ambitions presented at the expo and the resources available to engineers trying to turn them into businesses remains substantial.

For Tandoh, Ghana’s immediate priority is to build the application layer: a satellite-data processing hub capable of serving ministries across government before the country moves further into designing and launching its own satellites.

“Space cuts across all the ministries,” he told Al Jazeera. “We should be able to build and validate our own tools first.”

For Tagborloh, the timeline is more urgent.

“We shouldn’t wait for tomorrow,” he told Al Jazeera. “Whatever decision we have to take, especially for human resource capital in the space industry, it has to be now.”

Ghana has the policy. It has engineers, research institutions and companies trying to build a space industry. What it does not yet have is the capital and manufacturing capacity to turn those capabilities into a domestic industry.

“We have the team, the knowledge, the research and the technical know-how,” Tagborloh told Al Jazeera. “We just need funds.”

articles.title: Michigan Dem Abdul El-Sayed wants Bill Maher to get his 'a-- whooped' if invited on show
articles.excerpt: Former Clinton advisor and pollster Mark Penn breaks down the latest election polling data, analyzing shifting voter sentiment, key demographic trends and critical economic concerns shaping the electo...
articles.body_text:
Former Clinton advisor and pollster Mark Penn breaks down the latest election polling data, analyzing shifting voter sentiment, key demographic trends and critical economic concerns shaping the electorate.

Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed told former NBC News host Chuck Todd on Friday that he would want to go on comedian Bill Maher's show to see his "a-- whooped" after his anti-Islam comments.

During the "Noosphere" interview, El-Sayed said he'd be willing to appear on Maher or Joe Rogan's respective shows despite them espousing what he considered to be "terrible" beliefs because he'd want to speak with their audiences.

In addition, El-Sayed claimed that he'd be willing to go on "Real Time" in order to watch Maher get his a-- whooped" by a Muslim.

HASAN PIKER ACCUSES BILL MAHER OF BEING AN 'ISLAMOPHOBE' AND DEMONSTRATING 'ANTI-BLACKNESS'

Abdul El-Sayed, U.S. Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan, called out "Real Time" host Bill Maher during an interview on Friday. (Sarah Rice/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"You know how many terrible things Bill Maher has said about people like me?" El-Sayed said. "Terrible, awful things. Of course, he's still got his show on Comedy Central, and everybody seems to be perfectly okay going on that show despite the fact that he said deeply terrible things."

He continued, "But you know who else would go on that show? I would go on that show. You know why? A: I wanna give people the image of watching him get his a-- whooped on his own show by a guy who prays like I do. And I'd also go on the show because I want to convince the people who watch his show, right, that a lot of the things that he says, just not viable."

Maher responded to El-Sayed's comments during his show on Friday and offered an invitation for the Michigan Democrat to appear on "Real Time."

ABDUL EL-SAYED GRILLED ON PAST STATEMENTS ON SHARIA LAW AND WHITE SUPREMACY, TAXING THE RICH

"It’s not people like you, I would love to have you on, sir, by the way," Maher said. "And I hope we can make that happen. I talk about Islam. It’s never personal, and it’s never about race. It’s about ideas. Religion is an opinion. That’s all religion is: a group of thoughts that form an opinion of something. I have different views on what, you know, how women should be treated and things like that, that we will discuss. I hope you will accept our invitation."

Bill Maher invited Abdul El-Sayed onto his show after seeing his comments. (Lionel Hahn/Getty Images)

Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed's campaign and Maher's representative for comment.

El-Sayed has frequently invoked aggressive language against his GOP rival Mike Rogers. Last month, El-Sayed challenged Rogers to a game of tackle football despite being more than 20 years younger than the Republican candidate.

MICHIGAN STUDENT CONFRONTS EL-SAYED OVER IRAN STANCE IN TENSE EXCHANGE: ‘DO YOU STAND WITH US?’

"Since you’re too afraid to debate me, how about you ‘hold me accountable’ on a football field instead," El-Sayed wrote on X. "Tackle, no pads like we used to play when we were kids. I’d be happy to show you [how] much I love football."

Speaking to Fox News correspondent Alexis McAdams earlier this month, Rogers dismissed the comment as "unserious" in light of real election issues.

Abdul El-Sayed (right) previously challenged Michigan's GOP U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers (left) to a game of tackle football. (Sarah Rice/Getty Images ; Jeff Kowalsky / AFP via Getty Images)

"I think that is so unserious. You think about what the problems are here. People are facing this affordability [sic] credit. He wants to thump his chest and show how macho he is, and he spends a lot of time talking about high school. This is not about high school," Rogers said.

Lindsay Kornick is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to lindsay.kornick@fox.com and on Twitter: @lmkornick.

articles.title: Be like Sophie Cunningham, not Chris Simms — never give in to the outrage mob
articles.excerpt:
Dan Dakich questions why Chris Simms is apologizing over his remarks on injured Oregon QB Dante Moore.

Sophie Cunningham understands something that very few others in the sports world seem to.

You n...
articles.body_text:
Dan Dakich questions why Chris Simms is apologizing over his remarks on injured Oregon QB Dante Moore.

Sophie Cunningham understands something that very few others in the sports world seem to.

You never, ever cave to the mob if you haven't done anything wrong.

The Indiana Fever guard proved as much this summer after she came out against biological males competing against females in sports.

Sophie Cunningham No. 8 of the Indiana Fever celebrates after making a three-point shot in the first half against the Minnesota Lynx at Gainbridge Fieldhouse on Sept. 22, 2026, in Indianapolis, Ind. (Getty Images)

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SPARKS SOCIAL MEDIA MELTDOWN BY SPEAKING OUT TO PROTECT WOMEN'S SPORTS

Her stance prompted her to garner the title "MAGA Barbie." It sparked fans to boo her when she entered the game in cities such as Seattle. It caused a sports reporter to say that she is "unafraid to be blatantly transphobic" and fans to call for her suspension.

Did Cunningham buckle? Hell no. She doubled down with an Instagram post that declared she isn't backing down for anyone.

This is the only way to do it. If there's one thing the mob hates more than anything, it's courage. You show it to them, they go away. It's just sad that so few seem to possess it.

NBC Sports football analyst Chris Simms was the latest to bow to online outrage over some perfectly reasonable comments. After Oregon quarterback Dante Moore was knocked out of Saturday's game due to a helmet-to-helmet hit by USC's Desman Stephens II, Simms did what an analyst is paid to do: analyze.

At halftime, Simms said that Moore's injury was a "Debbie Downer" moment because fans want to see teams at full strength. He then shared some advice his father told him about how to "make sure you get down in time and don't take any big hits." He added how Moore's late slide put Stephens in a "no-win situation."

Quarterback Dante Moore of the Oregon Ducks runs with the football and slides to avoid a tackle from linebacker Desman Stephens II of the USC Trojans during a game at Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum on Sept. 26, 2026, in Los Angeles, Calif. (ISI Photos via Getty Images)

DAN DAKICH CALLS CHRIS SIMMS' APOLOGY OVER DANTE MOORE SLIDE ANALYSIS 'SOFT A-- BULLS--T'

This is an ex-football player talking football. But apparently all Oregon fans wanted to hear was that this was the dirtiest hit in the history of the sport, so Sunday, Simms took to social media to write "I clearly did not show enough sympathy for the situation. I mishandled the situation and I was wrong. I'm sorry for that."

It seems like we see a new one of these every week. Earlier this month, Texas quarterback Arch Manning laughed at an AI meme of ESPN reporter Holly Rowe getting slapped by Longhorns coach Steve Sarkisian. He was shamed into apologizing two days later. In July, Sandy Brondello, coach of the WNBA's Toronto Tempo, wanted a foul to be called on Atlanta's Angel Reese, and could be heard telling refs that Reese was a "protected species."

This is common lingo in Australia — Brondello's home country — where it's meant to express frustration over a player getting special treatment. But Brondello still issued a written apology to Reese, saying "I used a phrase that I shouldn't have used, and I take full responsibility for that."

And then, of course, there was Lions receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown caving last year after doing the Trump dance after a touchdown in a game vs. Commanders. Said St. Brown: "First of all, if I offended anyone, I do apologize. I did not mean to offend anyone. It was just, we're having fun."

It's hard watching these sports figures shed their dignity with each one of these mea culpas. What they don't understand is that they are losing respect from the public every time they issue one. The outrage mob simply sees them as people who will fold the next time they want to sink their hooks into them. And the folks who would have supported them if they stood strong? They now see a spineless pushover.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

This doesn't mean that people should never apologize. During his time in Seattle, Richard Sherman was infamous for his inability to ever take accountability for his wrongdoing. That's also a form of weakness — it's just wearing a different costume.

But to surrender when you've done nothing wrong? It's not noble, it's nauseating.

CHARLES BARKLEY DECLARES WNBA IS 'FOR WOMEN ONLY' AFTER ONGOING TRANSGENDER ATHLETE DEBATE

Charles Barkley says WNBA players dislike Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham, blaming a mix of jealousy, race, and sexuality for the hostility. (Getty Images)

People like Cunningham know this. Charles Barkley, too. The Hall of Fame hooper is on record saying trans athletes don't belong in women's sports, and the blowback has been almost nonexistent because everyone knows he is going to hold firm in his position. That's the power of integrity.

The vocal minority shouldn't have the influence that it does. Yet it regularly turns titans of the sports world into mush. Don't be like Chris Simms, who gave into the mob. Be like Cunningham, who decided to stand up to it. Sophie's choice is the only choice.

Matt Calkins is a columnist for Outkick, where he focuses on the overlap between sports and culture. Before joining the Fox team, he spent 11 years as a sports columnist for the Seattle Times, where he extracted a two-word quote from Marshawn Lynch and got a Seahawks draft pick to design his apartment.Matt also served as a sports columnist at the San Diego Union Tribune after working as the Blazers beat writer for the Vancouver Columbian. You can follow him on X at matt_calkins.

articles.title: Dan Wilson announces his own firing as Seattle Mariners manager in rare postgame moment
articles.excerpt:
Dan Dakich questions why Chris Simms is apologizing over his remarks on injured Oregon QB Dante Moore.

Seattle Mariners manager Dan Wilson personally broke the news to his team and the media Sunday t...
articles.body_text:
Dan Dakich questions why Chris Simms is apologizing over his remarks on injured Oregon QB Dante Moore.

Seattle Mariners manager Dan Wilson personally broke the news to his team and the media Sunday that he will not return for the 2027 season.

Before Game 162 against the Los Angeles Angels, Wilson held a closed-door meeting to inform players and staff.

Postgame, he stepped to the podium to deliver the news publicly and face questions before front-office executives addressed reporters.

Standard MLB protocol calls for front-office executives to issue a news release or hold a solo news conference while the ousted manager stays out of sight.

Manager Dan Wilson of the Seattle Mariners looks on before the game against the Los Angeles Angels at T-Mobile Park on Sept. 27, 2026, in Seattle, Wash. (Getty Images)

A manager taking the microphone to announce his own dismissal is virtually unheard of in modern sports.

"This season has been very difficult, and of course, the results have not been what any of us have expected," Wilson said. "As a result, it's concluded that today is my last day as manager of the Seattle Mariners."

Wilson, a former Mariners catcher who took over as manager in August 2024, acknowledged his deep roots in the organization.

"I'm still processing this with my family, and it's a very difficult day," Wilson said. "We love this city. We love this community and we appreciate the organization for what it has meant to the family since coming here as a player in '94. We feel extremely blessed by all the opportunities we've been afforded."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Expectations were sky-high entering 2026.

Coming off a 2025 AL West title and reaching Game 7 of the ALCS, Seattle fell just one win short of the World Series. Instead, the club collapsed to a 76-86 third-place finish.

The downward spiral was driven by offensive regression among core players, inconsistent starting pitching, a second-half bullpen collapse and some of the worst defensive metrics in Major League Baseball.

Manager Dan Wilson removes pitcher George Kirby during the seventh inning against the Philadelphia Phillies at T-Mobile Park on Aug. 25, 2026, in Seattle, Wash. (Getty Images)

Late-season comments from players highlighted a lack of clubhouse accountability as a core failure. Pressed on whether leadership failed to enforce standards, Wilson faced the criticism directly.

"That's always a necessary component, and I think accountability comes in a lot of different ways," Wilson said. "Obviously, I think you look back, and there's a lot of things that you can point to, and perhaps that's one of them."

When asked if the front office made the final decision, Wilson accepted the reality of sports leadership.

Mariners manager Dan Wilson stands before a game against the Brewers at American Family Field in Milwaukee, Wis., on Aug. 18, 2026. (Getty Images)

"I've been in baseball a while, and this is what happens," Wilson said. "Managers shoulder the blame and shoulder the responsibility. And this is obviously difficult."

RED SOX REMOVE INTERIM TAG FROM MANAGER CHAD TRACY AFTER THE TEAM'S REMARKABLE SUMMER TURNAROUND

Seattle Mariners President of Baseball Operations Jerry Dipoto and General Manager Justin Hollander will return in 2027.

Dipoto noted that "collectively we failed to meet our own expectations" and agreed a leadership change was necessary.

Wilson finishes his tenure as Mariners manager with a 187-171 career record.

Send us your thoughts: alejandro.avila@outkick.com / Follow along on X: @alejandroaveela

Alejandro Avila is a longtime writer at OutKick, living in Southern California.

articles.title: Questions remain over Iran’s link to alleged RAF Fairford bomb plot
articles.excerpt:
Tehran has been trying to step up attacks on targets in the west but its track record has been mixed

Investigators may be some way from determining exactly what led five men with three vans to a vill...
articles.body_text:
Tehran has been trying to step up attacks on targets in the west but its track record has been mixed

Investigators may be some way from determining exactly what led five men with three vans to a village just outside RAF Fairford in the small hours of Sunday – but the fact they have all been released on bail without immediate charge suggests they are not deemed to pose a serious and violent threat.

In a moment where wider geopolitical tensions mean external threats are perceived to be close, the question of whether Iran had a hand in the alleged plot remains open. Nonetheless, the bailing of the men is a mercifully lower-key development in an investigation that appeared of the utmost gravity.

Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform, had earlier insisted that the Fairford incident “proves my point on Iran” and argued that anybody arriving on small boats should not be allowed to move around in the UK. The latter point was an irrelevant argument, already weakened when police said at lunchtime that all five were UK nationals from London.

Though the five were arrested on suspicion of carrying explosives and involvement in a terror plot, after more than 24 hours of searches, nothing had been discovered that would prompt further police action – perhaps explaining why MI5 had no idea that the men and their vans would turn up a mile from the base with unclear intent.

British officials admitted on Sunday the arrests were not led by intelligence, but rather last-minute warnings on the ground. Counter-terror police said they were first aware of three vehicles travelling to the base at 12.45am on Sunday, while a local farmer phoned 999 at 1.36am after the vans blocked the entrance to her drive.

The next day Trump made a characteristically inflated claim that the US and UK had been monitoring the men for “a long time” and that they had been trying to do “big damage”. Threat levels at Fairford have been at the highest level for several days, apparently backing this up – but UK sources say this was related to wider concerns about threats to US bases, not specific to the site.

RAF Fairford is the European home for US air force bombers, essentially an American base on British soil. It has been used by the US in its bombing campaign against Iran, after the former prime minister Keir Starmer agreed to allow American strikes on Iranian missile launch sites in the war Donald Trump started in the spring.

The base has also been a source of explicit interest to Tehran. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) issued a statement on 23 July, as the US carried out a 13th day of consecutive bombing attacks. It said that any bases used by the US to attack Iran, including Fairford, were “legitimate targets”.

That would give Fairford an obvious value, though it is not clear why anyone from London would feel bold enough to attack a military base, given it would be expected to be protected by armed personnel. Rational plotters probably would not expect to survive, and would at least expect the most serious penalties available under law.

When the suspects’ release was announced, there was no firm information from UK counter-terror police about what explosives were found or whether there was deemed to be viable devices in the vans – the kind of information that would immediately point to the degree of intent in any terror plot. Subsequently, it emerged no explosive material had been found.

Tehran has been trying to step up attacks on targets in the west over the past three years, as fighting in the Middle East has sprawled and expanded after October 2023, and particularly after Trump joined Israel to start a full-scale war on Iran in February. But while its propagandists make heavy threats about British military bases online, Iran’s actual threat is mixed.

A year ago, Ken McCallum, the head of MI5, said the Security Service had “tracked more than 20 potentially lethal Iran-backed plots in just the one year”. Two Romanian men were found guilty in July of stabbing the Iranian journalist Pouria Zeraati in the leg in Wimbledon two years earlier in a state-directed attack; he worked for the independent Persian channel Iran International.

Yvette Cooper, then home secretary, sanctioned an IRGC-backed terror group, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia, in July after it claimed responsibility for a series of attacks in the UK, including the burning of four Jewish community ambulances in March. But while four men have pleaded guilty, evidence in the case has yet to be heard in court, with prosecutors only saying so far there was a “terrorist connection”.

In April police closed and searched part of Kensington Gardens near the Israeli embassy in London after an online video appeared to suggest the building had been targeted by drones containing hazardous substances. On that occasion, nothing was found.

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, has defended his economic record on the eve of what is widely expected to be the fourth interest rate rise of 2026, as the Reserve Bank remains concerned about persistent inflation.

The RBA board is poised to hike the cash rate from 4.35% to 4.6% on Tuesday, which would be the fourth increase in 2026 and push typical home loan interest rates to 6.5%.

Speaking on the ABC’s 7.30 program last night, Chalmers emphasised the factors contributing to inflation, saying that Australia was performing well considering what was going on in the world, particularly in the Middle East.

double quotation markWe have a lot going for us and we’ve got a lot of work to do to make sure that in these difficult global circumstances Australia continues to out-perform the world.

We have a big inflation challenge in our economy. It’s made much worse by decisions taken on the other side of the world.

From an economic point of view this war in Iran has been an absolute disaster for Australian families, because they have been asked to pay a hefty price.

The wife of an Australian activist missing in Cambodia has implored the Albanese government to find him and bring him home, Australian Associated Press reports.

Tran Hiep, a 50-year-old Australian-Vietnamese democracy campaigner, was due to return to Bangkok, Thailand, to reunite with his wife Chloe Dang after a short trip to Phnom Penh, Cambodia, to meet with human rights defenders.

But he never boarded his flight and has not communicated with his wife since September 18, leaving her worried for his safety.

double quotation markMy husband deserves protection, and I really hope the Australian government will continue to put pressure on Cambodia to do an investigation to find out where he is right now.

Hiep, a freelance IT professional who founded the Australian Alliance to Combat Human Trafficking, was travelling with another human rights activist Nguyen Duc Thuan, who is also Vietnamese and holds a Norwegian passport.

The pair travelled to Cambodia to meet with dissident Vietnamese activists for training.

Chalmers says Australians understand there are ‘inflationary challenges’ in our economy

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said the inflationary challenge in the economy is being made “much worse” by the war in the Middle East.

Chalmers, speaking on Channel 7’s Sunrise this morning ahead of the RBA announcement, said the government has focused on savings and delivering surpluses to get government debt down.

double quotation markBut we know that there’s always more work today. I think people understand, people who might be bracing for an interest rate rise later today. … I think people understand that there are inflationary challenges in our economy.

But when you see what’s happening with global oil prices … obviously, factually, that is one the big drivers of inflation that people are having other deal with right now.

Chalmers said he knows that people are under pressure and that interest rate rises add to that pressure.

double quotation markThat’s why we accept our part, our responsibility for our part in this fight against inflation. … And it also means dealing with these longer term economic challenges.

Mia Lay, the Sydney police officer who was killed in a car crash last week, will be among those mourned at National Police Remembrance Day 2026 in Sydney.

New South Wales’ premier, Chris Minns, governor, Margaret Beazley, and police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, will be among the guests at Sydney’s Domain.

Minns said he felt incredibly gratitude for the service of police officers across the state:

double quotation mark[Police] start a shift not knowing what you are going to face, and we ask these young men and women to put themselves in harm’s way to keep the rest of us safe.

Police and counter-terrorism minister, Yasmin Catley, said:

double quotation markMy thoughts are with the families of Constable Lay, Sergeant [Mark] Bransgrove and everyone else who has lost a loved one in the line of duty. Their sacrifice will never be forgotten.

Lay, 20, had worked as a police officer for just 16 months when she was killed “instantly” in the crash in Redfern on Friday. Sgt Mark Bransgrove, who died in July, served in the police service for 38 years, including 30 years in the Forensic Services Group.

Remembrance events will also be held in Broken Hill, Bourke, Orange, Lithgow, Inverell, Dubbo and Tamworth.

Good morning, and happy Tuesday. It’s Nick Visser here to take over the blog. Let’s get to it.

There were 30 drowning deaths in 2025-2026, the highest number in almost a decade, according to a Royal Life Saving Australia report that Australian Associated Press reports on.

Of them, 14 involved more than one death, often related to boating, driving through floodwater, or people exploring unfamiliar environments, chief executive Justin Scarr said.

Over the past decade there have been with 229 deaths, or an average of 23 per year.

In the most recent year, 83% of drowning victims were men, 37% were born overseas and a quarter were aged between 65 and 74.

Nearly one-third of the fatal events were related to boating, while driving through floodwater and swimming were the other leading circumstances.
