articles.title: ‘Thrilled’: huge swarms of bogong moths surprise NSW residents and may point to species’ recovery
articles.excerpt:
Researcher says sightings of the endangered moth have increased over the last two years but ‘this year has blown them out of the water’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Sw...
articles.body_text:
Researcher says sightings of the endangered moth have increased over the last two years but ‘this year has blown them out of the water’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Swarms of bogong moths have surprised New South Wales residents over the last few days – with experts saying sightings of the endangered native insect are cause for excitement rather than alarm.

Hundreds of moth sightings in coastal areas were posted over the weekend to the iNaturalist page for Bogong Watch, a citizen science initiative run by Invertebrates Australia.

Spring marks the beginning of an annual bogong moth migration: huge numbers of the insects migrate up to 1,000 km to a small number of cool caves in the Australian Alps, where they spend the summer escaping the heat.

Bogong Watch project manager Linnea Emneby said their bogong “sentinels” – dozens of volunteers spread in all directions from Mount Kosciuszko, who use non-lethal bug lanterns to monitor the moths – were reporting high numbers of the insects. Three NSW households each reported dozens of moths on Monday, while one sentinel sighted more than 200 bogongs on Sunday night, she said.

Emneby said the moths – which are about the size of a 50-cent piece and weigh a third of a gram – were important both “culturally and ecologically”, playing a critical role as pollinators and also a key food source for the critically endangered mountain pygmy possum.

“We’re absolutely thrilled with what we’re seeing,” said Dr Marissa Parrott, a reproductive biologist at Zoos Victoria, which runs a separate citizen science program Moth Tracker. “The reports just keep coming in … one of my team members was in tears with excitement this morning.”

Sightings of the endangered moth had increased over the last two years, but “this year has blown them out of the water”, Parrott said. “In September alone … we’ve had more bogong moths sightings come in than all of last year.

“We’re hoping this means a stronger recovery of this endangered species.

“Those big numbers really are in NSW and the ACT – Victoria is still behind,” Parrott said, adding that “wetter, cooler weather” had likely yielded favourable conditions for the moths.

“They do come in waves,” Parrott said, with the insects taking days to weeks to complete their migrations to the Alps.

“This is what should have happened in the past, seeing these big swarms of moths coming through Canberra, Sydney, Newcastle and Melbourne, across those south-eastern Australian migratory zones.”

An estimated 4 billion moths used to arrive in the Alps each year, until the population collapsed catastrophically – by up to 99.5% – between 2017 and 2019.

They were once found in huge numbers, periodically swarming into Parliament House in Canberra. During the closing ceremony of the Sydney Olympic Games in 2000, a swarm of bogongs drawn by stadium lights was so huge that weather forecasters mistook it for a rain cloud.

The moth has been listed as endangered by the International Union for the Conservation of Nature since 2021, but is not listed as a threatened species under federal conservation laws.

“They migrate generally more inland, but they can move around depending on weather and wind,” Parrot said. Moth Tracker sightings from last year showed that “they even get blown across to New Zealand”.

The nocturnal moths are the only invertebrate known to navigate using a map of the stars as a compass. “Hopefully the ones blown off course will be able to navigate back safely,” Parrott said.

The strongest El Niño on record, and the drier, hotter conditions the climate pattern can bring to Australia, was cause for concern, Parrott said. “While the [bogong] numbers are looking good now, and I think that’s something we can all celebrate, we do worry what’s going to happen over the next couple of years.”

For members of the public who encounter bogongs on their migration, experts suggest turning off unnecessary outdoor lights, refraining from insecticide use, and uploading sightings to the Moth Tracker or Bogong Watch platforms.

“If any come into the house, gently place them back outside,” Parrott said. “Females can have 2,000 eggs, so every moth is precious.

“They don’t do any damage, they don’t eat clothes. They pollinate the plants as they go through, so that’s a big help for people who love their gardens.

“The moths are gentle, beautiful little animals that will move on on their own.”

articles.title: Extra 1,000 prison beds announced in NSW as union warns against arresting ‘our way out of domestic violence’
articles.excerpt:
Minns government to spend $47.1m to recommission part of Silverwater jail while PSA says prison alone will not end violent behaviour

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our br...
articles.body_text:
Minns government to spend $47.1m to recommission part of Silverwater jail while PSA says prison alone will not end violent behaviour

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The reopening of part of Sydney’s Silverwater jail will deliver hundreds of extra beds amid record numbers of prisoners on remand, the state government says, as the prison officers’ union warns against “arrest[ing] our way out of domestic violence”.

The Minns government, responding to a surge in prisoners awaiting trial since domestic violence bail laws were tightened, announced on Monday it would spend $47.1m to recommission the 515-bed Dawn de Loas correctional centre at the Silverwater complex by early next year.

It said alongside the “fast-tracked delivery” of more than 360 additional beds at Parklea correctional centre, returning to public hands next month, this would add nearly 1,000 beds to New South Wales’ prison capacity.

The premier, Chris Minns, told reporters at Dawn de Loas on Monday he believed the expansion was “a necessary decision for NSW, [which] we believe in the long run will keep the public safe.

“Not arresting people for violent domestic violence offences will not solve them either.”

But after the announcement, the Public Service Association (PSA) of NSW said the additional beds were “a response to a DV crisis that demands far more than extra prison capacity”.

The PSA general secretary, Stewart Little, said, “We can’t just arrest our way out of domestic violence.

“Prison can contain someone who poses a serious risk. It cannot, by itself, protect a person before violence occurs or stop an offender returning to violent behaviour after release.”

The additional beds come amid desperate calls for action on domestic and family violence after the alleged murders of three women and two children this month.

On 11 September this year, Daniel Billings was sentenced to 28 years in jail for the 2024 murder of Forbes woman, Molly Ticehurst. Ticehurst’s killing by her ex-boyfriend, who had been freed on bail a fortnight before, prompted strengthened domestic and family violence laws, with serious alleged offenders now needing to “show cause” as to why they should be released, and registrars no longer able to make bail decisions.

The changes have driven record numbers of prisoners on remand, totalling 6,398 people – 46% of NSW’s adult prison population – as of September.

The PSA has called for the government to run domestic violence services in-house through 15 centres across the state, as well as compulsory diversionary programs for alleged offenders on remand, and dedicated courts for domestic violence cases amid a backlog of cases.

While it called for “properly resourced” domestic violence programs for people leaving custody on parole, the premier said the government had increased funding for domestic and family violence services.

“People pitch these arguments as: ‘Look, it’s a waste of money to have the criminal justice system in place or to have long sentences for violent domestic violence offenders’. I don’t agree with that,” Minns said on Monday.

Amid concerns that DV offenders were not being rehabilitated and about the effectiveness of rehabilitation programs in general, the premier said he could not make programs compulsory for prisoners on remand.

Dawn de Loas temporarily closed in November 2022 amid a declining prison population and staff shortages during the pandemic. The government says about 150 staff will be recruited to support the reopening in early 2027.

The government anticipates fast-tracking an additional 360 beds at Parklea correctional centre, one of two privately managed correctional centres in NSW, after Corrective Service resumes management in October.

It says the 1,000 additional beds, which will be for minimum security remand and sentenced prisoners, will take the strain off Silverwater’s 24-hour Metropolitan Remand and Reception Centre (MRRC).

On Monday, the corrections minister, Anoulack Chanthivong, ruled out closing Long Bay correctional centre’s Metropolitan Special Programs Centre (MSPC), where a 19-year-old man took his own life in May while on remand.

The independent watchdog had previously recommended the unit be closed because it “simply cannot provide a safe environment”.

The NSW opposition has proposed to close all of Long Bay to build 10,000 homes, calling for an upgrade to Goulburn correctional centre. Chanthivong confirmed the government had closed four Victorian-era wings at Goulburn which he said were “no longer fit for purpose”.

articles.title: Virat Kohli passes 15,000 ODI runs as India beat West Indies
articles.excerpt: Virat Kohli has become only the second batter after Sachin Tendulkar to reach 15,000 runs in men’s one-day international (ODI) cricket, achieving the milestone with an unbeaten century as India cruise...
articles.body_text:
Virat Kohli has become only the second batter after Sachin Tendulkar to reach 15,000 runs in men’s one-day international (ODI) cricket, achieving the milestone with an unbeaten century as India cruised to an eight-wicket victory over West Indies.

Kohli struck 139 not out from 88 balls and Shubman Gill made 110 as India chased down 296 with 50 balls to spare to take a 1-0 lead in the three-match ODI series on Sunday.

The milestone comes just days after Kohli announced that he would retire from national duty after next year’s 50-over World Cup. The leading century-maker in ODIs has already retired from T20 internationals and Test cricket ⁠⁠and now represents India only in the 50-over format.

Rohit Sharma and Gill launched the chase with a 74-run opening stand before Sharma was dismissed in the 12th over. Gill, the world’s top-ranked ODI batter, then took control, maintaining the aggressive approach and bringing up his 10th ODI century with a sweep.

Kohli came in at number three and notched his 86th international century, while Gill struck 110 in 108 deliveries as the pair put on a dominant 151-run stand off 132 balls that all but sealed the contest on Sunday.

Roston Chase eventually removed Gill, but Ruturaj Gaikwad made 13 off 19 balls and helped Kohli steer India home without further alarm. Kohli sealed victory with successive boundaries.

Put in to bat after the toss, Justin Greaves and John Campbell gave the West Indies a strong start, adding 135 from 117 balls for the opening wicket.

India struggled to find a breakthrough for much of the first 20 overs as the pair dominated the bowling and provided a solid platform.

Greaves, who was dropped by Sharma on 16, made India pay with a maiden ODI century and top-scored for the visitors.

The momentum shifted when Kuldeep Yadav dismissed Campbell in the 20th over, beating him in the air as he swept a catch to short fine leg. Yadav and Prasidh Krishna then applied the brakes on the West Indies innings as they lost four wickets for 22 runs between the 31st and 36th overs.

Yadav finished with 4-40 on his ODI return, but Amir Jangoo counterattacked with 58 off 43 balls. With support from Chase, he helped the West Indies recover from 198-5 and post 295.

articles.title: ‘Still a lockdown’: Deadly floods hit Nepal tourism as peak season begins
articles.excerpt:
Kathmandu, Chitwan and Nuwakot, Nepal – Like every year, Pushpraj Rimal, a tour planner and taxi driver in Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu, was looking forward to September for his business to boom.

But w...
articles.body_text:
Kathmandu, Chitwan and Nuwakot, Nepal – Like every year, Pushpraj Rimal, a tour planner and taxi driver in Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu, was looking forward to September for his business to boom.

But what he got instead was a series of cancellations by tourists after catastrophic floods last month killed more than 1,450 people and destroyed key highways, deeply impacting the Himalayan nation heavily dependent on tourism.

“It is still a lockdown kind of situation,” the 42-year-old told Al Jazeera nearly a month after the disaster.

Pushpraj, who speaks Nepali and Hindi, works on commission for several hotels and trekking companies in Kathmandu and the scenic town of Pokhara, known for its lake nestled in the Annapurna mountain range. Pokhara also serves as a base for Himalayan trekkers.

Nepal’s tourist season peaks after the monsoon ends in August and the skies are clearer. Tourism attracts thousands of international travellers, accounting for nearly 8 percent of Nepal’s gross domestic product and employs more than 1 million people.

Last year, Nepal saw more than 1.15 million tourists visiting the country, nearly a third of them during the September-November season.

But the floods this year, triggered by a glacial mountain collapse along the Nepal-Tibet border in the north, have pushed tourists away from the unaffected areas as well.

“I had rented two cars for two months, but I have done one fourth of the business I usually do in a season. Tourists generally start pouring in from September, but most of them have cancelled this year,” he said.

“I will get no commissions from the hotels or trek organisers, nor has the taxi business worked well. … I am now waiting for the season to end.”

Rimal has two children, Hema, 14, and Rahul, 12, whom he had promised a tablet this Dussain, a prominent Hindu festival that usually falls in October. “But it seems impossible now. I will have to break their hearts and my promise to them for the very first time.”

Seeta Nepali, 61, and her husband, Ramakant Nepali, 68, sell homemade buttermilk on the highway connecting Kathmandu to the tourist towns of Pokhara and Chitwan. The couple, who also sells cottage cheese in their neighbourhood, depend on these daily sales to make ends meet.

“Our town may not have been destroyed by the floods, but the floods reached us by way of no buyers. We could earn nothing for 11 days after the flood because the road was blocked,” Seeta told Al Jazeera.

“Even after it reopened, only government vehicles were allowed to pass. Now, some tourists are coming in, and we are able to sell, but it is not even half of what we used to sell earlier because there are far fewer people. … We are making barely one-fourth of what we would usually do,” she added.

British national Alexa, who goes by a single name, had planned to visit Pokhara and Dhulikhel, a hill town near Kathmandu known for its cultural experiences and homestays, with five of her friends. But the flooding forced the group to cancel their trip.

“It was going to be our first time in Nepal, and we had booked two cabs from Kathmandu airport to Pokhara in July itself along with hotels, trekking and camps. When we learned about the disaster on the 26th [of August], we had to cancel everything,” she told Al Jazeera.

A traveller from Japan, who asked to remain anonymous, said the washed-out roads and bridges were the least of his concerns.

“We could have taken flights, but the situation and environment due to the floods, the stranded dead bodies could be deadly for me and my family, so we chose to cancel this time,” the father of two said.

Others like Tapas Kumar from India changed their itineraries instead of cancelling their trips.

“Our son is based in the United States. He was concerned about us and insisted that we cancel Nepal for now. So we found a middle ground. We cancelled Pokhara and extended our Kathmandu stay for all of the seven days,” Kumar, who was travelling with his wife and friends, told Al Jazeera.

Many foreign tourists said they were also checking travel advisories issued by their embassies in Nepal before cancelling or rescheduling their trips.

“Some people also got scared and misunderstood the information and safety measures issued by the embassies of other countries in Nepal and chose to cancel their travel plans. But we want people to know that Nepal is open and safe. Only some parts need to be avoided,” Surendra Thapa, charge d’affaires at the Indian embassy, told Al Jazeera.

On the other hand, the embassy of the United Kingdom issued an advisory on September 11, warning that the floods had made many areas unstable and it was difficult to guarantee safe travels within Nepal.

The US embassy issued a similar advisory, stating many areas were unsafe and designated no-travel zones.

“We had ensured all the rooms were furnished with the best utilities. Special staff was hired, and the best supplies were bought since I had all the rooms sold out for September. But 23 days in and we are already in a lot of loss,” said Pramila Chhetri, who works at a resort in Chitwan, about 150km (90 miles) from Kathmandu’s airport.

She said her resort lost significant business this year because many travellers misunderstood the flood-related warnings as an advisory to avoid the entire country.

“We really wish people across the globe would understand that it is not all of Nepal that is facing the floods and there are many small and big businesses that depend on travellers to make ends meet, especially in the months of September and October,” Chhetri told Al Jazeera. “Even parts unaffected by the floods are bracing for a disastrous season.”

Chhetri said 80 percent of her resort’s reservations were cancelled within hours of the floods because the main highway to Chitwan was damaged and closed for nearly two weeks.

“A group was supposed to come in the first week of September, but instead of cancelling, they postponed their trip to October. So we are keeping our fingers crossed for now,” she said.

While the full economic impact of a decline in tourism is still being assessed, small-business owners such as Pushpraj and Seeta are already on the edge. Seeta is back on the road with her bottles of buttermilk, but there are not many buyers.

“We are eating only flattened rice and buttermilk for lunch since the income has been drastically reduced and we are not able to buy enough vegetables,” Seeta said.

“Every day, we come here with the hope that more tourists might have come to see our beautiful Nepal and buy from us. But we don’t see many.”

articles.title: Russian strikes kill eight, injure dozens across Ukraine
articles.excerpt: A Russian military strike on northeastern Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, has injured at least 22 people, including children, less than a day after eight people were killed in attacks nationwi...
articles.body_text:
A Russian military strike on northeastern Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, has injured at least 22 people, including children, less than a day after eight people were killed in attacks nationwide.

Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekov said on his Telegram account that a guided Russian aerial bomb hit an apartment block early on Monday, destroying two floors of the multistorey building.

He said six children were among the injured.

Russian attacks were also reported across Ukraine on Sunday.

Ukrainian Minister of Internal Affairs Ivan Vyhivskyi said three people, including a 16-year-old girl, were killed in air strikes that damaged a children’s centre in the northern city of Sumy.

Authorities in the Odesa region, meanwhile, said a “massive strike” on the south of the Black Sea region killed one person and damaged residential buildings, a shop, a hotel, a medical building, and a grain warehouse.

And in the capital, Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a woman and two 16-year-olds were injured and hospitalised.

“The enemy continues to relentlessly attack the Kyiv region with strike drones,” the city’s administration said.

“Sixteen sites have been damaged”, including 12 houses, a warehouse and a production facility, it added.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Sunday that three people were killed in strikes in the southern Zaporizhia region and that a Russian drone strike had killed one man in Kyiv.

Zelenskyy said in a post on his X account that Russia had launched more than 2,200 attack drones, 1,630 aerial bombs and 38 missiles of various types against Ukraine in the past week.

“If Russia were truly preparing for any real steps towards de-escalation, as it claims, particularly to American negotiators, this wave of Shahed terror would not be happening,” Zelenskyy said in later comments, referring to the Iran-developed drones Moscow has used against Ukraine.

In Moscow, Russia’s Ministry of Defence said it had bombed a Kyivstar data centre in Kyiv and another belonging to the Omega Telecom company. It said that the firms were providing services to the Ukrainian army.

Russian Minister of Foreign Affairs Sergey Lavrov told the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Saturday that Moscow intended to continue its military campaign “to the end”.

Ukrainian drones struck an oil depot in Russia’s Krasnodar region on Monday, according to local reports.

Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ published footage of a large fire and identified the facility as the Pavlovskaya oil depot.

Ukraine has intensified its targeting of Russian oil infrastructure in recent weeks.

United States-led talks to end the war, which began with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, have failed to produce a breakthrough, and the UN has highlighted the growing civilian toll.

articles.title: Should you lock into a fixed-rate savings account paying 5.25%?
articles.excerpt:
Savers face a dilemma: lock down the deals now or wait, with offers tipped to ‘get even better’

Returns on the top fixed-rate savings accounts are at their highest level in years and still climbing, ...
articles.body_text:
Savers face a dilemma: lock down the deals now or wait, with offers tipped to ‘get even better’

Returns on the top fixed-rate savings accounts are at their highest level in years and still climbing, with some now paying up to 5.25%.

It leaves those with money to put away facing a choice: lock into some of the best interest rates on offer in several years or hold your nerve in the hope they get even better?

While new fixed mortgage rates have jumped in recent months – dealing a blow to many homebuyers and those aiming to remortgage – their pain has been savers’ gain.

This month, the data provider Moneyfacts said fixed savings rates were at “multiyear highs”, fuelled by strong competition, and this trend has continued: on Thursday the average new one-year fixed savings bond rate was 4.41%.

With a fixed-rate savings bond, you typically have to tie up your money for between six months and five years, and they provide a clear, guaranteed return. The one-year version tends to be popular as many people do not want to tie up cash for long periods.

The top-paying accounts are offering a fair bit more than that average: at the time of writing, GB Bank had a one-year fixed-rate bond paying 5.05%. Meanwhile, Kent Reliance had a 13-month acciunt offering 5.06%. (With both, the minimum deposit is £1,000.)

The best-buy rates are even higher if you tie up cash for longer. This week, GB Bank, Shawbrook Bank and Vanquis were among those paying 5.25% on a five-year fixed bond.

However, some savers will recall that as recently as late 2023 there were fixed bonds paying 6%, and if and when the Bank of England base rate goes up, that could push returns on savings higher than they are now.

Many economists predict the Bank will lift the base rate before the end of this year, with further rises thought likely next year.

Rachel Springall at Moneyfacts expects the deals on offer to savers “to get even better”. However, she cautions that we do not know the path interest rates will follow, and that anything could happen in the next few months or so.

Those with cash to stash may want to hedge their bets by putting some into a competitive fixed-rate bond now and keeping another chunk in a high-paying easy access account. There are easy access accounts paying up to 5%.

Some fixed-rate savings bonds will let you “drip-feed” cash in – for example, some will let you add money while the account is still open to new customers, while others have a specific “funding window”, which might be a few weeks but can be just a few days.

The cost of living is still a big issue, with many worried about the prospect of higher energy bills this winter – so it could be a mistake to put all your savings cash out of reach. Springall suggests spreading your money across fixed-rate products and accounts that are accessible, plus also making use of tax-free cash Isas.

If you are aiming to put some money into savings or switch providers and are not using your Isa allowance at all, you are missing out on valuable tax benefits.

Rates on fixed cash Isas are often slightly lower than for similar non-Isa accounts, although not always: Shawbrook Bank’s five-year fixed savings bond and five-year fixed cash Isa pay 5.25%.

Every tax year you can save up to £20,000 in Isas, but from April 2027, the rules will change for anyone under 65. Instead of being able to put all of the money into a cash Isa, that element will be capped at £12,000. If you are 65 or over, all £20,000 can still be put into a cash Isa.

articles.title: Attorney for lone holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy mistrial pushes back on claims of refusing the law
articles.excerpt:
Attorney Edward Paltzik tells Fox News host Kayleigh McEnany that Lindsay Clancy holdout juror Michael Desronvil had "zero doubt" and "a mountain of evidence" behind his decision.

The attorney for th...
articles.body_text:
Attorney Edward Paltzik tells Fox News host Kayleigh McEnany that Lindsay Clancy holdout juror Michael Desronvil had "zero doubt" and "a mountain of evidence" behind his decision.

The attorney for the lone holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial is pushing back on a claim that his client refused to follow the law, telling Fox News host Kayleigh McEnany that the juror had no doubt about his decision.

In a preview of an interview airing Monday on "Fox & Friends," McEnany asks attorney Edward Paltzik whether juror Michael P. Desronvil ever had reasonable doubt after the jury foreperson sent the judge a note accusing him of refusing to follow the law on reasonable doubt.

LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT PRAISED AS 'AMERICAN HERO' BY LAWYER WHO SAYS HE REPRESENTS HIM

Attorney Edward Paltzik represents Michael Desronvil, the lone holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial. (Fox News)

"Zero doubt. No doubt. And he had evidence to back up his position?" McEnany responds.

"A lot of evidence. A mountain of evidence," Paltzik says.

LINDSAY CLANCY JUROR ADMITTED 'REASONABLE DOUBT' BUT STILL REFUSED INSANITY VERDICT, FOREPERSON SAYS

Michael P. Desronvil, the lone holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial, which ended in a mistrial. (Fugitive TV)

Desronvil was the lone holdout after seven days of deliberations in Clancy’s trial. Eleven jurors were prepared to find the former labor and delivery nurse not criminally responsible for killing her three children, while Desronvil held out for a conviction. Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial Sept. 4.

Clancy admitted killing 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan at the family’s Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. Her defense argued that postpartum psychosis left her not criminally responsible. Prosecutors argued she understood what she was doing and planned the killings.

LINDSAY CLANCY DA RARELY DOES PLEA DEALS, BUT HER CASE COULD BE THE 'EXCEPTION,' VETERAN ATTORNEY SAYS

Lindsay Clancy in court last month. (Boston Globe via Getty Images)

Desronvil later said he believed the physical evidence and witness testimony showed Clancy knew what she was doing. Prosecutors have not announced whether they will retry her. She is due back in court Sept. 29.

Watch McEnany’s full interview with Paltzik Monday on "Fox & Friends."

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

articles.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon told friend if he killed anyone he’d dump belongings in bin and take bodies to bushland, court hears
articles.excerpt:
Former police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in early 2024 – nine months after discussion with friend Georgia Cook

Follow our Australia news live blog for lat...
articles.body_text:
Former police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in early 2024 – nine months after discussion with friend Georgia Cook

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

A Sydney police officer told a friend he would hide the bodies of anyone he killed in bushland and put their belongings in a dumpster, months before allegedly murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies, a court has been told.

Beau Lamarre-Condon, 31, has been accused of fatally shooting the couple with a police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.

He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

At his double murder trial on Monday, Georgia Cook, a close friend of Lamarre-Condon, told the NSW supreme court about a dinner in May 2023.

The brief relationship between Baird and Lamarre-Condon had ended when the accused asked her what she would do if he told her he’d killed someone, Cook told the jury.

He then asked what she would do if she killed someone and what she would do with their bodies, the court heard. Cook responded she had no idea.

She said on Monday that Lamarre-Condon replied: “After I’d killed them I would take their stuff, I would put it in a dumpster, and I would take their bodies in bushland where nobody would ever find them.”

Asked about her response, Cook said the situation in 2023 felt “very surreal”.

“I didn’t know whether to believe anything I’d heard, or whether it was true,” she told the jury.

“Hearing a person of power in the police force [say that] – it felt like I didn’t have anywhere to go and I was really scared by what I had heard.”

After Lamarre-Condon allegedly shot Baird and Davies in February 2024, he dumped Baird’s bloodied belongings and furniture into a skip bin in Cronulla, the prosecution said during its opening statement last week.

The two bodies were found on the fence line of a Greek orthodox monastery in remote bushland in Bungonia – about 200km from Paddington.

Cook on Friday told the court that Lamarre-Condon told her he had been watching Baird from outside his home. The crown alleged in its opening that the police officer began planning to murder Baird in early 2024.

The defence team has claimed he was acting in self-defence after he disguised himself as an UberEats rider and entered Baird’s home on the day of the shootings.

The trial before justice Natalie Adams continues.

articles.title: Trump asked Xi Jinping if China would like to buy US weapons, American ambassador says
articles.excerpt:
David Perdue’s remarks come after a Taiwanese minister spoke of the ‘severe’ military threat posed by Beijing to the self-ruled island

Donald Trump offered to sell weapons to China while hosting its ...
articles.body_text:
David Perdue’s remarks come after a Taiwanese minister spoke of the ‘severe’ military threat posed by Beijing to the self-ruled island

Donald Trump offered to sell weapons to China while hosting its leader, Xi Jinping, last week, the US ambassador to China said on Sunday.

David Perdue told Fox News on Sunday: “President Trump continues to say, hey, we sell arms to other people around the world. He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some at one point.”

The extraordinary claim came during an interview about US policy on Taiwan, which has been waiting for months for Trump to approve a new arms sales ⁠package worth $14bn, after a record multi-billion dollar deal was unveiled in December last year.

Trump’s level of commitment to protecting Taiwan has previously been questioned. At a meeting with Xi in Beijing in May, ⁠Trump said he was keeping the $14bn Taiwan arms sales package in abeyance, describing it as a “very good negotiating chip” in dealings with China.

Washington has long maintained a strategically ambiguous stance on whether it would defend Taiwan in the event of an invasion. But under the decades-old Taiwan Relations Act, it is required to provide Taipei with sufficient military equipment to defend itself.

Beijing has repeatedly said it “resolutely opposes” Washington’s arms sales to the island democracy, which it regards as a breakaway province, despite never having ruled it, and has not renounced the use of force to take. During their Washington meeting last week, Xi urged Trump to oppose “Taiwan independence,” according to a readout from the official Chinese news agency Xinhua.

After Purdue’s interview, the White House told the New York Times that the US had no plans to sell arms to China, while the state department said: “US law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China.”

Before the interview, Taiwanese deputy foreign minister Chen Ming-chi spoke of the severe military threat China posed.

“Taiwan faces a severe situation in the Taiwan strait. Even though China’s economy is declining, it continues investing more resources into building military capacity. Under ‌this context, the US very much understands our defence needs,” he told reporters in Taipei.

Trump ​has not mentioned the sale ‌since last week’s summit, saying ‌only on Saturday that Xi understands his position on Taiwan.

Perdue himself told CNBC ​on Friday that there had been ​no change in Taiwan policy by Trump, including on arms ​sales.

articles.title: Houston Astros secure the most embarrassing kind of Major League Baseball history with AL West win
articles.excerpt:
The "MLB on FOX" crew discussed Aaron Judge potentially missing the Wild Card Series for the New York Yankees and how the team can find success.

When Major League Baseball changed the schedule to ens...
articles.body_text:
The "MLB on FOX" crew discussed Aaron Judge potentially missing the Wild Card Series for the New York Yankees and how the team can find success.

When Major League Baseball changed the schedule to ensure that the final day of the regular season featured all 15 games starting within a few minutes of each other, Sunday is what they envisioned. Mostly.

While most postseason spots and seeds were decided either within the last week or the last few days, there were two races that came down to the final day of the year. The American League West race featured the Houston Astros and Texas Rangers entering the day tied at 80-81, remarkably, and the third wild card spot in the National League between the Philadelphia Phillies and Arizona Diamondbacks.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

The Phillies, who as recently as last week had a 99.1% chance of reaching the postseason, per FanGraphs, avoided a historic collapse and clinched a wild card series appearance with a 7-3 win over the Tampa Bay Rays.

Houston Astros catcher Yainer Diaz motions to his teammates after hitting a double against the Athletics during the third inning at Sutter Health Park in West Sacramento, Calif., on Sept. 27, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

WITH ONE MONTH LEFT, AMERICAN LEAGUE TEAMS ARE HEADING TOWARDS AN EMBARRASSING, HISTORIC LOW

But the Astros, even with a win, did in fact make an embarrassing type of history: they are officially the worst division-winning team in baseball history.

The previous low-water mark was the 2005 San Diego Padres, who won the NL West with an 82-80 record. And while the Astros won 9-0 over the long-eliminated Athletics to avoid the 80-82 record, 81–81 marks a new low winning percentage for a division winner over a full season.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Even crazier? The Astros were extremely fortunate to finish the season at .500.

Houston Astros' Yordan Alvarez celebrates with Christian Walker after hitting a grand slam during the first inning against the Kansas City Royals in Kansas City, Mo., on June 12, 2026. (Charlie Riedel/AP)

While wins and losses are what decide the standings and outcomes, run differential has proven over time to be a significantly better predictor of future win and loss records than the previous standings. Essentially, the better you are at outscoring the opposition, the more likely it is that you'll win more games moving forward. One-run outcomes are not sustainable, but blowouts are illustrative of team quality.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Run differentials are also used to build "expected" records. Meaning that in the history of baseball, a specific run differential is expected to result in a given number of wins and losses. The Miami Marlins, for example, outscored the opposition by just three runs over the course of the season, which is an "expected" record of 81-81. Makes sense, they were even with the other teams in the league, they should finish at an even .500.

By contrast, the Milwaukee Brewers finished with a league-best +214 run differential, good for an "expected" record of 103-59. They finished 103-59.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

But teams frequently over perform or underperform against their expected win-loss record, for any number of reasons. A bad bullpen could mean a team wins blowouts, but loses more than their fair share of close games. Bad luck. Poorly timed injuries. Poor defense. Inconsistent hitting with runners in scoring position. The randomness of baseball. Or a dominant closer who shuts the door consistently in close games.

This year's 81-81 division winning Astros team was so bad they were outscored 32 runs over the course of the season, good for just an 78-84 expected win-loss record. While the Rangers and their fans are sure to be disappointed with the outcome, missing out on the final day, they were even worse. Texas had a -46 run differential, and a 76-86 expected record.

Houston Astros pitcher Tatsuya Imai celebrates after clinching the AL West division title in a game against the Athletics on Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026, in West Sacramento, Calif. (AP Photo/Sara Nevis)

So it's a near-certainty that Houston will make a quick postseason exit, right?

Yeah, no, not at all. Houston plays the Chicago White Sox in the best-of-three wild card series, which the Astros now host as division winners. Chicago's a better team, but the randomness inherent in the small sample size of a playoff series makes the result effectively a toss up. In fact, FanGraphs gives the Astros a 55% chance of advancing to the ALDS.

Should Houston win that series, they'd play the extremely mediocre Cleveland Guardians, who finished with a +11 run differential and 85-77 record. Cleveland may be slight favorites in that series, maybe 57-43, but hardly a foregone conclusion. Which means we could be staring down the barrel of an 81-81 team reaching the ALCS.

MLB always hoped for last-minute drama by starting every game around the same time on the final day of the regular season. They got it.

They also got the worst-ever division winning team because the league's financial incentives and playoff structure encourage owners to do the bare minimum and spend as little as possible to win 85 games and hope for the best. Or in Houston's case, 81. The Astros benefited, and fans were forced to watch the AL West "battle" lost.

articles.title: Foiled terror plot at bomber base signals wider threat to US military installations: expert
articles.excerpt:
Former FBI investigator Bill Daly discusses the investigation into an alleged terror plot after five suspects were arrested near an airbase in southwest England on ‘Fox Report.’

Five men arrested nea...
articles.body_text:
Former FBI investigator Bill Daly discusses the investigation into an alleged terror plot after five suspects were arrested near an airbase in southwest England on ‘Fox Report.’

Five men arrested near a key U.S. bomber base in the U.K. on Sunday may have planned a "complex," coordinated attack with potentially far-reaching security implications for American military installations globally, a former U.S. intelligence official warned.

As counterterrorism police investigated after officers detained the suspects near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, a former Pentagon official also said President Donald Trump will ultimately be the one to decide the consequences if indeed the "trail leads to Tehran."

The men were initially held on suspicion of offenses under Britain’s Explosives Act before being arrested on terrorism charges in connection with the airfield, a key U.S. Air Force hub and the primary European base for American strategic bombers.

On Sunday, Trump said U.S. authorities had been monitoring the suspects prior to their capture.

FORMER UK PRIME MINISTER TONY BLAIR WARNS EUROPE ‘WE DON’T WIN’ IN WAR WITHOUT US SUPPORT

Police at a road block on the road to RAF Fairford after a major incident was declared, with armed police manning a cordon near the village of Whelford in Gloucestershire, near RAF Fairford on Sunday, September 27, 2026. (Ben Birchall/PA Images via Getty Images)

"We had them under investigation," Trump told reporters in Chicago. "They were looking to do big damage to our fort."

"It may have been Scotland Yard. I don't know. We worked with a lot of them. We had them under view for a long time, and we got them," Trump added.

According to Sky News, counterterrorism police were investigating whether Iran is linked to the suspected bomb plot.

Former Trump White House official Morgan Murphy told Fox News Digital that British authorities are leading the investigation alongside U.S. law enforcement and intelligence.

"Every phone, bank record and rental receipt will be run through British and American intelligence, and if the trail leads to Tehran, it will be found," Murphy clarified.

"But as American airmen and bombers seem to have been the target, Air Force investigators on the base, the FBI in London, and American intelligence will likely all work the case."

"If conclusive evidence proves Iran is behind an attempted attack on U.S. forces, the American President will ultimately decide how Tehran pays," Murphy added.

BRITAIN INTRODUCES SWEEPING NEW POWERS TO TARGET FOREIGN STATE-LINKED GROUPS INCLUDING IRAN'S IRGC

A US Air Force Boeing B-52 Stratofortress bomber jet lands on the runway, beyond a USAF Rockwell B-1 Lancer bomber jet, at RAF Fairford in southwest England on March 9, 2026. (Henry NICHOLLS / AFP via Getty Images)

Former Defense Intelligence Agency official Andrew Badger told Fox News Digital the number of suspects and vehicles involved raised the possibility of a sophisticated operation.

"We are going to see elevated security protocols across Europe, across the U.K., and across the entire world for any U.S. installation," he said.

"This is a very significant threat, and again, seeing that we had five individuals involved and three different reported vans at the scene, this could have been a very complex, highly orchestrated operation," Badger added.

"This isn't just some type of amateur lone wolf operation," he said, noting Fairford’s strategic importance to the U.S. military. "Fairford is also where the U.S. houses its strategic bombers for Europe as well as the rest of the world."

He said a potential attack posed broader risks beyond the airfield itself which he said "could have had significant security implications. It could have damaged the nearby area."

HOW IRAN ATTACKS ARE FORCING THE PENTAGON TO RETHINK ITS DECADES-OLD MIDDLE EAST BASE STRATEGY

RAF Fairford is in the spotlight after five men were arrested near the key U.S. bomber base in the U.K. on Sunday. (Reuters)

"They could have tried to use a VBIED or a vehicle-borne explosive device where the first van could have gone off at the front gate, and then the other vans would have gone in and tried to go for the strategic bombers," Badger said.

British authorities have not publicly identified who they believe was behind the suspected plot or announced a motive, but RAF Fairford had taken on greater strategic importance during the war with Iran.

The U.K. government previously authorized U.S. forces to use the Royal Air Force bases Fairford and Diego Garcia for limited defensive operations, including destroying Iranian missiles and launchers at their source.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) later warned that any base used to attack Iranian territory would be considered a legitimate target.

"Any base used to launch attacks on Iranian territory is a legitimate target for our forces," the IRGC said, according to reports.

"Tehran warned London in July to keep American bombers off Fairford, and if this plot traces back to Iran, the answer must be more bombers, not fewer," Morgan said.

IRAN EXPERT BRANDS ISLAMIC CENTER OF ENGLAND IRAN'S 'UK OFFICE,' URGES IMMEDIATE CLOSURE

Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Chief Justice of Iran Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Eje'i, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, and an IRGC commander general Mohsen Rezaee attend a ceremony in Tehran, Iran, on July 3, 2026. (Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

A local councilor told Reuters there had been a recent security alert at Fairford and surveillance had been stepped up.

"So there was a specific threat about six weeks ago from the Iranians on this base. At the time, there was increased surveillance around the area," he told the outlet.

Badger, however, cautioned against assuming Iran was responsible while pointing to other potential threats.

"This could be Iran trying to gain strategic leverage in negotiations, but there are other actors as well," Badger added.

"But there's Russia, who's been launching a campaign of gray zone or hybrid warfare attacks across Europe, as well as Islamic extremists, which are still a significant threat here in the U.K."

"Was this some type of retaliation by Iran to perhaps try to gain leverage or to try to inflict a cost for the U.S. withdrawing from these negotiations? Again, we don't know for sure, but it is a possibility," Badger said.

Badger also pointed to RAF Welford, a major U.S. ammunition storage facility that primarily supports operations at RAF Fairford.

US EMBASSIES IN MIDDLE EAST WARN AMERICANS OF 'UNFORESEEN ESCALATION' AS LATEST STRIKES HIT IRAN

Members of the US military offload equipment from a US Air Force C-5 Galaxy at RAF Fairford in south west England on March 6, 2026. Britain's Prime Minister Keir Starmer has given approval for Washington to use the bases of Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean and RAF Fairford in southwest England to bomb Iranian missile sites, after several Gulf countries were targeted by Iranian retaliations. (Justin Tallis/AFP via Getty Images)

"RAF Welford is actually the second-largest weapons and ammunition depot in all of Europe," Badger said, noting that the facility where the U.S. stores ammunition "could have been a target as well."

"Other bases across Europe, including European and U.S. partners, have already been on a heightened state of alert," Badger continued.

"But of course, after this attack, I think they're going to be in an even more heightened state. You're going to have more frequent security patrols."

"There are reports that RAF Fairford was put onto what's called the Delta alert, which is the highest state of security alert within the military base system," Badger said.

"So this is basically that 'an imminent terrorist attack is inbound,'" he concluded.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title: Refugees in South Africa fear new attacks as September 30 deadline looms
articles.excerpt:
Durban, South Africa – Bishop Raphael Bahebwa is in hiding, afraid he could be attacked for speaking out for the rights of foreigners in South Africa.

“I am in hiding now because they say they are go...
articles.body_text:
Durban, South Africa – Bishop Raphael Bahebwa is in hiding, afraid he could be attacked for speaking out for the rights of foreigners in South Africa.

“I am in hiding now because they say they are going to kill me for speaking about the rights of foreigners,” he told Al Jazeera.

Bahebwa has lived in South Africa for 26 years, after arriving as a refugee from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

In that time, he has watched antiforeigner sentiment flare repeatedly in the country he came to call home. But he says this year feels different.

A September 30 deadline declared by March and March, an anti-immigration movement that has led protests across South Africa this year, has renewed fears of violence among migrant communities.

The group has called for undocumented foreign nationals to leave South Africa and has warned of further demonstrations if its demands are not met.

For Bahebwa and other refugees in Durban, however, the distinction between documented and undocumented migrants offers little comfort. They say the hostility they experience on the streets rarely begins with a request to see their papers.

South Africa will hold local government elections on November 4, in a campaign in which migration has become an increasingly prominent political and social issue.

For months, Bahebwa was among hundreds of refugees and asylum seekers who slept on the pavement outside the Durban Refugee Reception Centre on Che Guevara Road.

Many were from the DRC and Burundi, with others from Uganda, Mozambique and Tanzania. They said they had fled their communities because they feared antiforeigner attacks.

They arrived outside the Department of Home Affairs (DHA) office seeking safety.

For roughly four months, men, women and children slept outside, exposed to the elements and dependent on civil society organisations and volunteers for food and other necessities.

“It has been very tough,” Bahebwa said. “Never before have I experienced something like this.”

Some of the migrants told Al Jazeera that conditions became desperate. They described irregular access to food and medication and said one man who had tuberculosis died while living at the camp. Al Jazeera has not independently established the circumstances of his death.

The camp was also not far removed from the hostility its residents said they had fled.

On September 3, members of March and March confronted refugees and asylum seekers living outside the centre. Violence broke out, and police intervened. At least four people were reported injured.

At another protest days later, police officers stood between the two groups, forming a barrier as tensions rose.

March and March has described its mobilisation as a campaign against undocumented immigration, crime and deteriorating conditions in South African communities.

The group says the government’s response to immigration enforcement has been insufficient.

Its leaders have repeatedly rejected accusations that their campaign is xenophobic and insist their target is undocumented migration rather than foreign nationals generally.

Bahebwa said documented and undocumented migrants alike have been caught in the hostility.

Earlier this year, six refugees working in salons around Durban’s Warwick Street Market were beaten by men carrying sticks, according to public-interest news outlet GroundUp. Two were hospitalised.

Bahebwa said the migrants had also struggled to obtain help from the authorities after earlier attacks.

“Police said we can’t open cases because we are foreigners. We had nowhere to go,” he alleged. Police have not publicly responded to that specific allegation.

In mid-September, the government moved to clear the makeshift camp outside the refugee centre.

The refugees were given a choice: return to the communities they had fled or accept temporary accommodation at the Lindela facility in Gauteng, hundreds of kilometres from Durban. Lindela is a government-run immigration detention facility used to hold people facing deportation.

Some feared going to Lindela, a facility historically associated with immigration detention and repatriation. Others felt they could no longer endure life on the pavement.

On September 15, 274 people were transported by bus from Durban to Lindela. About 150 others chose to remain in Durban and began trying to find alternative accommodation.

For those who stayed behind, leaving the pavement did not resolve the problem that had brought them there in the first place.

Kafuti Muyumba, a small business owner from the DRC and a representative of the refugee community, said many were afraid to return to neighbourhoods where they had built businesses and lives.

People are afraid, he said. “Even the police allow March and March violence. They came with sticks and say we are attacking them,” Muyumba told Al Jazeera.

He said many refugees had lost their livelihoods during the months of upheaval and were now desperate to find accommodation.

“This is not the first time we are experiencing xenophobia,” he said. “In 2008 and then in 2015 we also experienced this.”

In 2008, xenophobic violence spread through townships and informal settlements, killing dozens and displacing thousands.

Further outbreaks of violence against foreign nationals followed in subsequent years.

For Muyumba, those memories make the rhetoric surrounding September 30 difficult to dismiss.

“We don’t trust the police. They are not being fair with us. Some of them are also saying we must go,” he said.

Police have said there are no plans to change their normal policing approach because of the September 30 deadline and that any protesters will be expected to remain within the law.

March and March said all it wants is for undocumented immigrants to leave the country and return home.

But Muyumba said returning to the DRC is not a viable alternative for many Congolese refugees.

In response to ongoing protests, the South African government said it had intensified its immigration enforcement.

Between June 14 and August 20, authorities processed 86,596 foreign nationals for deportation and repatriation, according to the government’s Inter-Ministerial Committee on Migration.

Malawians made up the largest group, followed by Zimbabweans and Mozambicans.

Government data says 90 percent of those repatriated had entered South Africa illegally, while 95 percent were classified as having crossed the border outside official ports of entry.

The government says the operations form part of a broader effort to strengthen border management and enforce immigration law.

At the same time, officials have repeatedly warned private groups against taking immigration enforcement into their own hands.

March and March’s September 30 deadline has no legal authority. The government says common citizens cannot deport anyone from South Africa.

But deadlines do not need legal force to create fear, as was the case for an earlier deadline of June 30. For the refugees who spent months sleeping outside the DHA office in Durban, September 30 is another uncertainty layered on top of many others.

Some have been moved hundreds of kilometres away.

Others are trying to find new homes in the same communities they once fled. But among the migrants Al Jazeera spoke to, there is a shared anxiety that paperwork may offer limited protection when anger is directed first at being foreign.

Bahebwa has spent more than a quarter of a century in South Africa. For now, he says he is hiding and does not know what September 30 will bring.

“They are scapegoating us as foreigners,” he said. “It is not going to end on September 30. It has to do with the elections.”

articles.title: South African police discover body of 11th woman near Johannesburg
articles.excerpt: South African police have discovered the body of another woman east of the country’s commercial capital, Johannesburg, bringing the total number of female bodies found near the city since mid-July to ...
articles.body_text:
South African police have discovered the body of another woman east of the country’s commercial capital, Johannesburg, bringing the total number of female bodies found near the city since mid-July to 11.

Police said on Sunday that the latest victim was found in an open field in the Ekurhuleni municipality at about midday local time (10am GMT).

“A security company vehicle patrolling the area noticed the body and alerted the police,” police spokeswoman Brigadier Brenda Muridili said.

Details about the woman’s identity, age and cause of death were not immediately available.

Just one day earlier, on Saturday, the body of a semi-naked woman was found near a cemetery in the same municipality.

The latest discoveries add to growing concern over violence against women in a country long plagued by violent crime. While police work to establish whether the killings are connected, there have been community concerns that the murders are being carried out by the same killer or killers.

Provincial police chief Tommy Mthombeni said the victim found on Saturday appeared to have been stoned to death, but a post-mortem examination would be conducted to determine the cause of death.

Police said a man linked to the killing was arrested almost 400km (250 miles) away. His arrest brings the number of people in custody in connection with the series of killings to four.

President Cyril Ramaphosa acknowledged the recovery of the body of the 10th victim while on the campaign trail for upcoming local elections, broadcaster eNCA reported.

“I’ve sadly heard about 10th body of a woman found in Thembisa,” Ramaphosa said on Saturday. “This continues to make us very sad, and in many ways, it’s a shame on the men of South Africa that we continue to kill the women of our beautiful country.”

South Africa has one of the highest femicide rates in the world, with an average of 15 women killed per day.

Two women have been charged with the murder of the woman whose body was the ninth discovered on September 17. Police have said the killing may have stemmed from a relationship-related matter.

Mthombeni, the provincial police chief, told state broadcaster SABC that investigators believe the ninth killing was an isolated case. However, he said it is possible some of the other killings are connected.

He added that some of the murders shared similarities, but cautioned that there is no conclusive evidence to suggest the same person or group is responsible.

Police discovered three bodies in July and August within 6km (4 miles) of one another in Ekurhuleni. Earlier this month, six bodies were found in 10 days, also in Ekurhuleni.

Prior to Saturday’s discovery, all of the deceased women were in their 20s or 30s. Several of them were found completely or partially naked.

The first body, discovered in mid-July, was found naked and restrained with cable ties. The victim’s boyfriend was subsequently arrested, but no charges were filed.

articles.title: Angels reach historic 100-loss low with season-closing defeat against Mariners as new era looms
articles.excerpt: Instead of ignoring the shots, ESPN fired back with a rare public statement to Awful Announcing—leading Le Batard to double down. Dan dissects the entire feud, calling out the massive holes in Le Bata...
articles.body_text:
Instead of ignoring the shots, ESPN fired back with a rare public statement to Awful Announcing—leading Le Batard to double down. Dan dissects the entire feud, calling out the massive holes in Le Batard's narrative and exposing what's really driving the conflict.

A season worth forgetting in Anaheim ended with a mark that will linger in baseball history forever.

With a 7-3 loss to the Seattle Mariners at T-Mobile Park on Sunday, the Los Angeles Angels (62-100) officially crossed a threshold they had evaded for 65 years: their first 100-loss season.

The defeat stripped the Halos of their standing as the last MLB franchise to avoid triple-digit losses, putting all 30 clubs on the century-mark ledger.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

For first-year manager Kurt Suzuki, Game 162 was the grim culmination of a grueling campaign, one that ultimately eclipsed the 63-99 mark set by Ron Washington’s 2024 squad.

Sammy Peralta No. 67 of the Los Angeles Angels looks on during the eighth inning against the Seattle Mariners at T-Mobile Park on Sept. 27, 2026, in Seattle, Wash. (Getty Images)

The finale carried an unmistakable layer of drama. Franchise star Mike Trout watched from the dugout on a scheduled day off as his young teammates fought to avert history.

Shortstop Zach Neto had insisted earlier in the week that organizational pride would propel them past the brink, and a 5-4 stretch in their final nine games gave Anaheim a flicker of hope. But Sunday proved unforgiving.

ANGELS SEEM COMPLETELY UNAWARE THEY ARE THE WORST TEAM IN MLB: 'OUR BEST BASEBALL IS AHEAD OF US'

Yusei Kikuchi #16 of the Los Angeles Angels pitches during a game against the Seattle Mariners at T-Mobile Park on Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026, in Seattle, Wash. (MLB Photos via Getty Images)

Former Mariner Yusei Kikuchi (1-7) was tagged early by his old club, surrendering three runs over five innings. After Angels' Bryce Teodosio trimmed the deficit to 3-1 with a sixth-inning sacrifice fly, Seattle quickly slammed the door. A costly throwing error and a two-run double by Randy Arozarena pushed the margin out of reach. A late solo shot by Jose Siri provided a brief spark, but the season expired when Dominic Canzone squeezed a fly ball off the bat of Christian Moore for the final out.

Following the June 26 firing of GM Perry Minasian, interim GM John Mozeliak tore down the roster, shipping out fan favorites Taylor Ward, Jo Adell, Logan O'Hoppe and Chase Silseth (and more) for prospects and leaving Suzuki with a stripped-down, youthful core down the stretch.

Cole Young of the Seattle Mariners slides into home plate to score during the second inning against the Los Angeles Angels at T-Mobile Park on Sept. 27, 2026, in Seattle, Wash. (Getty Images)

Yet, hitting rock bottom arrives with a sudden shift in momentum.

The end of Arte Moreno's era is officially underway following an agreement to sell the controlling interest of the franchise to Stan Kroenke’s group for a record $4 billion.

For a fanbase enduring its lowest historical point, Kroenke’s proven track record of constructing championship rosters across professional sports offers what Anaheim has lacked for decades: a real vision forward.

Life is pretty sweet if you're a Jacksonville Jaguars fan as of late.

Last year, the Jags went 13-4, their best season since 1999, and sit atop the AFC South three games into this season with one of the best coach-quarterback combos in the NFL.

Duval's finest absolutely crushed last year's AFC Champions, the New England Patriots, thanks in large part to the play of that aforementioned quarterback.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

JACKSONVILLE JAGUARS SET AT 8.5 WIN TOTAL AFTER SURPRISING 13-4 SEASON AND WILD CARD LOSS TO BUFFALO

Jacksonville Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence (16) stands in the pocket against the Tennessee Titans during the first half at Nissan Stadium on Nov. 30, 2025. (Steve Roberts/Imagn Images)

Trevor Lawrence tossed three touchdowns in a blowout 35-6 victory on Sunday, but he could have added a rushing touchdown midway through the fourth quarter as well.

With the Jaguars leading 28-6 with just under nine minutes left in the game, Lawrence took a designed quarterback keeper on third and three and broke into the clear.

NFL'S DUMBEST MOMENT OF WEEK 2 GOES TO JETS COACH AARON GLENN WHO PLAYED NOT TO LOSE AT END OF REGULATION

Then the flaxen-maned signal caller did something pretty inexplicable by all accounts: he slid at the one-yard line.

Okay, analytics nerds, I'm ready for any and all explanations on this one.

I get that you want to burn as much time as possible when you're holding a lead, but a touchdown there gives you a four-score lead with just over half a quarter left in the game.

Jacksonville Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence (16) gets past Kansas City Chiefs defensive tackle Chris Jones (95) as he runs the ball during the second half of an NFL football game. The game took place in Jacksonville, Florida, on Oct. 6, 2025. (Phelan M. Ebenhack/AP Photo)

The Patriots looked downright anemic on offense, mustering two field goals the entire game, and even if they somehow miraculously found the end zone four times in the next eight minutes, they still would've needed at least one two-point conversion just to tie the ballgame.

So again, I ask, what's the thought process here.

I've never been one to get too up in arms when it comes to things like this, but luckily the internet did it for me, as a bunch of angry fantasy football owners and amateur gamblers were ready to throw their phones through a wall after this one.

RAIDERS STAR BROCK BOWERS SHOCKINGLY UNDERGOES MENISCUS TRIM SURGERY AS FANTASY MANAGERS FUME AHEAD OF WEEK 1

I don't get the move, but I certainly don't think there's anything nefarious going on here.

Lawrence likely wanted to burn as much time as possible, and although I think it was ultimately a pointless endeavor, I can understand the logic.

Trevor Lawrence of the Jacksonville Jaguars throws a pass during the first quarter against the Buffalo Bills in the AFC Wild Card Playoff game at EverBank Stadium on Jan. 11, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Mike Carlson/Getty Images)

I would say to put your tinfoil hats away, folks, but Lawrence actually gave a tongue-in-cheek answer about it when speaking during his postgame interview

Stand up and take a bow, conspiracy theorists. You were right this time.

articles.title: Kathy Griffin says Ed Sheeran should have told Robert Kraft to 'go f--- yourself' over Macklemore
articles.excerpt:
Comedian Kathy Griffin argued that Ed Sheeran should have pushed back against stadium owner Robert Kraft when the latter wanted Macklemore removed from the tour.

Comedian Kathy Griffin said on Wednes...
articles.body_text:
Comedian Kathy Griffin argued that Ed Sheeran should have pushed back against stadium owner Robert Kraft when the latter wanted Macklemore removed from the tour.

Comedian Kathy Griffin said on Wednesday that singer Ed Sheeran should have told Gillette Stadium owner and billionaire Robert Kraft to "go f--- yourself" after barring Macklemore from performing as his opening act over his "Free Palestine" stunt.

In an interview with Queerty, Griffin commented on Macklemore being pulled from the rest of Sheeran's tour earlier this month after he repeatedly pushed for a "Free Palestine" during his act and performed his anti-Israel song "Hind's Hall." The decision came after Kraft barred Macklemore from performing at Gillette Stadium.

Though Sheeran has said that the decision ultimately came from the concert promoter and venues rather than him, Griffin argued that Sheeran could have, and should have, defended Macklemore at the time.

MACKLEMORE'S LONG HISTORY OF CONTROVERSY FROM GRAMMY WINS TO 'FREE PALESTINE' CONCERT REMARKS

Kathy Griffin criticized Ed Sheeran and defended Macklemore during an interview with Queerty. (Gilbert Flores/Variety via Getty Images)

"I wish that Ed Sheeran had not taken the advice of the ones who told him to fire Macklemore," Griffin said. "Let’s not be listening to f------ Robert Kraft. When Robert Kraft says I’ve called all the other stadium owners and they’re not gonna let you do the show with Macklemore either, Ed Sheeran should’ve said go f--- yourself, I can go to Brazil and perform for 250,000 people. He had more options."

Griffin added that Macklemore's comments were protected under the First Amendment and professed her own support for a "Free Palestine."

"I don't think 'Free Palestine' is such a controversial thing to say because that's a genuine genocide that is happening there, in my opinion. I don't want Israel to be eradicated. I love the Israeli people as I hope the rest of the world likes the American people but hates [President Donald] Trump and his cabinet and our current SCOTUS. So I can't stand [Israeli Prime Minister] Bibi Netanyahu. I think he's ruined the Knesset which is their Congress. But I certainly don't have a beef with the Jewish people or the Palestinian people. They're both trying to survive. I personally think that Palestine should be its own country," Griffin said.

ROBERT KRAFT PLEDGES $2M FOR HUMANITARIAN AID AS MACKLEMORE FACES FALLOUT OVER VENUE BAN

Macklemore (right) was removed from Ed Sheeran's (left) tour earlier this month. (Kevin Mazur/WireImage)

Fox News Digital reached out to Sheeran's and Kraft's representatives for comment.

In response to being removed from Sheeran's tour, Macklemore announced on Thursday that he would be launching his own "Free Palestine Tour." As of now, he has three shows scheduled: in Dublin on Oct. 26, in Paris on Oct. 29 and in London on Oct. 30.

Though Macklemore has received support from progressive figures for his political actions, the singer has also faced criticism from pro-Israel organizations who accused him of supporting antisemitism.

MACKLEMORE BAN BY ROBERT KRAFT DRAWS FIRE FROM AOC AND CAIR WHO ADVOCATE FOR FREE SPEECH ONLY WHEN CONVENIENT

The Israeli-American Council (IAC) released a statement to Fox News Digital supporting Kraft's actions pushing back against Macklemore.

The Israeli-American Council (IAC) supported Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft after he barred Macklemore from performing after his "Free Palestine" chant. (AFP via Getty Images)

"The Israeli-American Council (IAC) applauds Robert Kraft and his fellow stadium owners for their moral leadership in expelling rapper Macklemore from the concert stage rather than allow him to promote antisemitism," the statement read.

It added, "Robert Kraft's moral leadership establishes what should be an obvious principle: a performer who traffics in antisemitism should not be given a stage. As a result, Macklemore will no longer be allowed to subject audiences to his hateful rants. The IAC salutes and thanks Mr. Kraft for setting an example for all to follow."

Fox News' Emily Trainham contributed to this report.

Lindsay Kornick is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to lindsay.kornick@fox.com and on Twitter: @lmkornick.

articles.title: Baker Mayfield leaves game after writhing in pain on turf in Tampa Bay when thumb on throwing hand injured
articles.excerpt: A devastating knee injury sidelines New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart, drawing attention to a growing league-wide health crisis. OutKick host Dan Dakich and medical expert Dr. Ann Bass join the ...
articles.body_text:
A devastating knee injury sidelines New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart, drawing attention to a growing league-wide health crisis. OutKick host Dan Dakich and medical expert Dr. Ann Bass join the broadcast to analyze the physical toll on modern NFL signal-callers. They examine the rising number of quarterback injuries across six different teams already this season.

Baker Mayfield was trying to lead a fourth-quarterback comeback against the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday when he found himself heaving a desperation fourth-down pass which got intercepted. And then something really bad happened.

As Vikings linebacker Andrew Van Ginkel was cradling the interception, back up field Mayfield was on the ground literally screaming in pain.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

He clearly injured the thumb on his throwing hand.

Baker Mayfield (6) of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers looks to pass in the third quarter of the game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on Oct. 20, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Gregory Shamus/Getty Images)

KYLER MURRAY CLEARS CONCUSSION PROTOCOL AND WILL START FOR VIKINGS AGAINST TAMPA BAY BUCCANEERS

The finger bent in a manner it should not.

After the game, Bucs head coach Todd Bowles announced Mayfield suffered a dislocated thumb.

"He'll get an MRI tomorrow just to see exactly what inside is wrong," Bowles said. "We'll know more tomorrow."

The "know more" part will determine how much rather than if Mayfield suffered ligament damage. The tests will also determine if Mayfield will need surgery.

If Mayfield needs surgery, he's probably looking at a stint on the injured reserve list, which would require him to miss four games.

His return to play will be determined by how long it eventually takes him to regain his grip.

WASHINGTON COMMANDERS FACE SEASON-DEFINING CRISIS AS JAYDEN DANIELS SUFFERS ANOTHER SERIOUS ELBOW INJURY

TAMPA, FLORIDA - DECEMBER 11: Baker Mayfield #6 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers warms up prior to a game against the Atlanta Falcons at Raymond James Stadium on December 11, 2025 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Julio Aguilar/Getty Images)

Mayfield left the game after the injury. He walked to the Buccaneers' locker room to have the digit examined.

That included an X-Ray within the Raymond James Stadium medical facility.

The Bucs turned to backup quarterback Jalon Daniels to play the final two minutes of the game, down 23-16.

Daniels, an undrafted rookie who made the club as something of a surprise, could not author the comeback win. He threw an interception on the game's final play.

The Buccaneers are 0-3 and in trouble, especially if their starting quarterback's condition means he'll miss the next month of games.
