articles.title: Irish PM rejects antisemitism concerns in Ireland amid dramatic vote over boycotting Israel game
articles.excerpt:
Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin speaks outlines Ireland's position on Israel, the war in Gaza, antisemitism concerns and the country's experience resolving conflict in Northern Ireland

Irish Prim...
articles.body_text:
Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin speaks outlines Ireland's position on Israel, the war in Gaza, antisemitism concerns and the country's experience resolving conflict in Northern Ireland

Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin rejected claims that Ireland's sharp criticism of Israel has crossed into antisemitism as tensions flared around a politically charged soccer match between the countries Sunday, with Irish players holding a last-minute vote over whether to boycott the game.

Martin, in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital this week in New York, outlined why Ireland has taken such a staunch position against the Israeli government's conduct of the war in Gaza, calling its military response "absolutely disproportionate" while pressing Israel to "change strategy" and calling for increased humanitarian aid to Gaza.

Martin argued that Ireland's own history — particularly its experience ending decades of conflict in Northern Ireland — gives the country a role to play as a voice for peace on the international stage, a theme he returned to while discussing Ukraine and the ongoing debate over Irish reunification.

"I think for the vast majority of people it does not," Martin said when asked directly whether anti-Israel sentiment in Ireland had crossed the line into antisemitism.

"We have no toleration for antisemitism, none," Martin added.

NEW YORK TIMES ISSUES CORRECTION, DELETES LINE QUESTIONING IF ISRAELIS WERE VICTIMS OF OCT 7 TERROR ATTACK

Celtic supporters display a "Stop The Game" banner during a match against Hearts at Celtic Park in Glasgow, Scotland, on May 16, 2026, as part of a campaign opposing Ireland's upcoming soccer fixtures against Israel. (Ross Parker/SNS Group via Getty Images; John Lamparski/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The extraordinary player vote came after months of pressure surrounding the UEFA Nations League fixture on Sunday, with more than 160 Irish sports figures calling for a boycott and players themselves publicly questioning whether the match should go ahead.

A "significant majority" of players ultimately voted on Saturday to play the game, while one player left the squad after expressing his wish not to take part.

In the interview, Martin strongly condemned Hamas' Oct. 7 terrorist attack and defended Israel's right to exist in security.

"First of all, we condemned, absolutely, the outrageous terrorist attack by Hamas in October," Martin told Fox News Digital.

"We believe in a two-state solution," Martin said. "We believe that Israel, of course, has a right to exist in security and its people need to be guaranteed of security. But likewise, Palestinians should have a right to live in their homeland in a peaceful way."

"There are many peaceful voices in Palestine that I've met who want peaceful coexistence with Israel."

Martin said Ireland's strongly pro-Palestinian position was rooted partly in its own history.

"There's a very strong pro-Palestinian position in Ireland," Martin said. "Ireland, the Irish government and the Irish people, probably because of our own history, but also because of a sense of right and justice and fairness."

Supporters protest during the international friendly soccer match between the Republic of Ireland and Qatar at Aviva Stadium in Dublin on May 28, 2026. (Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile)

Thousands have taken to the streets across Ireland since the war began, while national broadcaster RTÉ refused to air this year's Eurovision Song Contest after Israel's participation was confirmed.

Ireland spent centuries under British rule before most of the island gained independence a little more than a century ago, while Northern Ireland remains part of the United Kingdom.

He said Israel's military response to the Oct. 7 attack had resonated deeply in Ireland and called for increased humanitarian aid into Gaza.

"We want humanitarian aid going into Gaza. There's not enough humanitarian aid going in," Martin said, pointing to the conditions facing roughly 2 million people there, including shortages of food and shelter and children without access to education.

Martin said Ireland wanted Israel to reconsider its conduct of the war, asking whether it would "change strategy" and "change its approach to the whole issue."

"So that's the background to the Irish position," he said. "People are angry in terms of what's going on in the Middle East and that's the manifestation of it."

Dublin , Ireland - 6 September 2025; Republic of Ireland supporters make their feelings know as they protest against Israel before the FIFA World Cup 2026 Group F qualifying match between Republic of Ireland and Hungary at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin. (David Fitzgerald/Sportsfile via Getty Images)

ANTISEMITIC VIOLENCE REACHES DEADLIEST LEVEL SINCE 1994, NEW GLOBAL REPORT FINDS

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrímsson said his players were uncomfortable with the games, declaring: "We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide." The Israeli Football Association accused him of "stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy," prompting Martin to call the remarks "unacceptable."

The FAI previously sought Israel's suspension from international competition. Separately, Irish soccer officials later voted to fulfill the Israel fixtures after being warned a boycott could cost the association at least $6.3 million and trigger UEFA sanctions.

Sunday's game will be played in Hungary, while Ireland's Oct. 4 home fixture has been moved to Serbia and will be played behind closed doors. Irish supporters will not have access to either game.

An organized campaign dubbed #StopTheGame has, meanwhile, spent months pressuring Irish soccer officials and players not to fulfill the Israel fixtures, staging protests and urging the national team to refuse to play.

The campaign has also spilled onto the field. During a friendly against Qatar in May, protesters threw tennis balls bearing "Stop The Game" messages onto the pitch in opposition to the Israel fixtures.

Martin has resisted calls for Ireland to boycott Israel, arguing that unilateral action could be "self-defeating" and may hurt Irish soccer without having any effect on Israel.

Republic of Ireland's Evan Ferguson looks on as play is halted after protesters threw tennis balls onto the pitch during an international friendly against Qatar at Aviva Stadium in Dublin on May 28, 2026. The protest targeted Ireland's upcoming soccer fixtures against Israel. (Charles McQuillan/Getty Images)

The dispute over the games reflects a broader debate over whether Ireland's criticism of Israel has crossed a line.

The American Jewish Committee raised concerns directly with Martin in Washington in March 2025 about antisemitism and what it called the "vilification of Israel in Ireland." An Anti-Defamation League official also participated in the meeting. The AJC alleged that antisemitism had become "pervasive" in Ireland.

Martin pointed to Ireland's annual Holocaust commemorations and the historic contribution of Jewish communities in Dublin, Cork and elsewhere in rejecting the suggestion that antisemitism was broadly tolerated in Ireland. He also pointed to Ireland's participation in international efforts against antisemitism and said the country campaigns against it globally.

"We cherish that contribution that the Jewish community has made to Ireland," Martin said.

Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin addresses the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York on Sept. 24, 2026. Martin used his address to criticize Israel's conduct in Gaza and Israeli settlement activity in the West Bank. (Angela Weiss/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Martin's defense of Ireland's position came before he addressed world leaders at the United Nations on Thursday, where he delivered a sharply critical assessment of Israel's conduct in Gaza and the West Bank, declaring that the international community had "failed Palestine."

"When the full truth of what has happened, what is still happening in Gaza, is finally known, when the evidence is gathered, when the testimonies are heard, when the true horrors are finally and fully revealed, it will shame the world," he said. "Nobody will be able to say that we did not know."

Martin accused violent Israeli settlers in the West Bank of acting with "near-total impunity" and said Palestinian communities faced displacement and destruction "amounting to ethnic cleansing."

He reiterated his support for a two-state solution, saying the only viable outcome was for "a State of Palestine and a State of Israel" to live side by side "in peace, security and dignity."

During his Fox News Digital interview, Martin connected Ireland's position on the Middle East to its experience ending decades of violence in Northern Ireland, saying "we feel we can make a contribution to that conflict resolution pathway."

That role has taken on added significance as Ireland holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union, giving it an elevated diplomatic role at a time of multiple international conflicts.

Martin also pointed to a personal experience that shaped his thinking, recalling meeting Israeli Rami Elhanan and Palestinian Bassam Aramin in Israel, two fathers who each lost a daughter in the conflict and later worked together for peace. Their stories are told in Colum McCann's novel "Apeirogon."

"That's an inspiration to me," Martin said, adding that he had met both men in Israel. He said their work reflected Ireland's own efforts to reconcile communities divided by generations of conflict.

Palestinians seek aid supplies from the U.S.-backed Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF), in the central Gaza Strip, Aug. 4, 2025. (REUTERS/Stringer)

Beyond the Middle East, Martin addressed Russia's war in Ukraine, saying a ceasefire along existing battle lines could provide a starting point for negotiations while rejecting territorial gains by force.

"Ukraine can't cede territory that Russia hasn't even conquered, despite four years of war," Martin said. "From our perspective, no one has the right to go into another country and take its territory."

Ireland has maintained its military neutrality while providing humanitarian and non-lethal assistance to Ukraine and taking in more than 120,000 Ukrainians since Russia's invasion. Martin rejected suggestions that such support compromised Ireland's neutrality, noting that Dublin has not supplied lethal weapons. "We want the war to end," he said.

Martin's focus on ending long-running conflicts also extends to Ireland's own divided island. He and his Fianna Fáil party support reunification with Northern Ireland, but he said greater trust between the two communities must come first.

"I believe in unity and my party believes in unity, but we have to work on it," Martin said. "We have to build reconciliation amongst the different traditions on the island of Ireland."

Under the Good Friday Agreement, a referendum would be called if it appeared likely that a majority in Northern Ireland supported reunification — an issue that gained fresh attention when Trump said during his recent visit to the country that he would "love" to see a united Ireland.

Martin also pointed to Ireland's unique relationship with the United States, crediting Washington with playing a "critical" role in the Northern Ireland peace process in the 1990s.

Asked whether Washington could play a role again in a future reunification process, he replied: "To a degree maybe, potentially, yeah."

Michael Dorgan is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business.

You can send tips to michael.dorgan@fox.com and follow him on Twitter @M_Dorgan.

articles.title: Tense standoff over loyalist march in Portadown as protesters block route
articles.excerpt:
Sinn Féin leaders join those on streets opposing decision to allow Garvaghy Road parade for first time since 1998

Hundreds of protesters spent the day blocking the route of a hugely contentious parad...
articles.body_text:
Sinn Féin leaders join those on streets opposing decision to allow Garvaghy Road parade for first time since 1998

Hundreds of protesters spent the day blocking the route of a hugely contentious parade in Northern Ireland after a court gave late-night clearance for the Orange Order to march on a historically significant road for the first time in nearly 30 years.

The loyalist Drumcree parade along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road in Portadown was given the go ahead by the Parades Commission for the first time since 1998, a decision denounced as “madness” by Sinn Féin.

It led to a weekend of intense legal wrangling which concluded at 2.15am on Sunday when the court of appeal said it could not interfere with the commission’s decision.

In driving rain on a cold Sunday morning, hundreds of nationalist protesters gathered to block the route. Many linked arms and sang songs as announcements were made over loudspeaker that they were liable to arrest and prosecution.

The Orangemen spent the day ensconced a mile away in a church, the proposed start of the march, and said they would wait until police told them the road was clear.

Among the protesters was the Sinn Féin president, Mary Lou McDonald, who said the decision to allow the parade was “madness” and “primitive treatment of any community in the year 2026. It is intolerable, and it will not be tolerated.”

She added: “The mood here has been peaceful. It has been united and orderly. This is a dignified and united community and they are absolutely determined that they and we will not be drawn back into the past.”

Michelle O’Neill, the Sinn Féin vice-president and Northern Ireland first minister, was also there and said reigniting the dispute brought “into question how this whole peace process works”.

She told reporters: “We’re meeting families who feel collectively traumatised, who feel individually traumatised. Does anybody think that this is a good idea?

“No right-minded person would make this decision. I still do not know the answer to this question – why, after 28 years of a determination to block a march down this road, that the Parades Commission thought that this was the right idea today to bring this mess back on to this community?”

The local Democratic Unionist party (DUP) MP, Carla Lockhart, accused O’Neill of “whipping up hysteria” at an “unlawful” protest.

“It is unreal that we have a first minister behaving the way she is behaving,” she said. “If I did it, or if any of my colleagues did it, I would be in the back of a Land Rover.”

Gavin Robinson, the DUP leader, said “we now have lawmakers acting as law breakers” and accused O’Neill of “giving two fingers to the courts, the police, the rule of law”.

The Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, cut short his attendance at the Labour party conference in Liverpool to travel to Belfast, but said he did not have the powers to call the march off unless police formally requested him to do so.

He said the nationalist protest was “unlawful” and called on politicians to “calm things down”.

Bryant said: “It is incumbent on everybody in political office to take this moment very, very seriously and to take the temperature down, to think twice before ... inflating any argument and to think about what somebody else who doesn’t share your opinion might think about the way you’ve put your case.”

The tense standoff also drew in the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who appealed for “calm on all sides”.

The Irish taoiseach, Mícheál Martin, echoed that but described the Parades Commission decision as “incomprehensible and wrong”.

He called for the situation to be mediated sensibly in a way “that protects the gains that have been made and the peace and harmony that has prevailed for so long”.

The Drumcree parade on the Garvaghy Road – a Catholic enclave in a largely Protestant town – sparked some of the most serious and violent disorder in Northern Ireland’s history.

On Friday, the Parades Commission granted permission subject to restrictions, including a limit of 35 participants, an 8am start time instead of 1pm and that it should be held in silence.

The decision was challenged and blocked on Saturday by a judge, Justice Patricia Smyth, who said the “long-running dispute has the potential to escalate” across Northern Ireland.

That decision was then challenged by the Orange Order, leading to two further hearings on Saturday night and Sunday morning.

The final time-limited sitting, which began at 0.20am on Sunday, was heard before Mr Justice Humphreys, who acknowledged the “unusual if not unprecedented circumstances … with a parade scheduled to begin in just over six hours’ time”.

Outlining his decision, Humphreys cited case law that as a public body the courts must respect the commission’s judgment and “their decisions will not be lightly interfered with”.

articles.title: Finding Desert Angels: Searching for the missing at the US-Mexico border
articles.excerpt:
An ageing trailblazer of search and rescue risks his life to find a woman’s missing son in the US-Mexico borderlands.

Search-and-rescue pioneer Rafael Larraenza runs a harrowing, high-stakes DIY resc...
articles.body_text:
An ageing trailblazer of search and rescue risks his life to find a woman’s missing son in the US-Mexico borderlands.

Search-and-rescue pioneer Rafael Larraenza runs a harrowing, high-stakes DIY rescue operation for those who have gone missing after crossing the United States-Mexico border. For 25 years, Larraenza has been the man people call when no one else has the will, instincts or know-how to find their loved ones.

Now, facing physical decline and limited resources, Larraenza races against time to help a mother find her missing son, knowing that every minute can mean the difference between life and death. Desert Angel follows his dangerous journey through the deadly landscapes few ever see and some never escape.

Finding Desert Angels is a documentary film by Vincent DeLuca.

articles.title: For Libya, the Hormuz crisis can be a trap or an opportunity
articles.excerpt: Amid the worsening global energy crisis triggered by the US-Israel war on Iran, European countries, desperate for alternative energy supplies, trade routes and partnerships, have looked across the Med...
articles.body_text:
Amid the worsening global energy crisis triggered by the US-Israel war on Iran, European countries, desperate for alternative energy supplies, trade routes and partnerships, have looked across the Mediterranean for solutions.

As a result, governments across North Africa have started to reassess their strategic value. Algeria is in an especially strong position as an established gas supplier, while Egypt can offer infrastructure, refining capacity and access through the Suez Canal.

Libya has also seen its strategic value increase. It has around 48 billion barrels of proven oil reserves, the largest in Africa, and produces 1.5 million barrels of oil per day. It also has substantial natural gas reserves.

Its oil reaches international markets through the Mediterranean, while the Greenstream gas pipeline connects its Mellitah complex directly to Europe.

Libya cannot replace the Gulf in terms of oil and gas exports, but it can become a major player in diversification efforts not just in Europe but elsewhere in the world. The challenge the country faces is how to take full advantage amid structural constraints and insecurity.

Libya is simultaneously a major energy exporter and an energy-insecure state. Although the country possesses vast oil and gas resources, Libyans experience regular electricity blackouts due to an inefficient domestic energy system.

More than 70 percent of Libyan gas production is consumed domestically, mostly for electricity generation. Production has struggled to meet both domestic needs and export commitments. Gas exports consequently fell year on year from around 200 billion cubic feet in 2019 to 35 billion in 2025, the lowest export levels in 22 years.

At the same time, the country is flaring at least 200 billion cubic feet of gas annually due to underdeveloped infrastructure. Gas that could generate electricity, support industry or increase exports is instead being wasted.

The International Monetary Fund has estimated Libya’s total energy subsidy burden at around $17bn, equivalent to roughly 35 percent of GDP – one of the largest in the world.

Much of these funds go into subsidising imported refined fuels, as domestic refining capacity is largely underdeveloped and cannot meet demand.

The domestic energy situation is compounded by political fragmentation, institutional disputes and periodic disruptions to production due to conflict.

Increasing exports without addressing these problems risks improving energy security abroad while neglecting it at home, and that is a recipe for more instability in an already fragile nation.

The global energy crisis triggered by the Iran war is surely a major opportunity for Libya to increase its revenues from hydrocarbons. But it also carries a risk.

As I pointed out during the 5th meeting of the Mediterranean Energy Experts Circle earlier this month, greater demand for Libyan oil and gas could reinforce the economic model the country has struggled to escape from for decades: producing hydrocarbons, exporting them, distributing the revenues and postponing structural reform.

This model does not allow Libya to capture the full economic potential of its resource wealth. It keeps the Libyan state stuck in the all too familiar “resource curse”, which promotes economic stagnation and inefficiency.

That is why when taking advantage of heightened demand for energy, it is crucial that Libya uses the proceeds to transform its energy system.

That means capturing flared gas, modernising electricity generation and transmission, expanding domestic refining where economically viable, reforming subsidies, investing seriously in renewable energy and participating in sustainable regional energy cooperation.

Libya’s National Sustainable Energy Strategy aims to have 22 percent of electricity generation from renewable sources by 2035, an ambitious target that requires major positive shifts in security and governance conditions. Increased revenue flows can help jump-start the process.

Another important consideration is how the country should approach heightened foreign interest. Libya’s first major oil and gas licensing round since 2007 was concluded in February, with the US’s Chevron, Italy’s Eni, QatarEnergy, Spain’s Repsol, Hungary’s MOL, Nigeria’s Aiteo, and Türkiye’s TPAO securing new licences.

Commercial and geopolitical interests are rarely completely separate in energy. For Libya, this creates bargaining power—if managed coherently by the Libyans. Rather than becoming an arena in which external actors compete for individual assets and relationships, Libya could use diversified partnerships to attract investment and technology while reducing dependence on any single partner.

The transformation Libya seeks should not be confined to its borders. Its strategic objective should be to become an integral player in a Mediterranean energy hub by expanding cooperation with neighbouring states and leveraging existing production capacities and infrastructure.

To Libya’s east, Egypt has a large electricity system and significant refining and processing capacity. To its west, Tunisia provides access towards the wider Maghreb and increasingly towards European markets. Libya sits between them with enormous hydrocarbon resources, considerable solar potential and existing energy connections with both neighbours.

Important steps have already been taken to deepen regional energy integration. In January, Egypt and Libya signed an energy cooperation agreement covering exploration and the development of crude-oil refining. The two countries are also discussing the construction of an 800km pipeline connecting Tobruk to Alexandria. The project is worth $1bn and would carry Libyan crude directly to Egyptian refineries.

Libya and Tunisia are also expanding cooperation. Earlier this month, the Libyan-Tunisian company Joint Oil opened an international licensing round covering around 3,000 square kilometres of shared offshore acreage and development of the cross-border Zarat oil and gas discovery. Formal awards are expected by the end of April 2027.

The risk here is that expanded cooperation could develop into dependence. How to avoid that is the lesson Libya can learn from the Strait of Hormuz crisis. The country still needs sufficient domestic electricity, refining and production capacity to protect itself. Regional integration should add alternatives rather than create new vulnerabilities: more markets, more electricity connections, more processing options and more export routes.

The objective should therefore be specialisation, connectivity and redundancy all achieved in the right sequence depending on needs and conditions.

The Iran war has given Libya something potentially more valuable than temporarily higher hydrocarbon prices: renewed strategic relevance. But greater strategic relevance does not automatically make the country a more reliable energy partner.

Converting the former into the latter requires a radically different approach not just to the domestic oil and gas industry, but also to overall economic development and regional geopolitics.

Libya must use this moment to pursue strategic redesign: to increase production while recovering wasted gas, improve electricity infrastructure, develop refining and renewables, strengthen regional connections and cooperation, and use competition among international partners to attract investment.

Libya already has the resources and the geography to become an even bigger player in the energy market. The question is whether it can build the rest.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Pope Leo urges healing of ‘deep wounds’ before meeting child sexual abuse survivors in France
articles.excerpt:
Pontiff also uses visit to Catholic shrine at Lourdes to criticise assisted dying as “false compassion”

The pope has called on the Catholic church to heal “deep wounds” and “painful errors”, before a...
articles.body_text:
Pontiff also uses visit to Catholic shrine at Lourdes to criticise assisted dying as “false compassion”

The pope has called on the Catholic church to heal “deep wounds” and “painful errors”, before a meeting with survivors of child sexual abuse as he continues his four-day visit to France.

Addressing a crowd in a large field near the Catholic shrine of Lourdes on Sunday, Pope Leo XIV called on the church to reckon with its past, without directly referencing sexual abuse scandals in France that affected at least 330,000 children over seven decades.

“In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and ⁠painful errors that have occurred within [the church], we must humbly place ourselves under the Lord’s purifying gaze,” the first US pope told the estimated crowd of 150,000 people.

Leo was due to privately meet seven survivors of child sexual abuse by French clergy on Sunday after leading an open-air morning mass at Lourdes, one of the most popular Catholic sites for pilgrims and reputed as a place of healing.

Meeting French bishops earlier on Sunday, Leo said they had acted with determination against “the painful scourge of abuse committed against minors by members of the clergy or in an ecclesial context against minors”. He urged them “to continue along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance”, according to a transcript of his remarks released by the Vatican.

During a homily to the faithful, the pope attacked medically assisted dying as immoral “false compassion”, in a staunch articulation of the Catholic church’s teaching that all human life must be defended from conception until natural death.

After years of debate, France formally adopted legislation last month allowing incurably ill adults the right to “aid in dying”, joining a small number of countries with similar laws, including Belgium, the Netherlands, Switzerland and Canada.

The pope said: “It is impossible to regard causing death as something normal. What is legal is not necessarily moral.”

The pope was due to take part in six events while in Lourdes, including a meeting with staff and patients at the shrine’s care centre.

Lourdes has drawn millions of sick and disabled believers seeking a cure from its spring waters since the Catholic church officially recognised visions of the Virgin Mary reported by a local girl in 1858. Arriving there in a white popemobile on Saturday night, however, Leo would have been reminded of the church’s dark and painful legacy, as he passed boarded-up mosaics by a Jesuit priest who is accused of abusing more than two dozen women over three decades.

Marko Rupnik, one of the Catholic church’s best-known mosaic artists, is on trial in a Vatican court, accused by more than two dozen women of having psychologically, spiritually and sexually abused them from the 1990s, including during the creation of his artworks. The bishop of Lourdes ordered the works covered up, reasoning that survivors of abuse seeking succour at the site should not be forced to see them.

Rupnik is not known to have commented publicly on the allegations, Reuters reported.

Among the survivors who will meet the pope is a former pupil of the nearby Catholic boarding school Notre-Dame de Bétharram, whose former students have recounted their experiences of violence, rape and sexual assault in what is thought to be the biggest child sexual abuse scandal at a school in French history.

In an interview published last year, the pope spoke of the “crisis” of clerical sexual abuse in the church. He also said “victims must be treated with great respect and with an understanding that those who have suffered very deep wounds because of abuse, sometimes carry those wounds for their entire life”, according to a transcript on Vatican News, the Holy See’s official news site.

The first official papal visit to France in 18 years follows an announcement last week by the country’s Independent National Authority for Recognition and Reparation that about 2,000 people who reported sexual abuse by clergy or other church representatives were seeking reparations.

France’s Catholic bishops conference agreed to provide compensation after a landmark report in 2021 estimated that 330,000 children were sexually abused over seven decades by predatory priests or other Catholic figures. The two-and-a-half-year independent inquiry found that vast numbers of children were subjected to sexual violence by priests and clergy and that the crimes were covered up in a “systemic way” by a deliberate “veil of silence” in the church.

On the day Leo arrived in Paris, a group of survivors published an open letter voicing fears that his visit would change nothing, criticising that the seven he was due to meet in Lourdes were “carefully selected” by the church, rather than survivors’ groups.

“You will merely ask us for forgiveness. This is not enough. One does not ask for forgiveness for a crime; one is responsible for a crime,” they wrote in the letter published in the newspaper Libération.

The pope arrived to celebrate mass on Sunday morning to a rapturous reception from the faithful, who waved flags and cheered, as they thronged the streets of Lourdes to catch a glimpse of him. The Holy See’s live stream showed Leo making stately progress in his popemobile, stopping frequently to greet and bless babies that were passed to him.

The south-western town near the Spanish border is one of the most important Catholic sites in the world, attracting 3 million pilgrims a year. The Associated Press reported that the pope’s visit had caused accommodation prices to soar, with the price of some one-night hotel stays reaching more than €2,000 (£1,700).

articles.title: Burnham refreshes the parts others can’t reach on the Andy and Laura show | John Crace
articles.excerpt:
The PM oozes confidence and easy-going charm as he tells Laura Kuenssberg the hill he’ll die on is fixing social care

In recent weeks there has been much speculation in some parts of the media that A...
articles.body_text:
The PM oozes confidence and easy-going charm as he tells Laura Kuenssberg the hill he’ll die on is fixing social care

In recent weeks there has been much speculation in some parts of the media that Andy Burnham would be calling an early general election. Speculation that existed largely in the heads of those writing the stories, as even the most favourable polls suggest that Labour would lose its huge majority and become the largest party in a coalition government. But to stop the chatter dominating his party conference, Burnham made it clear there would be no early election. His reward? Headlines in the rightwing press that he had bottled it. By not calling an election he had never planned to call. Sometimes you just can’t win.

There again, you might call this a first-world problem for the prime minister. This time last year, Burnham had been hanging around the fringes of the conference as he and his allies attempted one of the most half-arsed coups in living memory. One that fizzled out almost before it had started and became the butt of many jokes among Keir Starmer’s inner circle. Andy looked to have blown himself up on the runway, leaving Keir safe for the duration of the parliament.

Fast forward a year and Burnham is in Number 10, Reform’s lead in the polls has disappeared, and Labour is looking a lot more competitive than even the most rose-tinted party members could have reasonably expected in such a short period of time. Andy must be pinching himself. Unable to believe his luck. All that’s changed has been him. Energy prices are still sky high as a result of the war in Iran. The cost of living is still way too high. Nigel Farage and Kemi Badenoch might have been a problem for Keir, but they aren’t for Andy. You might even call them assets.

No wonder then that Burnham was looking relatively chipper as he kicked off the party conference with the traditional lengthy interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg. Only relatively chipper, because you’d need to be a halfwit not to be a little wary. These interviews can go hideously wrong – Liz Truss’s at the Tory conference in 2022 is a collector’s item – and prime ministers generally regard them as exercises in damage limitation. To survive without generating the wrong kind of headlines is the dream.

“You look like you’re loving the job,” observed Laura. Somehow biting her lip and refraining from adding that it is early days and we’ll see how much you’ve aged by this time next year. Andy smiled. He was, he said. Not because he had the job he had always coveted. But because now he had a chance to make a difference. To end the drift and division of the decade since Brexit – he could have gone back another five years and included austerity. To do politics differently. To bring back hope. You’re going to hear a lot of the H word in the next four days. It’s plastered over every wall of the conference centre.

And Burnham speaks as if he genuinely means it. He has the easy-going charm and self-confidence of a man who is comfortable in his own skin. He reaches parts that other politicians don’t get near. Nige has the same quality. Only where he speaks to people’s fears and grievance, Andy has a way of making you feel better about yourself. You may still struggle to pay your bills, you may still fight to get a hospital appointment, but somehow you can believe in better days ahead. The triumph of hope over experience.

All of which is a much in demand – if not essential – skill for a politician. One that gives you a fighting chance of success. People feel both heard and seen by him. It’s almost uncanny. Burnham talks of being a different sort of politician when the reality he is the archetypal career politician. You’d imagine he had spent years doing what he calls a real job as a hospital porter, but he’s been a politician almost all his adult life. Few understand the Westminster system better than him, he also suggests. You can’t escape the irony. Keir Starmer actually had a long and successful career outside politics, but he is the one who always sounded like the career politician. Speaking in soundbites and half-truths. You’ve either got it or you haven’t.

The message Burnham really wanted to get across on Sunday morning was that social care was the hill he would die on. Other politicians had said they would tackle the issue but had recoiled when they realised how difficult it was. “I will grasp the nettle,” he said, opening his eyes still wider, hoping that viewers would fall into them. He would create a national care system that incorporated the NHS and social care. Old people were either paying through the nose for their own care, falling through the cracks or ending up bed blocking in hospitals. It was unsustainable and undignified.

How this would be paid for would be laid out in due course. It would be what Labour would campaign on in 2029. But make no mistake, people were already paying for it. Here he was preaching to the converted. My sisters and I had to sell my mother’s house to pay for her care during the last seven years of her life as she suffered from Alzheimer’s. We didn’t mind so much, but my mother would have been gutted had she been aware. It had mattered to her that she could leave her house to the three of us. Paying a little extra in tax to make sure that other people – possibly even you – don’t have to burn through their assets seems the kind of thing any fair-minded society would do.

Burnham ended by saying he very much hoped to work cross-party on all this. It was too important not to. This aspiration lasted all of five minutes. Because that’s how long it took the ever ridiculous Chris Philp – Kuenssberg’s next guest – to start going on about a “death and dementia tax”. Like clockwork. The Philpster becomes more and more a parody of himself. The Tory party’s very own Alan B’Stard. Venal, self-serving and not very bright. A man whose answer to everything is to cut the welfare bill still further, seemingly unaware his leader has already spent the cuts her party has proposed.

It’s as if Philp regards getting dementia as a personal failing, just as he sees being on benefits as morally deficient. If you get dementia then you deserve to pay for your own care. Now is not a good time to be one of Chris’s relatives. If you find yourself in need of care, then you’re very much on your own. There’s no way the Philpster is missing out on his inheritance.

articles.title: Swiss voters reject stricter neutrality rules that would curb Nato cooperation
articles.excerpt:
70% vote against tightening centuries-old neutrality, which far right said was being eroded by sanctions against Russia

Swiss voters have decisively rejected a proposal for a strict definition of neu...
articles.body_text:
70% vote against tightening centuries-old neutrality, which far right said was being eroded by sanctions against Russia

Swiss voters have decisively rejected a proposal for a strict definition of neutrality that would have required Switzerland to curb cooperation with Nato and abandon sanctions against Russia.

All cantons and about 70% of voters rejected the proposal for a strictly defined version of neutrality to be ⁠written into the Swiss constitution, final results from the Federal Statistical Office showed. The motion had been promoted by the far-right Swiss People’s party (SVP).

Although the defeat was expected, it will be a relief across Europe, amid increasing strains in maintaining EU unity on sanctions against Russia.

Switzerland’s centuries-old neutrality was formally recognised after the end of the Napoleonic wars in 1815. Critics of current government policy claim that status has been eroded by Switzerland’s decision to mirror EU sanctions against Russia, after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Voters were asked to decide on enshrining the principle of “perpetual and armed neutrality” in the constitution and barring Switzerland from joining any military alliances or imposing sanctions on warring states, unless mandated by the United Nations.

The outcome is a heavy defeat for the SVP’s billionaire backer, Christoph Blocher, who was a prominent supporter of the initiative, reported by Bloomberg to have spent 2 million francs (€2.1m, £1.8m) on the campaign

Opponents welcomed the results. “Voters understood what the SVP wanted: it wanted Switzerland to isolate itself internationally and shirk its responsibilities when international law is being trampled on,” said Sibel Arslan, a lawmaker for the Green party.

The Swiss government, along with most political parties, opposed the measure, arguing “Switzerland would cease to be a reliable partner in international security policy” leaving the country less secure in the event of an attack and heavily restricting its ability to cooperate with Nato.

Although not a member of Nato, Switzerland has cooperated with the transatlantic military alliance for 30 years.

Analysts said the result showed Swiss people were content with how the government interpreted Swiss neutrality. “The people have spoken: they accept that neutrality is an instrument that can evolve, leaving the government with room for manoeuvre to adapt its application faced with geopolitical upheavals,” wrote Katy Romy, a correspondent for SwissInfo, the online service of the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation.

She also wrote that the yes campaign was unable to shed perceptions it was acting in Russian interests.

Russia’s foreign ministry had praised the initiative, while criticising Switzerland’s adoption of EU sanctions and claiming the country was abandoning neutrality.

The SVP accepted the defeat and said it had no current plans for further action.

articles.title: Hugh Hefner's 'most sexy' Playboy model reveals how Anna Nicole Smith changed her life
articles.excerpt:
Sandra Taylor reveals how her friendship with Anna Nicole Smith unexpectedly helped launch her Playboy career and recalls the star’s sweeter side.

Anna Nicole Smith unknowingly transformed the life o...
articles.body_text:
Sandra Taylor reveals how her friendship with Anna Nicole Smith unexpectedly helped launch her Playboy career and recalls the star’s sweeter side.

Anna Nicole Smith unknowingly transformed the life of the woman Hugh Hefner once called his "most sexy model."

Sandra Taylor, who made hearts race as a Playboy cover girl during the '90s, is now the head sommelier at Allegiant Stadium, home of the Las Vegas Raiders. But long before then, her friendship with the 1993 Playmate of the Year changed the course of her life.

Taylor recently appeared on Sports Illustrated Swimsuit model Kim Alexis' podcast, "Unexpired," where she reflected on her life and career.

LARRY BIRKHEAD CELEBRATES DAUGHTER DANNIELYNN'S 20TH BIRTHDAY WITH RARE PHOTOS

Sandra Taylor attends the "Raising Helen" Los Angeles premiere arrivals at El Capitan Theatre in Hollywood, California. (WireImage)

"I was friends with Anna Nicole Smith, and she was such a darling," Taylor recalled to Fox News Digital. "We shared two makeup artists. One was in New York, one was in LA. And they introduced us very, very early on to her coming here from Texas, and we became friends. She needed a place to stay when she first came out here."

Anna Nicole Smith in a publicity portrait for the movie "Naked Gun 33 1/3: The Final Insult," 1994. (Getty Images)

A visit to Smith on the set of "Naked Gun 33 1/3: The Final Insult" changed the course of Taylor's career. After Smith's makeup artist urged her to meet with Playboy during its 40th anniversary search, Smith encouraged her friend to go for it. The opportunity led Taylor to Playboy and launched a new chapter in her life.

WATCH: SANDRA TAYLOR REVEALS HOW ANNA NICOLE SMITH LED HER TO PLAYBOY

"It was my friendship with Anna Nicole Smith ... it led me right there," said Taylor.

Model Sandra Taylor attends the Playboy Magazine party honoring her on June 8, 1995, at Gauguin at the Plaza in New York City. (Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

"I never, in a million years growing up, thought I would ever be in Playboy," she said. "It just seemed so out of the realm of reality. I was full speed ahead to be a mathematician just like my dad. ... I studied macroeconomics, microeconomics, statistics, differential equations, and I was a dream dancer."

Actor Sandra Taylor arrives at the National Lampoon premiere of "One, Two, Many" at the Arclight Theatre on April 10, 2008, in Los Angeles. (Getty Images)

"I was only 19 years old when my dad passed away," she continued. "It was on my college campus at SUNY Purchase. He was walking with my mom, and he had a heart attack just out of the blue and passed away. And then I never went back to that campus again. Books in locker; never went back. Never looked back. I always used to joke, 'I wonder if my books are still in my locker,' because I never cleared it out. But after that, when he passed away, the math died along with him, and I just didn't want to do it anymore."

Actress Sandra Taylor appeared on "The Tonight Show with Jay Leno" on Aug. 30, 1995. (NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal via Getty Images)

After her father's sudden death, Taylor abandoned her plans to pursue math and embraced a career in modeling. Looking back, she remains grateful for her friendship with Smith, whom she credits with helping open the door to Playboy before Smith died in 2007 at 39.

"I remember how sweet she was," said Taylor. "She was really, really a sweet girl and loved her son so much. She really wanted to be a great mom. She was really a sweetheart, just a really nice girl. I don't think she could hurt a fly."

Anna Nicole Smith appears with her son Daniel on the Harald-Schmidt Show on June 24, 1997, in Germany. (Frank Hempel/United Archives via Getty Images)

For Taylor, posing for Playboy was only the beginning. She said it led to a friendship with Hefner that lasted until his death in 2017 at 91.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Sandra Taylor is seen here with Playboy founder Hugh Hefner. (Courtesy of Sandra Taylor)

"Even when you do the magazine, it doesn't end there," Taylor explained. "Hef opens up his home for years to come. ... Because I was good friends with Kimberley, his wife, I was able to fly on their jet. I was able to really experience him as a family man, and how kind he was, too. I loved his laugh. If I look back, his laugh to me was the most infectious, wonderful thing about him. And I miss him. I really think he changed the trajectory of things for me. I'm sure it closed some doors ... but I wouldn't change it for the world."

Sandra Taylor told Fox News Digital she had a lasting friendship with Hugh Hefner. (Courtesy of Sandra Taylor)

Decades later, Taylor said she learned what Hefner thought of her Playboy photos.

Sandra Taylor is seen here on the cover of the July 1995 issue of Playboy magazine. (Alamy)

"You know Traci Bingham from 'Baywatch?'" said Taylor. "She had told me when she went in to discuss doing Playboy, it was right around the time my layout was [going] to press. She goes, 'I want to do a layout just like that! Who's that?' And he was like, 'Oh, this is Sandra Taylor. She's our most sexy model we've ever had.' I go, 'Why did you wait all these years to tell me that amazing piece of trivia? I would've loved to have known years ago what Hef thought about me.'"

Traci Bingham from Seasons 7 and 8 of "Baywatch," which aired from 1989 to 2001. (Courtesy Everett Collection)

"I always knew he was so into blondes, like real blondes," said Taylor. "So to think he was a fan of my photos as well. I just thought he had to use diversity in the magazine. Brunettes, blondes ... every single walk of life you want to represent in the magazine. But I always thought he favored blondes. So, when she told me that, it was so beautiful. ... I was like, 'Traci, could you tell me that one more time?'"

Hugh Hefner and actress Tracy Bingham pose for a photo outside the Barfly on Aug. 17, 2002, in Hollywood. (Getty Images)

Becoming a sought-after model had plenty of perks for Taylor — like catching Fabio’s eye.

WATCH: SANDRA TAYLOR RECALLS DATING FABIO, POSING FOR ROMANCE COVERS

"Shooting the romance covers with Fabio was exactly what you would imagine it would be," said Taylor. "These elaborate wardrobes — the fan, the hair, everything. It was so wonderful. It was in New York. I met Fabio at this gym called the Vertical Club. He was so sweet. We dated a few times, and he was lovely. He said, 'Have you ever thought about doing a romance novel cover?' And I was like, 'No, but I would love to.'"

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Italian actor and fashion model Fabio Lanzoni poses for a portrait with Brenda Joyce's book "Scandalous Love" in New York, on Nov. 8, 1992. (Getty Images)

"I was on the yes train from the get-go," said Taylor. "I always was interested. I always had an open mind, and I always kept myself very interested in anything that came my way. ... I don't know how many romance novel covers we did together, but it was a lot. You shoot many, many in one [day]. So that was really fun. That was a great experience."

As an actress, Taylor frequently worked with director Garry Marshall. She also appeared in projects with Steven Seagal, Robert De Niro and other Hollywood stars.

From left: Victoria Silvstedt, Carmen Electra, Sandra Taylor and Miss March Tina Jordan pose together at an event, date unknown. (WireImage)

"Steven Seagal was really kind to me," said Taylor. "He was a real gentleman to me. Every time I went to audition, and it was multiple times, there were more beautiful women. The rooms were just packed with beautiful women. I just braced myself. But he was so professional. I remember I wore my lucky pink Chanel suit. The first thing he said to me was, 'Oh, my wife has a suit similar to that.' He was just so chivalrous and kind to me."

Canadian comedian and actor Dan Aykroyd with Playmate Sandra Taylor, circa 1992. (Getty Images)

"And Dan Aykroyd, I remember he was incredibly generous too. He bought me my SAG card for my first movie. Dan was like, 'I would love to pay for that for you and one day be able to say that I bought you your SAG card.' That was a beautiful surprise. He was also very kind and welcoming. I'll never forget that."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Sandra Taylor is the head sommelier for the Las Vegas Raiders. (Courtesy of Sandra Taylor.)

Taylor's life today is "a little different," she said. She lost her home of 24 years in the 2025 Palisades Fire. She continues to rebuild and has embraced a new role as a professional sommelier. She also helped create Raider Rosé.

Sandra Taylor is seen here holding a bottle of her rosé. (Courtesy of Sandra Taylor)

Today, Sandra Taylor is embracing the next chapter of her life. (Courtesy of Sandra Taylor)

"I'm proud of the life I've led," said Taylor. "I've faced ups and downs, but I've been blessed. And I'm always ready for what life throws at me."

Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: One Nation boss called David Farley an ‘asshole’ in lead-up to Farrer byelection, text messages reveal
articles.excerpt:
Exclusive: Documents seen by Guardian Australia show that Kelvin Morton has also clashed with party HQ staff and Brisbane volunteers

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

One N...
articles.body_text:
Exclusive: Documents seen by Guardian Australia show that Kelvin Morton has also clashed with party HQ staff and Brisbane volunteers

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

One Nation’s general manager, Kelvin Morton – brought in by the party to improve its vetting processes – referred to David Farley as an “asshole” just days before Farley’s historic Farrer byelection win for the party in May.

In a series of text messages seen by Guardian Australia, Morton responds to a news article published in the Sydney Morning Herald about infighting among senior party figures over Farley’s previously undeclared support for the Labor party.

“We need to do way better with our candidate selection – we need to stop finding these assholes … or letting them find us.

“I guess this might nail David’s colours to us a little more. He’s sworn allegiance in the face of all the concerns being raised – he’d look like a completely untrustworthy snake if he jumped ship after the election – he’d be ruined forever.”

A One Nation party spokesperson said that Farley was “a dedicated One Nation MP”.

“The comments made do not reflect the view of the party.

“The only untrustworthy snake is the person who leaked the text messages.”

Tensions between Farley and other One Nation MPs and staff have reportedly been high since he was elected to parliament, with the party having to publicly criticise him after he claimed One Nation’s migration policy was not dissimilar to the Labor government’s.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Morton, who claims on his LinkedIn to be a “strategic business transformation leader” with vast experience with some of the world’s biggest companies, was appointed as general manager in February.

At the time, he said the party’s national executive had wanted him to build a “professional, scalable, and legally robust organisation capable of outright victory at the next general election”. He claimed to be introducing a new vetting process and was in his position when Farley was preselected.

But while his appointment was heralded as a turning point for the professionalisation of the party, the Guardian can reveal that Morton has since clashed with staff at the party’s Brisbane headquarters and officials at one of the party’s most active branches.

He was recently appointed to the One Nation national executive, replacing former treasurer Alex Jones.

Documents seen by the Guardian show he wrote to the Lilley branch in Brisbane advising it of federal intervention, which included removing the entire committee of volunteers. This came after a dispute about access to promotional materials and a local fundraiser that raised $12,000 for the party.

The dispute arose after Morton and the Lilley branch coordinator, Mark McGuire, clashed over access to promotional materials for a different event, which prompted Morton to suspend him.

“Your membership will continue to remain suspended until a formal written apology is received by you,” Morton said, accusing him of removing promotional materials from head office and clashing with a staff member.

McGuire told the Guardian he had accessed policy flyers to take to an event being run by the party’s Brisbane branch.

Other volunteer branch members and the president, Deb Dalton, complained about McGuire’s treatment, advising head office that the branch committee would cease volunteering in protest.

The letter from Morton sent in response stated that he accepted the board’s “resignation”, despite the branch members only advising they would cease volunteering.

“The Federal Executive is now intervening in the management of the Lilley branch as its functioning and compliance are in question,” he writes.

“All branch decisions and actions are now subject to direct review and management by the Federal Executive, which reserves the right to overturn any local decision which is not in the best interest of the Party.”

Morton also accused the branch of not handing over $12,000 raised at a branch fundraising dinner last year and demanded it be transferred to party headquarters where it would be controlled by the party’s national executive.

“You are reminded that … branches are strictly prohibited from maintaining independent bank accounts,” Morton said in a letter to the branch president.

“All branch funds – including the $12,000 referred to by Mark McGuire in his phone call to me – must be managed centrally.”

He said he would revoke the membership of all branch committee members, and that “ongoing membership is contingent upon the full and transparent return of all party property, financial records, and the $12,000 in raised funds”.

McGuire told the Guardian that he believed the party’s volunteers had been treated unfairly and the $12,000 had already been paid automatically to central office when people bought tickets.

“They were treated with no procedural fairness and total disrespect,” McGuire said. “They all put their own time in, they make a sacrifice for their own family.

“The fact is that he’s got it wrong, the question is, where’s the 12 grand? Who’s had their sticky fingers in the pie? He needs to stand up and be accountable to show the whole of the branch where the 12 grand is.”

A One Nation spokesperson said the party “does not provide comment on internal disciplinary actions”.

“All branch donations are managed through a microsite that tags funds with the corresponding branch. Branch funds are quarantined for localised campaigns.”

articles.title: British celebrities beat AI companies lobbying to get free use of their work. They have a warning for Australia
articles.excerpt:
‘People care about the songs, books and pictures that influence the critical moments in their lives,’ says the architect of the fightback in the UK

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news...
articles.body_text:
‘People care about the songs, books and pictures that influence the critical moments in their lives,’ says the architect of the fightback in the UK

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

If you want to state the case against copyright reform in Australia, get Kylie Minogue’s phone number.

If there is one lesson to be learned from a similar battle in the UK, high-profile members of the creative industries make a difference. They get your argument on the front of newspapers, in the news bulletins and on social media.

In the face of this onslaught, the UK government backtracked on plans to let AI firms use copyright-protected work without permission.

The many artists who put their name to various letters and protests against the reforms to create a virtual red carpet, included: Sir Elton John, Sir Paul McCartney, Abba’s Björn Ulvaeus, the actor Julianne Moore and the Radiohead singer Thom Yorke.

John had one of the most memorable soundbites, calling the government “absolute losers” who were on course to “rob young people of their legacy and their income”.

Overall, the campaign was more sophisticated than just rounding up irritated celebrities. Beeban Kidron, a member of the upper house of the UK parliament and an award-winning film director, marshalled an effective political campaign against the proposals by pushing legislative amendments that would have spiked the plans. She also helped organise celebrity opposition.

Kidron says the campaign struck a chord with the public.

“People care about the songs, books and pictures that influence the critical moments in their lives,” she says.

Polling backed this up, with seven out of 10 adults in the UK supporting the payment of royalties to copyright holders whose work had been used to train AI models.

The Australian prime minister should take heed, Kidron says.

“Albanese has been a leader in standing up to tech. He should not squander his reputation by selling Australian creatives down the river.”

The campaign against copyright reform also benefited from the ingenuity of an industry that knows how to grab people’s attention. One of the most prominent figures in the movement against the proposals, Ed Newton-Rex, organised a “silent” album and an “empty” book, to warn of the consequences of watering down copyright law.

“There is no one out there, who does not work for an AI company, who thinks AI companies should not pay for the content they use,” he says. “What we did in the UK was make the government understand that was the case.”

Newton-Rex, a composer and former AI executive, put together an album featuring recordings of dormant music studios and performance spaces, called Is This What We Want? It was backed by more than 1,000 musicians, including Damon Albarn, Kate Bush and Annie Lennox.

The author stunt, called Don’t Steal This Book, involved 10,000 writers listing their names in an otherwise empty paperback. Contributors included Kazuo Ishiguro, Philippa Gregory and Richard Osman.

“The only way the government gets something like this copyright proposal through is if no one notices what they are doing. It will take just a moment for people to understand this is not fair,” says Newton-Rex.

Albanese’s government needs to be wary of committing the same mistake as its centre-left UK counterpart, says Pierre Andrews, a former adviser on culture policy under Rishi Sunak’s Conservative government in 2023-2024.
 “The [UK] Labour government’s mistake was that it thought it could convince the creative industries to go along with it,” he says.
 Instead, the nation’s assembled artists and authors recoiled at a perceived betrayal by a party they thought would be on their side.
 “There was a strong sense of surprise within the creative community that Labour would even consider changing copyright to their detriment,” he says, adding that he foresees another government U-turn, but in Australia this time.

The tech industry still believes in the win-win argument; that the UK could get behind a policy where domestic AI companies are able to train models on British shores using copyright-protected content, while the holders receive adequate compensation for their work.

“The government recognised that it didn’t frame the initial consultation very well,” says Antony Walker, deputy chief executive of trade association techUK. “But I also think rights holders were extremely effective at shouting down the debate. It was a one-sided argument.”

In March the then UK technology secretary, Liz Kendall said the key proposal to let tech companies train on copyright protected material unless artists “opt out” of the process beforehand was no longer the government’s preferred option. The new prime minister, Smiths-loving Andy Burnham, has yet to set out a new policy on copyright but would face a battle-hardened opposition if he took the unlikely step of taking on the creatives again.

articles.title: RBA expected to hike cash rate to 4.6%, its highest level since 2011
articles.excerpt:
Outcome of meetings of Reserve Bank on Monday and Tuesday will affect Australian mortgage rates, household budgets and house prices

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Austra...
articles.body_text:
Outcome of meetings of Reserve Bank on Monday and Tuesday will affect Australian mortgage rates, household budgets and house prices

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australia’s key interest rate is expected to hit its highest level since 2011, drag down house prices and add more than $100 to typical monthly mortgage repayments.

The Reserve Bank board is poised to hike the cash rate from 4.35% to 4.6% on Tuesday, which would be the fourth increase in 2026 and push typical home loan interest rates to 6.5%.

For someone with an average-sized new mortgage of $731,000, now paying a rate of 6.2%, an increase would add about $119 to their $4,477 monthly repayments. That would take the total rise in repayments since January to nearly $480.

The share of borrowers behind on their home loan repayments is small but rising, S&P data analysed by Westpac shows.

Household budgets have also been strained by rising petrol prices amid the US war on Iran, now 80c higher since the start of the year, adding $44 to the cost of filling up a vehicle with a 55-litre tank.

Consumer spending is already slowing, with Commonwealth Bank data showing households cut back on purchases of education, motor vehicles and household goods in August.

House prices would fall further after a fourth rate rise. Comparison website Canstar estimated a hike would cut $11,200 from the borrowing capacity of someone earning an average annual full-time wage of $108,650, taking the total lost borrowing power to $47,400.

Shrinking borrowing capacities have locked buyers out of markets. Three rate rises and the Albanese government’s investor tax reforms have seen home loan inquiries slump from nearly 15,000 a week at the start of 2026 to just over 12,000 in August and September, Equifax data shows.

Home prices around Australia have fallen more than 4% from their peak earlier this year, Cotality data shows.

On Friday, the bank predicted prices would fall 7.3% by mid-2027, then begin rising again if the RBA prepared to cut rates.

Westpac has predicted falls of 10% in Sydney and 8% in Melbourne, suggesting new buyers in some areas may find housing more affordable even after accounting for higher interest rates.

But most capital cities are not expected to see significant price drops, meaning housing affordability would not improve after accounting for higher interest rates and repayments.

When the cash rate last rose above 4.35% in 2010, inflation was 3%, housing markets were buoyant and the mining boom was boosting household incomes. Rates stayed above that level until the end of 2011.

Nearly 15 years later, the RBA is poised to return interest rates to the same level despite a weak economy and slumping house prices because inflation has persisted above the target range of 3%.

Senior RBA staff in recent weeks have highlighted the risk households could be starting to expect high inflation will endure beyond the disruptions to oil prices from the conflict in the Middle East.

Shane Oliver, AMP’s chief economist, said on Saturday the central bank was at risk of losing financial markets’ confidence if it did not raise rates again.

“After more than five years of inflation being above target, threatening RBA credibility, it does not have the luxury of continuing to wait and assess,” Oliver said.

Financial markets expect an additional cash rate rise early next year.

Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Justin Cooper was eight years old when he began experiencing the not-so-friendly side of fame.

Cooper, who starred as Jim Carrey's son in the 1997 comedy "Liar Liar," revealed one dark side of the business during an appearance on the "Not So Little Rascals" podcast.

The "Brother's Keeper" actor told co-hosts Jordan Warkol and Blake Collins that his mother did a "really good job" of protecting him from the outside world while growing up in front of the cameras, but that there were still scary moments associated with fame.

'GROWING PAINS' CHILD STAR ASHLEY JOHNSON REVEALS 'DARK' MOMENT ARMED FAN TRIED TO ABDUCT HER FROM SET

Justin Cooper worked alongside Jim Carrey in the '97 film "Liar Liar." (Everett Collection)

"She would tell me later on about, like, prison mail that I would get that she never showed me," Cooper said before explaining that he would receive "letters from people in jail."

'BOYHOOD' CHILD ACTOR LIVES 'IN THE MIDDLE OF NOWHERE' AFTER LEAVING HOLLYWOOD BEHIND

"Dudes in jail talking about how they're such a big fan of me ... and you're such a cute kid," he remembered.

Cooper praised his mother for protecting him during a pivotal time in his career, and noted that she "never, ever left me alone with anybody on set."

Carrey portrayed a pathological liar-lawyer who couldn't tell a lie for 24 hours in the comedy "Liar Liar." (Universal City Studios)

"You know, there's a lot of acting parents that you hear of back in the day that are just like, 'OK, ya, go. Do whatever they tell you to do. Bye!' and my mom was not like that," he said. "Almost to a fault."

"I remember a story that just blew my mind. So Don Rickles played Mr. Wilson in 'Dennis the Menace Strikes Again,' and he's known for being a, you know, foul-mouthed comic," Cooper recalled.

"She went up to him and, is like, 'I don't want you to use any language like that in front of my kid.'"

During the peak of his fame, Cooper appeared on "The Tonight Show with Jay Leno" alongside Melissa Joan Hart. (Margaret Norton)

After years in the business, Cooper stepped away from the spotlight when auditions started to feel like work.

"You've got to sit in the car for 45, 50 minutes to get out there, and then I've got to do this, and then I gotta go home and start my homework, and I want to just go home right now and talk to girls on AIM," he said.

"After a while of me kind of just being like, I got another audition, my mom was like, 'Look, if you don't want to do it anymore, you don't have to.'"

Cooper feared his mother may have been disappointed by his decision to step away from the business due to her close connection to his career.

Justin Cooper starred in a string of '90s hits, including "Dennis the Menace Strikes Again!" with Carly Schroeder. (Ron Galella)

"My relationship with my mom was great for most of the time," he said. "In high school it got a little strange ... I stopped acting, I started smoking weed."

He remembered how she found his "stash" and admitted "that put a little strain" on their relationship for a while.

"Throughout my whole acting phase, she was always there ... taking me on auditions, all the stuff, helping me, running lines," Cooper said.

articles.body_text:
Former PGA Tour star Hunter Mahan talks about getting into posting golf content online and eyeing a return to professional golf.

There is a very real chance that the International team wins the Presidents Cup for just the second time in the biennial event's history on Sunday, but one of the team's most important players likely won't be around to witness the finish.

Tom Kim, who has earned three of a possible four points at Medinah this week, is slated to compete in the Asian Games at Kasugi Country Club in Japan beginning on Wednesday. While a Presidents Cup victory would be quite meaningful for Kim, a top finish in the Asian Games would undoubtedly trump it.

If Kim were to win a gold medal in the men's individual or team competition in Japan, he would be excused from his mandatory military service in South Korea.

Tom Kim of South Korea and the International Team plays his shot from the fifth tee during Saturday's Foursome matches on day three of the Presidents Cup 2026 at Medinah Country Club on September 26, 2026 in Medinah, Illinois. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images) (Luke Hales/Getty Images)

SCOTTIE SCHEFFLER SQUASHES 'VERY MUCH UNTRUE' NARRATIVES ABOUT AMERICANS AHEAD OF PRESIDENTS CUP

According to the Associated Press, Kim is set to fly to Japan late Sunday afternoon, with the Asian Games beginning Wednesday. He will be taking on Wyndham Clark in the second match of the day during Sunday's singles matches.

Under South Korean law, most able-bodied men must perform 18 to 21 months of military service. Special exemptions, however, are granted for both athletes and classical artists who excel in international competitions.

Athletes can receive exemptions by earning any medal at the Olympics or a gold medal at the Asian Games.

Tom Kim of the International Team reacts to a made putt on the 12th hole green during Day Three of the Presidents Cup at Medinah Country Club Course No. 3 on September 26, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by James Gilbert/PGA TOUR via Getty Images) (James Gilbert/PGA TOUR via Getty Images)

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Kim, who was born in Seoul, South Korea, came close to earning a bronze medal at the 2024 Olympics in Paris after shooting a final-round 68, missing out on third place in the individual competition by four shots. American Scottie Scheffler earned the gold medal in Paris.

Sungjae Im and Si Woo Kim, both competing on the International team this week, won a gold medal for South Korea in the team competition during the 2023 Asian Games.

Tom Kim will be joined by Do-yeob Moon and S.H. Kim on the South Korean team for this year's Asian Games.
