articles.title: Australian backlash to datacentres is faux import from US, officials say: ‘We are not the United States’
articles.excerpt:
Pro-datacentre officials argue scale of Australia’s buildout is smaller, more regulated and less damaging than in US

Australian politicians and business leaders are arguing that their populace’s grow...
articles.body_text:
Pro-datacentre officials argue scale of Australia’s buildout is smaller, more regulated and less damaging than in US

Australian politicians and business leaders are arguing that their populace’s growing resentment of AI datacentres is an inauthentic import from the United States.

Like the US, Australia is seeing community resentment grow in response to a surge in the construction of massive AI datacentres. However, pro-datacentre officials and executives argue the scale of Australia’s buildout is smaller, more regulated and therefore less damaging than that in the US. They say the burgeoning negative reaction is being tainted and inflamed by a heated US debate that has arrived down under via social media feeds.

When the backlash began in earnest in the United States last year, it echoed slowly in Australia. In 2026, though, it has exploded into national conversation across the country, leading to calls for a national moratorium, community protests, three government inquiries, state frameworks being developed and the Australian government moving to set the rules for how the datacentres can be built, and how they consume energy and water.

Australian state governments, desperate for economic growth, have been broadly welcoming of the investment for the new centres, in some cases overriding local council approval processes, given the size of the projects being developed.

In July, Victoria’s then-minister for economic growth, Steve Dimopoulos, boasted that his state was second only to New South Wales in terms of datacentres, and was outstripping Australia’s most populous state in growth for new centres. He expressed concern that the growing resentment toward new developments was a result of US social media influence.

“We’re seeing some US states move to ban new large datacentres. And those campaigns and mega-developments in the US shape public opinion in Australia,” he said. “Because when it’s on your phone, you think it’s right here, or you think it might just come here.”

The minister declared: “We are not the United States. Our planning, energy and water systems are much more carefully monitored, managed and regulated.”

Leaders in the datacentre sector have also complained about the backlash, calling it misleading and disingenuous.

“Australia’s datacentre debate is being fought on America’s facts,” Belinda Dennett, the head of the peak lobby group for the sector, Data Centres Australia, declared in a speech in March.

Dennett said reactions to datacentres from everyday people range from curiosity to confusion and fear, and the news around the sector was “alarming”.

“The industry is depicted as energy vampires, water hogs and job killers,” she said. “The problem is that most of those headlines originate in the United States, where the industry is operating at a completely different scale, under completely different market rules. They are being transplanted wholesale into Australian debates as though the contexts were interchangeable.”

Dennett said the US has 5,400 datacentres, with 53.7 gigawatts of total capacity, compared with 252 in Australia with 1.4 gigawatts of capacity. Measurements of the number of US datacentres vary.

“When people read about datacentres straining the grid, driving up bills and consuming vast amounts of water, they are reading about America’s challenges, applied uncritically to an Australian market that bears almost no resemblance to it,” she said.

What Dennett omitted was that Australia, with a population of 28 million, has just under one datacentre per 100,000 people, compared with 1.5 per 100,000 people in the US, population 342.7 million.

The pace of datacentre construction is increasing rapidly in Australia, with several large datacentres with 1 gigawatts or more capacity in the planning.

Trending videos on TikTok and Instagram highlight major local community concerns including a 2.4 gigawatt centre planned for outer Melbourne, and a 2 gigawatt gas-powered centre in the Northern Territory.

That is the equivalent of 2m households’ annual electricity consumption, said Rob Nicholls, professor and senior research associate in digital policy at the University of Sydney. The NT’s population is just over 265,000.

The Australian government – seeing the US gas boom fueled by datacentres’ demand for power – has planned to override states and ban gas being used to power centres. New rules would require datacentres’ operators to bring as much new renewable energy into the system as the centre would otherwise take.

Some experts find the backlash justified in following the US example.

“The social media input from the US is very vocal and rationally based: ‘It’s going to increase the cost of electricity and it’s going to increase the cost of water and I don’t get a benefit from it.’ And that’s a rational position,” said Nicholls.

Nicholls said the hurdle facing the Australian government is explaining to its constituents how the issues faced in the United States differ from local ones.

Legislation for the framework is unlikely to arrive until next year, and has led to calls for Australia to follow the lead of New York and implement a moratorium on new development until proper rules are in place.

Until then, there are now two state inquiries and one federal inquiry into the sector, along with the steady stream of new development applications leading to pushback from locals.

Many of Australia’s datacentres are US-owned. The federal assistant minister for technology, Andrew Charlton, said that Australians may be cynical about datacentres in their communities because many of the companies that operate the facilities are not Australian. Microsoft and Amazon operate several, and OpenAI and Anthropic are eyeing their own developments.

“Simply building datacentres in Australia does not necessarily mean that Australia captures the economics of AI,” he said in a speech this week. “We can supply the land, we can supply the electricity, we can host the machines, and still find that much of the value – and many of the economic rents – flow offshore.”

Charlton called for datacentre providers who want to build in Australia to enable access to compute for Australian start-ups, researchers and not-for-profits, on favourable terms, and flagged that Australia could build its own local AI capability based on open-weight models.

“We risk becoming dependent on imported intelligence itself,” Charlton said.

articles.title: Trump says he is rolling back Biden-era US fuel economy rules for cars
articles.excerpt: United States President Donald Trump has announced new fuel economy standards that roll back requirements adopted under his predecessor, arguing they will lower automobile prices and encourage manufac...
articles.body_text:
United States President Donald Trump has announced new fuel economy standards that roll back requirements adopted under his predecessor, arguing they will lower automobile prices and encourage manufacturers to expand production in the US.

In a social media post on Saturday, Trump said the new standards would “TERMINATE” what he called former US President Joe Biden’s “EV (electric vehicle) mandate”, accusing the previous administration of imposing costly requirements on carmakers and steering consumers towards electric vehicles.

“These new Standards will take the waste out of building cars in America. That means LOWER PRICES, saving families thousands on a new, beautiful, and safe car,” Trump wrote.

The changes form part of a broader Trump administration effort to reverse Biden-era policies supporting lower-emission vehicles, increasing the gap between US policy and global trends favouring electric vehicles.

While Trump and US Republicans have used the term “EV mandate” to describe higher fuel efficiency requirements instituted under Biden, a Democrat, there are no federal guidelines or laws that require Americans to buy electric cars or bar the sale of ones powered by petrol.

At the centre are Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards. This system, established by the US Congress in 1975, requires automakers to meet average fuel economy targets across all cars and light trucks they sell, meaning that a brand that sells an inefficient vehicle would also have to sell a more efficient one to help comply with the government’s standards.

Under rules finalised by the Biden administration in 2024, the required fleetwide fuel economy was scheduled to rise from 39.1 miles per gallon (mpg) to about 50.4mpg by 2031. The administration said then the measures would reduce fuel consumption and emissions to combat climate change while helping motorists save money at the pump.

As a result, auto manufacturers have ramped up production of EVs to help meet the Biden-imposed fuel economy requirements. The Republican-controlled US Congress, however, gutted consumer tax incentives last year for electric vehicles as part of Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

Trump did not provide details regarding what the new fuel economy standards would be. But in December 2025, he announced a proposal that would set the industry fleetwide average for light-duty vehicles at roughly 34.5mpg by 2031, more than 30 percent lower than the Biden-era rule.

In a reposting of Trump’s announcement, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said an announcement would be “COMING MONDAY”.

Al Jazeera has reached out to the White House for comment.

A Costco membership is best known for bulk grocer...
articles.body_text:
‘Outnumbered’ reacts to reports that Costco is becoming an unexpected dating hotspot as singles look to make face-to-face connections while shopping.

A Costco membership is best known for bulk groceries, the $1.50 hot dog combo and towering packs of paper goods, but some of the biggest savings can happen well beyond the winding checkout lines.

From travel and gas to gift cards, optical services and warranty coverage, Costco members can access a range of discounts and services, according to the company’s website and news reports.

Here are five lesser-known ways shoppers can stretch their Costco membership outside of the warehouse aisles.

WEALTHY AMERICANS CHOOSE ONE GROCERY STORE CHAIN OVER RIVALS, SURVEY FINDS

Costco members can check local gas prices and station hours through the retailer’s app. (Zak Bennett/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Buying Costco gas can help households offset the annual membership free, according to Money Talks News. It often costs less than competitors, though the actual savings vary by location and driving habits, according to the outlet.

An additional perk is that Costco members can check local gas prices and station hours through the Costco app before heading to the pump.

And another secret at the pump is that the warehouse’s long hoses also allow drivers to fuel up from either side of their vehicle. "Whether your gas tank is on the left or right side of your car, you can choose the shortest line," Costco's website reads.

COSTCO FOOD COURT ITEM PACKS MORE PROTEIN THAN ANYTHING ELSE ON THE MENU, BUT THERE'S A CATCH

Costco’s Executive membership costs more than a Gold Star membership but includes a 2% annual reward on qualifying purchases. (Tim Boyle/Getty Images)

Upgrading from Costco's annual $65 membership to the $130 Executive membership includes an annual 2% reward — up to $1,250 — on certain purchases.

Since the upgrade costs $65 more than a Gold Star membership, shoppers would need about $3,250 in qualifying annual spending to cover the added upgrade cost.

COSTCO BRINGS BACK A FAN-FAVORITE FOOD COURT TREAT AFTER YEARS OFF THE MENU

Executive members also receive earlier warehouse access, beginning at 9 a.m. at many locations, plus additional discounts on select Costco Services.

Costco Travel offers members access to vacation packages, cruises, hotels and rental cars. (Lindsey Nicholson/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

Costco Travel lets members book vacation packages, cruises, hotels and rental cars through Costco. Executive members can also earn their 2% annual reward on qualifying travel purchases, though the reward is credited after the trip is completed.

One member who booked a Costa Rica trip reported getting a $200 Shop Card after returning, paying for more than three years of membership, Money Talk News Reported.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Costco sells gift cards for a variety of activities, from theme park tickets to city exploration passes, according to its website, for a discounted price.

Discounted gift cards and tire services are among the additional benefits available to Costco members. (Getty Images)

"Costco offers deals like two $50 gift cards for $79.99 or four $15 gift cards for $44.99," Linda Chavez, founder and CEO of Seniors Life Insurance Finder, told Real Simple. "These offers make stocking up on gift cards for Christmas or birthdays a breeze," she added. "Gift cards for movie theaters, theme parks, performances, activities and more are also available."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Costco shoppers who buy tires through its tire center receive free rotation, balancing, pressure checks and flat repairs for the life of those tires, according to Money Talks News.

Costco memberships can offer savings that extend beyond bulk grocery purchases. (Lindsey Nicholson/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

Those services can add up over time, though shoppers should compare tire prices and available services locally before buying, the website noted.

Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Arch Manning does interview with Holly Rowe after controversy over AI slapping video comment

Craig breaks down why Arch Manning shouldn't have to apologize for laughimg at the Holly Rowe/Steve Sarkisian AI video

Texas quarterback Arch Manning did a postgame interview with ESPN reporter Holly...
articles.body_text:
Craig breaks down why Arch Manning shouldn't have to apologize for laughimg at the Holly Rowe/Steve Sarkisian AI video

Texas quarterback Arch Manning did a postgame interview with ESPN reporter Holly Rowe on Saturday, less than two weeks after apologizing for calling an AI-generated video that depicted her being slapped "hilarious."

Rowe interviewed Manning on the field after No. 1 Texas survived a late comeback attempt by No. 14 Tennessee to earn a 20-17 victory at Neyland Stadium.

"I know this was a hard-fought win. This was dramatic down the stretch, but that long drive, you guys punch it in, you go over, and you're hyping up your offensive line. How huge was that moment for you guys in this game?" Rowe asked.

NO. 1 TEXAS ESCAPES TENNESSEE WITH THRILLING SEC VICTORY AS PRESIDENT TRUMP WATCHES ON FROM NEYLAND STADIUM

ABC sideline reporter Holly Rowe prior to the game against the Tennessee Volunteers and the Arkansas Razorbacks at Donald W. Reynolds Razorback Stadium on Oct. 5, 2024. (Nelson Chenault/Imagn Images)

"It was fun," Manning said. "I thought they battled the whole time. Shout out to our defense. Colin Simmons, that's a real player right there."

Rowe then asked Manning about the significance of winning at the stadium where his uncle, Peyton Manning, became a college football legend.

"He was terrific today. Your whole team was," Rowe said. "But I know a lot of people think this is a special day for your family. You made your own history out on this field today. What was that like for you, Arch?"

"It's not about me," Manning responded. "I didn't play very well, but our team played great. Defense played well. SEC road win, that's what it's all about."

Manning completed 14 of 19 passes for 201 yards and an interception. He was sacked six times as Texas finished with just 262 total yards and committed 11 penalties for 115 yards. The Longhorns’ defense recorded 10 sacks, including a program record-tying five by Simmons.

Rowe closed by asking Manning about the encouragement he offered Tennessee quarterback Faizon Brandon after the game.

TEXAS' STEVE SARKISAN'S FIRST INTERVIEW WITH HOLLY ROWE GOES OFF WITHOUT A HITCH AFTER VIRAL POSTGAME INCIDENT

"I just said keep going," Manning said. "He's a great player. I wish him all the best."

"Thank you. Appreciate it," Manning responded.

The interview garnered mixed reactions on social media, with some praising the cordial nature of it despite the context, while others shared concerns that Manning's personality appears depleted after the controversy and subsequent apology.

ARCH MANNING ISSUES APOLOGY AFTER FACING HEAT FOR LAUGHING AT AI VIDEO OF STEVE SARKISIAN SLAPPING HOLLY ROWE

The exchange attracted additional attention because of the controversy that followed Texas’ dramatic 24-23 comeback win over Ohio State on Sept. 12.

After that game, Longhorns coach Steve Sarkisian interrupted Rowe’s opening question, shouted, "Texas fight" and "Hook ’em," and walked away from the interview. An altered video subsequently circulated on social media that falsely showed Sarkisian slapping Rowe.

When Manning was asked about social media edits during a press conference two days later, he brought up the fabricated clip.

"I saw an AI edit of Sark’s interview," Manning said. "Y’all seen that one? That’s a good one. Of him slapping Holly Rowe. It’s hilarious."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Manning apologized the following day, acknowledging that there was "nothing funny about it" and that his comment had been hurtful.

"I specifically want to apologize to Holly Rowe for what she has personally had to deal with because of my comments," Manning wrote. "I have a ton of respect for her and appreciate her showing me grace in this moment. I need to do better and will be more thoughtful going forward."

Rowe publicly accepted the apology and revealed that she and Manning had spoken privately.

"Thank you Arch," Rowe wrote. "I appreciate our conversation about this — which will remain private. Apology accepted. We move forward with respect and kindness for one another."

Saturday’s interview appeared to reflect that sentiment, with Rowe praising Manning and the quarterback thanking her before they parted ways.

articles.title: Arch Manning revels in cigar smoke: Texas leaves Neyland with win—and a warning for college football
articles.excerpt: Tennessee Volunteers fans told OutKick's Trey Wallace they're excited for President Donald Trump to attend a key SEC matchup against the Texas Longhorns on Saturday, and they left with their final sco...
articles.body_text:
Tennessee Volunteers fans told OutKick's Trey Wallace they're excited for President Donald Trump to attend a key SEC matchup against the Texas Longhorns on Saturday, and they left with their final score predictions.

KNOXVILLE, TN - Cigar smoke was coming from the Texas locker room following their win over Tennessee on Saturday afternoon that came down to the final play.

The only offense that we really got on a consistent basis Saturday between Tennessee and Texas came when the Secret Service was clearing an area for President Trump to walk through while the national anthem was being played.

A slugfest of wacky proportions played out inside Neyland Stadium, with Arch Manning doing just enough to get his Longhorns out of Knoxville with the win.

SEC CROWD GREETS TRUMP WITH MASSIVE CHEERS AHEAD OF TENNESSEE-TEXAS SHOWDOWN

The entire morning was filled with anticipation, as the President would finally make his way from the airport to Tennessee's campus for what would turn out to be a first half appearance.

But, it was the Texas defense that showed up for the party with a reckoning on its mind, finishing with ten total sacks, which Steve Sarkisian said led to eight Tennessee players being helped out of the field in what turned out to be another physical SEC game.

TENNESSEE FANS EXCITED FOR TRUMP'S ATTENDANCE AT GAME VS TEXAS: 'I HOPE HE STAYS THE WHOLE GAME'

Texas QB Arch Manning talks about the Longhorns win over Tennessee (Via: Trey Wallace. OutKick)

The Longhorns have the two-best wins in college football this season, after defeating Ohio State just fourteen days ago.

Steve Sarkisian, will not apologize for how his team wins, nor should he.

"For us, we’ve got more of these to go..We have 7 ranked opponents we have still yet to play..That's why I’m not gonna apologize for how we beat a top-15 team on the road, when others don’t even play them," Sarkisian said postgame.

Head Coach Steve Sarkisian of the Texas Longhorns looks on during the first half against the Tennessee Volunteers at Neyland Stadium in Knoxville, Tenn., on Sept. 26, 2026. (Getty Images)

We wondered how the Longhorns would react to a hostile environment, with over 100,000 fans starting to enter the gates in hopes of taking advantage of alcoholic beverages that were 50% off , thanks to the Tennessee athletic department enticing fans to enter the stadium before traffic got out of hand due to Trump's arrival.

That answer was provided on the defensive side of the ball for Texas throughout the entire game, as Tennessee quarterback Faizon Brandon scrambled for his life on what felt like every other play for the Vols.

DONALD TRUMP ADDS POLITICAL STAKES, ANTICIPATION AND POTENTIAL SIDELINE CHAOS TO TEXAS-TENNESSEE SHOWDOWN

Heck, Texas' Colin Simmons had five sacks on the day, making life extremely difficult for the Vols freshman QB.

If you were under the impression that this Steve Sarkisian led football team wasn’t prepared for their first road trip of the season, you were sorely mistaken. There were some that wrote about how this physical test on the road would be to their detriment.

NO. 1 TEXAS ESCAPES TENNESSEE WITH THRILLING SEC VICTORY AS PRESIDENT TRUMP WATCHES ON FROM NEYLAND STADIUM

I guess they aren't watching the same Texas team. This group continues to find ways to win, in the most difficult era of college football. Whether it was on the final play of the game, or holding off an offense on the last series, the Longhorns have figured it out early this season.

Sure, he might have only thrown for 127 yards in the first half, taking a 10-3 lead into halftime. But, that didn’t stop him from finding pockets of success in the second half, which kept his team ahead when the final whistle blew.

And yes, Manning only finished the game with 201 yards passing with zero touchdowns, but he put Texas in a position to win once again.

Whether it was Cam Coleman or Ryan Wingo, Tennessee did not seem to have an answer for the talented pair on a consistent basis, which came back to bite the Vols during the second half.

Seven total sacks for the Texas defense also kept the Vols offense in check for a majority of the game.

This was the first road test, and they passed. At the end of the day, when Texas boards the plane home for Austin, that's all that matters for this team.

We can talk about some of the sloppy offensive line play, or the weird unsportsmanlike penalty on Colin Simmons, but that's just noise right now.

What we witnessed on Saturday afternoon was two teams who are still working out the glitches. The problem for Tennessee is that they do not have a veteran starter, while Arch Manning is finding different ways to get his squad into the end zone.

KNOXVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 26: Arch Manning #16 of the Texas Longhorns carries the ball during a game between the Tennessee Volunteers and the Texas Longhorns at Neyland Stadium on September 26, 2026 in Knoxville, Tennessee. (Photo by Roger Wimmer/ISI Photos/ISI Photos via Getty Images) ( )

All the while, Texas once again proved they might be the best overall team in college football in one of the hardest places to play in this sport.

As the equipment staff began loading the truck for its ride back to Texas, you can hear the noise coming from inside the Longhorns locker room.

"We're the real UT, so they can stop talking," one player said aloud.

On Saturday afternoon in Knoxville, this Texas team once again proved it could find another way to win.

But, in the end, it still came down to their defense. Just as it did against Ohio State.

You don't rack up 12 sacks on an SEC opponent without having a stellar group on that side of the ball. Maybe we should be talking more about the unit who has provided four wins on the season, with two against Top-15 teams.

It's easy to get lost in Arch. We might wanna get used to this defense.

Trey Wallace is the Sr. College Sports Reporter for OutKick.

The mother of a woman found hanging in a tree in Mississippi has...
articles.body_text:
Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old mother of four, was found hanging from a tree in August

Warning: This story contains distressing details

The mother of a woman found hanging in a tree in Mississippi has spoken of her shock after authorities said they believed her daughter was dead before her body was placed at the allegedly "staged" crime scene.

Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old mother of four, was found hanging from a tree at an abandoned home in Jackson in August.

The discovery sparked widespread fears in the majority-black city because of the state's deep history of racial violence and lynchings. But on Friday, police said that Fortune had been dead before her body was hanged from the tree.

"I have more questions now than what I did before," her mother Christy Spivey told the BBC.

The Jackson Police Department said that the medical examiner who conducted Fortune's post-mortem examination had determined that her death was a homicide and that "the scene and the hanging were staged".

Officials have not disclosed the exact cause of death or shared any potential motive behind the allegedly staged hanging.

Three people have been arrested in the case, all of whom are black.

"I was hoping to be more relieved," Spivey said, adding that the police had not specified how the three suspects were connected to her daughter - or why her death was allegedly staged in this way.

"Still no cause of death, no date of death - nothing," she said. "What actually killed her?"

Fortune's death left the local community on edge and lawmakers demanding federal probes. But the latest developments have created more confusion.

Christy Spivey told the BBC she was upset at how the police had handled the investigation

Spivey told the BBC that getting the update from the coroner that her daughter did not die by hanging initially gave her peace - at least her daughter did not die in such a gruesome manner, she thought.

"When the police called me, I started crying and thanked them and felt a little more at peace than I had before," she said. "I just hope they've got the right person/people."

When the latest details surrounding her death emerged this week, she said she was "starting to break down".

Police told a court on Friday that Fortune's death was thought to be as a result of a drug-related dispute. A detective said Fortune may have been killed over allegations she stole drugs.

Spivey rejected those allegations, but did acknowledge her daughter suffered from addiction.

"Tasia has an addiction - had - an addiction problem. She was trying to get better," Spivey said.

"If she still was doing drugs, which I'm sure she probably was, she still didn't deserve to be done like that. Nobody does."

She said her daughter was homeless at the time of her death, but typically bounced around other people's homes.

Her four sons, whose ages range from one to seven, are now living with a mix of family and friends. Two are in the process of being adopted.

Vi...
articles.body_text:
World champions Spain came from behind to beat England 3-2 in an entertaining Nations League encounter at Wembley on Saturday, denying the hosts a cathartic win after their painful World Cup exit.

Victory for Luis de la Fuente’s men extends Spain’s astonishing unbeaten run to 39 matches – a record for a European team.

Thomas Tuchel’s men got off to a nightmare start when Lamine Yamal pounced on a gaffe by defender Marc Guehi, and they could easily have been three goals down as silky Spain created multiple chances.

But England, criticised for their ultra-defensive tactics in their World Cup semifinal defeat to Argentina, showed adventure of their own and got their reward in the 36th minute when Barcelona winger Anthony Gordon finished a fine team move.

Four minutes later, the home side were ahead after Kane headed home Nico O’Reilly’s cross via a Marc Cucurella deflection.

Kane had a golden chance to give England a two-goal cushion from the penalty spot 10 minutes into the second half but slipped slightly, crashing his shot against the bar.

Spain, who beat England in the Euro 2024 final, took full advantage, with substitutes Alex Baena and Mikel Oyarzabal putting their side ahead, taking advantage of more sloppy defensive play from the home side.

England boss Thomas Tuchel was adamant ahead of the match that it did not signal a new start, but he will have been dismayed by his team’s nervy start.

Manchester City’s Guehi, with a chance to clear in the second minute, inexplicably turned back towards goalkeeper James Trafford, apparently unaware that Yamal was just behind him.

The teenager collected the ball and curled a left-footed effort off the inside of the post.

Ferran Torres was in the thick of the action, with an effort ruled out for offside and another shot saved by Trafford, in for longtime number one Jordan Pickford.

He also squandered a golden opportunity with just the goalkeeper to beat.

Yamal then set up Dani Olmo, who flashed wide as Spain rued yet another miss.

England, who had shown plenty of promise down the wings, made the visitors pay with an incisive counter-attacking goal after winning the ball back deep in their own half.

Gordon was involved early in the move and surged forward, collecting Jude Bellingham’s pass to steer the ball decisively past goalkeeper Unai Simon.

And, with the atmosphere now totally changed, England were in front when Kane rose to head home.

Tuchel’s men started the second half brightly and had a chance to extend their lead from the spot when they were awarded a penalty for a Rodri foul on Bellingham following a VAR check.

But Kane crashed his shot against the bar, and England paid the price when Baena steered home on the hour mark after O’Reilly had given the ball away to Olmo.

Worse was to come for the home side when Baena turned provider for Oyarzabal, who dinked the ball over Trafford.

articles.body_text:
Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Maren Morris is sharing photos from her healing journey.

In a recent Instagram post, the 36-year-old country singer revealed photos from her recent trip to Bali, telling her followers she's "not healed but healing."

"Thank you @rachelbeauregard + @hotyogaeastnashville for the most beautiful journey to Bali with so many new friends for life," she wrote in the caption. "And it’s not over yet :)"

One of the photos featured Morris showing off her toned abs in a black string bikini, as she stood on a deck with lounge chairs behind her, with a drink in her hand.

Morris shared a series of photos from her wellness trip to Bali, including one of her in a black bikini. (Maren Morris Instagram)

MAREN MORRIS' INFANT SON RECEIVED 'SCARY' DEATH THREATS AFTER THE MUSICIAN CALLED OUT MORGAN WALLEN

Others showed her taking part in a group meditation, standing under a waterfall, being silly with her friends and other snaps from her trip.

"She's thrivinggggggg (and surviving)," one fan wrote in the comments section. Another added, "So happy to see this journey for you 🥹."

Morris also shared photos of her in a meditation session. (Maren Morris Instagram)

Morris shot to stardom in 2016 with the release of her breakthrough song "My Church," which led to her debut album, "Hero," which also featured hits such as "80's Mercedes," "I Could Use a Love Song" and "Rich."

She has since released four studio albums, including "D R E A M S I C L E," "Humble Quest" and "Girl," and has received 17 Grammy Award nominations, with one win.

She also shared photos of her being silly with her friends. (Maren Morris Instagram)

While it is unclear what she is healing from now, she spoke to People in August 2025 while promoting "D R E A M S I C L E," about how the album was very personal, as it dealt with her sexuality and how she made it through her divorce from her ex-husband Ryan Hurd.

"It’s just cool; it’s a very intimate record, very vulnerable, not the easiest to make — so the fact that people are receiving it this well and healing from my healing is really special, to get to see the live form of that that place now."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Morris said she has stopped going to award shows because they have become "dicey." (Tibrina Hobson/Getty Images)

As an outspoken liberal, she also spoke about how her mental health has suffered due to her being "so deeply concerned and uncomfortable with the weird status quo of country music," in a TikTok she shared in January.

Morris shared that she doesn't attend very many award shows anymore, saying they have become "dicey" since the political atmosphere of country music has changed after President Trump's first term in office.

"I've lost a lot of fans over the years because of my viewpoints and I think that's fair," Morris said. "If you don't agree with me, and you can't enjoy my music because of my viewpoints, you are absolutely allowed to do that."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Morris has received criticism for her political views in the past, and in 2024 was told she should be arrested after she took her young son to a drag show.

Morris previously received backlash for taking her young son to a drag show. (Ralph Bavaro/NBCUniversal via Getty Images)

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

After getting backlash, she defended herself during an appearance on "The Kelly Clarkson Show," telling the host the drag show her son attended was "family friendly."

"I think it's just such an amazing expression of artistry, and so I just think like normalizing it and making it seem like these are just people that love dressing up, too, is an amazing thing," she said. "It was an all-ages show, so it was completely family-friendly."

Lori A. Bashian is an entertainment news writer at Fox News Digital.

Justin Verlander’s final start of his illustrious career brought out all the emotions, including some tears from the 42-year-old. Detroit Tigers manager A.J. Hinch came out of the dugout to pull the legendary starter after 5 1/3 innings of two-run ball in the Tigers’ 4-3 win over the Pittsburgh Pirates on Saturday but didn’t walk to the mound.

Hinch instead brought out someone special to Verlander to remove him from his last start: his daughter, Genevieve.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Genevieve Verlander runs to hug her father, Detroit Tigers starting pitcher Justin Verlander, as catcher Dillon Dingler looks on during the sixth inning of a baseball game against the Pittsburgh Pirates on Sept. 26, 2026, in Detroit. (AP Photo/Jose Juarez)

Genevieve came sprinting out of her seat and gave her dad a hug by the pitcher’s mound. Verlander embraced his daughter for more than 15 seconds as his body shook with emotion and the tears began to flow. The emotional Verlander then composed himself as he hugged his infielders one final time.

After hugging his teammates, he walked off the mound hand-in-hand with his daughter as the raucous Tigers crowd gave their longtime ace a rousing ovation.

Before greeting his teammates, he hugged his wife, Kate Upton, who was holding their second child. The 2011 American League MVP then high-fived all of his teammates and coaches, who had all come out of the dugout, before walking down the dugout steps with Upton and Genevieve.

Genevieve Verlander hugs her father, Detroit Tigers starting pitcher Justin Verlander, during the sixth inning of a game against the Pittsburgh Pirates on Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026, in Detroit. (AP Photo/Jose Juarez)

As he walked down the steps alongside his family, he saluted the fans with his hat.

The whole scene felt like something out of a movie – and a fitting end for one of the best pitchers of his generation.

Verlander, who was making just his second start of the year due to injury, still flashed a 95 mph fastball and struck out six Pirates hitters. His final career start was his first at Comerica Park in 3,324 days.

Detroit Tigers starting pitcher Justin Verlander acknowledges the crowd after being taken out of the game during the sixth inning of a baseball game against the Pittsburgh Pirates on Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026, in Detroit. (AP Photo/Jose Juarez)

With Verlander riding off into the sunset, he also takes with him the era of the workhorse starting pitcher.

In addition to his MVP Award, he won three Cy Young Awards and a Triple Crown, was named Rookie of the Year, made 10 All-Star teams, won two ERA titles and is a two-time World Series champion.

Ryan Canfield is a digital production assistant for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Shaun Cassidy says teen idol fame trapped him before he made drastic career move at 21
articles.excerpt: Ryan Cassidy, the younger brother of teen idol David Cassidy, has written a children's book titled "James Cagney Was My Babysitter." He is the son of the "Partridge Family" matriarch Shirley Jones and...
articles.body_text:
Ryan Cassidy, the younger brother of teen idol David Cassidy, has written a children's book titled "James Cagney Was My Babysitter." He is the son of the "Partridge Family" matriarch Shirley Jones and Tony Award winner Jack Cassidy.

Shaun Cassidy had the screaming fans, the hit record and the television stardom. Then, at 21, he walked away from it all.

The former teen heartthrob revealed why he stopped touring at the height of his fame, saying the celebrity lifestyle had become less appealing than staying home, raising his children and creating television behind the scenes.

"I stopped touring when I was 21. Astrodome was my last show — not because I didn't love touring. I did, I loved performing, loved singing, but I found that writing and producing TV gave me, frankly, a much better life," he shared on the "Naked Lunch" podcast.

That decision came after Cassidy had already become one of the biggest teen stars of the late 1970s. His 1977 self-titled debut album spawned the No. 1 hit "Da Doo Ron Ron," while his role as Joe Hardy on ABC's "The Hardy Boys/Nancy Drew Mysteries" made him a familiar face in homes across America.

FORMER TEEN IDOL SHAUN CASSIDY CALLS OUT FATHER AS ‘PHONY’ AFTER GROWING UP ALONE IN HOLLYWOOD SPOTLIGHT

Former teen idol Shaun Cassidy says growing up in the Hollywood spotlight left him feeling alone. (John Atashian/Getty Images; Brad Elterman/Getty Images)

But Cassidy wasn't interested in spending the rest of his life inside the teen-idol machine.

"I got to stay home. I had kids at a young age. And I love writing," he said about his decision to give up touring.

For Cassidy, writing and producing offered something performing couldn't.

"I was a magician as a really young kid … when you write something, it's like magic. You pulled something out of the air and 200 people have a job on a sound stage."

FORMER TEEN IDOL SHAUN CASSIDY HAD TO RELEARN HIS OWN HITS FOR FIRST MAJOR TOUR IN 45 YEARS

Shaun Cassidy opened up about childhood, family struggles and the career path that changed his life. (Brad Elterman/FilmMagic)

By the mid-1990s, Cassidy had largely traded the stage for the writers' room and producer's chair, working on shows including "American Gothic," "Roar" and "New Amsterdam."

Cassidy said life as a teen idol left him feeling increasingly isolated.

He explained, "Because once you are well-known — at least in my case — I became insulated. I couldn't go out … kind of a prisoner in your house."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Shaun Cassidy reflects on his early years in Hollywood and the complicated relationship he had with his father. (Getty Images)

He added, "And that's one of the reasons again, like I don't want to be Elvis — not that I was Elvis, but you know what I mean — like I don't want that life. I don't want the Michael Jackson isolation, it's not healthy."

Instead, he said, he chose family and a life outside the glare of the spotlight.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"I'm glad I made the choice I did because now I've got a great life, I've got a great family, I've got … 107 children, and I'm a lucky man," Cassidy, who is father to seven children, laughed.

"The Partridge Family" stars Shirley Jones, Brian Forster, Suzanne Crough, Susan Dey, Danny Bonaduce and David Cassidy pose leaning out of the windows of a bus in a group portrait circa 1973. (Silver Screen Collection/Getty Images)

Cassidy's complicated relationship with fame began long before he became famous himself.

He grew up as the son of Broadway and television star Jack Cassidy and Oscar winner Shirley Jones, who became a television icon as Shirley Partridge on "The Partridge Family." Jack Cassidy and Jones married in 1956 and divorced in 1975.

American actress and singer Shirley Jones, alongside her husband, actor and singer Jack Cassidy, circa 1972. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)

Cassidy has previously described his late father as a "phony," saying Jack's larger-than-life showman persona didn't necessarily translate into fatherhood.

The former teen idol said that he and his brothers, including actor Patrick Cassidy and the late David Cassidy, experienced a very different reality behind the family's Hollywood image.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

He has also recalled essentially raising himself while his parents pursued their careers.

Cassidy is currently preparing for his "Unwrapped: Songs & Stories for the Holidays" tour, which is scheduled to kick off in November.

Stephanie Giang-Paunon is an entertainment reporter for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Hamas slams Board of Peace for refusal to work with UNRWA in Gaza
articles.excerpt:
Palestinian group Hamas has condemned the Board of Peace’s decision not to work with the United Nations agency for Palestinians, UNRWA, and for saying that the agency will have no role in Gaza.

The U...
articles.body_text:
Palestinian group Hamas has condemned the Board of Peace’s decision not to work with the United Nations agency for Palestinians, UNRWA, and for saying that the agency will have no role in Gaza.

The US-created Board’s decision is “a complete alignment with the Zionist [Israeli] position”, aimed at ending UNRWA’s operations, preventing it from delivering aid to Palestinians and eliminating the right of return, Hamas spokesperson Hazem Qassem said on Saturday.

On Friday, the Board of Peace said that “UNRWA’s involvement in Gaza is unchanged.”

“We will only work with trusted partners who will deliver for the people of Gaza and contribute to a deradicalized Strip,” it said in a post on X, adding that “UNRWA fails on those litmus tests”.

In his statement, Qassem said it was “strange for the Peace Council to adopt this hostile stance towards UNRWA while simultaneously failing to provide aid to Gaza or compel the occupation to abide by the ceasefire agreement and halt the daily killings of Palestinians in the Strip”.

UNRWA, set up in 1949, has for decades provided aid and education services to Palestinian refugees and preserved their national rights.

Palestinians see the agency as safeguarding their right of return to their homeland, while Israel wants it dismantled.

The Associated Press reported on Friday that Board of Peace members had been more willing to work with UNRWA behind the scenes than their public stance suggested.

At the Board of Peace briefing to the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, officials named several UN agencies as partners. UNRWA was not among them.

However, a Board of Peace official, speaking to The AP on condition of anonymity, confirmed that board members had met UNRWA officials several times.

The official said the agency’s programmes could continue if they served Gaza’s residents well, but maintained that “UNRWA’s days are over”.

Philippe Lazzarini, who led UNRWA until earlier this year, told The AP that members of the Palestinian technocratic committee appointed by the Board to govern Gaza wanted to work with the agency.

On Thursday, Lazzarini accused the Board of failing to deliver on its mandate, saying in a post on X that Israeli authorities are still blocking basic aid “as part of a wider plan to keep Gaza unlivable for Palestinians”.

“Grandiose plans is what the Board of Peace does best. Plans however will not keep the people of Gaza warm this winter,” he added, urging that crossings into Gaza be opened and supplies let in at scale.

On the ground on Saturday, Israel’s pattern of violations against Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank continued.

Israeli attacks killed seven Palestinians across the Gaza Strip in the past 48 hours, including one person who succumbed to wounds sustained prior, Gaza’s Ministry of Health said.

In northern Gaza, Israeli forces shot dead a Palestinian in Jabalia, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported. An Israeli drone strike near Joulis Street and al-Nouri Tower in the Nuseirat refugee camp killed another person and wounded others.

In al-Mawasi in Khan Younis, an Israeli drone strike wounded several Palestinians, including a girl, while Israeli artillery shelled areas east of the city.

An Israeli quadcopter also opened fire on Salah al-Din Street in central Gaza, wounding three people, including another girl.

Meanwhile, in the occupied West Bank, Israeli forces stormed Ramallah-based Birzeit University, raiding one of its buildings while students sat final examinations, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.

In Tulkarem, forces arrested resident Bashar Odeh after raiding his home in Shuweika, and interrogated others during home searches in Zeita.

In Bethlehem governorate, Israeli forces closed the military gates at the entrances to western villages, stopping residents, including pedestrians, from passing.

Raids continued across other localities, including the Qalandiya and Am’ari refugee camps.

articles.title: Maher blasts ‘intolerant left’ after Massachusetts lesbian bar faces fury for tweaking COVID-era mask policy
articles.excerpt:
Fox News host Greg Gutfeld and the ‘Gutfeld!’ panel discuss a Massachusetts lesbian bar bullied out of town after lifting its mask mandate.

Comedian Bill Maher took aim at his own side of the aisle F...
articles.body_text:
Fox News host Greg Gutfeld and the ‘Gutfeld!’ panel discuss a Massachusetts lesbian bar bullied out of town after lifting its mask mandate.

Comedian Bill Maher took aim at his own side of the aisle Friday night, mocking far-left critics who torched a struggling Massachusetts lesbian bar for daring to go mask-optional one night a week.

During Friday’s episode of HBO’s "Real Time," Maher weighed in on the viral story regarding Last Ditch Bar and Arts Venue — a lesbian bar in Greenfield, Massachusetts that drew national headlines this week after the Boston Globe reported on a slew of community backlash surrounding the businesses’ decision to lift its COVID-era mask mandate for one night each week.

"Here's what's going on at the Last Ditch Bar," Maher said, adding, "It's a very woke bar, which is fine. Their mission statement [is], ‘For dykes, transsexuals, gender freaks, workers and friends.’"

NEWSOM'S ADMISSION THAT INFAMOUS COVID MOVE WAS 'INSANE' TRIGGERS VIRAL FURY: 'WE ALL TOLD YOU'

Comedian and television host Bill Maher arrived for the 27th Mark Twain Prize for American Humor gala at the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts on June 28, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Alex Wroblewski/AFP via Getty Images)

"I love the way workers and friends are fourth and fifth on the list," Maher joked.

The comedian went on to delve into the bar's financial struggles. The Boston Globe reported that more patrons had said they could not afford the cover charge, and the bar allowed them in anyway.

MAHER SKEWERS WEALTHY CELEBS WHO PREACHED 'WE'RE ALL IN IT TOGETHER' DURING COVID AS AMERICANS STRUGGLED

Last Ditch Bar and Arts Venue recently removed its mask requirements on Saturdays in an effort to boost business. (Google Maps)

"But economically, it wasn't working," Maher said. "Because even though there was a cover charge, if you couldn't pay, they wouldn't make you pay. Homeless, they were welcome in there. Not the cops, but the homeless. But also, it was masked"

Maher later pointed out that ‘because they're losing money, one of the owners was living in her truck."

BILL MAHER BREAKS WITH THE LEFT TO HAMMER ANTHONY FAUCI AFTER EXPLOSIVE SENATE HEARING

Maher said of the reaction to the bar's policy change: ‘And of course, the tolerant left did what they always do — became very intolerant and left’  (Lionel Hahn/Getty Images)

In an attempt to keep the doors open, Last Ditch made the decision to lift its strict KN-95 mask mandate one night each week — Saturdays — and allow patrons inside without the COVID-era face coverings, according to the Boston Globe.

"It is with love we inform our immunocompromised disabled divas we will be opening Saturday nights as mask optional," Last Ditch wrote in an Aug. 31 Instagram post.

‘COVID 2.0’: LAWMAKERS PUSH BACK ON SWEEPING HEALTH 'POLICE POWER' IN KEY BATTLEGROUND STATE

The backlash was swift, with locals flocking to a monthly community meeting on Sept. 11 to air their grievances, the outlet reported.

Virtual attendees were quick to criticize the bar owners for their decision, with the meeting taking another turn when some critics objected to a mediator, a licensed therapist who is White.

BILL MAHER BLAMES THE FAR-LEFT FOR PUSHING OUT LIBERALS LIKE JOE ROGAN, ELON MUSK OVER TO CONSERVATIVES

"A lot of people are calling for an acknowledgment of harm and I’m hearing a WHITE therapist … center[ing] the feelings of a majority white and white adjacent staff," one person said, the newspaper reported.

Maher took issue with the far-left bar patrons' apparent lack of understanding of the situation and blasted their intolerance toward the business.

BILL MAHER WARNS THAT THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY IS BEING 'COLONIZED' BY SOCIALISTS, SAYS HIS 'VOTE IS IN PLAY'

"And of course, the tolerant left did what they always do — became very intolerant and left," Maher said.

He went on to point to comments reportedly made by critics of the bar.

"And statements like, ‘People like you kill disabled people in the name of your own leisure and convenience,’ and ‘I hope your venue gets firebombed.’ This is what I'm talking about. This level of hatred that is out there."

Maher's criticism of the political left was noted by NewsBusters Executive Editor Tim Graham, who pointed out what he viewed as hypocrisy on both sides.

"This whole story went viral because it's shocking that a mask mandate is still in place at a bar in 2026. I imagine many people can feel more than a hint of the old COVID authoritarianism in the virulent leftist reaction to a single mask-optional night at this establishment," Graham told Fox News Digital. "These same people are probably furious at the Boston Globe for publishing this story. They don't care that the bar was a financial mess."

Graham added that Maher seems to have a pet peeve about liberals who preach tolerance but, in Maher's view, fail to practice it.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"Bill Maher has a tendency to go against the dominant grain and can be savage about left-wing intolerance even though he was a massive supporter of Barack Obama," Graham said. "He's been very rough on organized religion, and can bring the pain to other strains of fundamentalism."

Fox News Digital reached out to Last Ditch Bar for comment.

Fox News Digital’s Landon Mion contributed to this report.

Julia Bonavita is a media and culture writer for Fox News Digital, and a Fox Flight Team drone pilot. You can follow her at @juliabonavita13 on all platforms and send story tips to julia.bonavita@fox.com.

articles.title: Tens of thousands attend right-wing protest over Ceuta migrant crisis
articles.excerpt:
Thousands of people have rallied in the Spanish capital to protest the government’s policy on irregular migration and its handling of a recent migrant influx into the North African enclave of Ceuta.

...
articles.body_text:
Thousands of people have rallied in the Spanish capital to protest the government’s policy on irregular migration and its handling of a recent migrant influx into the North African enclave of Ceuta.

Saturday’s protest in Madrid was organised by right-wing civil society group Sociedad Civil Espanola and backed by the mainstream conservative People’s Party (PP) and far-right Vox.

According to the government, 20,000 people attended, while protest organisers put the turnout at 180,000.

At the end of July, more than 70,000 migrants stormed into the autonomous Spanish city of Ceuta from neighbouring Morocco, before most of them were returned. However, thousands remain stranded.

Demonstrators accused Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez and his government of failing to protect the borders of Ceuta.

They are calling for an early election to be held by mid-November, with Vox demanding Sanchez be tried for treason. Spain’s next general election is not due until August 2027.

PP’s secretary-general Miguel Tellado said there was a “widespread feeling that the government has not acted responsibly; there has been a dereliction of duty, extreme negligence”.

“Spanish society has to take to the streets to ask the government to defend our territorial integrity,” he added.

The July 30 and 31 surge of people into Ceuta led to unprecedented scenes and the deaths of dozens of migrants.

Sanchez said on Tuesday that Moroccan border control failed to adequately handle the incident and that an investigation was still under way, adding that Rabat had been asked for answers.

The Spanish government estimates that between 6,000 and 10,000 stranded migrants remain in Ceuta.

Vox leader Santiago Abascal is demanding that everyone who arrived in late July be deported to their country of origin.

Abascal said Ceuta remained “invaded because Sanchez continues to be Morocco’s servant”.

Spanish newspaper El Pais reported on Saturday that the government is planning to approve a decree on Tuesday to accelerate the return of migrants from Ceuta to Morocco.

The protest is the second under the March for Dignity banner. That demonstration was held in late May before the incident in Ceuta and attracted 40,000 protesters, according to the government.

articles.title: Private colleges around Australia offering last-minute discounts for diploma allegedly ‘misused by shonks’
articles.excerpt:
Federal government to deregister graduate diploma of management in October over fears it was being used by ‘non-genuine’ students to remain in country

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily n...
articles.body_text:
Federal government to deregister graduate diploma of management in October over fears it was being used by ‘non-genuine’ students to remain in country

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Private colleges are offering discounts to rush students into a diploma the federal government is cancelling over concerns it is being “misused by shonks”.

The government announced in early September it would deregister the graduate diploma of management (learning) which it suspected was being used by “non-genuine” students to remain in Australia. The course is taught by close to 450 institutions, has over 15,000 students studying currently and more than 40,000 students registered for future enrolment following completion of a different vocational course.

Ads posted to social media and shared among agents and students in recent days encouraged students to join the course or expedite their start date before cancellation on 5 October. Any students already enrolled and studying by that date are allowed to complete it.

Some immigration education agents have offered promotions for the month of September, including in WhatsApp messages and texts, encouraging students to join the course or those who have a future enrolment to study now. Several ads promote discounted course fees or a free certificate of enrolment to join immediately.

One private college has sent immigration agents a promotion offering “attractive” commissions with same-day offer letters and confirmation of enrolment for students, with two “special intakes” on 21 September and 2 October – just three days before the course is cancelled.

Phil Honeywood, the chief executive of the International Education Association of Australia (IEAA), supported the decision to cancel the course and said it could put some private providers trying to loophole the system into financial trouble.

“The government for all the right reasons moved to stop non-genuine international students from using this course to stay in the country,” Honeywood said.

“High-quality providers will always have a place in the international education ecosystem … they would rather have these factory-type private providers out of the system for all the right reasons.”

Some education migration providers are encouraging the more than 40,000 international students with a future enrolment to start the course now before it is cancelled. Some of those students would need to do so, or choose a different course such as a bachelor’s or master’s with a high qualification level to maintain their visa conditions. That could mean completing two courses at the same time.

Students who have “packaged” a lower-level vocational course with the graduate diploma to be completed after, will need to enrol into a higher-level course to maintain their visa requirements.

One student who spoke to Guardian Australia on the condition of anonymity said they had initially come to Australia to study a bachelor’s degree but unenrolled after one semester on the advice of a migration agent to do a VET course in carpentry, followed by the graduate diploma in management. The graduate diploma and the VET course would fulfil the qualification level required to maintain a valid international student visa.

They said they were being told to commence the graduate diploma now.

“I talked to the agent, and they told me the new rules. They want me to study concurrently, [so] I can study both courses at the same time. I don’t know if I can take this much study load,” the international student said.

They said other friends doing the same course pathway were also given the same advice, and were also stressed by the potential workload.

A migration agent, who asked not to be named, said they had heard of other agents and institutions pushing students to expedite their enrolment, but they warned the government would view this suspiciously. They said they were concerned that this behaviour would damage the reputation and credibility of the rest of the sector.

They also said private institutions might look at setting up other courses such as the graduate diploma of strategic leadership that just over 34 colleges currently teach or the graduate diploma of portfolio management that is taught by just a few, that have the same visa requirement level.

Julian Hill, the assistant minister responsible for cancelling the course, said the department and education regulator would be “closely watching student and provider behaviour”.

“Students and providers are on notice that curious patterns of early commencement or new enrolments will be investigated and action taken against those doing the wrong thing,” Hill told Guardian Australia.

At the time of the announcement in September that the course would be deregistered, Hill said in a statement: “The Coalition left behind a shocking mess in 2022, with unsustainably high growth in student numbers in the least reputable parts of the sector, and our high-quality student visa being degraded into a low-rent illegal work visa and misused by shonks.”

Melanie McFarlane, New South Wales president of the Migration Institute of Australia, said some education agents were helping their students into master’s courses to maintain their visas.

“Those students needing to find an alternate course, they’re being placed by, I would say, reputable agents, into a master’s degree within the same institution where that graduate diploma was otherwise available,” she said.

“But then you’ve got the other side where there are migration agents who are potentially going out of business because of all the changes to the industry … and might be rushing students into that course in the time that they can.”

It is part of a wider crackdown by the government to curb visa-hopping and overstayers in Australia.

The government has now banned international students from starting one qualification and then transferring to a lower-value qualification which would allow them to remain in the country and work more hours instead of studying. This would help prevent a student enrolled in a bachelor’s degree from downgrading to a vocational course.

Hill said the government had also banned commissions for agents transferring students between courses in Australia.

“This has helped but the quantum and pattern of transfers remains concerning, so from next year international students looking to change providers will have to apply for [a] new visa.”

articles.title: Palestinian careers adviser who was allegedly told to stop wearing keffiyeh at Sydney school sues for racial discrimination
articles.excerpt:
Wasim El-Haj alleges NSW government school ordered him to stop wearing symbolic garment as it ‘may cause discord’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A Palestinian careers ad...
articles.body_text:
Wasim El-Haj alleges NSW government school ordered him to stop wearing symbolic garment as it ‘may cause discord’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A Palestinian careers adviser who was allegedly directed to stop wearing a keffiyeh at a Sydney government school because it was a symbol that “may cause discord” has lodged a racial discrimination case in the federal court against the state of New South Wales.

Wasim El-Haj, a former careers adviser at Sydney Girls High School – an inner-city selective government school – alleges the then acting principal told him in 2024 that the keffiyeh was seen as a symbol of conflict. He alleges the state’s conduct is unlawful for breaching the Racial Discrimination Act.

El-Haj began wearing the keffiyeh – a traditional scarf linked to the struggle for a Palestinian state for decades – at school in January 2024, three months after Hamas’ 7 October attacks and Israel’s subsequent war on Gaza.

His statement of claim, filed in the federal court last month, alleges Geoffrey Denyer, the then acting school principal, met with him on 15 May 2024 and said words to the effect of “I have been directed to direct you to remove this item of clothing”, indicating to El-Haj’s keiffeyh.

Denyer also said words to the effect of the direction had come “from above, possibly from the minister” and that action would be taken if El-Haj did not comply, the statement of claim alleges.

In an email sent the same day, after El-Haj requested the issue be laid out in writing, Denyer outlined the terms of the direction he had received.

“Consistent with the Department’s Controversial Issues and Code of Conduct policies, the staff member in question should be given clear advice, from you, that this item of clothing should not be worn at school, nor in the performance of any duties in connection with his employment. That advice should be complied with immediately,” the email said.

“It is understandable that, in such times as these, feelings and emotions are strong. However, our schools need to remain free of symbols which stir these emotions, and which may cause discord.”

El-Haj alleges that in a further conversation with Denyer he said words to the effect of “any symbol of Palestine is seen as a symbol of conflict”.

In August 2024, El-Haj met with Maria Serafim, a NSW Department of Education official, who detailed six anonymous concerns, including that he had worn a symbol of “partisan conflict” by wearing the keffiyeh, the statement of claim alleges.

An internal complaint El-Haj made about the direction did not lead to its withdrawal. The careers advisor appealed the decision about the complaint to the secretary of the NSW Department of Education, Murat Dizdar.

Responding to this, Dizdar upheld the school’s decision. In a letter to El-Haj in February 2025, he recognised the keffiyeh “is a garment of cultural significance for the Palestinian community” but said the department did not want to compromise the “safety, wellbeing and security in all our school communities”.

“Unfortunately, our schools are not immune to external events, such as the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, with the tragic loss of innocent lives,” he said.

“Regrettably, within our school communities, some individuals and groups may seek to politicise global conflicts or others may form that perception, and as such we always remain politically neutral in public schools when such events can impact on operations.

“It is with this context that the senior officers and the school advised you to not wear the keffiyeh to school.”

El-Haj took leave from his employment from May 2024 until the end of the year and resigned from Sydney Girls High School in March 2025.

El-Haj alleges the state of NSW has engaged in unlawful conduct under section 9(1) of the Racial Discrimination Act.

The state of NSW is yet to file its defence in the federal court.

The matter is due to be next heard for a case management hearing on 3 November, federal court records show.

A spokesperson for the NSW Department of Education said it was “committed to maintaining neutral and apolitical school environments, in line with its policies.”

Guardian Australia understands the department is not able to make further comments while the matter is before court.

articles.title: Trump claims stunning casualty numbers in Russia-Ukraine war
articles.excerpt:
President Donald Trump told reporters Saturday that last month, 25,000 people died in the Ukraine-Russia war and said the month before that 32,000 people died.

President Donald Trump said Saturday th...
articles.body_text:
President Donald Trump told reporters Saturday that last month, 25,000 people died in the Ukraine-Russia war and said the month before that 32,000 people died.

President Donald Trump said Saturday that 25,000 people were killed last month and another 32,000 the month before in the war between between Ukraine and Russia

"Last month, 25,000 people died in the Ukraine-Russia war, okay? 25,000," he told reporters on the White House lawn Saturday.

"The month before that, 32,000 people died … mostly soldiers, 97% soldiers. But whether they're soldiers or civilians, think of it: 32,000. Two months ago, 33,000 people; this month, 25,000 people died. What a shame," he added.

PUTIN UNLEASHES NEW FURY ON UKRAINE AS REPORT EXPOSES FEAR HANGING OVER WAR’S END

Russia alone has lost as many as 450,000 soldiers since invading Ukraine in 2022, according to the Center for Strategic & International Studies (CSIS).

U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to the media as he departs the White House on the South Lawn in Washington, DC, US, September 26, 2026. (Annabelle Gordon/Reuters)

Trump also told reporters he wants to see an end to the war soon, revealing he spoke to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy recently.

KUSHNER, WITKOFF SET FOR KYIV TALKS AFTER PUTIN MEETING IN US PUSH FOR PEACE

"I spoke to him a lot, and he's going along and Putin's going along. And someday, hopefully in the not too distant future, maybe before the heavy winter, they'll make a deal," he told reporters.

He claimed that he pushed Zelenskyy to try to make a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

TRUMP NEGOTIATORS WITKOFF, KUSHNER MEET WITH PUTIN IN MOSCOW AS US PUSHES FOR END TO RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR

"I agreed with Zelenskyy that we talked about a lot of different subjects, and many of those subjects, very strong agreement. But you know what I want him to do? Make a deal. I want him to settle with Putin, and I want Putin to settle with him.

President Donald Trump greets Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at the White House Aug. 18, 2025 in Washington, D.C. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

Zelenskyy announced Friday that Trump had agreed to give approval to Ukraine to license and produce U.S. Patriot missile interceptors.

TRUMP SAYS US WILL LET UKRAINE MAKE PATRIOT MISSILES IN MAJOR POLICY SHIFT

"There are concrete agreements regarding Patriot licenses. At our meeting, President Trump stressed that he had made his final decision: Ukraine will receive licenses to produce Patriot missiles,'" Zelenskyy posted Friday.

"There are concrete agreements regarding Patriot licenses," Zelenskyy wrote. (Jens Büttner/Getty Images; Antonio Masiello/Getty Images)

President Trump had previously hesitated to grant Ukraine the licenses.

Fox News Digital contacted the White House for comment.

articles.title: Former UK Prime Minister Tony Blair warns Europe ‘we don’t win’ in war without US support

Former U.K. Prime Minist...
articles.body_text:
Former British Prime Minister Tony Blair joins ‘Saturday in America’ to discuss the Gaza rebuilding plan, ending the Iran conflict and confronting challenges presented by AI.

Former U.K. Prime Minister Tony Blair warned that Europe could find itself unable to prevail in a conflict with Russia if it loses the backing of the United States, saying British leaders should preserve their alliance with President Donald Trump.

"If we get drawn into a conflict without the support of America, we don't win," Blair told "Saturday in America" host Kayleigh McEnany.

"This is an essential relationship," he continued. "And the reason why I thought we should have supported President Trump when he asked for the use of our bases is in circumstances where your ally is an indispensable part of your security, and they come asking for help, it’s wise to give it to them."

RUBIO QUESTIONS ‘POINT’ OF NATO AFTER ALLIES BLOCKED US FROM USING BASES DURING IRAN CONFLICT

Founding member of the Board of Peace Executive Board and former British Prime Minister Sir Tony Blair speaks at a Board of Peace High Level Briefing on Sept. 23, 2026 in New York City. (Ryan Murphy/Getty Images)

Blair, who served as Britain’s prime minister from 1997 to 2007, called the U.S.-U.K. relationship "an essential" part of the West’s security as European nations debate the threat Russian President Vladimir Putin could pose to NATO countries.

While Blair personally believes Putin poses no real threat to countries outside of Ukraine, he acknowledged that others across Europe hold a different belief.

US INTEL WARNS RUSSIA COULD LAUNCH LIMITED ATTACK ON NATO ALLY IN EFFORT TO FRAGMENT ORGANIZATION: REPORT

President Donald Trump attends the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Sept. 22, 2026. Blair pointed to Britain's alliance with the U.S. as crucial to success should conflict arise. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

"I might be wrong [about Putin]. And there are a lot of people in Europe who think he's got malicious intent towards NATO countries," he said.

Blair's comments come as some European leaders have raised their voices in concern over Russia, including after one recent instance in which an explosives-laden drone was discovered near a Ukrainian cargo plane at an airport in Germany.

A series of other events — including airspace violations, arson and more — have similarly raised eyebrows and pointed toward escalation, per USA Today.

The U.S. and European nations continue to seek ways to bolster Ukraine's defense and deter Russia while refraining from complete involvement in the conflict.
