articles.title: Jill Dando murder: technological advances allow police to review CCTV 27 years later
articles.excerpt:
BBC broadcaster was shot in 1999 in case detectives have previously said may never be solved

Technological advances are allowing police to review old CCTV footage in the unsolved murder of the BBC br...
articles.body_text:
BBC broadcaster was shot in 1999 in case detectives have previously said may never be solved

Technological advances are allowing police to review old CCTV footage in the unsolved murder of the BBC broadcaster Jill Dando, Scotland Yard has revealed.

Advances in CCTV enhancement technology have allowed detectives to return to 27-year-old footage of Putney Bridge Underground station, Scotland Yard said. But detectives stressed that the review was part of existing inquiries – not a new investigation.

The former Crimewatch presenter was 37 years old when she was shot and killed outside her home in Fulham, west London, on 26 April 1999. An unidentified person, referred to as “Man X”, was captured on camera near Putney Bridge station – about a mile from Dando’s home – shortly after the attack.

A driver had seen a man “running for his life” on Fulham Palace Road around the time of the shooting, the Mirror reported. She later picked out Man X in the station CCTV as the person who had been sprinting.

A Met spokesperson said: “In the 27 years since Jill Dando’s murder, the investigation has been subject to numerous reviews, aiming to identify whether matters could be progressed with advances in technology and forensics.

“Recent advancements in CCTV enhancement technology have provided investigators with the opportunity to re-examine original footage from Putney Bridge train station.

“The review of CCTV footage forms part of ongoing inquiries and should not be interpreted as a significant line of inquiry nor as a new investigation being opened on this matter.”

Outside her work on Crimewatch, Dando was also seen during the 1980s and 1990s on BBC shows including travel show Holiday and The Antiques Inspectors.

She began as a reporter at her local paper The Weston Mercury in Weston-super-Mare, Somerset, before moving to the morning programme Breakfast Time, which later became BBC Breakfast.

In 2019, the detective who led the inquiry into Dando’s murder expressed doubt the case would ever be solved. Speaking in a BBC documentary to mark 20 years since the television presenter’s shooting, Hamish Campbell said he did not think any new suspects would ever be brought to court.

“Do I think somebody will come back to court? Probably not, no. Sometimes, I felt we were a day away from solving it and other times, I thought: ‘No, we’re a long way away’. Senior officers were asking: ‘What are the likelihoods of this case being resolved?’

“We had over 2,000 people named as potential suspects or responsible. Some actions to trace and eliminate one person might take a day. One action might take two weeks. But there’s thousands of them and that’s the issue of managing stranger homicides.”

articles.title: Security lapses at Utah campus where Charlie Kirk was killed, review says
articles.excerpt:
Kirk's Utah Valley University event was held in a courtyard surrounded by tall buildings

An independent review has pointed to a number of security shortcomings at the Utah campus where conservative a...
articles.body_text:
Kirk's Utah Valley University event was held in a courtyard surrounded by tall buildings

An independent review has pointed to a number of security shortcomings at the Utah campus where conservative activist Charlie Kirk was shot dead last year.

The report said Utah Valley University (UVU) did not carry out a proper written security assessment nor prepare an event action plan, deferring key decision-making about the event to Kirk's conservative organisation Turning Point USA.

It also said that Kirk's aides had insisted on a outdoor venue, overriding security concerns from campus officials, who then failed to properly assess the dangers.

The 31-year-old activist had been addressing thousands of people in an Orem campus courtyard when he was shot from a nearby rooftop on 10 September 2025.

Kirk's family said the report reinforced their concerns about how the event was managed.

University officials had raised concerns in August 2025 about holding the event at a location surrounded by tall buildings and had suggested alternative venues, including some indoors, the report, external - published by UVU - says.

"But a Turning Point representative insisted that Kirk speak at a campus courtyard because he had been there previously and the organisation was familiar with the location," it adds.

Despite the "significant protective operations considerations", no line-of-sight assessment was documented in the planning process, the external consultants note.

They also identified shortcomings in the co-ordination between university police and Kirk's private security team.

A proposed meeting between the university's police chief and Turning Point security shortly before the event did not take place, the report said.

The reviewers described the absence of a joint security briefing and walk-through as a missed opportunity to have identified risks, clarified responsibilities and considered additional security measures.

However, the review concluded that no university employee or representative had acted in bad faith or shown "willful and wanton disregard" for anyone's safety.

Charlie Kirk was addressing about 3,000 people when he was shot in the neck

Kirk's family has previously accused the university of serious security failures and has filed a wrongful-death notice, a step that can precede legal action.

The family's lawyer, Brett Parkinson, said the independent report released on Friday backed up the concerns raised by Kirk's loved ones.

"The buck stopped with UVU leadership and law enforcement," Parkinson said in a statement to the Associated Press. "Justice for Charlie and his family requires true accountability for UVU's fatal shortcomings that day."

When asked for comment on the findings, Turning Point USA referred to Parkinson's statement.

The review makes numerous recommendations aimed at improving security for major campus events.

UVU President Jon Anderson said the university must "learn from the findings of this review, and follow through on its recommendations".

It has previously been reported that the campus police failed to conduct security procedures now common practice at high-profile events, including flying a drone to monitor rooftops or security screening like bag checks and metal detectors.

Kirk had been debating UVU students about US mass shootings, as part of a series of events across different university campuses, when he was shot in the neck shortly after noon. He was rushed to hospital but later pronounced dead.

His alleged killer, Tyler Robinson, has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder in connection with Kirk's death. Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty.

articles.title: Green shoots? Burnham cultivates rural links in attempt to ‘build back trust’ with farmers
articles.excerpt:
Ministers have been speaking to farming activists to try to build bridges after relations were soured by the tax changes introduced under Keir Stamer

As an arable farmer, Olly Harrison’s WhatsApp mes...
articles.body_text:
Ministers have been speaking to farming activists to try to build bridges after relations were soured by the tax changes introduced under Keir Stamer

As an arable farmer, Olly Harrison’s WhatsApp messages are normally concerned with the more mundane matters of working the land: logistics, supplies and the occasional chat about the weather.

So when a recent message came through from Andy Burnham, it was more than a little unexpected.

The personal touch wasn’t just the act of a politician on the campaign trail – Burnham was fighting the Makerfield byelection at the time – Harrison said it showed a change of approach to farmers.

“He’s trying to meet farmers, he wants to meet up,” said Harrison, who farms near Liverpool.

Under the Starmer administration farmers had been hit with new taxes, including a loathed inheritance tax. Harrison said the dialogue between the government and agricultural workers had been nonexistent.

And now? Burnham appears to have sown the seeds for a better relationship, telling farmers on a visit this summer that government had “long way to go to build back trust” with farmers and the UK needed to “guarantee our own food production”. Green shoots, perhaps.

Harrison was one of a group of activist farmers who took umbrage at the 2024 budget. His fellow protesters, who included Jeremy Clarkson, rolled furiously into Westminster on tractors after the chancellor’s announcement to yell and beep at No 10 and the Treasury.

Their protests garnered crowds of tens of thousands, arguing the new taxes would lead to the closure of farms as the tax bill would significantly outstrip revenue.

Since then, the group become a thorn in the government’s side, following former environment secretary Steve Reed when he spoke at farming events, to beep their tractor horns loud enough to drown him out.

Burnham’s team appears to have weighed the benefits of keeping this noisy, tractor-driving community of dissenters on side and is actively working to repair the fractured relationship.

It may already be yielding results, as there is no planned protest by farmers at this year’s budget. A bridge may have been built, but is by no means guaranteed to last.

Last year, a record 6,300 forestry, fishing and farming businesses closed, according to the Office for National Statistics. This has been linked by some to the tax changes, though extreme weather and rising inflation have undoubtedly played a part.

Former Labour cabinet minister Lord Blunkett recently said at a Countryside Alliance event: “It’s very strange because we’ve never won so many rural seats since 1945 – around 135 Labour MPs are either rural or semi-rural – and their voices need to be heard much more clearly.”

It seems Burnham is trying to do this. The Mail on Sunday recently reported that a U-turn on the inheritance tax is on the table for the next budget. Government sources have confirmed to the Guardian that it is a possibility, and that ministers are looking for a sweetener for farmers. This could be a reduction in inheritance tax, or more money for nature-friendly farming.

One rural Labour MP said: “There are other things you could do for farmers that could be significantly better than changing inheritance tax again – new money for farming would be great and also meaningful progress on procuring public food from British farmers.”

The farming budget that replaced EU subsidies has been a shambles. Earlier this week, thousands of farmers were left empty-handed with the government’s £253m annual budget spent in just six hours.

“I have had some very upset emails from farmers,” the MP said. “The current system creates an exclusionary aspect, for those who can afford a land agent to get the email in. We need a new system.”

They added that Starmer froze out rural MPs who questioned his decision on inheritance tax: “Under Keir it wasn’t just farmers who felt shut out, it was rural MPs too. There has been a step-change since Andy came in with the relationship with backbenchers.”

The new environment secretary, Angela Eagle, appointed by Burnham, has been on the road in recent weeks to visit farms and strike up a rapport with farmers.

Martin Williams, one of Harrison’s fellow activists, farms arable crops on the banks of the River Wye in Herefordshire. Eagle came to visit him in recent weeks: “It is surprising what you can achieve if people actually speak to each other,” he said. Of Burnham, he added: “He is a savvy politician, he knows that you can’t throw away a whole contingency of voters. It was very difficult to get any meaningful dialogue with government but under the new regime it has changed quite markedly.”

Harrison also had a visit from Eagle: “When Angela turned up it was just like I knew her. The Defra team said ‘she wants to know what’s going on and hear your opinion’, she brought policy advisers.”

It helped that the Defra secretary is a nearby MP: “Angela only lives over the river from me, we didn’t disagree on anything.”

Though Burnham and his team seem to have avoided a protest, they may have an uphill battle winning back the farming vote. A recent poll from the Country Land and Business Association found that 0% of farmers would vote Labour again.

Harrison said: “I’ve had a few comments saying don’t trust them, they haven’t got a vote left in the countryside, that is totally understandable. There are some farmers who are so angry still.”

But the government may have something left to fear from Jeremy Clarkson, who was recently spotted filming an episode of his popular Amazon show, Clarkson’s Farm, with David Cameron. The former prime minister issued a rare rebuke against the government, calling the inheritance tax on farm assets “stupid”. Clarkson declined to comment when the Guardian asked if, like Keir Starmer, Andy Burnham would be banned from his Cotswolds pub.

articles.title: PRESIDENT PAZ: Bolivia has rejected socialism and is open for business
articles.excerpt: Amid President Trump’s Western Hemisphere policy success, Bolivian Minister of the Presidency Fernando Aramayo says Bolivia is defending democracy, fighting organized crime and drawing White House sup...
articles.body_text:
Amid President Trump’s Western Hemisphere policy success, Bolivian Minister of the Presidency Fernando Aramayo says Bolivia is defending democracy, fighting organized crime and drawing White House support.

For nearly two decades, my country was governed by the Movement Toward Socialism. That period reshaped Bolivia’s economy, institutions, and relationship with the United States. Today, my government is taking a different direction: rebuilding confidence, strengthening institutions, opening the economy to investment, and creating more room for private enterprise and entrepreneurship.

When I took office, Bolivia’s Central Bank had only $51 million in reserves. Ten months later, reserves had risen to close to $1.2 billion, and our objective is to continue rebuilding them. Inflation remains high, fuel shortages have tested our people, and the work ahead is difficult. But the direction is clear: Bolivia is putting its economic house in order.

TRUMP ADMIN BACKS BOLIVIA STATE OF EMERGENCY AS LEFTIST EX-LEADER'S LOYALISTS FRACTURE NATION

During my campaign, I described our approach as "capitalism for everyone." By that I mean access to capital, the ability to invest, the freedom to build businesses, and the opportunity to create jobs and prosperity. Ideology does not put food on the table. Employment does. Production does. Investment does. Economic growth does.

Bolivia's President Rodrigo Paz delivers a speech in La Paz on June 3, 2026, after naming Ernesto Justiniano as defense minister following the resignation of Marcelo Salinas amid protests. (Claudia Morales/Reuters)

This new economic direction is also creating the basis for a new relationship with the United States. My discussions in New York with Secretary of State Marco Rubio reflected an important change in the relationship between our countries. Bolivia seeks cooperation with the United States based on mutual respect, economic opportunity, security, investment, and shared interests.

THE UNLIKELY SOUTH AMERICAN ALLY HELPING LEAD TRUMP'S DRUG CARTEL CRACKDOWN

The Trump administration has placed renewed attention on the Western Hemisphere, including economic strength, security, and cooperation among the nations of the Americas. Bolivia intends to engage constructively in that conversation while pursuing its own national interests and rebuilding relationships that can contribute to growth and stability.

Bolivia is open for business. But opening our economy does not mean selling our future.

RESOURCE-RICH NATION PRAISES US TIES AMID WASHINGTON-BEIJING CRITICAL MINERALS RACE

Our country possesses extraordinary natural wealth. We have natural gas, agricultural capacity, forests, and strategic minerals including lithium, copper, and tin that are increasingly important to the global economy. But we do not want to repeat the history of countries that exported their natural resources for decades while remaining poor.

Bolivia cannot simply remove minerals from the ground, ship them abroad, and watch other countries create the technology, manufacturing, jobs, and value from them. We want long-term partnerships built around employment, training, technology, infrastructure, productivity, and value added in Bolivia.

AFRICAN GROWTH BOOM FOLLOWS TRUMP PUSH TO REPLACE AID WITH TRADE

Our message to American and international investors is straightforward: Bolivia welcomes investment, capital, technology, and expertise. We want companies that are prepared to build, produce, employ, train, and grow alongside Bolivian workers and businesses.

As I told the United Nations, Bolivia wants to be open to the world with dignity.

US, SHIELD OF THE AMERICAS CONDEMN 'ONGOING EFFORTS' TO OVERTHROW BOLIVIA'S ELECTED PRESIDENT AMID UNREST

That means economic growth must also serve the Bolivian people. A stronger private sector does not mean abandoning social responsibility. Our objective is to create better jobs, stronger institutions, better education, greater security, and more opportunity. We must protect our forests and the Amazon, respect our Indigenous communities, and ensure that development creates tangible benefits for the people who live here.

The same principle applies to our young people. Bolivia’s future will depend on whether they can find purpose, work, and opportunity at home. Investment should help create that future.

TRUMP ALLY 'EL TIGRE' SWORN IN AS COLOMBIA'S NEW PRESIDENT AMID CONTINENT'S RIGHTWARD SHIFT

Bolivia’s economic direction is therefore based on a simple proposition: work with the United States, our neighbors, and the wider world; welcome productive investment; encourage entrepreneurship; expand private enterprise; and ensure that the wealth created in Bolivia also improves the lives of Bolivians.

Not everything has been resolved. We are only beginning.

But Bolivia will not remain on its knees. We will stand up, move forward, and build again.

Rodrigo Paz Pereira was elected president of Bolivia in 2025. A member of the Christian Democratic Party, he has pledged to move the South American nation away from socialism.
