Leigh Steinberg tells OutKick in a recent interview that Jim Harbaugh is the reason he isn't concerned about the Los Angeles Chargers slow start.

The Los Angeles Chargers are one of eight teams to begin the season 0-2 and are desperate for a spark.

Since the expansion of the playoff format in 2020, just 16% of 0-2 teams have reached the postseason. Even though the Chargers lost to the Arizona Cardinals and Las Vegas Raiders, two games in which they entered as heavy favorites, legendary agent Leigh Steinberg is not willing to write off the Chargers just yet.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

LEGENDARY AGENT LEIGH STEINBERG HAS SIMPLE ADVICE FOR GIANTS STAR JAXSON DART AFTER CRUSHING KNEE INJURY

Los Angeles Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh reacts from the sideline during the second half of an NFL football game against the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026, in Inglewood, Calif. (AP Photo/Caroline Brehman)

"At the end of the day, I think, Jim Harbaugh is one of the most effective and unique coaches in the history of pro football," Steinberg told OutKick in a recent interview.

"And the fact that they’ve lost two games, there are 15 left, and they’ll make adjustments, they can see what’s happening on the film, they understand that if you’re fumbling the ball multiple times and (committing) turnovers, but, I’d be very surprised if they weren’t in the playoff hunt."

The Chargers entered the season with hopes of contending in the AFC, with plenty of excitement surrounding Mike McDaniel as their offensive coordinator. In McDaniel’s first two games, the Chargers have a minus-4 turnover differential and have averaged just 14 points per game.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Los Angeles Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh speaks during a news conference after an NFL game against the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026, in Inglewood, Calif. (AP Photo/Caroline Brehman)

The Chargers have gone 11-6 in each of Harbaugh’s first two seasons at the helm, losing in the wild-card round each time. Right now, finishing 11-6 seems like a tall task for a Chargers team that has struggled, especially considering they have a difficult upcoming schedule.

In their next six games, the Chargers play the Buffalo Bills, Seattle Seahawks, Denver Broncos, Kansas City Chiefs, Los Angeles Rams and Houston Texans.

With the slow start and the grueling schedule, some are wondering if Harbaugh is already on the hot seat. Steinberg said any talk of Harbaugh, or any coach, being on the hot seat is premature.

Leigh Steinberg attends the 39th Annual Leigh Steinberg Super Bowl Party at Storek on Feb. 7, 2026 in San Francisco, California. (Jesse Grant/Getty Images)

"There’s not a ton of storylines at this point in the season, so people have a tendency to overreact to 2 weeks. It's only been two weeks, it's just too early to consign someone," Steinberg said.

While it’s still early in the season, if the offense doesn’t turn things around over the next six games and the Chargers find themselves a few games under .500 at the midpoint of the season, falling behind in a strong AFC West, it could get late early for Harbaugh and Los Angeles.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Steinberg, who was inducted into the California Sports Hall of Fame in 2017, has had many high-profile clients throughout his impressive career. Across football and baseball, Steinberg’s clients include Steve Bartkowski, Steve Young, Troy Aikman, Warren Moon, Bruce Smith, Thurman Thomas, Kordell Stewart, Jeff George, Ben Roethlisberger, Myron Rolle, Matt Leinart, Mark Brunell, Ricky Williams, Howie Long, Eric Karros and Dusty Baker, among others.

Ryan Canfield is a digital production assistant for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: NFL legend Brian Urlacher rips Colin Kaepernick, says protests wouldn't have flown in his locker room
articles.excerpt: Chicago Bears legend Brian Urlacher opens up about Colin Kaepernick kneeling during the national anthem, exposing how the controversy shattered NFL locker room unity and why he couldn't stomach those ...
articles.body_text:
Chicago Bears legend Brian Urlacher opens up about Colin Kaepernick kneeling during the national anthem, exposing how the controversy shattered NFL locker room unity and why he couldn't stomach those antics on his own team.

Colin Kaepernick's infamous protests during the 2016 NFL season are still talked about to this day, but Hall of Famer Brian Urlacher made it clear something like that wouldn't have flown if he was in the same locker room.

The legendary Chicago Bears linebacker talked about Kaepernick's knee-taking and locker room dynamics in general during an appearance on OutKick's "The Craig Carton Show."

Carton asked Urlacher if politics were a big thing in the Bears' locker room while he was playing in the league.

PATRIOTS LEGEND ROB GRONKOWSKI REVEALS THE IMPACT POLITICS HAS ON LOCKER ROOM DYNAMICS

Chicago Bears legend and Pro Football Hall of Famer Brian Urlacher said that Colin Kaepernick's infamous anthem protests would not have gone over well in his locker room. (Photo by Jonathan Daniel/Getty Images and Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images)

"No," Urlacher said. "Politics — I didn't even know what I was (politically) back then. I didn't care, man... You can't have the racial divide in the locker room. It's just not going to work. If you do, your team is going to be s---."

Urlacher pointed out that everyone in the room is coming together to work toward the same goal, but Kaepernick's anthem protests? That wouldn't have flown with him.

Colin Kaepernick and Eric Reid of the San Francisco 49ers kneel in protest during the national anthem before an NFL game against the Los Angeles Rams at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara, Calif., on Sept. 12, 2016. (Getty Images)

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"The thing with him taking a knee would have been really, really f---king hard for me to put up with in the locker room," he said. "That would have been something that would have probably been a line in the sand for me when it comes to stuff like that."

He and Carton both agreed that in the locker room, all that matters is that you're there, not how you got there; an idea that Carton said should probably be applied to society at large.

Brian Urlacher is honored with a Ring of Excellence ceremony for his recent induction into the Hall of Fame at Soldier Field. (Photo by Quinn Harris/Getty Images)

"We have to get along (in the locker room)," he said. "There are going to be spats, don't get me wrong. There are some times where you get into it with your teammates, but then literally 30 minutes later it's squashed. You're over it. You're moving on."

But again, that whole thing with Kaepernick was different. In fact, it turned him off from the league for years.

"I'd retired, so I was watching all this happen on TV, and we quit watching. There were probably two, two and a half, three years where we didn't watch football. I was like, as long as this s---'s taking place, I'm not watching. My wife was fully on board. She's all about that as well. So we just didn't watch pro football for a few years there because of all the s--- that was going on."

articles.title: UN adds 61 firms to settlements blacklist over alleged human rights violations against Palestinians
articles.excerpt:
Israel ‘categorically rejects’ publication and says businesses on database have committed no wrongdoing

The UN human rights office has added 61 more companies to a blacklist of firms that it says are...
articles.body_text:
Israel ‘categorically rejects’ publication and says businesses on database have committed no wrongdoing

The UN human rights office has added 61 more companies to a blacklist of firms that it says are involved in violating Palestinian human rights through business ties to Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

The vast majority of the total 214 companies, which are based in 11 countries, are Israeli. Five of the 158 companies listed last year were removed in the latest update.

The blacklist, first published in 2020, was born of a vote by the UN’s human rights council, which has no ability to force companies to act. Its main goal is to name and shame businesses with ties to the settlements.

It is unclear how the inclusion on the list has affected the companies financially.

“This report is another reminder to companies that they have human rights responsibilities and are expected to conduct due diligence to ensure that they do not become involved in human rights violations or abuses,” said Volker Türk, the UN human rights chief, in a statement.

Israel said it “categorically rejects” the publication. “This database is meant to serve as a blacklist against businesses that have committed no wrongdoing,” the Israeli diplomatic mission in Geneva said in a statement. “We call on friends not to yield to this ugly attempt to blacklist Israeli firms.”

The UN office said it had advised the companies of their listing and given them a right of reply.

The latest report comes as Israeli settlements in Palestinian areas have faced new scrutiny.

Earlier this month, Britain banned trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, where it says “settler terrorists” are carrying out “ethnic cleansing” of Palestinians. France and Canada announced they would take similar action.

articles.title: Pezeshkian says Iran ‘no longer trusts talks with Washington’
articles.excerpt: President Masoud Pezeshkian has told Al Jazeera that Iran no longer trusts negotiations with the United States after previous rounds of talks were followed by attacks and sanctions, as Tehran awaits a...
articles.body_text:
President Masoud Pezeshkian has told Al Jazeera that Iran no longer trusts negotiations with the United States after previous rounds of talks were followed by attacks and sanctions, as Tehran awaits a response to its latest proposal to end the war.

“We have no trust in the American side and do not know on what basis an understanding can be reached with it,” Pezeshkian told the Qatar-based broadcaster in an interview aired on Saturday.

Pezeshkian and Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi visited the US this week for the United Nations gathering of world leaders and proposed a deal that would end fighting in the US-Israel war on Iran and unblock the Strait of Hormuz within seven days.

Araghchi told reporters on Friday that initial steps would take four to five days, the Strait of Hormuz would reopen on the sixth day and “on day seven, the talks with the US will be started for the final deal on mutually agreed subjects,” referring to Iran’s nuclear programme.

Under the plan, Washington would lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, release an estimated $12bn in frozen Iranian assets and observe a ceasefire covering the region, including Lebanon and Yemen.

In return, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas passed before the war, and which has become Tehran’s main point of leverage.

Pezeshkian told Al Jazeera that mediators Qatar and Pakistan are conveying Iran’s messages to Washington. He said the negotiations are based on the previous memorandum of understanding (MoU) reached by the two sides in June, and the US must clarify its position on that agreement, which lapsed last month.

The war began in late February, when the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran that killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

Pezeshkian also denied that Iran was responsible for blocking the Strait of Hormuz, saying the US “closed the routes before us”. He described the closure as “a natural response when routes are cut off to Iran”.

He said the crisis could be resolved through negotiations rather than force, and that the waterway would reopen to commercial shipping if talks ended the war.

Pezeshkian called the US the aggressor in the conflict, saying Iran “has not attacked any country in 200 years”. He said the US and Israel had dragged regional countries into the war in the belief that the Iranian system “would collapse within days”.

“We withstood the American and Israeli attacks, and we will continue to stand firm,” he said, adding that neither the killing of an Iranian commander nor economic pressure had caused Iranians to retreat.

He said Israel and the US had attacked Iran from the airspace of Islamic countries, and that Iran targets bases used by US forces in the region because operations against it are launched from them. Tehran seeks nothing outside international law, he said, and responds only when others violate the rules.

Pezeshkian also linked the imposition of sanctions on Iran to the tactics used by Israel in its genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza.

“Those who deny Iranians medicine and raw materials are the same people who cut off food and water from Gaza,” he said, adding that anyone who believed Iranians could be targeted through sanctions had “miscalculated”.

Pezeshkian also said regional security could be achieved through cooperation among the region’s own countries. “We do not need a regional policeman,” he said.

He accused the US and Israel of seeking to pit Islamic countries against one another to control the region’s resources. He also said Saudi Arabia is capable of playing a role in uniting the Islamic world.

Regarding Yemen, where fighting has escalated between the Iran-aligned Houthi rebels and Yemen’s Saudi-backed government forces, he said the actions of the Houthis were not connected to Iran, and that Tehran stands in solidarity with “everyone subjected to injustice”.

He urged the Houthis and Saudi Arabia to resolve their differences through dialogue, saying “a brother should not fight his brother,” and offered Iran’s help in ending the dispute. “We will not be warmongers,” he said.

On domestic politics, Pezeshkian accused Iran’s “enemies” of trying to stir disagreements among Iranian officials, insisting the country is witnessing “unprecedented unity and cohesion”.

He said he had met twice with Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not appeared in public since the war began, including one meeting that lasted seven hours and covered pivotal issues. He pledged to overcome what he called “accumulated imbalances in Iran’s internal conditions”.

The US and Israel want to stop Iran from becoming self-reliant, he said, “but we will invest in our people”.

articles.title: Put down those textbooks and turn off the screens. Here is a great way for kids to learn
articles.excerpt: Manhattan Institute senior fellow Chris Rufo discusses 1619 Project founder Nikole Hannah-Jones admitting she regrets enrolling her daughter in a high-poverty public school in Brooklyn on 'America Rep...
articles.body_text:
Manhattan Institute senior fellow Chris Rufo discusses 1619 Project founder Nikole Hannah-Jones admitting she regrets enrolling her daughter in a high-poverty public school in Brooklyn on 'America Reports.'

It’s late September. Kids are firmly back in school; routines are established and reading lists set. But what exactly is on the menu? The usual textbooks, which, if they’re in a government school, are often written by committee (with an agenda), range from uninspiring to outright woke.

Or maybe most of your child’s school curriculum is delivered via lifeless and impersonal computer screens.

But there is an alternative, a source whose advocacy first transformed the task of educating children over one hundred years ago. Virtually unknown to public school parents, the British 19th-century reformer Charlotte Mason (1842-1923) has long been the hero of modern homeschooling in America, and the movement’s best-kept secret weapon.

WE GREW UP BEFORE SCREENS TOOK OVER. OUR KIDS DESERVE THAT CHANCE TOO

But her ideas and theories are not just applicable to the home-schooling community. Parents and educators can greatly benefit from Mason’s ideas about children and reading, which are even more relevant today.

Students who read the great books will find them far better than the dull stuff of textbooks. (Ryan McVay/iStock)

Creating a thirst for knowledge, and lifelong love of learning was Mason’s goal. If children developed an early hunger for ideas, she reasoned, it would sustain them through their lives. Mason believed that in addition to the proper vitamins and nutrients needed to thrive, children require ideas to chew on, to properly grow. And the source of these ideas, she reasoned, was not typical textbooks.

BEN CARSON, RILEY GAINES FIGHT SCRUBBING OF FAITH FROM KIDS' US HISTORY BOOKS FOR AMERICA'S 250TH

That’s a perspective as true today as it was in Mason’s time. Most if not all textbooks which children encounter in public schools are either bland by design, so as not to arouse controversy, or the opposite: brazenly geared to advance a woke agenda.

Mason believed that the best resource for the ideas that will benefit children most came from a regular exposure to great art, great music, and, above all, books of "literary quality" or great books. "For the best thought the world possesses is stored in books," she wrote in "Parents and Children." "Children must have books, living books ... the best is not too good for them; anything less than the best is not good enough."

DOLLY PARTON'S BELOVED LITERACY MISSION SEES SURGE OF SUPPORT AFTER COUNTRY ICON'S DEATH

Her idea of "living books" was about books written by a single author (not a committee), ones that actively engage the mind, imagination and spirit, rather than simply presenting factual material.

For example, a list of "living books" for early learners (grades 1-4) might include: "The Trumpet of the Swan," "Black Beauty," and "A Little Princess." Titles for middle schoolers include: "My Side of the Mountain," "Around the World in 80 Days," "To Kill a Mockingbird," and C.S. Lewis’s classic "Narnia" series.

CLASSICAL EDUCATION AND AI COULD RESHAPE HOW AMERICA PREPARES ITS CHILDREN

High school students can gain most from reading "Pride and Prejudice," "David Copperfield," and, "Through Gates of Splendor," as well as the "Lord of the Rings" trilogy.

Living books like these can spark kids’ curiosity, thanks to their authors’ genuine passion for their subject.

WILLIAM BENNETT, JON HAGE: AI CAN MIMIC A TEACHER, BUT IT CANNOT SHEPHERD A SOUL

Unlike textbooks, they use a compelling, even spellbinding style that draws the student into the plot and characters, triggering their imagination and emotions.

Her idea of "living books" was about books written by a single author (not a committee), ones that actively engage the mind, imagination and spirit, rather than simply presenting factual material.

Living books like "My Side of the Mountain" and "To Kill a Mockingbird" weave sometimes complex concepts and subjects into an approachable narrative, in ways that allow children to more easily connect and identify with the material. Like those of us who grew up with favorite books, children are bound to remember details and themes, long after the work has been returned to the shelf.

GEORGIA SCHOOL DISTRICT DEFENDS PULLING 'SEXUALLY EXPLICIT' BOOK DEPICTING CHILD RAPE AMID 'CENSORSHIP' CLAIMS

Living books often feature unfamiliar words and language that challenge young readers to expand their vocabulary. Contrary to what lazy teachers may think, old-fashioned forms of communicating in English, like Charles Dickens’s novels or even the King James Bible, don’t turn off young minds. They broaden and deepen a reader’s grasp of the English language, which is crucial for their intellectual, even moral, growth.

For instance, E. B. White, author of classics like "Charlotte’s Web," and "The Trumpet of the Swan," never hesitated to challenge his young readers with new words like "radiant" and "humble," because he believed, like Charlotte Mason, that children were smart, capable readers.

AMERICAN SCHOOLS COST MORE THAN EVER BUT OUR STUDENTS STILL KEEP FAILING

White once said, "Anyone who writes down to children is simply wasting his time. You have to write up, not down. Children are demanding. They are the most attentive, curious, eager, observant, sensitive, quick, and generally congenial readers on earth.... Children are game for anything. I throw them hard words and they backhand them across the net."

Finally, unlike typical textbooks, living books help students move from a passive learning mode to an active learning mode. Instead of simply memorizing what they need to know to pass a test, having students retell a story like "The Little Princess" in their own words, builds lasting communication and analytical skills.

Try some living books out on your children if you haven’t already. Books like Louisa May Alcott’s "Little Women" will teach them lessons about the importance of family, sacrifice, and generosity. Mark Twain’s "The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn" teaches about friendship, loyalty, and moral courage.

Charlotte Mason used to say, "Education is an atmosphere, a discipline, a life." If our current educators have abandoned that hopeful vision, turning to living books can restore it, not just for children, but for all of us.

Beth Herman is a visiting fellow at Independent Women's Education Freedom Center. She is completing her master's degree in Classical Education at the University of Dallas.

CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM ARTHUR HERMAN

Arthur Herman is a historian and Pulitzer Prize finalist. His latest book is "Founder’s Fire: From 1776 to the Age of Trump" (Center Street, April 21,2026).  Follow him on X at @ArthurLHerman.

articles.title: Wave of overlooked 'left-wing' lawsuits could come with an unexpected price tag for Americans
articles.excerpt: Heritage Foundation Chief Economist EJ Antoni and Power The Future founder Daniel Turner spoke to Fox News Digital about their new report estimating the potential cost to American families if climate ...
articles.body_text:
Heritage Foundation Chief Economist EJ Antoni and Power The Future founder Daniel Turner spoke to Fox News Digital about their new report estimating the potential cost to American families if climate lawsuits and climate "superfund" laws succeed.

FIRST ON FOX: American households could end up paying $1,465 more per year on average in energy costs if "anti-energy" climate lawsuits against oil and gas companies are successful, according to a new report first obtained by Fox News Digital.

Americans will "pay a lot more" if the far-left "get their way," warned Heritage Foundation chief economist E.J Antoni, who co-authored the report with Power The Future founder Daniel Turner.

Hundreds of lawsuits and other state-level "climate superfund" laws could increase the cost of gasoline, electricity and other everyday necessities Americans rely on, the report estimates.

SUPREME COURT CAN RESTORE SANITY AND STOP THE LEFT’S RADICAL CLIMATE AGENDA

North Dakota's oil boom transformed the state's economy and now generates billions of dollars in tax revenue each year. (Jim West/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

The new analysis, obtained by Fox News Digital, comes as the Supreme Court prepares to hear a closely-watched lawsuit next month out of Boulder, Colorado, which could drastically shape the future of climate litigation.

"If those folks on the radical left wing who are anti-energy, if they get their way, your costs are going to go up," Antoni told Fox News Digital. "Your household is going to pay a lot more. The energy is going to get much more expensive."

"You may think it's bad now, but it will get significantly worse," he added.

The report estimates energy companies could face an additional $194 billion in annual costs, which the authors argue would ultimately be passed on to consumers through higher prices rather than absorbed entirely by companies or their shareholders.

Those costs could add roughly 41 cents to a gallon of gasoline and increase residential electricity rates by about 8.6%, according to the analysis.

"Every single time a company is sued, yes, they pay some damages, but ultimately they will just charge people more for their product to recoup those losses," Turner told Fox News Digital.

LAWSUITS COST EVERY AMERICAN HOUSEHOLD THOUSANDS OF DOLLARS. SUPREME COURT CAN HELP

Gas prices are shown, Tuesday, March 31, 2026, in Detroit. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya)

The report examined more than 300 pending lawsuits, three state "climate superfund" laws, 12 state legislative proposals and one federal bill. Its estimate reflects a "full-success scenario" in which all of those measures prevail; it does not predict that they will.

The analysis counted each lawsuit only once and excluded duplicate filings. In fact, Antoni said the estimate may be conservative because some lawsuits do not specify the damages they are seeking, leaving potential court awards open-ended.

The legal efforts include New York’s Climate Change Superfund Act, which was blocked by a federal judge in August, and the Supreme Court’s pending Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County case.

That case could determine whether state and local governments can pursue climate lawsuits against fossil fuel companies in state court.

GAVIN NEWSOM'S 'HIDDEN CLIMATE TAX' HITTING AMERICANS NATIONWIDE, LAWMAKER WARNS

People march as they take part in a strike to demand action on the global climate crisis on September 20, 2019 in New York City. (ALEX KENT/AFP via Getty Images)

Turner argued the lawsuits could also shift responsibility away from state and local leaders.

"The concern about these superfund lawsuits is that they absolve elected leaders from doing the bad, boring part of governing, which is infrastructure and mitigation strategies," he said.

Despite the rise in climate lawsuits and state "superfund" laws, Antoni said the issue has largely flown under the radar.

"It really is important that we start ringing the alarm bells now before these things actually come to pass and American families have to foot the bill for it," he said.

Kiera McDonald is a Production Assistant for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Mistress may have handed prosecutors missing ‘why’ in ‘American Idol’ alum’s wife murder case: expert
articles.excerpt:
Fox News contributor Josh Ritter explains why the latest testimony could influence jurors, from motive and text messages to the missing murder weapon.

The explosive testimony of Caleb Flynn's former ...
articles.body_text:
Fox News contributor Josh Ritter explains why the latest testimony could influence jurors, from motive and text messages to the missing murder weapon.

The explosive testimony of Caleb Flynn's former mistress may have handed Ohio prosecutors a critical piece of their murder case against the former "American Idol" contestant – a potential answer to why he would allegedly kill his wife, a former prosecutor told Fox News Digital.

"Motive. She provides a motive," Josh Ritter, a former prosecutor, criminal defense attorney and Fox News contributor, said of Alleigha Botner's testimony. "She gives jurors a reason for why would this man murder his wife."

"She seems like she was, by all accounts, a very nice woman," Ritter said about Ashley Flynn. "She's the mother of his children. Yes, he wanted out of the marriage."

"Perhaps there was some financial gain in the idea of life insurance, but, you know, jurors oftentimes struggle with that question," he added.

DAD OF 'AMERICAN IDOL' CONTESTANT'S SLAIN WIFE MADE EERIE GOOGLE SEARCH AFTER HEARING OF HER MURDER

Caleb Flynn becomes emotional in court during his murder trial in Ohio. Flynn is accused of killing his wife, Ashley Flynn, in February 2026 and staging the scene to look like a break-in. (COURTESY: WKEF)

Flynn is accused of fatally shooting his wife in the back of the head inside their Ohio home on Feb. 16 and staging the scene to look like an intruder had broken in. He has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and other charges.

Botner, who testified she carried on an affair with Flynn for roughly a year and a half, spent two days walking jurors through many of the 107,000-plus messages exchanged during their relationship.

NEW JERSEY MAN ACCUSED OF KILLING WIFE WITH BARBELL ALLEGEDLY CONFESSED IN MESSAGES TO RELATIVES: REPORT

Some contained explicit discussions about Ashley's death.

In one May 2025 message, Flynn allegedly wrote, "If I could literally kill her and not go to hell, I would do it in a heartbeat."

RUSSIAN SPIES ORCHESTRATED $40K MURDER PLOT IN NATION’S CAPITAL, US ALLEGES

Days later, he allegedly wrote, "I hate her, loathe her. I want her dead."

In June, Flynn allegedly told Botner, "Please hire someone to take [her] out. I need you in my life, I need you."

Alleigha Botner wipes away tears while testifying about messages exchanged with Caleb Flynn during his murder trial in Ohio. (CREDIT: WKEF)

SCOTT PETERSON'S DEFENSE LOSES BID TO INTRODUCE WITNESS TESTIMONY IN LONG-RUNNING FIGHT TO OVERTURN CONVICTION

Botner responded, "So tempting. I can't live without you. And I've had this thought so often lately. How do we figure this out?"

Botner also became emotional while reading one of her own messages to Flynn, expressing regrets that she wished she never wrote it.

ALEX MURDAUGH LAWYERS ALLEGE ‘FABRICATED’ EVIDENCE WAS USED TO SECURE MURDER INDICTMENTS

"I want to kill her, Caleb," she had written.

"That makes two of us," Flynn allegedly responded.

Body camera footage shows Caleb Flynn reacting to his wife’s murder inside their home in Tipp City, Ohio on Feb. 16, 2026. (Tipp City Police Department)

ALEX MURDAUGH MAKES 'EXPLOSIVE' BID TO BLOW UP MURDER CASE HINGING ON DNA, DIRTY MONEY AND LIES: EXPERT

Ritter said it is the substance of those exchanges – rather than simply the existence of the affair or sheer volume of messages – that could prove significant for prosecutors.

"It's the idea that he's even discussing her being dead," Ritter said. "He went as far as to saying I literally would kill her. That's far beyond someone voicing their frustrations and venting to a lover that I wish my wife wasn't around, I wish she would leave, I wish we could get a divorce."

"This is saying you want that person dead, that, in your view, that is your solution to the problem that you have," he added.

Ashley Flynn, a Tipp City Schools substitute teacher and volleyball coach, was found dead in her Ohio home. (Tipp City Schools)

The messages grew particularly significant as prosecutors moved jurors closer to the night Ashley was killed.

FLORIDA PLASTIC SURGEON FOUND GUILTY OF MURDERING ATTORNEY WHO VANISHED FROM BLOODY OFFICE

Botner testified that Flynn told her in an August message he had stayed up until 4 a.m. "literally thinking of ways to kill her and not go to jail."

Months later, Botner gave Flynn a Jan. 11 ultimatum to leave Ashley or she would end their relationship. When he failed to do so, Botner cut off communication until Feb. 14 – just two days before Ashley's death.

By the night of Feb. 15, the two were communicating again.

Botner testified that Flynn discussed his plans for the following day, including telling family members about the divorce and obtaining a burner phone.

Ashley and Caleb Flynn in an undated photo with their two children. (GoFundMe)

Shortly after midnight, Flynn allegedly wrote to Botner, "It's happening."

He then wrote, "February 16th – day I'll never forget."

"You're about to be free," Botner responded.

Those were some of the final messages Flynn sent Botner before she learned Ashley had been killed, she testified.

Ritter pointed to that timing as among the most significant evidence Botner brought to the prosecution's case.

He noted that Flynn had spent months allegedly talking about wanting Ashley dead before the messages reached the eve of her killing.

"The day before the murder takes place, he tells his mistress that tomorrow is going to be a big day, that he chooses her," Ritter explained. "He's made a decision and that tomorrow, meaning February 16th, the date his wife was murdered, will be a day that he will never forget."

Alleigha Botner testifies Wednesday in the Ohio murder trial of former "American Idol" contestant Caleb Flynn. Prosecutors say Botner had an affair with Flynn before his wife, Ashley Flynn, was killed. (CREDIT: WKEF)

But Ritter said the same enormous volume of messages prosecutors are using against Flynn also gives his attorneys an argument.

The defense can contend prosecutors have cherry-picked the most damaging statements from more than 100,000 messages exchanged during an intense affair and stripped them of the broader context of two people using exaggerated and sometimes ugly language.

Flynn's attorneys can also argue that when he talked about what would happen Feb. 16, he was referring to finally leaving Ashley – not killing her.

WATCH: Caleb Flynn had ominous response when mistress said ‘I want to kill her’

"That could be true," Ritter said. "It could be that he is just the unluckiest man on earth, that the day he tells his mistress he's going to announce to his wife that he's leaving her after months of saying that he wants her dead, that some random home burglar happens to break in with no signs of forced entry, goes to his vehicle, knows exactly where to find his handgun, marches upstairs, puts two bullets in the back of his wife's head while she's sleeping, and leaves the rest of the house undisturbed."

During cross-examination Thursday, Flynn's attorneys began putting Botner's own language before the jury.

"I'm so done with you. You have murdered my heart," Botner acknowledged writing Flynn during one argument. "I hope you're glad you took my virginity and also my heart and stomped all over it. Enjoy your marriage. I'm done."

The defense also has another potentially important distinction to emphasize, Ritter said. Despite Flynn's repeated statements about wanting Ashley dead, he never explicitly told Botner he intended to carry out her killing.

"There was never an explicit mention of, 'I'm going to do it, I'm gonna follow through on it,'" Ritter said.

Caleb and Ashley Flynn are pictured in an undated photograph. (Ashley Flynn/Facebook)

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"I think they are also going to concentrate on the idea, as they have since opening statements, that this might have been a rush to judgment, that once police uncovered the affair, they stopped their investigation," Ritter said. "And once they knew that he was planning on leaving his wife, they thought, 'Well, that's enough for us. We're not going to pursue other leads.'"

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

"I'm not saying that's a convincing argument, but I'm saying that that is at least something for them to stand on and mount a defense on his behalf," he added.

WATCH: Caleb Flynn mistress drops bombshells in dramatic testimony

The defense can also point to the absence of the alleged murder weapon, an eyewitness to the shooting and gunshot residue on Flynn.

Botner testified, however, that Flynn had previously shown her a gun he kept inside the center console of his truck, though she could not remember what it looked like.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"In an ideal world, would the prosecution want the murder weapon? Sure," Ritter said. "But ... it's something that the defense is obviously going to lean into."

But for Ritter, Botner's testimony ultimately comes back to the question prosecutors hope jurors will ask when they consider the killing – why?

"Motive," Ritter said. "She provides motive."

Greg Wehner is a reporter for Fox News Digital covering U.S. news and crime, with a focus on breaking developments, law enforcement, public safety and major stories shaping communities across the country.

articles.title: Work intensifying on UK laws to stamp out concert ticket touts, say sources
articles.excerpt:
Artists including Tinie Tempah and the Smiths’ drummer Mike Joyce ramp up pressure on government to keep its pledge to outlaw for-profit resales

The government has stepped up work on new laws to stop...
articles.body_text:
Artists including Tinie Tempah and the Smiths’ drummer Mike Joyce ramp up pressure on government to keep its pledge to outlaw for-profit resales

The government has stepped up work on new laws to stop ticket touts fleecing fans, as the prime minister came under pressure from artists including the drummer from the Smiths, one of his favourite bands.

Keir Starmer said last year that the government would “stop fans from being ripped off” by outlawing the for-profit resale of tickets on sites such as Viagogo and StubHub, a pledge Labour first made in its 2024 election manifesto.

Despite support from a host of globally renowned artists, including Radiohead, Dua Lipa and Coldplay, the measure was not included in this year’s king’s speech, prompting concern among music industry figures that the proposal had been shelved.

But multiple sources told the Guardian that the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) has assembled a sizeable “bill team”, a group of civil servants who are drafting the policy and will help shepherd it through parliament.

They are understood to be considering ways to mitigate the risk that touts and resale platforms simply base themselves offshore to bypass any new legislation.

The culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, told the House of Commons this month that Andy Burnham “feels particularly passionate” about the issue and the government would treat it as a priority. Nandy is due to give a speech at Labour conference on Wednesday, at which she could provide further detail.

On Friday, industry figures and artists including the rapper Tinie Tempah and the Smiths’ drummer Mike Joyce called on the prime minister to act fast, citing new evidence of touts targeting small venues in Greater Manchester.

Research examined 300 events across 13 venues where tickets were being touted on Viagogo, including Band On The Wall, Gorilla, YES, Rebellion, New Century and the White Hotel.

All were advertised at significantly over cost price, while some did not feature information about the seller, an apparent breach of competition rules. Under government plans, companies would face much tougher penalties for failing to enforce these rules.

Other tickets appeared to be “speculative”, meaning that they had been fraudulently listed by touts who do not have them but hope to procure some once they have agreed a sale.

The most expensive was £5,899 for Mica Millar’s show at New Century – a 19,728% mark-up.

Tickets to a 40th anniversary celebration of the Smiths’ The Queen Is Dead, featuring a conversation between Joyce and the producer Stephen Street, were being touted for £549 each.

Joyce said it was “time to stop this for good”, while Tempah said fans and artists deserved better than to see tickets “siphoned away by people who contribute nothing to live music but are happy to profit from it”.

Just three touts – based in Latvia, North America and Germany – were responsible for more than 75% of the listings, research by the music industry group FanFair Alliance found. Viagogo dispute the claim, saying the proportion held by the trio was significantly lower.

Viagogo also listed tickets for tiny, obscure events, including an evening with the “world’s greatest psychic” in Inverness, a rum tasting in Devizes, and stargazing in Tavistock.

The company said actual sale prices were much lower than the high-priced listings identified by FanFair Alliance.

“Viagogo takes its obligations under the law seriously and is fully compliant in the UK. Our policies prohibit speculative listings,” it added.

If the government does go ahead with a ban on ticket touting, it would bring the UK in line with Ireland, which outlawed touting in 2021.

At present, the unauthorised resale of football tickets is illegal across the UK.

Resale of concert or theatre tickets without authorisation is permitted, although individual touts have been prosecuted and jailed in rare instances where they have been judged to have committed fraud.

Fans lost £60m to touts between Labour’s announcement of the policy and April this year, the telecoms company and venue sponsor O2 has estimated, with fans of acts including Olivia Dean, Bad Bunny and Ariana Grande “fleeced” by markups of up to 1,000%.

The Guardian has repeatedly exposed exploitative tactics in secondary ticketing, including speculative selling and the use by touts of specialist software to hoover up tickets and flip them for profit, often via sites such as StubHub and Viagogo.

A DCMS spokesperson said: “We are fully committed to stamping out ticket touting for good. For too long, fans have been ripped off and we’re determined to right that wrong.

“That’s why we are bringing forward draft legislation in this parliamentary session to ensure that our measures are truly effective, enforceable and future-proof and fans get the protection and security they have always deserved.”

articles.title: We followed five people in Gaza from dawn to dusk – this is what the headlines don’t tell us
articles.excerpt:
Behind the stories of bombings and mass deaths, the everyday challenges facing Palestinians living under siege portray a quieter tragedy we rarely hear

What does it take to make a morning cup of tea ...
articles.body_text:
Behind the stories of bombings and mass deaths, the everyday challenges facing Palestinians living under siege portray a quieter tragedy we rarely hear

What does it take to make a morning cup of tea in Gaza?

For Alaa Hessi, in her final month of pregnancy, this small ritual begins with a calculation of gas rations. Her family gets a ration of 6kg of gas every three months – enough to heat a pot for 18 precious minutes a day. That’s needed for cooking – so for tea, a fire must be built instead.

For 12-year-old Ramadan, the process begins with a hunt for anything flammable, in an environment where there is almost no wood left. He scouts through the sand dunes where he lives, snaps off a few twigs from a thorn bush, and feeds the flames with pieces of discarded plastic that wash up on the beach.

Before you boil the kettle, though, there is the matter of the water – with none running, the question is whether a water truck visits your area that day, and if not, how far you must walk to find it. Then there is transporting that water – how will Ramadan store it, given all of his family’s large water containers have been chewed through by rats? And how does a small boy carry the weight of it – enough liquid for a family to wash, brush teeth, cook with and drink through the next 30C summer day?

Finally, the water is boiling, but still there is the question of whether you even have tea or coffee or sugar to brew. Holding the paper bag of rationed sugar sparks a memory of what those goods have sometimes cost to acquire. Crouched over the teapot, Ramadan recalls last year’s famine, when aid points became death traps, and he and his brother risked everything to sprint for a bag of flour or sugar. He remembers the boys he saw shot beside him, because they moved too soon or too late.

Most of the headlines we encounter about Gaza are the extreme events: bombings, mass deaths, targeted assassinations. These demand attention.

There are some things, however, that rarely make the headlines, but have come to define life in Gaza. They are grinding, cruel realities that only really emerge when you inspect the minutia of a day – like a cup of tea. Over the course of this week, we documented the daily routines and mundane tasks of five ordinary Palestinians: a child, a pregnant woman, a teacher, a skateboarder and a grandmother. We followed them from sunrise to dusk, through the small, ordinary moments that rarely make international news – and through them, hoped to get a different, deeper understanding of what life is like now for Gaza’s people.

There is a lot you can understand from the anatomy of a day in Gaza. One thing that comes sharply into focus is the effect of dismantling or withholding those things – higher education, books, arts, museums, hobbies, musical instruments – that take human life beyond pure survival.

Israel continues to control everything that passes into Gaza, deciding how many calories it will allocate to its citizens, how much gas can be eked out to heat a minimum of hot meals.

Along with restricting the essentials required for life, the blockade bans a plethora of ordinary objects from entering Gaza, classing them as “dual use” items that could be used by Hamas. The blacklist and its criteria are opaque, arbitrary and ever-changing. At various times they have blocked the import of ventilator machines, medications for cancer, wedding dresses, sewing machines, toys, musical instruments, spices, dates and crutches.

From the story of Rajab al-Reefi’s day, we learn how the ban on skateboards has reverberated through his life. The 30-year-old has spent the past five years running Gaza Skate Team, a youth club that teaches children how to skateboard. During the war, their weekly gatherings became a lifeline and outlet for displaced children. Even after their skatepark was demolished, the team continued, posting videos of landing tricks on the rubble, kickflips executed on collapsed beams of concrete and tangled metal pylons.

But skateboards only have a lifespan of a couple of years: one by one, their layers snapped, wheel bearings wore out, parts salvaged from one broken board could no longer be fitted to another. With none left, the club went on a salvage mission, to dig some equipment from the rubble of a bombed building. Now, they have a handful of working boards again, and the girls are back to skating. But even these boards are on their last legs. When they wear out, there is nothing coming to replace them.

A skateboard is not essential to live – its absence will not make headlines like the systematic deprivation of food. But their absence illuminates the nature of the blockade in a fuller way: its random cruelties, the curtailing of opportunities for lightness, fun, self expression.

Still, against the odds, each person finds ways in their day to keep hold of the things that make them feel human. Prof Mahmoud Seydam wires a solar panel to power a laptop, uploading lectures over WhatsApp and taking oral presentations instead of written exams – battling to provide an education with no paper, no notebooks, no university campus. Alaa Hessi does her best to prepare a safe crib for her baby, in a tent pitched above the rubble where her three children were killed in a strike. Mansoura Ibrahim Mohammed Abdel Dayem, living in the back of a truck, tells her grandchildren stories of their history. Ramadan watches the ocean and dreams of becoming a lifeguard.

You can read all five of their days here.

articles.title: Thomas Jefferson letter goes on the market – containing a prescient warning for Trump today
articles.excerpt:
Third US president wrote in 1787 about importance of peace, paying off debt and supporting agriculture

A remarkably prescient letter written by Thomas Jefferson, the third US president, advising how ...
articles.body_text:
Third US president wrote in 1787 about importance of peace, paying off debt and supporting agriculture

A remarkably prescient letter written by Thomas Jefferson, the third US president, advising how the newly created country could prosper, has been put up for sale by a private collector. The handwritten document from 1787 warns specifically against many of the missteps Donald Trump has taken to drag down his own second term of office.

Written in Paris, where Jefferson was the fledgling government’s minister to France, the note to David Rittenhouse, a friend and fellow member of the American Philosophical Society, muses on the priorities and principles he believed future presidents should follow.

Previously on display at Texas A&M University, the letter and a book described as “a major European scientific work”, an accompanying gift from Jefferson to Rittenhouse, have a guide price of $285,000 through the Raab Collection, a Pennsylvania-based dealer in historical artifacts and documents.

“Peace should be our plan, and the payment of our debts, improvement of our constitutions and extension of agriculture our principal objects,” Jefferson wrote, sharing his thoughts about that year’s landmark federal convention in Philadelphia, later known as the constitutional convention, which debated and signed the US constitution.

Almost 240 years later, Trump, who has frequently hailed Jefferson as one of his political heroes, and installed a lifesize bronze statue of him in the White House Rose Garden in July to mark the US semiquincentennial, appears to have eschewed every element of his predecessor’s advice.

His hugely unpopular war in Iran endures; the national debt has surpassed $40tn for the first time; Trump’s “blitzkrieg” on the constitution continues; and he is at odds with American farmers over his administration’s treatment of the agricultural sector.

Nathan Raab, president of the Raab Collection, said it was difficult not to draw parallels between Jefferson’s caution contained in a highly personal document drafted barely a decade after the dawn of the new nation, and the volatility of politics in 2026.

“Leaving out the various partisan positions, the prescience here is that the same issues that the founding fathers were dealing with during the constitutional convention of the founding of our country are issues that still make headlines today,” he said.

“Things change, yet things stay the same, and here we are confronting many of the same issues that were on the lips of our founding fathers, or the tip of their quills, back in 1787.

“These are fundamental issues that, really, have faced our country for a long time. Of all the issues that have come and gone – isolation, war, peace – on the other end spending and debt have remained.”

Jefferson’s letter covers more ground than only his thoughts on the nation’s future direction. He shares with Rittenhouse, a fellow scientist and avid astronomer who built precision telescopes and early models of the solar system, his love of “the west”, and fear of another conflict with England four years after the end of the revolutionary war.

“Digging out of a hole of debt, funding not only the war debts but also the creation of this new country, was something that was very much an issue,” Raab said.

“What I love about this letter is it’s kind of a general warning. He’s not saying, ‘So and so said this, and therefore we must counter with this message.’ He’s giving in one broad stroke what he feels should be the priorities of the convention and the country.

“He kept in contact with people who were involved in the convention and was in the loop as much as you could be when a letter took three weeks or so to reach England. But he certainly didn’t have updated information, which is illustrated by the fact that the day he wrote this letter, the convention finished.

“He had no way of knowing. He wouldn’t know for weeks.”

Raab’s company has handled numerous Jefferson documents previously, including the sale in 2024 of a letter written in 1802 revealing his precarious financial situation, and last year’s uncovering of a note he wrote to Virginia’s then governor Benjamin Harrison in 1783 expounding the rights of citizens to bear arms in revolutionary causes.

But Raab said he has never seen anything as impressive as the letter and book given to Rittenhouse.

“This is at the very top,” he said. “The breadth of knowledge that [Jefferson] brought to this letter, the many subjects in which he is completely conversant. He’s talking to a prominent scientist as well.

“The important warning that he offers at the end is just so relevant today, it’s impossible to miss. I think it’s intentional that he saved that to the end of the letter. And the idea that Jefferson, a very famous book buyer and collector, is sending books to another founding father, David Rittenhouse, and the book is still together with the letter, that’s just incredible.”

articles.title: Delivery drones could be waiting before you even order
articles.excerpt:
FOX Business correspondent Madison Alworth reports on drone food delivery services launching in New Jersey on ‘America Reports.’

Your next food delivery could start moving before you even place the o...
articles.body_text:
FOX Business correspondent Madison Alworth reports on drone food delivery services launching in New Jersey on ‘America Reports.’

Your next food delivery could start moving before you even place the order. Flytrex is rolling out a system in Dallas-Fort Worth that sends drones to restaurant rooftops ahead of expected demand. AI predicts which locations are likely to get busy, then positions an aircraft nearby. If the prediction is right, the drone is already waiting when your food is ready. Flytrex says its new Rooftop Dock and predictive fleet positioning can cut its own delivery costs by 60%. The company also says customer delivery times can drop by half. The idea makes a lot of sense. Stop wasting time sending a drone to the restaurant after the food is ready. So how does Flytrex know where to put a drone before anyone orders, and how could this expand beyond Texas?

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Get Better Healthcare With AI replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare With AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay now at CyberGuyLive.com

PILOTLESS CARGO AIRCRAFT COULD CHANGE HOW PACKAGES MOVE

Flytrex is rolling out AI-powered drone positioning in Dallas-Fort Worth, sending aircraft to restaurant rooftops before customers place orders. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Flytrex uses machine-learning models to study past demand, location and the time of day. The software also looks at other activity across its delivery network. It then predicts which restaurants are most likely to receive upcoming orders. Instead of leaving every available drone at a central location, Flytrex can send aircraft closer to restaurants before customers order anything. That could make a big difference during busy meal periods. A pizza restaurant that usually sees a rush around dinner time could already have a drone waiting nearby. Once an order comes through and the kitchen finishes the food, the aircraft can get moving quickly. The current process can take longer. An operator may have to send a drone from another location after the restaurant has the order. The aircraft then flies to the restaurant before it can start the customer delivery. Flytrex wants to cut out that extra trip.

Once Flytrex decides where a drone should wait, the aircraft lands on its Rooftop Dock. The company says the system can go on an existing rooftop or another elevated area near the restaurant. According to Flytrex, the setup does not require additional real estate or structural changes. The company also says it can operate without placing a Flytrex employee at each restaurant. After the drone lands, it shuts down its motors and waits. When the food is ready, the aircraft lowers a hook into position. A restaurant employee clips the packaged order onto it without handling the drone. Then the aircraft takes off and heads directly toward the customer. That also removes the need for someone to carry the food to a separate drone launch site. Flytrex co-founder and CEO Amit Regev says those last few hundred feet between the restaurant kitchen and the aircraft have been one of the harder parts of drone delivery. "The truly challenging part has never been the flight; it's the last few hundred feet between the kitchen and the aircraft," Regev said.

Sending a drone to a restaurant before an order arrives could save more than time. Flytrex says its new setup cuts its cost per delivery by 60%. The company also says it can reduce customer delivery times by half. The drone no longer has to make a separate pickup flight from a central location. Meanwhile, restaurant workers can load the order without a dedicated Flytrex employee standing there. That could let each aircraft handle more deliveries over the course of a day. There is one big variable, though. The AI needs to put the drone in the right place. Customer demand can change quickly. Weather can shift ordering patterns. A local event could suddenly make one restaurant much busier than expected. If a drone ends up waiting at the wrong location, Flytrex may have to move it again.

Flytrex is launching the technology at active merchant locations across Dallas-Fort Worth. The company says it is also installing the system at more than 100 additional sites. That makes North Texas an important test for something Flytrex wants to expand much further. The company says it has completed more than 250,000 U.S. deliveries. It has also been building relationships with some of the biggest names in food delivery. In 2025, Uber invested in Flytrex through a partnership focused on Uber Eats orders. We covered that move when Uber Eats began preparing for drone deliveries.

Flytrex also partnered with DoorDash in Dallas-Fort Worth. DoorDash has since expanded its own drone ambitions. We recently covered how DoorDash received FAA approval for its commercial drone delivery operation.

CLEVELAND CLINIC LAUNCHES PRESCRIPTION DRONE DELIVERY

Flytrex says its Rooftop Dock system could cut its delivery costs by 60% and customer delivery times by half. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Flytrex has another important piece in place as it looks beyond Texas. The company received Federal Aviation Administration approval for beyond visual line of sight operations, also known as BVLOS. That allows Flytrex to conduct approved flights without requiring a visual observer to keep each aircraft in direct sight throughout the trip. Instead, Flytrex can monitor multiple drones remotely from an operations center under the conditions of its authorization. Flytrex says the approval gives it a path toward expanding into the 37 largest U.S. metropolitan areas. That does not mean rooftop drone delivery will appear across all 37 markets at once. Flytrex still has to build out its network as it expands. The new rooftop system gives the company a setup it hopes to repeat from one market to the next.

The rooftop system comes after several other moves from Flytrex. In April 2026, the company introduced its Sky2 delivery drone through a partnership with Little Caesars. The aircraft can carry up to 8.8 pounds, enough to handle two large pizzas. Flytrex also opened a manufacturing facility in Pilot Point, Texas. The company says the site can produce about 1,000 drones per year. Now Flytrex is tackling the next problem. Building more drones only gets you so far if those aircraft spend too much time traveling to pickup locations. Putting them closer to the restaurants before orders arrive could keep more of that fleet moving toward customers.

If Flytrex gets this right, you could spend less time staring at a delivery timer. The drone may already be waiting at the restaurant when your food is ready, so it can head toward your home almost immediately. That could also mean your meal spends less time sitting around before pickup. Then there is the cost. Flytrex says the system cuts its own delivery costs by 60%. The company has not said whether those savings will eventually lead to lower fees for customers, but a cheaper delivery model could make drone delivery easier to expand. Don't expect a drone hovering over your takeout spot tomorrow. Flytrex is starting in Dallas-Fort Worth, and expanding this kind of service will take time. The bigger takeaway is what happens before the drone ever takes off. If AI can put the aircraft where the next order is likely to happen, Flytrex could make the whole process faster without asking customers to do anything differently.

CHINA’S GRIP ON RARE-EARTH MAGNETS COULD CRUSH US DRONE INDUSTRY BEFORE IT GROWS

AI predicts which restaurants are likely to get orders, allowing Flytrex drones to wait nearby before food is ready for pickup. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

What gets my attention here is how simple the problem sounds once Flytrex points it out. The drone may be fast in the air, but that does not help much if it has to spend part of the delivery flying to the restaurant first. Moving drones ahead of demand could change that. The AI looks for where orders are likely to come from, while the rooftop dock gives the aircraft somewhere to wait. If Flytrex can get those predictions right consistently, it could cut a lot of wasted time out of each delivery. Dallas-Fort Worth should give us a good sense of whether this works beyond a handful of restaurants. Flytrex says more than 100 additional installations are underway, which should give the company plenty of chances to prove whether those big claims about speed and cost hold up.

Would faster food delivery be worth having drones waiting on restaurant rooftops around your community, or would you rather keep all that buzzing out of your neighborhood? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.
