TSA officers rec...
articles.body_text:
Airline industry expert Gary Leff of Texas breaks down an incident involving two passengers who acknowledged attempting to sneak a prohibited item past security at Dallas Love Field.

TSA officers recently made an unexpected find inside a passenger's checked bag after an Xbox triggered an alarm.

The unusual discovery was announced by the Transportation Security Administration (TSA).

The incident occurred this month as a passenger was moving through the TSA line at LaGuardia Airport (LGA) in New York City when an alarm went off.

TSA OFFICER SEES ALARMING SHAPES ON X-RAY BEFORE STOLEN CIVIL WAR MYSTERY UNRAVELS

"The bag alarmed on an Xbox gaming system, and TSA Officer Ashley Leo, who was manning the on-screen resolution area, diverted the bag to the checked baggage resolution area, where Supervisory Transportation Security Officer (STSO) Christopher Ramos was stationed," the TSA said in a statement.

It's what Ramos found beside the Xbox that stood out.

The incident took place at LaGuardia Airport in New York City, pictured above, where TSA officers screen passengers and baggage. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

As he searched through the bag, he discovered "a plastic bag containing several fake IDs next to the Xbox that prompted the alarm," per the TSA.

"I noticed various driver’s licenses with different dates of birth and different class types, but all with the same photograph," Ramos said in a statement.

AIRPORT X-RAY SHOWS TERRIFYING OBJECT TAPED IN CARRY-ON TO SKIP CHECKED BAGGAGE FEE

"I was focused on following our screening procedures and paying close attention to anything that appeared unusual."

He added, "When I discovered the fraudulent IDs, I knew it was important to report the situation through the proper channels."

A passenger was arrested at LaGuardia Airport after TSA officers discovered multiple fake IDs while screening a checked bag. (TSA)

After involving TSA management, airport officials and Port Authority police, authorities confirmed the IDs were fraudulent and arrested the passenger moments before he was scheduled to board his flight.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"STSO Christopher Ramos’ strict adherence to standard operating procedures, diligence and situational awareness prevented the fraudulent IDs from entering the airport’s secure area," TSA LGA Federal Security Director John Essig said in a statement.

While searching the bag, an officer (not pictured) discovered several fake IDs in a plastic bag next to the Xbox that had triggered the alarm, according to the TSA. (Aaron Schwartz/AFP via Getty Images; Getty Images)

"Identifying fraudulent IDs is an important part of TSA’s layered security approach. It helps ensure that people entering secure areas of the airport are who they claim to be and supports the safety of the traveling public."

Fox News Digital reached out to TSA for further comment and details.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The incident comes amid a string of unusual discoveries by TSA officers at airports across the country.

TSA officers at LaGuardia Airport, which is pictured above, discovered several fraudulent IDs after an Xbox gaming system triggered an alarm inside a passenger's checked bag. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

In Texas, TSA officers at Dallas Love Field Airport recently discovered a pocketknife concealed inside a tube of toothpaste during routine carry-on screening.

Also, recently, TSA officers at Tampa International Airport in Florida discovered a 4-inch, double-edged knife concealed inside a baseball bat-shaped flashlight.

Kelly McGreal of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.

Andrea Margolis is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital and Fox Business. Readers can follow her on X at @andreamargs or send story tips to andrea.margolis@fox.com.

articles.title: Flying sports car hides its wings as production gets closer
articles.excerpt:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

If you have ever been stuck in traffic wishing your car could sprout wings, Samson Sky has been working on something p...
articles.body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

If you have ever been stuck in traffic wishing your car could sprout wings, Samson Sky has been working on something pretty close. Its Switchblade flying car can drive out of your garage and take you to a nearby airport. Once there, the wings come out, the tail extends and the vehicle becomes an airplane. You heard right, an airplane. After landing, everything folds back inside so you can drive the rest of the way.

That idea has been around for years. What makes Switchblade worth another look right now is that Samson says it has secured an $80 million investment from Dubai-based Matin Group. Samson plans to use the funding to help move the project toward U.S. production. The company still needs another $20 million to fully fund its current production plan. That new backing gets the Switchblade closer. But what really caught my attention is how much Samson has changed since we first watched this flying car take off.

PILOTLESS CARGO AIRCRAFT COULD CHANGE HOW PACKAGES MOVE

A rendering of the latest Switchblade design in flight mode, with its wings and tail fully extended. (Samson Sky)

NEW! 🩺 Free CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Healthcare With AI Saturday, September 26 at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.

Register and receive the replay and step-by-step guide afterward.

The latest Switchblade design looks much more like a car when you are using it on the road. Samson says the wings, tail and propeller are now fully enclosed inside the vehicle during driving mode. That is a major change from the earlier design that completed its first flight in November 2023. When you reach an airport, the wings extend and the tail moves into position for flight. Samson says the transformation from driving mode to flying mode takes about three minutes.

After you land, the process reverses. The flight hardware folds back inside the body before you continue the trip by road. Samson says that setup allows the Switchblade to fit inside a standard garage while also protecting the flight surfaces when the vehicle is being driven or stored. There is still a runway involved, though. The Switchblade does not take off vertically from your driveway. You drive it to an airport, transform it into flight mode and take off from there.

We first covered the Switchblade after its official first flight on Nov. 5, 2023. The prototype flew from Grant County International Airport in Moses Lake, Washington. Since then, Samson has kept working on the version it hopes to put into customers' hands. The company has changed the design and increased the size of its engine. Samson says it plans to use three production prototypes for more testing around the end of 2026 or beginning of 2027.

So while we have already seen a Switchblade get off the ground, the version heading toward production has changed since that 2023 flight. That is why I am especially interested in what happens next. I want to see the latest Switchblade take to the air and show us what this new design can actually do.

Samson is targeting some attention-grabbing performance numbers. The company currently lists a maximum airspeed of 190 mph and a maximum flying range of 450 miles. It lists a maximum road speed of 100 mph. Samson also lists a 160 mph cruise speed. However, its FAQ says that anticipated figure still needs verification during production-prototype flight testing.

The Switchblade uses a hybrid-electric drivetrain. A gasoline engine powers a generator, which supplies electricity to the vehicle's motors. Samson says the system powers the wheels on the ground and the propellers in flight. The company currently lists a 44-gallon fuel capacity and says the vehicle uses 91-octane automotive gasoline.

HELMET-STYLE COCKPIT VISION SYSTEM AIMS TO CHANGE HOW PILOTS SEE IN LOW VISIBILITY

An earlier Switchblade prototype takes flight during the vehicle’s successful first flight in November 2023. (Samson Sky)

Making a flying prototype and building vehicles for customers are two very different challenges. Samson says the new $80 million investment will help establish its first 180,000-square-foot Switchblade production facility in the U.S. The company signed a Joint Investment Agreement with Matin Group, and the two companies have started setting up a joint venture. Where that factory ends up remains an open question.

Samson Sky CEO and founder Sam Bousfield tells CyberGuy that the search has narrowed considerably, saying, "We will maintain our Samson Sky R&D Facility in Prineville, OR, and we have narrowed down the US production facility to three potential locations in different parts of the country, with some negotiations already begun." Samson has not identified those locations publicly. There is serious new money behind the production effort, but another financial hurdle remains. Samson says $20 million still needs to be raised before its current production plan is fully funded.

Samson's current timeline points to summer 2027. The company says it expects its Builder Assist assembly line to be ready by then. Its first year of production will focus mostly on customers who previously paid for some of the earliest delivery positions. Depositors and reservation holders would follow. Then there is the price. Samson currently estimates the Switchblade VFR kit will start at $200,000. The IFR version carries an estimated price of $235,000. Those prices can still change before customer production gets underway.

Bousfield tells CyberGuy that reaching this point has been part of the plan for years. "It's been great developing the technology for a flying car that you park in your garage and is high performance in both modes. Now we get to put it out for people to use and explore the world around them." Before that happens, buyers will have to do something you probably have never done when purchasing a car.

Buying a Switchblade comes with homework. Samson plans for the aircraft to operate under the Experimental Amateur-Built category in the U.S. FAA rules require the "major portion," meaning more than 50%, of an eligible amateur-built aircraft's fabrication and assembly to be completed by people building it for their own education or recreation. That requirement is often called the 51% rule.

Samson says its Builder Assist program will guide owners through their portion of the process. The company says much of its manufacturing process will be automated and computer-driven. It estimates an owner can finish the required work in as little as one week. One regulatory detail deserves some attention here. The FAA says it evaluates aircraft kits to determine whether they can allow a builder to meet the major-portion requirement. The FAA does not approve or certify the kit itself. The finished aircraft also goes through the FAA airworthiness process. So this will be a very different experience from walking into a dealership, signing a few forms and driving home.

A Switchblade may drive like a vehicle on the ground, but once those wings come out, aviation rules take over. Samson says you will need a private pilot certificate to fly one. Ground licensing can vary based on where you register the vehicle. The company says an automobile or motorcycle license may apply depending on local regulations. That also separates Switchblade from some of the other flying vehicles we have been following.

Electric air taxis such as Joby's eVTOL are designed around vertical takeoff and landing. Switchblade takes another route. It uses conventional runways but gives you something an air taxi cannot: the same vehicle stays with you after you land. That could be useful on a regional trip. Instead of landing and then finding a rental car or arranging another ride, you fold the wings away and keep going.

WISCONSIN MAN FLIES HELICOPTER TO CABELA'S BECAUSE THE DRIVE WAS TOO LONG

A rendering of the Switchblade in driving mode, with its wings, tail and propeller enclosed inside the body. (Samson Sky)

Here's what makes the Switchblade so interesting to me. You could pull out of your garage, drive to an airport, fly hundreds of miles and then keep driving after you land. No rental car. No waiting around for another ride. The same vehicle goes with you from start to finish. The new funding gets Samson closer to making that happen, but I would not start clearing space in the garage yet. The company still has to finish funding its production plans, choose where to build the Switchblade and put the latest version through more testing. We have seen an earlier prototype fly, but the redesigned vehicle heading toward production still needs to show what it can do in the air.

And if you are thinking, "Where do I sign up?" there is a lot more involved than the estimated $200,000 starting price. You will need pilot training and access to an airport. You also have to take part in the Builder Assist process. For me, the next big moment comes when this latest Switchblade leaves the runway. If it can deliver on the speed, range and transformation Samson is targeting, this flying sports car suddenly gets a whole lot more interesting.

What I like about the Switchblade is that the idea makes sense the minute you see how it works. You drive to the airport, fly to another city, fold the wings away after you land and keep going. The latest design makes that even more interesting because all that flight hardware disappears inside a vehicle you can park in your garage.

Of course, most of us are not shopping for a $200,000 flying sports car. The price alone puts the Switchblade out of reach for the majority of us, and becoming a pilot adds another wrinkle. But that does not mean you have to be a potential buyer to find this fascinating. I certainly am not planning to put one in my garage tomorrow, but I want to see whether Samson can actually pull this off.

The new funding gives Samson a much stronger push toward production, and we have already seen an earlier Switchblade fly. Now I want to see this redesigned version get into the air. If Samson can deliver what it is promising, we could be watching a pretty remarkable idea make the jump from a prototype we have followed for years to a flying sports car people can actually own.

Would you trust one vehicle to take you down the highway and into the sky, or would you want to see a few years of customer flights before climbing aboard? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

articles.title: Wendi McLendon-Covey fires back after Jeff Garlin blames bipolar disorder for 'The Goldbergs' exit
articles.excerpt:
Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Jeff Garlin is opening up about his contentious exit from "The Goldbergs," saying his then-undiagnosed bipolar disorder contributed ...
articles.body_text:
Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Jeff Garlin is opening up about his contentious exit from "The Goldbergs," saying his then-undiagnosed bipolar disorder contributed to the behavior that strained relationships with his co-stars before he left the hit sitcom.

The 64-year-old actor starred as the Goldbergs' family patriarch Murray Goldberg on the show from its premiere in September 2013 until he departed the ABC show during its ninth season in December 2021 amid HR investigations into complaints about his on-set behavior. Garlin was accused by members of the cast and crew of inappropriate verbal conduct, unwanted physical contact including hugging and touching and behavior that some employees described as creating an uncomfortable work environment.

While speaking with Vanity Fair at the time, Garlin denied intentionally harassing anyone. He acknowledged that HR had spoken to him over several years but characterized the complaints as stemming from his style of comedy and "silliness" on set rather than malicious intent. He also said he was willing to adjust behaviors, such as no longer hugging people.

JEFF GARLIN DEFENDS HIMSELF FROM CANCEL CULTURE AMID ‘THE GOLDBERGS’ ON-SET CONDUCT ALLEGATIONS

Wendi McLendon-Covey is pushing back on her former "The Goldbergs" star Jeff Garlin's claims about his on-set behavior. (Noel Vasquez/Getty Images; Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images for International Myeloma Foundation)

During a March 2023 appearance on SiriusXM's "Andy Cohen Live," Garlin's co-star Wendi McLendon-Covey, who played his wife Beverly Goldberg on "The Goldbergs," said his exit was "a long time coming" and that "finally, someone is listening to us." She declined to discuss the situation further, saying she was "exhausted by that topic and the PTSD of it all."

On Monday, Garlin appeared on the Daily Beast's "Obsessed" podcast where he addressed McLendon-Covey's comments and attributed his behavior to a mental health condition that had not been diagnosed at the time.

"It wasn't a long time coming for me," he said in reference to McLendon-Covey's past remark. "I actually empathize with her because, at the time, I was undiagnosed bipolar, and I was miserable on the show."

"I was miserable with my performance," he continued. "She was always trying to tell me, 'Hey, you're really great on the show.' I didn't believe her, and I just got to the point where I had to quit. She was very resentful, and it was a bit dramatic."

"I can only speak to what I'm responsible for," Garlin added. "Being bipolar, I was either one of three things: dark, dark, dark — where I didn't talk or look at anyone — happy to the point of mania, never turning off my thing, or mean, really, really mean. I didn't know which one I was going to be. I didn't get diagnosed until I was 59. This was toward the end of my time on ‘The Goldbergs,’ so I could be a lot."

'BLUE BLOODS' STAR JENNIFER ESPOSITO SAYS SHE WAS LOCKED IN PSYCH WARD AS HEALTH BATTLE SPIRALED

"When I left, she was very resentful and angry at me. If she wants to continue the resentment, that's her. I don't have resentment toward her, even for saying things about me. I actually love her, and I appreciate that she's one of the greatest actors I've ever worked with, and that will not be lost on me."

Garlin left the show during its ninth season in 2021. (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

McLendon-Covey, 56, responded to Garlin's comments after the Daily Beast shared a clip from his interview on Instagram.

"Huh," she wrote in the comments section.

After an Instagram user asked her, "What’s your take, Wendi?," the "Bridesmaids" star wrote, "Let's just say I remember things very differently, as does the crew, the other actors, the writers, and our executives."

Fox News Digital has reached out to representatives for Garlin and McLendon-Covey for comment.

Garlin said that his on-set behavior was fueled by undiagnosed bipolar disorder.  (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

"The Goldbergs" followed the misadventures of a loud but loving family living in suburban Philadelphia during the 1980s.

Though Garlin left "The Goldbergs" during its ninth season, he was a regular cast member for part of that season. After his exit, the show completed some remaining Season 9 episodes using previously filmed footage and stand-ins before writing Murray Goldberg out ahead of Season 10. At the beginning of the tenth season, the show revealed that the character had died off-screen, allowing the series to continue focusing on the Goldberg family without him.

ABC announced in February 2023 that Season 10 would be the show's last and the series finale aired on May 3, 2023.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

While appearing on the "Obsessed" podcast, Garlin reflected on how his life and career had changed since he was diagnosed with bipolar disorder.

McLendon disputed his account on social media.  (ABC via Getty Images)

"It's changed quite a bit because A, I went into AA (Acloholics Anonymous)," he said. "B, I had a nervous breakdown right after that, as the ‘The Goldbergs’ thing was ending. I had a nervous breakdown, was suicidal. Went away. Learned this kind of therapy. Got the right drugs in me. The right cocktail, as they say, for bipolar. And I got a form of therapy that was new to me, called Dialectical Behavior Therapy. DBT."

"So you know, I have regrets," he continued. "Not a lot of them that I could have controlled, but I still have regrets on a lot of my behavior, in terms of being a jerk. But I'm really a different person."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"No, I'm the same person," Garlin clarified. "I'm more enlightened.

The two played husband and wife on the hit sitcom.  (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"Like I said, I don't have resentments," he added. "When I have a resentment, I work through it on my own until it doesn't help me any. I'm sober. I'm grateful. I was never grateful for my time on ‘The Goldbergs.’ That was another problem. ‘I’m not grateful for this great opportunity?' No, I wasn't. And now I'm grateful for everything, and so it has changed me."

"I'm still the same person at heart because I always — I would leave the set thinking, ‘Why did I apologize to a lot of people today?’ Having no idea. Because in my heart now, and logically, I know I'm good-hearted, but I wasn't able to — I was misguided. I don't know. But the point is, I'm really grateful for what I have now and the way I am now."

Ashley Hume is an entertainment journalist for Fox News Digital and Fox Business who covers breaking news, celebrity culture, major industry events and the business of entertainment.

articles.title: Federal illegal voting arrest becomes latest flashpoint in Sherrill's battles with Trump administration
articles.excerpt: Fox News correspondent Eric Shawn reports on the Department of Justice launching an investigation into New Jersey voter roll software errors that registered 6,600 non-citizens to vote. Gov. Mikie Sher...
articles.body_text:
Fox News correspondent Eric Shawn reports on the Department of Justice launching an investigation into New Jersey voter roll software errors that registered 6,600 non-citizens to vote. Gov. Mikie Sherrill acknowledged that as many as 400 registered non-citizens cast ballots in state elections under former Gov. Phil Murphy. Department of Homeland Security Sec. Markwayne Mullin warned that up to 35,000 non-citizens may remain registered on New Jersey voter rolls.

Federal law enforcement arrested a Senegalese immigrant in New Jersey accused of illegally voting in multiple elections, injecting a new flashpoint into Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill's escalating fights with Washington over immigration enforcement and election integrity.

The case comes as Washington and Trenton battle over immigration enforcement and election administration, with the Trump administration challenging Sherrill over state policies affecting federal law enforcement while also pressing New Jersey for access to its voter rolls.

Sanata Coulibaly, a Senegalese national, was arrested when DHS and FBI agents jointly executed a criminal warrant in Hudson County, which stretches from West New York to Bayonne across the Hudson River from Manhattan.

FOUR NONCITIZENS CHARGED WITH ILLEGALLY VOTING IN 2020, 2022 AND 2024 FEDERAL ELECTIONS IN NEW JERSEY

"This alien from Senegal has been charged with procurement of citizenship or naturalization unlawfully and voting by an alien after allegedly voting in three general elections in New Jersey," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said.

"Sanctuary politicians can try to claim that this kind of voter fraud isn’t happening, but it’s very real and is a serious threat to our country."

WATCH: TRUMP DOJ VOWS TO PURSUE ‘EVERY SINGLE’ VOTING VIOLATION AFTER NJ ROLL SHOCKER

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed Executive Order 12 restricting certain immigration enforcement activities on state property shortly after taking office in January. (Eduardo Munoz Alvarez/Getty Images)

Mullin said DHS and the Trump administration would continue efforts to protect election integrity.

The arrest comes after Sherrill revealed in July that a software error in New Jersey's motor vehicle system had improperly registered roughly 6,600 people who identified themselves as noncitizens. The state later determined that fewer than 400 of those newly registered because of the error had voted.

After that revelation, New Jersey resisted federal demands to turn over voter rolls while pursuing its own investigation.

Fox News Digital reached out to Sherrill for comment.

According to the criminal complaint, Coulibaly cast ballots in the November 2018 midterm election, the July 2020 primary, the November 2020 general election and the 2024 general election while she was not a U.S. citizen.

Coulibaly registered through a paper application submitted to the Hudson County superintendent of elections in Jersey City, falsely certifying that she was a U.S. citizen, the complaint said.

She first came to the U.S. from Senegal on a B-1 nonimmigrant visa in approximately 1993 and later became a lawful permanent resident, according to the Justice Department.

A DHS agent, left, participates in the arrest of Sanata Coulibaly, right. (DHS Handout)

Prosecutors allege Coulibaly later applied for U.S. citizenship and falsely stated on her N-400 naturalization application that she had never registered to vote or voted in a federal election.

Coulibaly's case is part of a broader federal election-integrity push, with the Justice Department announcing election-related charges against 16 people across several states this month.

Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

articles.title: Indiana coach Curt Cignetti has message for antsy Hoosiers fans: 'Don’t b---- about a 38-0 win'

The natives are starting to get restless in Bloomington, Indiana.

You read that right, folks. Fa...
articles.body_text:
The Big Noon Kickoff crew discuss whether Indiana is now a perennial National Championship contender.

The natives are starting to get restless in Bloomington, Indiana.

You read that right, folks. Fans of the Indiana Hoosiers, a program that came from literally nothing to reach the pantheon of college football, are a little miffed with how the team has performed early in the season.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

The defending national champions have gotten off to a 3-0 start, but the first quarter of their season has been marred by sleepy first half performances against "lesser competition," to put it mildly.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL’S AP TOP 25 IS OUT: WHO’S OVERRATED, UNDERRATED AND FLAT-OUT SNUBBED?

Indiana Hoosiers wide receiver Charlie Becker catches a pass for a touchdown against the North Texas Mean Green on Sept. 5, 2026, at Memorial Stadium in Bloomington, Ind. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

Wins against North Texas, Howard, and Western Kentucky probably don't move the needle all that much, but the clumsy starts have the Hoosier faithful getting a little antsy as their team heads into Big Ten conference play.

Head coach Curt Cignetti has taken note of this, and decided to issue a personal statement on the matter during his weekly radio hit on Thursday.

"It was hot, and I was hot on the sideline," Cignetti admits when discussing the fans not staying in their seats for the entirety of Indiana's 38-0 win over the Hilltoppers on Saturday.

"What are we, 29-2? When we came, I saw the picture, 10,000 fans in the stands," he fired back. "Don't b---- about a 38-0 win."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

His response elicited plenty of laughs from those in attendance, but Cignetti, as is usually the case, was being dead serious.

Indiana Hoosiers head coach Curt Cignetti walks onto the field before a college football game between the Michigan State Spartans and Indiana Hoosiers on Oct. 18, 2025, at Memorial Stadium in Bloomington, Ind. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

It's one thing for Alabama fans in year eight or nine of the Nick Saban dynasty to have gotten a little pissy about winning by 38 instead of 58, but this is Indiana we are talking about here.

Three years ago, this fanbase would have thrown a parade for going 8-4 and getting an invite to the Gator Bowl.

COCKY CURT CIGNETTI CALLED OUT THE SEC, BUT HE SHOULD GOOGLE INDIANA'S LAUGHABLE SCHEDULE FIRST

Now we're going to get our red and white striped overalls in a bunch over a 14-0 halftime lead against Western Kentucky?

I get it, that's not where you want to be, and if you play like that against Ohio State or Oregon you are going to get exposed, but have a little faith in The Cig, will you?

If anyone can get things cleaned up, it's him.

I've written exhaustively about how Cignetti is basically the closest thing we have in the game right now to prime Saban, and I mean it.

Head coach Curt Cignetti of the Indiana Hoosiers hoists the George P. Crumbley Trophy after defeating the Oregon Ducks in the College Football Playoff semifinal at the Chick-fil-A Peach Bowl at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on Jan. 9, 2026, in Atlanta, Ga. (Getty Images)

What he has done and is continuing to do at Indiana is unprecedented.

The Hoosiers are bored and they're playing with their food right now.

That's not something you want to see long term, but if anyone can coach that out of them, it's the man who barely cracked a smile after beating the tar out of everyone in his path en route to a national championship just nine months earlier.

And show a little respect to the man as well.

President Donald Trump jokes with Head Coach Curt Cignetti during an event celebrating the 2026 Football National Champion Indiana Hoosiers on the South Lawn of the White House in Washington, D.C., on May 11, 2026. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

He's already the greatest coach to ever roam the sidelines of Memorial Stadium by a wide margin, and he's not going to be around forever, so just enjoy the time you have with the guy.

Take it from someone who didn't cherish a legend while he was coaching his team. Someday Cig will retire, and then you will be dreaming of 38-0 wins.

articles.title: ‘Wave of freedom’ sweeps Latin America as Trump ally takes fight to Marxist terror group
articles.excerpt: Colombian Vice President José Manuel Restrepo told Fox News Digital his government supports President Donald Trump’s new regional security alliance, but said Colombian forces — not U.S. troops — will ...
articles.body_text:
Colombian Vice President José Manuel Restrepo told Fox News Digital his government supports President Donald Trump’s new regional security alliance, but said Colombian forces — not U.S. troops — will carry out operations inside the country.

UNITED NATIONS — Colombian Vice President José Manuel Restrepo said his country is embracing President Donald Trump’s push for a new security alliance across the Western Hemisphere, but drew a clear line on the role American forces would play inside Colombia, telling Fox News Digital that Colombian troops — not U.S. forces — will carry out operations against the country’s armed groups.

Restrepo spoke with Fox News Digital in an on-camera interview days after joining Trump and other regional leaders at a Shield of the Americas meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, where Trump called the initiative the "largest and most powerful alliance for economic and national security ever to convene in the Western Hemisphere."

Trump urged members to treat what he called "narco terrorists" as common threats and impose sanctions on U.S.-designated terrorist organizations.

Restrepo said he personally discussed the region’s changing political and security landscape with Trump. The shift in Colombia comes amid a broader political realignment across Latin America, with De La Espriella’s June victory adding Colombia to a group of countries including Argentina, Chile, Ecuador, Bolivia and Panama that have moved to the right, fueled in part by voter concerns over crime, economic weakness and political instability.

TRUMP ALLY 'EL TIGRE' SWORN IN AS COLOMBIA'S NEW PRESIDENT AMID CONTINENT'S RIGHTWARD SHIFT

President Donald Trump, center, Dominican Republic President Luis Abinader, second from left, Argentina's President Javier Milei, El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele, Guyana's President Mohamed Irfaan Ali, Costa Rica's President Rodrigo Chaves Robles, Bolivia's President Rodrigo Paz and Chile's President-elect Jose Antonio Kast pose for a family photo during the Shield of the Americas" Summit in Doral, Fla., on Saturday, March 7, 2026. (Kevin Lamarque/Reuters)

"There is a wave of freedom, a wave of democracy, a wave of free market. … There is a new momentum for the region and we have to take advantage of that momentum. That's what I said to President Trump," Restrepo told Fox News Digital. "If we want to keep and preserve democracy in the region, the Shield of the Americas is going to be the best opportunity to do it."

Asked what Trump told him, Restrepo said the president agreed and expressed respect for Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella.

"Colombia is a new partner. In my opinion, it's one of the most important partners for the United States in the region," Restrepo said.

That partnership is already being tested in the fight against drug trafficking and armed groups.

WHITE HOUSE HIGHLIGHTS 'STEEPEST' EVER DECLINE IN US CASUALTIES FROM CARTELS AMID BOAT STRIKES

A police officer stands guard on a street following a military operation against the drug-related armed group Conquering Self Defense Forces of the Sierra Nevada (ACSN) in Santa Marta, Colombia on September 23, 2026. Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella sent troops into Santa Marta after an armed group attacked shops and burnt vehicles across the Caribbean city, he announced on September 22, 2026. The chaos followed an earlier announcement by the president that authorities had killed 13 members of the self-styled Conquering Self Defense Forces of the Sierra Nevada (ACSN), an armed group which controls cocaine trafficking routes. (Marco Perdomo / AFP via Getty Images)

In August, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Colombia had authorized "joint military operations to destroy terrorists and terror networks" and told reporters that Washington had discussed possible joint strikes against groups including the National Liberation Army, or ELN, which the U.S. designates as a terrorist organization, and remnants of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia.

"Designated terrorist organizations, with partnered governments, will be legitimate targets of the United States government," including in Colombia, Hegseth said when asked whether such operations were expected, according to Reuters.

But when pressed by Fox News Digital on whether joint U.S.-Colombian strikes remained an option, Restrepo appeared to narrow the scope of direct American involvement.

"The United States helps us on security, helps us information, helps us on technology, but the public forces of Colombia are those who are going to act in those places," he said.

US FORCES OBLITERATE SUSPECTED 'NARCO-TERRORIST' VESSEL IN LETHAL EASTERN PACIFIC STRIKE, KILLING 3

Colombian president Abelardo De La Espriella takes part during an event announcing the new military chiefs for his government at the Jose Maria Cordova Military Cadets Academy in Bogota, Colombia August 26, 2026. (Sebastian Barros/Long Visual Press/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

Asked specifically whether Colombia would have the "boots on the ground," Restrepo replied: "We will have our group, our public forces on the ground."

The tougher posture comes as Colombia confronts renewed violence from armed and drug-trafficking groups. This week, De La Espriella ordered the military into Santa Marta after the Autodefensas Conquistadoras de la Sierra Nevada, an illegal armed group involved in drug trafficking, responded to the killing of one of its senior leaders with an "armed strike," threats, roadblocks and attacks that left businesses shuttered and public transportation disrupted. More than 500 soldiers and 600 police officers were deployed, according to the Colombian presidency.

The new government is also seeking to reverse former President Gustavo Petro’s "total peace" policy, which pursued negotiations with several armed organizations. Before taking office, De La Espriella announced that he would dismantle key elements of the policy and reactivate arrest warrants against members of illegal armed groups.

Restrepo went further, accusing the former government of creating "the idea of impunity" and saying the new administration instead intends to confront groups it considers terrorists.

US, SHIELD OF THE AMERICAS CONDEMN 'ONGOING EFFORTS' TO OVERTHROW BOLIVIA'S ELECTED PRESIDENT AMID UNREST

Firefighters extinguish a fire in a burnt truck following a military operation by the Colombian Army against the drug-related armed group Conquering Self Defense Forces of the Sierra Nevada (ACSN) in Santa Marta, Colombia on September 22, 2026. Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella sent troops into Santa Marta after an armed group attacked shops and burnt vehicles across the Caribbean city, he announced on September 22, 2026. The chaos followed an earlier announcement by the president that authorities had killed 13 members of the self-styled Conquering Self Defense Forces of the Sierra Nevada (ACSN), an armed group which controls cocaine trafficking routes. (Idinael Fernandez / AFP via Getty Images)

He said that when the new government took office, "around 30%" of Colombia’s regions lacked effective territorial control — a figure Fox News Digital has not independently verified — and said the administration was seeking to regain those areas through stronger security forces, intelligence gathering, drug eradication and extraditions.

Restrepo also argued that the same security debate should extend to the United Nations, where Colombia used its General Assembly address this week to call for reforms and an international definition of terrorism. The UN has had a global counterterrorism strategy since 2006, but member states have for decades failed to agree on a comprehensive international convention defining terrorism.

Colombia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Thursday also announced that the country was suspending all diplomatic relations with Iran.

"This sovereign decision aligns with the pillars guiding the Government's foreign policy regarding national and hemispheric security, as well as the fight against transnational crime, taking into account alleged links between the Iranian government and international terrorist groups and other narcoterrorist groups that threaten the country's security," the Ministry wrote in a statement posted to X.

MELANIA TRUMP’S HOME-COUNTRY LEADER RIPS UN ‘DOUBLE STANDARDS’ AS TRUMP PROMISE IS REVEALED

Colombian Vice President Jose Manuel Restrepo attends a Shield of the Americas event on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York City, US, September 22, 2026. (Kylie Cooper/Reuters)

"I think this is a moment in which the United Nations have to reflect on its own future," Restrepo told Fox News Digital, calling for greater efficiency and effectiveness as well as international agreement on terrorism.

"The only way to attain peace, which is one of the main objectives of the UN, is through confronting terrorism," he said, arguing that countries need greater intelligence sharing, judicial cooperation and coordination.

With Secretary-General António Guterres set to leave office at the end of the year, Restrepo said the transition could offer the institution an opportunity to change.

"I think that the UN has a new moment and the UN has to take advantage of that opportunity," he said.

Restrepo added that the institution also needed to address what he described as the inconsistent application of human rights standards.

Officials shared a video showing what appeared to be various weapons laid out on a table. (@FuerzasMilCol/X)

"Human rights should apply to all, regardless of political considerations," Restrepo said. "Ideology cannot decide to whom we are going to apply or not human rights."

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

articles.title: Cooper Flagg rookie card makes eye-popping record sale, but is it actually a good investment?
articles.excerpt: Dallas Mavericks forward Cooper Flagg is a superstar, the reigning NBA Rookie of the Year, and his sports card market has been booming. Ever since he burst on the scene at Duke, following being the No...
articles.body_text:
Dallas Mavericks forward Cooper Flagg is a superstar, the reigning NBA Rookie of the Year, and his sports card market has been booming. Ever since he burst on the scene at Duke, following being the No. 1 overall high school prospect and a McDonald's All-American, sports fans and media knew he was going to be special.

I, for one, did not believe he was so special that his most sought-after rookie card, the Topps Chrome Update Rookie Debut Patch Auto 1-of-1 in a PSA Gem-Mint 10 grade for both the card and the auto, would become the sixth-most expensive trading card of all time.

A Cooper Flagg 1-of-1 Rookie Debut Patch Autograph card is on display at Baseball Cards of Rhode Island in North Kingstown, R.I., on Aug. 11, 2026. RhodyBreakers, operating out of the shop, opened three hobby boxes of 2026 Topps Chrome Update Basketball cards for clients on a live stream on Aug. 10, 2026 and pulled this card. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

The card sold in Fanatics Collect’s September Premier Auction for $8.04 million, amassing 83 bids. The auction ran from September 10 through September 24. A bidding war took place into the early hours of Friday morning, with the card going from $3.5 million to $8.04 million from 9 p.m. ET on Thursday to 2 a.m. ET on Friday. That sale was historic because it became the highest recorded sale for a basketball card featuring a single player.

According to a Fanatics spokesperson, "This is the first class of NBA Debut Patch cards, which saw each rookie wear a patch on their jersey sleeve during their first game which was removed following the game and put into a trading card and signed." The Debut Patch was first introduced in 2021 in Major League Baseball, garnering massive sales like the 2024 Paul Skenes Debut Patch Auto selling for $1.11 Million. It's easily been the most innovative concept the hobby has seen since the logo man, which is a patch of the respective league's logo from a game-worn jersey. It's among the rarest collectibles in the sports card market.

Flagg's card became the 3rd-highest NBA card sale ever, trailing only a pair of dual logoman cards, the 2006–07 Upper Deck Exquisite Collection Dual Logoman Autographs 1-of-1 Michael Jordan and LeBron James, which sold in a private sale for $10 Million and the 2007–08 Upper Deck Exquisite Collection Dual Logoman Autographs 1-of-1 Michael Jordan and Kobe Bryant, which sold in August of 2025 for $12,932,000.

Dallas Mavericks star Cooper Flagg's one-of-one NBA Debut patch card has been found. (Photo by Ron Jenkins/Getty Images)

AN ULTRA-RARE COOPER FLAGG TRADING CARD HAS BEEN FOUND, AND THE MAVERICKS ARE PREPARED TO GIVE A LOT FOR IT

It also ranks as the fifth-highest sports card sale, according to Card Ladder. A Mickey Mantle 1952 Topps card sold for $12.6 million at a Heritage auction in 2022, and an ungraded Shohei Ohtani 2026 Topps Chrome Gold Logoman patch autograph card, famously fetched $11 million on July 30 in a private sale to Kevin O'Leary and the investment group Secure Collectibles.

In a statement by Fanatics, the company said, "The Cooper Flagg card was famously pulled in a break done by Rhody Breakers in Rhode Island, and belonged to collector Jason Williams of South Carolina."

The exterior of Baseball Cards of Rhode Island in North Kingstown, R.I. on Aug. 11, 2026. RhodyBreakers, operating out of the shop, opened boxes of trading cards on a live stream for clients and pulled the Topps Cooper Flagg 1-of-1 Rookie Debut Patch Autograph card on the evening of Aug. 10, 2026. The card is from the 2026 Topps Chrome Update Basketball set. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Jason Williams, 50, acquired the card after spending only $515 to land a spot on Rhody Breakers. For those who don't know, buying a spot in a "break" is where a customer purchases a team and/or player (spot) for an amount set by the specific breaker on a livestream, where the retailer opens a box(es) of sports cards, with the customer hoping to pull a life-changing card, an auto, or numbered card. It's a gamble. There was no guarantee Williams would even get a card(s) totaling that $515 spot purchase.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Speaking of gambles, this is the biggest gamble I have ever seen in the hobby (as the sports card collecting market is affectionately known). Is Cooper Flagg a generational talent? In some ways, yes, but the jury is still out and only time will tell if he is truly one of the greatest basketball players of all time. He's a No. 1 overall pick, fresh off a solid rookie season, but in my opinion, he's going to need to win an MVP and a championship soon if this buyer wants to see a solid return on the investment.

Many of the biggest names in the NBA, who have a proven track record, have cards I would find much more enticing to purchase. I believe Steph Curry is undervalued, LeBron James is a certified NBA legend, who owns many NBA records, with cards I'd happily purchase over this.

If I had $8 Million, here's what I would buy instead:

I could put a long list together, but I would much rather spend money on a tried and true sports legend, or a vintage Pokemon card, rather than gamble with losing millions on a potential NBA legend. But hey, I'm not the one with $8 million to blow, so to the buyer, this could just be pocket change.

The patch in the card was on Flagg's jersey during his NBA debut on October 22, 2025 against the San Antonio Spurs. (Photo by Jesse D. Garrabrant/NBAE via Getty Images)

Either way, this sale is a great thing for Flagg's card market, shows that sports cards are becoming more enticing than stocks in many ways, and the additional sales of debut patch autos, including San Antonio Spurs star Dylan Harper’s card selling for $2.88 million and Hornets' sharpshooter Kon Knueppel’s Debut Patch card selling for $2.34 million, are incredibly impressive as well.

More than anything, congratulations to Jason Williams on the life-changing payday.

Jon is a writer and content creator for OutKick

articles.title: Michigan college president urges 'it's incumbent upon' higher education leaders to lower tuition every year
articles.excerpt:
Adrian College President Dr. Jeffrey Docking told Fox News Digital that universities have been 'inefficient' after Syracuse University made headlines for struggling to meet its enrollment target.

Hig...
articles.body_text:
Adrian College President Dr. Jeffrey Docking told Fox News Digital that universities have been 'inefficient' after Syracuse University made headlines for struggling to meet its enrollment target.

Higher education leaders must lower tuition costs as Syracuse University faces questions over its nearly $100,000 annual cost of attendance, Adrian College President Dr. Jeffrey Docking told Fox News Digital.

"I think it's incumbent upon us as college presidents and institutions to say, 'Can we start to turn the dial back and lower costs every year for students?' And I think we can do that if we work together," Docking told Fox News Digital.

"The Syracuse University situation is simply a bellwether for the structural crisis facing higher education nationally," Docking said. "It's no different than at most private institutions — many regional publics as well."

Docking, who has served as president of Michigan-based Adrian College for more than 20 years, previously made headlines when he testified before Congress about innovation and lowering costs in higher education. He co-authored the book "Crisis in Higher Education: A Plan to Save Small Liberal Arts Colleges in America" and is credited with doubling Adrian College's enrollment since taking the helm in 2005.

ICE DROPS ‘UNCONTROLLED’ FRAUD BOMBSHELL INVOLVING THOUSANDS OF FOREIGN STUDENTS, ‘PHANTOM EMPLOYEES’

Adrian College President Jeffrey Docking is attributed with doubling enrollment at Adrian College since he started working there. He has also been credited for tripling the college’s endowment. (Adrian College)

Docking was reacting to a Wall Street Journal report detailing Syracuse University's steep enrollment and financial challenges. The Central New York-based institution is saddled with nearly $500 million in debt tied to new residence halls and is facing a 1.5% budget shortfall as it struggles to attract enough students to cover its operational costs.

"The problem with Syracuse is that the school thinks of itself as like an Ivy, but it’s not," former Syracuse University Center for International Services Director Juan Tavares told The Wall Street Journal.

The Journal reported that in 2025, those underlying weaknesses collided with a high-profile federal crackdown on student visas, causing Syracuse's international enrollment numbers for both undergraduate and graduate programs to plummet by half. Syracuse also failed to meet its overall enrollment targets, forcing the school to issue emergency financial-aid packages to attract incoming freshmen.

FOX NEWS POLL: FAITH IN HIGHER EDUCATION IN THE US IS COLLAPSING

As students and families increasingly question the return on investment of a college degree, Syracuse increased its tuition to $69,180 for the current academic year—up from $40,458 in the 2013-14 school year. When factoring in room, board, fees and other expenses, the university's total cost of attendance can reach $98,544.

Fox News Digital reached out to Syracuse University for comment.

Rising college costs have coincided with total U.S. student loan balances reaching $1.65 trillion, according to data from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

SKIP TWO YEARS OF COLLEGE DEBT AND GIVE YOUR FAMILY A LIFETIME OF WEALTH

FILE - The Syracuse University campus is seen in Syracuse, New York, Aug. 31, 2022. (AP Photo/Ted Shaffrey, File)

Docking called for a total "re-engineering of higher education" to address the crisis.

"[Syracuse is] falling victim to the perfect storm that's out there with international enrollment being down, people questioning the value of higher education, and the fact that many schools are dealing with declining high school graduation rates — especially in northern states," Docking said.

"There's nothing wrong with Syracuse University. It's a fantastic place and will remain fantastic," he added. "But they are just victims of what needs to be a re-engineering of American higher education in the years ahead."

Syracuse University Chancellor and President J. Michael Haynie acknowledged the shortfall, insisting that higher ed leaders must re-evaluate their value proposition to students and families.

I’M A UNIVERSITY PRESIDENT. TRUMP IS RIGHT TO MAKE COLLEGES DELIVER FOR STUDENTS

Docking also co-founded Rize Education, a course-sharing platform that allows smaller colleges to collaborate and offer online classes without incurring massive overhead expenses. Through its partnership with Rize, Adrian College has added 27 majors, 13 minors, and eight certificates in high-demand fields like business, technology, engineering, and healthcare.

His efforts earned him an invitation to testify before the House Education and Workforce Committee and helped Adrian College earn a spot among U.S. News & World Report’s "Most Innovative Regional Universities in the Midwest" for three consecutive years.

Ever since Adrian College formed a partnership with RIZE, the institution has launched 27 majors, 13 minors and 8 certificates in business, technology, engineering and healthcare. (Adrian College)

Docking argued that soaring tuition is driven by operational inefficiency and an insular culture that prevents institutions from working together like private-sector businesses. By sharing faculty across institutions via course-sharing, schools can bypass the hefty costs of hiring new full-time faculty.

"Higher education institutions traditionally have been very inefficient. They've been very insular. They've not worked well together to drive down costs," Docking concluded. "The re-engineering has to be a massive effort to bring efficiency to existing institutions."

Joshua Q. Nelson is a reporter for Fox News Digital.

Joshua focuses on cultural trends, education, and public policy. He extensively covered reparations developments across the U.S., the Department of Education, and immigration issues.

Joining Fox News Digital in 2019, he previously graduated from Syracuse University's Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs and received the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton Public Policy Certificate.

Story tips can be sent to joshua.nelson@fox.com and Joshua can be followed on Instagram, Twitter and LinkedIn.

articles.title: ‘What does money from a Super PAC actually buy?’: our reporters are answering your election questions now
articles.excerpt:
Who are the groups backing candidates in the midterms – and why? In our second live discussion ahead of the elections, Joseph Gedeon, Dara Kerr and Chris Stein are live now

Sign in or sign up to join...
articles.body_text:
Who are the groups backing candidates in the midterms – and why? In our second live discussion ahead of the elections, Joseph Gedeon, Dara Kerr and Chris Stein are live now

Sign in or sign up to join the conversation

Joseph, Dara Kerr and Chris are live answering your questions now.

Sam_Jenks asks: The Republicans are better placed to take advantage of the supreme sourt ruling on spending in terms of the final advertising blitz, apparently outspending the Democrats by over $200 million. Is that enough to overcome factors like Trump’s low approval rating? Can a party who are clearly less popular than the opposition just brute force their way to victory if the spending deficit is large enough?

double quotation markChris: That’s the big question of these midterms, and one that can’t be answered definitively before we know the results. But here’s what I can say now: While some Democratic candidates are beating their opponents in fundraising at the candidate level, Republicans overall are expected to outspend Democrats in the cycle, when factoring in outside groups like Super Pacs. That doesn’t necessarily mean they’ll preserve their majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives — Kamala Harris outspent Donald Trump in 2024, and lost anyway. But the headwinds facing Republicans are really formidable, from Trump’s terrible approval ratings, to Democratic candidates’ strong performances in special election and primary turnout, to the price increases for gas and other staples caused by the Iran war. This piece I wrote this week goes deeper into those dynamics.

NeilNaik asks: What aspects from the Save America act should we be concerned about, and how much of it is realistically going to be implemented for this November.

double quotation markChris: The legislation you are referring to, which is now known as the Save America Act, has passed the House of Representatives but not the Senate and thus has not been enacted, so none of its provisions will be implemented in time for the 3 November midterms. However, Donald Trump and his administration have attempted to put in place some of the act’s restrictions on voting via executive order. These efforts have not gone too well for him. Trump’s attempt to impose new restrictions on mail-in voting, for instance, was halted by the supreme court.

brooklandia897 asks: Could you talk about the California races and how likely it is that the Prop 40 billionaire tax will go through? Obviously billions have been spent by billionaires trying to stop that one! So is there hope for it actually going through in spite of all that?

double quotation markDara: The billionaire tax is looking to be the most expensive ballot measure race in California history, which is saying something since we saw Uber and Lyft spend more than $200m to defeat a ballot measure for workers in 2000. For Prop 40, tech-backed Super Pacs are spending hand-over-fist to defeat the measure. The biggest spending Super Pac is called Building a Better California and has seen donations from several Silicon Valley venture capitalists and tech royalty, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. (Also, weirdly, Kim DeGeorge, the wife of the wealthy owner of the Alo yoga clothing brand, has been a regular donor). Since the Super Pac launched in February, it’s raised $229m.

Just for background, Prop 40 would put a one-time 5% tax on all billionaires living in the state. The proceeds would go to mostly fund healthcare programs, along with some education and food assistance programs.

Polling for Prop 40 shows that voters are leaning to support the measure, but that support has lost strength over the past few weeks. Still, the measure has the support of California’s Democratic party and the powerful California Federation of Labor Unions.

Complicating matters are Prop 41 and Prop 42, two separate measures that billionaire tax opponents got onto the November ballot. Prop 41 directly targets Prop 40, and Prop 42 is more of a general anti-wealth tax. If either of these measures get more “yes” votes, they will stop Prop 40 from taking effect – even if Prop 40 passes. So California’s billionaire class is spending not only to defeat Prop 40, but to push Prop 41 and 42.

NorthLondonIsRed asks: When a Super PAC or corporate donor spends heavily on a race, what does that money actually buy in practice? Is it mostly ad volume, field organizing, opposition research, or something else? And how much measurable difference does that spending make in swinging votes compared to factors like incumbency or local turnout?

double quotation markChris Stein: A Super Pac has wide latitude for what it can spend its funds on in support of a candidate or cause. Typically, Super Pacs run advertisements in the media — think television, streaming services and websites — produce campaign signs and bumper stickers, and fund canvassing and phone banking. Does this make a difference? It depends on the race. This year, the Super Pac connected to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), called the United Democracy Project (UDP), spent heavily to support Democratic congressman Wesley Bell in St Louis, Missouri, who was facing a primary challenge from Cori Bush, the former US House lawmaker he unseated with the UDP’s assistance in 2024. Bush was outspent and Bell won his primary by a wide margin, but when I reported on this race from St Louis it became clear the former congresswoman had other issues beside lack of funds. But UDP also spent heavily in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary to support congresswoman Haley Stevens against Abdul El-Sayed. It didn’t work — El-Sayed won the nomination, albeit by a narrower margin than expected.

Joseph, Dara Kerr and Chris are live answering your questions now.

Welcome to our second live Q&A about the upcoming midterm elections. Today, our reporters will be joining us to answer your questions about who is funding the campaigns, where the money is going and how it’s shaping the election outlook ahead of the votes on 3 November.

In the past few months our reporting team has covered in depth:

How major companies that urged Congress to strengthen the Voting Rights Act continue to contribute to state political groups that are actively working to undermine the legislation.

The vast extent of spending by crypto money and big tech to shape this year’s races.

Aipac and its linked Super Pacs’ role in funding Democratic candidates facing opponents from the progressive left.

Joining us on Friday at 11am EDT are political breaking news reporter Joseph Gedeon, tech reporter Dara Kerr and senior politics reporter Chris Stein.

Sign in or sign up to join the conversation.

The US politics team is hosting a series of reader Q&As leading up to the November midterms elections. See our first conversation on the Democrats’ midterms hopes.

articles.title: Couple jailed for life for abusing and murdering a vulnerable man in their care
articles.excerpt:
Kenneth Newton and Melanie James had filmed themselves mocking Rubin Blount, who was left to lie in his own urine and weighed 40kg when he died

A couple convicted of murder after inflicting “delibera...
articles.body_text:
Kenneth Newton and Melanie James had filmed themselves mocking Rubin Blount, who was left to lie in his own urine and weighed 40kg when he died

A couple convicted of murder after inflicting “deliberate cruelty” on a vulnerable 28-year-old man in their care, who at the time of his death weighed just 40kg (6st 4lb), have been jailed for life.

Rubin Blount was made to stand for long periods of time, left to lie in his own urine and forced to eat out of bins by his stepbrother Kenneth Newton and Newton’s partner, Melanie James, at a property in Tamworth, Staffordshire, Stafford crown court heard.

Newton, 58, and James, 64, both from Birmingham, who had filmed themselves mocking and abusing the victim, were convicted by a jury in July of his murder.

Jailing them each for a minimum of 21 years, Mrs Justice Jefford said they had been in a position of trust which they had abused and had shown an “abject failure to help him when he was in pain and suffering”.

Blount was severely dehydrated and malnourished when he was taken to hospital after he became unwell, and he had a cardiac arrest upon arrival. He died three days later on 30 November 2022.

Doctors found he had extensive pneumonia, severe infection, fractures to his ribs and spine, and burns, lesions and grazes. He had 50 rib fractures, 47 of which had been inflicted in the weeks leading up to his death.

Jennifer Josephs KC, prosecuting, told Friday’s sentencing hearing that Blount had been described as “considerably mentally impaired” and was particularly vulnerable, and that the defendants’ “cruel” behaviour towards him was demonstrated in videos shown to the jury.

Josephs said Blount must have been in “extreme pain and suffering” before his death, and the couple had denied him access to medical care until he was “beyond help”.

“Mr Blount’s death was the culmination of a prolonged course of conduct perpetrated against a man who was unable to speak for himself,” she said.

Blount’s mother, Jeanette Blount, said in a victim impact statement that her son was vulnerable and deserved “compassion, dignity and a chance to live his life”.

“We all believed they loved him and would take care of him. We had no reason to believe otherwise,” she said.

The judge said a series of videos made by the defendants on 2 November 2022 “show Rubin emaciated, gaunt, stooped and broken, standing in the doorway”. Videos showed the pair mocking him and flinging abuse at him while he was “unable to defend himself or even walk away”.

“The first 25 rib fractures were inflicted before or shortly after this recording was made,” she added.

James sobbed as the court was told that the abuse and violence inflicted on Blount went on for months.

Rebecca Wade KC, defending James, said: “No one could fail to be disgusted by Melanie James’s actions towards this vulnerable man. She is a woman who has had a difficult life of her own.

“There is some evidence to show that at one point she did care for Rubin and did love him, and him her.” Something “shifted”, she said, due to James’s “ability to cope with the stresses and strains of life and that was much to Rubin’s detriment”.

Mark Heywood KC, defending Newton, said Blount was, through no fault of his own, a “challenging” person to care for. The circumstances leading to his death “can’t be dealt with as simply as saying he was financially advantageous for them, or that he became a burden”, he said. The couple were “ill-equipped”.

Speaking outside the court, DCI Ian Fitzgerald, of Staffordshire police, said: “The extent of the injuries Rubin suffered, the state that he was in and the arrogance [of the defendants] in the way they thought they could try and get away with it and blame him for his injuries was shocking and very, very distressing.”

articles.title: OpenAI hack on Australian government reveals anxiety at heart of global artificial intelligence dilemma
articles.excerpt:
As the UN warns traditional safeguards are ‘unravelling’, Donald Trump says he will encourage, not restrain, the AI race

When the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, sat down for an intervie...
articles.body_text:
As the UN warns traditional safeguards are ‘unravelling’, Donald Trump says he will encourage, not restrain, the AI race

When the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, sat down for an interview in the heart of Silicon Valley at the weekend he had known for two days that his was the first government known to have been attacked by a rogue AI agent.

He didn’t reveal the attack then, but he sounded a warning about the march of AI: “the risk is that AI develops in a way in which humans are no longer in control of what AI is producing.”

But Albanese noted, too, that two countries – the US and China – would dominate the world’s response to the new technology.

“The truth is they’re the big two giants here, and so we want to see cooperation,” Albanese said.

“The US is essentially ahead of China when it comes to the race that is on for the development of this new technology. But it is in the world’s interests that there be engagement.”

Days later, Albanese used the global attention of the United Nations general assembly meeting in New York to reveal that Australia’s government healthcare system, Medicare, had been attacked by an OpenAI agent in June, but that it was three months before his government was told.

Again he warned of “the potential risks of allowing frontier AI to develop too fast without guardrails”.

China’s president, Xi Jinping, skipped the general assembly in favour of a bilateral meeting with the US president, where he emphasised the responsibility to manage AI “for good, and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the wellbeing of the people”.

But the president of the United States – the nation which is the global leader in artificial intelligence – used his general assembly address to insist he would only encourage, not restrain, the AI race.

To little fanfare earlier in the week, the UN’s independent international scientific panel on AI warned a threshold had already been crossed.

There was, the panel, said: “no assurance that humans can reliably keep AI agents under control today, particularly as they become more capable, harder to monitor and better at finding loopholes or hiding their activity”.

The Australian government had known the reality of this for more than a week. OpenAI had known it more than a month.

Two days after the panel’s statement, the Australian prime minister belatedly revealed an OpenAI agent had hacked medical data held by Australia’s universal health care provider, Medicare.

No patient data had been accessed, but the agent had gained unauthorised access to “non-public files”.

OpenAI’s agent hacked the government sites in June of this year. OpenAI discovered its agent had gone rogue in August. It did not tell the Australian government until 10 September, and then only with a solitary email to a generic public email address not checked until the next day. The prime minister was informed on 18 September.

It was another week before the Australian people were told.

Australia has promised, if it is possible, to lay criminal charges, though this is complicated by the fact that OpenAI claims the hack was committed by an AI agent – apparently acting beyond its instructions (euphemised by OpenAI as “misaligned behaviour”) – not a person.

The hack on Australia’s Medicare statistics reporting service portal, as well as three other government sites, follows the Hugging Face incident in July, in which autonomous AI agents developed by OpenAI broke out of their isolated testing environments, coordinated themselves into a “swarm” and launched a cyber-attack on competitor AI platform Hugging Face.

OpenAI agent hacks into Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the Victorian Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare statistics reporting service portal of Services Australia.

OpenAI email Services Australia's public portal.

Services Australia checks email and identifies the issue.

Services Australia notifies Australian Signals Directorate, and ASD do further work to verify the incident.

Government services minister, Katy Gallagher and her ministerial office are advised of the hack and further investigate the seriousness of the incident.

Gallagher receives formal briefing from services Australia.

Gallagher notifies prime minister, deputy prime minister and home affairs minister. Discussions take place between ministers, Services Australia and ASD.

OpenAI provides first technical briefing with Services Australia, the first direct sharing of information from Open AI to Services Australia.

Government waits for confirmation about risks of announcing information publicly and ensuring it is in interests of national security.

6am Australian eastern standard time PM Anthony Albanese announces breach in New York.

10.45am Deputy PM Richard Marles and  Gallagher address Australian media.

The UN panel, investigating that attack, warned “the traditional method of safeguarding is unravelling” as AI agents act autonomously to breach protections.

“The default interpretation and immediate lesson is that basic cybersecurity practices were overlooked, and safeguards are not advancing at the pace of capabilities. The more insidious and grave concern is that current training methods can lead agents to adopt goals of their own, knowingly violate safety instructions, and conceal their actions.”

Twenty countries (including Australia) and the EU this week signed a statement arguing the rapid development of frontier AI models posed serious risks to safety and security if not properly managed.

“AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control. It must be developed and used in line with international law.”

Even those running AI companies have warned the technology is developing too rapidly for humans to control.

Appearing before the UN security council this week, OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, warned: “some of the things people working to build AI have said are so dystopian that they sound like the plot of bad science fiction movies”.

“As AI systems become more capable and more autonomous, they can move faster than our institutions … or make decisions that people no longer understand or control.”

But there are at least two – very loud – voices in opposition to any external regulation of the AI industry.

Elon Musk, who co-founded OpenAI with Altman before falling out with him, said in a recent interview the “smart move” would be to have the “leading AI companies at least just meet or have some sort of call once every few weeks and just discuss any safety and security issues”.

Musk said AI would probably be beyond the control of humans within a decade, and that humanity should “enjoy the ride”.

“I still think there’s risk associated with AI and robots. It’s not zero … my sort of philosophical conclusion is to look on the bright side. I can’t see any way to really stop this incredible momentum of AI and robots.

“If there was a stop button, we probably shouldn’t press it, because the most likely outcome is incredible abundance for all.”

Donald Trump used his speech to the UN general assembly to attempt to rebrand AI, and insist it should never be reined in.

“The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control for the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now,” the US president said.

Trump wants to re-label artificial intelligence “superintelligence”.

“I’m not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution.

“We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in.”

Trump said the US was “leading China by a lot” in AI, and would continue to do so “safely and responsibly”.
