articles.title: Trump and Xi exchange warm words at state dinner but little progress on key issues
articles.excerpt:
Watch: The world’s two most powerful men just met. How did it go?

US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping exchanged warm words at a lavish White House state dinner but gave little ...
articles.body_text:
Watch: The world’s two most powerful men just met. How did it go?

US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping exchanged warm words at a lavish White House state dinner but gave little indication of progress on pressing issues.

Xi stressed that the countries should ensure AI remain "under human control" and act "as responsible major countries", while Trump toasted a future of "harmony, peace and success" for both nations.

But tensions remain despite the diplomatic niceties, including over Taiwan - with Xi urging Trump earlier in the day to take the "correct position" on the self-governing island which Beijing claims, amid a weapons package paused by Trump.

Billionaire business leaders and US tech CEOs joined the leaders at the extravagant dinner late on Thursday.

Their arrival was marked by protesters shouting from just outside the White House gates, some of whom were arrested.

Trump lavished praise on Xi during his first visit to the US in over a decade, telling those attending the dinner that while the two countries had "different systems", they had "never gotten along better".

Xi meanwhile welcomed the "historic juncture" in US-China relations - and said both leaders' ambitions could "surely be mutually reinforcing".

"China and the United States must act as responsible major countries to meet the expectations of our peoples, keep pace with the trend of our times, and explore a new approach for major countries to get along with each other," he said.

But little to no mention was made of key issues which divide the leaders of the world's two most powerful countries.

China believes the US is trying to contain its rise as a superpower, and it wants Washington to stay out of its way - particularly when it comes to trade, technology and Taiwan.

Xi thanked his hosts for receiving him and his wife with "meticulous care and consideration"

Trump has been blunt about his ambitions for artificial intelligence (AI) - and clear that he considers China to be the US's main rival for its development.

But beyond Xi's reference to AI remaining under "human control", little indication was given of what progress the two leaders may have made on the issue - if any - during their talks.

The dinner also came just hours after Chinese state media reported Xi had, behind closed doors, advised Washington to handle "with prudence" its approach to Taiwan.

Washington is yet to comment publicly on the remarks, and the matter was another neither leader addressed late on Thursday.

The US is legally bound to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself, but Trump delayed approving a $14bn (£11bn) arms package for it after Xi in May warned that mishandling the issue could cause the two countries to "collide or even enter into conflict".

At the time, Trump called it a "very good negotiating chip" with Beijing, but has yet to make a public comment on the issue during this visit.

Xi visit to Washington all pomp but little progress so far

Trump and Xi come face-to-face as US and China battle to win the AI race

Xi got Trump's red carpet welcome - but not everything he wanted

The evening instead marked a continuation of the lavish welcome Xi has so far received in the US.

Trump presented the Chinese president with a sculpture of a bald eagle - America's national symbol - saying it embodied "the free and soaring spirit of America". First Lady Melania had participated in its design, Trump added.

Others in attendance included key White House figures, such as Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, chief of staff Monica Crowley, and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

They were joined by scores of US officials, as well as conservative broadcasters, tech industry bosses, social media CEOs and corporate executives.

Apple's Tim Cook and Nvidia's Jensen Huang were seated at the same table as Trump and Xi, as was Elon Musk, who previously worked in Trump's administration leading the effort to shrink government.

OpenAI's Sam Altman, Google's Sundar Pichai, and Amazon's Jeff Bezos were also present, as were Mark Zuckerberg and Jeff Yass, the American billionaire who owns a share of TikTok.

Musk was seen mingling with guests, alongside US Secretary of State Marco Rubio

The leaders of companies including General Motors, Visa, Paramount Skydance and ExxonMobil could also be seen in the room.

"Everybody wanted to be there," Trump said ahead of the event. "I would say you have the entire tech world, the entire banking world, and a lot more."

One notable absence was Anthropic - one of the biggest and most valuable AI firms in the world. The BBC has asked Anthropic if it was invited, or if they chose not to be there.

Business leaders and tech bosses were among those in attendance

The office of the First Lady Melania Trump, which planned the event, said the dinner menu would showcase "American ingredients with subtle Chinese influence".

The first course was yellow squash, wild mushrooms and crispy pancetta. The guests ate off red tablecloths - red being a symbol of luck and good fortune in China.

For their main course they dined on a sesame-crusted sea bass, braised bok choy and roasted eggplant.

Dessert featured the two leaders and their fellow diners tucking into vanilla crémeux with sour cherry confit, with an accompanying ice cream "made with harvested White House honey".

The wine chosen by the first lady included Schramsberg Blanc De Noir - a nod to President Nixon's 1972 "Toast to Peace" with former Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai, when they used a bottle from the same vineyard.

Watch: Trump puts on a warm reception for Xi in Washington

Trump and Xi will begin the final day of their visit on Friday with tea at the White House's Red Room with their wives.

The group will then head to the US National Archives for a tour of the building and its exhibits.

Formally called the National Archives and Records Administration, the building holds some of the most important documents regarding the founding of the United States - including the US Constitution, the Declaration of Independence and the Bill of Rights.

Xi and his wife will depart Washington later in the day.

articles.title: Frontline NATO ally shares shocking take on Russian invasion threat
articles.excerpt: In a Fox News Digital exclusive, Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna says Moscow is relying on hybrid tactics, including cyberattacks and GPS interference, instead of preparing for a full-scale i...
articles.body_text:
In a Fox News Digital exclusive, Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna says Moscow is relying on hybrid tactics, including cyberattacks and GPS interference, instead of preparing for a full-scale invasion of NATO.

NEW YORK — Fears that Russia is preparing for a broader war with NATO aren't rattling Estonia's foreign minister, who told Fox News Digital that his country’s intelligence sees no signs Moscow is preparing for a full-scale invasion of the alliance.

"We have more and more this kind of panic in Europe that Russia will invade and will be full-scale aggressive against NATO and Europe and the Baltic states, Poland," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said in an interview on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York City before quipping, "But we don’t see it."

Estonia shares a roughly 180-mile border with Russia and has long been among NATO’s most vocal members warning about the threat from Moscow under President Vladimir Putin. But Tsahkna drew a distinction between preparations for a conventional attack and the growing campaign of drone incursions, sabotage, cyberattacks and other provocations that European governments have blamed on Russia.

BATTLE-TESTED ZELENSKYY SOUNDS CHILLING ALARM ON WHERE PUTIN’S WAR COULD HEAD NEXT

"Our intelligence, we see very, very deep into Russia, we don’t see any change," Tsahkna said. "We don’t see that Russia is preparing a full-scale invasion or aggression. The other side of our borders is pretty empty."

Estonia Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna spoke with Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. (Fox News Digital)

Tsahkna, who served as Estonia’s defense minister from 2016 to 2017, contrasted the current picture with what he saw a decade ago, when he said roughly 120,000 Russian troops were positioned across the region’s borders and could be ready to move within 48 hours.

"It’s empty," he said of the Russian side of Estonia’s border today.

His assessment comes as European officials grapple with a series of Russian airspace violations and suspected hybrid attacks, including a Russian military helicopter that crossed into Polish airspace Wednesday. Poland’s military said the incursion appeared to be another attempt to test the readiness of its air defenses.

RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT

European and NATO officials have also warned that Russia could rebuild sufficient military capability to pose a direct threat to the alliance in the coming years. Estonia’s own intelligence service said earlier this year that it saw no Russian intention to attack a NATO member in the immediate term, while warning that Moscow’s military reforms are increasing its longer-term capabilities.

Tsahkna argued that the more immediate threat is a Russian campaign of provocations and hybrid attacks designed to remain below NATO’s Article 5 threshold.

"What Russia is doing now is waging these attacks, which are not crossing Article 5," he said. "It’s sabotage attacks, terror attacks."

"The main purpose for Putin is to play with the Western part of the fear of escalation," Tsahikna went on. "He’s trying to divide the Western parts of the world. Divide the unity, divide this kind of consensus."

European and NATO officials have also warned that Russia could rebuild sufficient military capability to pose a direct threat to the alliance in the coming years (Remko de Waal /ANP/AFP via Getty Images)

Estonia has dealt with GPS interference, cyberattacks and disinformation it has attributed to Russia, while drones have also crossed into its airspace as the war in neighboring Ukraine continues.

Tsahkna said Estonia recorded roughly 40,000 cyberattacks last year, a particular challenge for a country where virtually all public services are available online.

"We are witnessing already, yes, any kind of different level attacks," he said. "Unfortunately, it’s already like normality."

Tsahkna said NATO needs to become more flexible in responding to attacks that fall below the alliance’s collective-defense threshold.

"NATO must be more flex and more dynamic, because these are the attacks which are not crossing Article 5," he said, pointing to sanctions, public attribution and political responses as tools available to the alliance.

"Putin wants to boil Europe and western part of the world as a frog," Tsahkna said. "Turning on the heat piece by piece is a test of us."

Tsahkna also pointed to an incident last year in which three Russian fighter jets violated Estonian airspace for roughly 12 minutes, prompting Tallinn to request consultations under NATO’s Article 4 and raise the incident at the U.N. Security Council.

Estonia has dealt with GPS interference, cyberattacks and disinformation it has attributed to Russia, while drones have also crossed into its airspace as the war in neighboring Ukraine continues. (Alexander Kazakov/Sputnik/Kremlin Pool Photo/AP)

He recalled President Donald Trump later saying Russian aircraft that violate NATO airspace should be shot down, and said Estonia has not experienced another comparable fighter-jet incursion since.

"We have now drones coming in," Tsahkna said. "NATO is working as a Swiss clock."

Tsahkna said NATO may need cheaper and more efficient ways to bring down drones rather than relying on expensive fighter aircraft.

On Ukraine, Tsahkna called for increasing pressure on Moscow, arguing that Russia’s economic and battlefield losses could eventually push Putin toward serious negotiations.

"What we see, and I also visited Ukraine last week, is that we need to put more pressure on Russia, because Putin understands only very clear language through strength," he said.

Tsahkna also pointed to Ukraine’s growing ability to strike targets deep inside Russia as a source of pressure on the Kremlin.

"If Putin is under heavier pressure, and also Ukraine is delivering more deep-strike capabilities and attacks, there will be a momentum when Putin may really start some kind of ceasefire or energy ceasefire, or real talks," he said.

Tsahkna said Trump had devoted significant effort to seeking an end to the war, but argued that Putin has used the diplomatic process to buy time.

"President Trump has put lots of energy during the last year to find a way, but Putin has just played with him and also winning the time," Tsahkna said.

He said Ukraine’s deep strikes are already weakening Russia economically, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly signaled his willingness to agree to a ceasefire.

"Putin can just decide like today or tomorrow to have a ceasefire," Tsahkna said. "Unfortunately, we don’t see any change for now."

Tsahkna also said Estonia has been assured that U.S. forces will remain in the region for the next rotation, amid the Trump administration’s broader review of the American military footprint in Europe.

"We got the information that it will happen soon," he said of the next rotation.

Tsahkna said the presence of American forces remains an important part of deterrence on NATO’s eastern flank.

"U.S. troops are keeping the peace in our region," Tsahkna said. "The flag of the troops is so important to give the message to President Putin" about the red lines between Russia and NATO.

articles.title: GOP handed new lifeline on biggest pocketbook fight of midterms
articles.excerpt:
Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., discusses how rising energy costs and persistent inflation are impacting families on the campaign trail ahead of the midterm elections.

FIRST ON FOX: Republicans are being g...
articles.body_text:
Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., discusses how rising energy costs and persistent inflation are impacting families on the campaign trail ahead of the midterm elections.

FIRST ON FOX: Republicans are being given a new playbook on an issue that is all but certain to be the biggest political lightning rod of the November midterms.

Conservative group Club for Growth is sending a memo to Capitol Hill lawmakers on Friday arguing that Americans' struggle with high living costs cannot be ignored — and that the fault lies with an expanding federal government.

"Americans are not asking whether the inflation rate has slowed; they are asking why the same basket of goods is permanently more expensive," the information packets being distributed to Republican lawmakers read. "[G]overnment made core costs higher through deficit spending, subsidies, mandates, and restrictions on supply."

It's an argument that could be a lifeline for the GOP as it fights an uphill battle to keep control of the House and Senate. While Democrats attack Republicans for how Americans feel about prices today, Club for Growth's memo is urging Republicans to point to the rapid federal expansion the Biden administration presided over during the COVID-19 pandemic.

REPUBLICANS JUST GOT A POWERFUL NEW PLAYBOOK FOR THE BATTLE FOR CONGRESS. HERE'S WHAT'S INSIDE

Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, R-La., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., attend the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum's National Commemoration of the Days of Remembrance ceremony in Emancipation Hall on April 14, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

The materials, a two-page memo for lawmakers and a more in-depth 76-page policy packet, also urge Republicans to push policies that Club for Growth says will actually lower those costs.

AMERICA’S BROKEN PERMITTING SYSTEM IS QUIETLY RAISING YOUR COST OF LIVING

The strategy would be a gamble, given the midterms are traditionally a referendum on how people feel about how they are doing under the party currently in power. But it gives Republicans a potential economic platform and a roadmap to pitch for lowering costs if they keep the majority for the next two years.

"The free-market answer is structural cost relief: spend less, build more, produce more energy, make healthcare compete, let workers earn, and let families choose," the memo said.

BILLIONS SPENT BY KEY FEDERAL AGENCY HASN'T MADE AMERICAN DREAM OF HOMEOWNERSHIP ANY EASIER: REPORT

It urged Republicans to resist calling for subsidies for areas of the economy where prices are skyrocketing, arguing that handing out taxpayer money would only increase costs in the longer-term. An example the memo used is Affordable Care Act (ACA) premium tax credits, which Republicans have long blamed for skyrocketing healthcare costs before the COVID-era subsidy expired at the beginning of this year.

"Subsidies and regulation function as a back door for government control and involvement in private industry," the memo argued. "The only way to address the affordability crisis properly is to undo misguided government intervention and stop pretending more of the same will suddenly work."

Gas prices are seen on a gas pump at an Exxon Gas Station in Falls Church, Va., Aug. 24, 2026. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images)

But it could put GOP lawmakers at odds with President Donald Trump and his promise to give each American adult $5,000 if Republicans win the midterms. Several GOP lawmakers who spoke with Fox News Digital last week were hesitant to embrace the idea.

Among the solutions offered are reforming Social Security, which fiscal hawks have long warned will soon run out of cash if changes are not made to current age requirements and other guidelines.

GOP FISCAL HAWK SOUNDS ALARM ON 'OUT OF CONTROL' FEDERAL SPENDING, SAYING 'BOTH PARTIES HAVE FAILED US'

On high housing costs, the memo urges lawmakers to increase supply by targeting land use and building regulations rather than offering subsidies to make existing housing more affordable.

Energy costs, which were a flashpoint in the 2025 off-year elections as well, could be brought down by furthering the Trump administration's goals to unleash U.S. energy sources rather than Democrats' push for net-zero carbon emissions, the memo said.

A focus on nuclear energy policies could also help drive down energy costs, which will be at the forefront of most Americans' minds during the November election.

President Donald Trump pauses as he walks alone along an ivy-covered wall during his final departure from Aras an Uachtarain on Sept. 12, 2026, in Dublin. (Artur Widak/Anadolu via Getty Images)

And while Democrats have pushed free early childcare as a solution for struggling families, the Club for Growth memo is urging Republicans to find a more lasting solution in reforming regulations surrounding the industry.

"Health and safety training in specific areas, adherence to building, fire, and health codes, and comprehensive background checks, including fingerprinting, are reasonable," the memo said. "However, strict and complex rules about work-child ratios, rigid staffing mandates, and regulations on facility specifications, including equipment requirements and zoning classifications, increase operating costs without demonstrable improvements in child wellbeing."

The election is less than 50 days away, and both sides are working overtime to prove they are best positioned to help ease rising costs.

Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

Follow on Twitter at @liz_elkind and send tips to elizabeth.elkind@fox.com

articles.title: Fast-food drive-thrus took over American mornings for these key reasons
articles.excerpt: Culinary storyteller Capri Cafaro shares how postwar development, expanding interstate travel and widespread automobile ownership helped turn ordering meals from behind the wheel into a lasting nation...
articles.body_text:
Culinary storyteller Capri Cafaro shares how postwar development, expanding interstate travel and widespread automobile ownership helped turn ordering meals from behind the wheel into a lasting national phenomenon.

For millions of Americans, grabbing breakfast or coffee from a fast-food drive-thru is an ordinary part of the morning routine — but not long ago, ordering a meal without leaving the car was a novelty.

So how did the drive-thru go from a novel idea to an everyday staple?

Convenience and an "on-the-go" lifestyle are two big factors, according to Capri Cafaro, the creator, executive producer and host of "America the Bountiful."

MORE AMERICANS NOW EAT IN THEIR CARS THAN EVER BEFORE AS EXPERT REVEALS WHAT IT SAYS ABOUT MODERN LIFE

Cafaro spoke with Fox News Digital about how and why the drive-thru, particularly drive-thru breakfast, became a daily ritual for many Americans.

The modern drive-thru is reflective of America's convenience and on-the-go lifestyle. (Gary Friedman/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

There is some debate over which restaurant pioneered the drive-thru concept.

West Coast chain In-N-Out Burger is widely credited with creating the first drive-thru, debuting a two-way intercom drive-thru system in California in 1948.

AMERICA'S LATE-NIGHT FAST-FOOD CULTURE MAY BE MAKING A COMEBACK — HERE'S WHY

However, Cafaro and other news publications, maintain that Springfield, Mo., restaurant Red's Giant Hamburg (the word "hamburger" reportedly didn't fit on the sign) actually introduced the drive-thru concept in 1947, narrowly beating In-N-Out.

Regardless of which establishment first created it, the drive-thru emerged at a time when Americans' relationship with the automobile was rapidly changing.

In-N-Out is said to have introduced the drive-thru concept in 1948, although a food historian claims it was started a year earlier at a Missouri restaurant. (Richard Hartog/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

During the mid-20th century, the country saw a surge in automobile usage due to the growth of suburbs and the rise of highways, particularly the interstate system and Route 66, which will celebrate its 100th anniversary in November.

More people took to the roads, not just for their daily commute to and from work, but also for road trips and family outings.

As Americans ended up behind the wheel, "that really created an opportunity for the rise of fast-food restaurants and certainly the drive-thru," Cafaro noted.

Despite McDonald's firm grip on the fast-food breakfast market in recent years, it was not the first chain to introduce the morning meal.

McDonald's is one of the most frequented fast-food chains for breakfast, even though the Egg McMuffin didn't arrive on menus until the early 1970s. (iStock)

McDonald's was actually beaten to the punch by Jack in the Box, which debuted breakfast in 1969 with the Breakfast Jack, a sandwich with egg, cheese and ham.

The Egg McMuffin, by comparison, wasn't on McDonald's menus until 1971, when it was invented at a Santa Barbara, Calif., location by franchise owner Herb Peterson, according to the McDonald's website.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"McDonald's, it seems to be the most prolific and the most recognizable, [but] they actually … were later adopters to some of these trends that are so embedded in our fast-food culture today," Cafaro said.

The golden arches didn't hover over a drive-thru window until 1975, when McDonald's added one to its Sierra Vista, Arizona, location to accommodate soldiers who weren't allowed to get out of their cars while wearing their uniforms off-base, its website said.

McDonald's didn't open its first drive-thru location until 1975. (Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

Today, drive-thru sales account for roughly 70% of McDonald's business, according to the corporate website.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Another late adopter of the drive-thru is Starbucks. The coffee giant didn't open its first drive-thru location until 1994.

Starbucks didn't open its first drive-thru location until 1994. (Carlo Allegri/Reuters)

Business Insider reported in 2022 that two-thirds of Starbucks sales happen via the drive-thru.

"The drive-thru and fast-food landscape has changed in the last 50 to 70 years, and it will continue to evolve as long as we have cars and as long as we want convenience," Cafaro said.

Sadie Chafe is a writer on the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Mistress told ‘American Idol’ contestant she wanted ‘to kill’ wife but testified divorce, not murder, was plan
articles.excerpt:
Jurors watched the final exchanges between Caleb Flynn and his former mistress before Ashley Flynn was killed, ending with a haunting remark after they met hours later. (Credit: WKEF).

Jurors spent h...
articles.body_text:
Jurors watched the final exchanges between Caleb Flynn and his former mistress before Ashley Flynn was killed, ending with a haunting remark after they met hours later. (Credit: WKEF).

Jurors spent hours Thursday listening to droves of messages exchanged between former "American Idol" contestant Caleb Flynn and his former mistress, Alleigha Botner, before defense attorneys sought to recast the relationship as an emotionally volatile affair centered on divorce – not murder.

The day ended with an Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation digital forensics expert beginning testimony about data recovered from Flynn's cellphone.

Here are the biggest moments from Day 6 of testimony:

‘AMERICAN IDOL’ CONTESTANT’S 100K TEXTS WITH MISTRESS SHOW MOTIVE IN WIFE’S MURDER, PROSECUTORS SAY

Ashley and Caleb Flynn in an undated photo with their two children. (GoFundMe)

Botner testified that she and Flynn exchanged messages about wanting his wife dead months before Ashley was killed.

"I just wish I didn't say this," she said as she became emotional on the stand.

Botner then read her message to Flynn: "I want to kill her, Caleb."

She said Flynn responded: "That makes two of us."

WATCH: Caleb Flynn had ominous response when mistress said ‘I want to kill her’

Prosecutors focused heavily on the final hours before Ashley Flynn was shot, walking jurors through messages exchanged the night before her death.

Botner repeatedly questioned whether Flynn was prepared to leave his wife.

‘AMERICAN IDOL’ CONTESTANT’S 100K TEXTS WITH MISTRESS SHOW MOTIVE IN WIFE’S MURDER, PROSECUTORS SAY

"I said, 'Caleb, I've never felt anything as deep as I felt with you. I trusted you with my heart. I'm terrified. But thank you for saying all that. We will see if your actions finally match your words,'" Botner testified, reading from the messages.

She said Flynn responded: "I've never felt anything like it either. It's why I know it's actually real ... I'm terrified as well, but tomorrow it all starts."

‘AMERICAN IDOL’ CONTESTANT’S 100K TEXTS WITH MISTRESS SHOW MOTIVE IN WIFE’S MURDER, PROSECUTORS SAY

When Botner asked whether he was "more excited or scared," Flynn allegedly replied: "Well, I got a pretty massive day tomorrow so I'm gonna head to sleep. Please be praying for me and I'll update you the whole time."

Later in the conversation, Botner testified she wrote: "You're about to be free."

MISTRESS SAYS SHE GAVE ‘AMERICAN IDOL’ CONTESTANT ULTIMATUM BEFORE WIFE’S KILLING BLEW UP AFFAIR

She said Flynn replied: "I choose you ... You're more than enough. Good night."

Caleb Flynn becomes emotional in court during his murder trial in Ohio. Flynn is accused of killing his wife, Ashley Flynn, in February 2026 and staging the scene to look like a break-in. (COURTESY: WKEF)

Botner testified she later went to Ashley's parents' home, where church staff had gathered after the shooting.

She said Flynn hugged her shortly after she arrived.

"The first thing he said to me was, 'It didn't happen the way we thought it would, did it?'"

She testified she immediately questioned him about what happened and became increasingly suspicious as he described hearing a gunshot, finding blood inside the home and discovering Ashley.

Alleigha Botner wipes away tears while testifying about messages exchanged with Caleb Flynn during his murder trial in Ohio. (CREDIT: WKEF)

Defense attorney Emily Smith sought to reframe the prosecution's key evidence, arguing Botner understood Flynn's messages to be about leaving his wife – not killing her.

Smith asked whether Flynn's repeated references to becoming "free," taking action and leaving Ashley meant he intended to divorce her.

MISTRESS SAYS SHE GAVE ‘AMERICAN IDOL’ CONTESTANT ULTIMATUM BEFORE WIFE’S KILLING BLEW UP AFFAIR

Smith then asked whether she understood those same messages to mean Flynn was planning a murder.

Smith also zeroed in on Botner's ChatGPT research before Ashley's death.

Botner testified she looked up divorce proceedings, deleting messages and digital evidence because she feared Ashley could discover their affair if Flynn followed through with a divorce.

She also said she was trying to keep the affair from becoming public – not cover up a homicide.

One of the defense's most significant exchanges came when Smith questioned Botner about Flynn's repeated statements that he wanted Ashley dead.

Ashley Flynn, a Tipp City Schools substitute teacher and volleyball coach, was found dead in her Ohio home. (Tipp City Schools)

Botner acknowledged she did not believe he actually intended to carry out those statements.

"I did not believe that he meant it," she said.

Asked why, Botner replied, "I don't think he could ever be capable of doing something like that."

Caleb and Ashley Flynn are pictured in an undated photo. (Ashley Flynn/Facebook)

Smith then turned to Botner's own messages, arguing she repeatedly pressured Flynn to leave Ashley.

"I'm so done with you," Botner wrote in one of the texts she read in court. "You have murdered my heart."

"I hope you're glad you took my virginity and also my heart and stomped all over it," she later continued. "Enjoy your marriage. I'm done."

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Smith also walked Botner through months of messages in which she acknowledged giving Flynn four or five separate deadlines to leave Ashley after he failed to follow through on earlier promises.

The defense also pointed to exchanges in which Botner demanded reassurance Flynn hated Ashley, questioned him whenever he spent time with his wife and threatened to end the relationship if he didn't leave Ashley.

Alleigha Botner testifies Wednesday in the Ohio murder trial of former "American Idol" contestant Caleb Flynn. Prosecutors say Botner had an affair with Flynn before his wife, Ashley Flynn, was killed. (CREDIT: WKEF)

After Botner stepped down, prosecutors called Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation Special Agent Joseph Wilhelm, a digital forensics examiner who spent the remainder of the day walking jurors through evidence recovered from Flynn's iPhone.

Wilhelm testified investigators ultimately extracted a full copy of Flynn's phone after earlier attempts failed, then analyzed browser history, location data, health information, application activity and other digital records to reconstruct what the device was doing in the hours before Ashley Flynn's death.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Jurors heard testimony that ChatGPT was uninstalled from Flynn's phone on Feb. 15, while GroupMe and Instagram were removed shortly after 1 a.m. on Feb. 16. Wilhelm also testified investigators found no text messages between Flynn and Ashley on the device.

Wilhelm also outlined phone location data, Apple Watch activity, AirPods connections and a timeline leading up to Flynn's 911 call, which prosecutors are expected to revisit as the trial continues.

Before court adjourned, prosecutors played two AI-generated songs recovered from Flynn's phone. Wilhelm testified the files were related to Flynn's relationship with Botner and matched lyrics investigators found saved in the phone's notes app.

Flynn's attorney, L. Patrick Mulligan, declined to comment while the case is ongoing.

Botner could not immediately be reached for comment.

A joint statement with lea...
articles.body_text:
The Premier League and three other top European leagues have called for governance reform of FIFA, following Gianni Infantino’s failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup.

A joint statement with leagues from Spain, Italy and Germany accused FIFA’s president of actively promoting “exploitative ideas rather than safeguarding against them”.

The Premier League is football’s richest and most popular league. Its collaboration with Europe’s other leading leagues adds to the growing pressure on Infantino, who plans to stand for re-election despite losing the support of many national federations over his controversial plan to sell profits in the World Cup through a commercial subsidiary.

“Football’s longstanding foundations have, in recent years, been threatened by a fundamental governance problem,” the statement said.

In the face of continued ‌criticism of his leadership at FIFA, Infantino posted on social ⁠media Thursday that ⁠he is ready to embrace discussions with member nations about reforms in the organisation.

Infantino has been under fire from a number ⁠of top national federations and governing bodies around the world, including UEFA in Europe and CONCACAF, which includes the United States, Canada and Mexico.

FIFA president ⁠since February 2016, Infantino caught the ire of member nations with a now-abandoned plan to sell 20% of FIFA’s commercial rights in the World Cup to private investors. The deal, which could have been worth a reported $4.2b, led ‌to UEFA and CONCACAF, among others, calling for Infantino’s replacement.

The latest development came last week when England’s Football Association asked Infantino to release all documents related to his plan to bring on private investors for the World Cup, as well as the controversial decision to overturn US striker Folarin Balogun’s red card during this summer’s tournament.

Currently at the Arabian ⁠Gulf Cup tournament in Saudi Arabia, Infantino praised the ⁠host nation and referenced a letter he sent to the FIFA council and member nations, proposing a discussion on reforms.

Writing on Instagram that he has received “positive messages” ⁠in reaction to the letter, Infantino stressed the need for open communication.

“We have a FIFA Council meeting next ⁠month, so we will continue to have a dialogue ⁠on these important matters,” he posted, in part. “There must be a culture of dialogue, of listening to each other and respecting one another.”

Infantino addressed potential cynics to his desire to discuss ‌reforms.

“This is not about generating positive headlines, it is about what is right for the game,” Infantino wrote. “I have never been more determined and committed ‌in ‌doing that. FIFA is always engaged. I am always engaged and want to hear how we can continue to grow football for the benefit of everybody, everywhere.”

articles.title: Jonathan Flora: The WNBA has a courage problem and it’s not Sophie Cunningham
articles.excerpt:
Do you ever notice ... how the WNBA has a courage problem?

The WNBA doesn't need another statement. It needs a definition.

The league says outside forces are trying to hijack women's basketball.

Bu...
articles.body_text:
Do you ever notice ... how the WNBA has a courage problem?

The WNBA doesn't need another statement. It needs a definition.

The league says outside forces are trying to hijack women's basketball.

But there is a remarkably simple way to stop them.

Clearly define who is eligible to play in the Women’s National Basketball Association.

THE WOMEN'S NATIONAL BASKETBALL ASSOCIATION CAN'T DEFINE A 'WOMAN,' AND IT'S BEYOND SHAMEFUL

WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert speaks before the WNBA basketball draft in New York on April 13, 2026. (Pamela Smith/AP)

Funny how quickly a hypothetical becomes real when somebody finally has to write the rule.

Last week, I wrote that the WNBA had backed itself into a corner.

Turns out somebody at league headquarters finally noticed the walls.

WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert has now told teams that the league is discussing transgender-player eligibility and expects those conversations to continue.

Because the WNBA doesn't need another statement.

The league's collective bargaining agreement says:

"Only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA."

Except it doesn't define what a woman is.

That might have been an amusing legal omission when the question was theoretical.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Turkish-American former basketball player and human rights activist Enes Kanter Freedom is seen prior to a game between the Indiana Fever and the Chicago Sky at Wintrust Arena in Chicago, Ill., on Aug. 23, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

Former NBA players Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White say they want to enter the WNBA Draft.

French transgender basketball player Julie Tétart, who is biologically male, is already playing professional women's basketball overseas.

Suddenly the question isn't something being shouted across cable-news panels.

The WNBA has a courage problem and it’s not Sophie Cunningham

And the answer can't be: We'll get back to you.

Because you can't have a professional women's league whose rule says only women may play

That's a future lawsuit with a basketball.

And while league officials figure this out, we're getting a pretty good demonstration of why this

subject has become so difficult for the WNBA to address honestly.

Just look at what's happening in Indiana.

Chicago Sky guard DiJonai Carrington commits a flagrant 2 foul against Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham. (Kamil Krzaczynski/Imagn Images)

DiJonai Carrington came up behind Sophie Cunningham on a fast break and clobbered her in the

head, sending her crashing to the floor and bloodying her mouth.

Carrington was assessed a Flagrant 2 and ejected.

It wasn’t even close to a basketball move.

Afterward, Fever coach Stephanie White defended Carrington's competitiveness and said she

didn't believe Carrington was trying to hurt Cunningham.

As White spoke, Makayla Timpson looked down.

Caitlin Clark buried her head in her hands.

White has since said she hadn't seen the foul when she made those comments.

Video appears to show White looking directly toward the play as it happens.

The WNBA has a courage problem and it’s not Sophie Cunningham

This time White talked about unity, love, grace and integrity while blasting the outside forces she

says are trying to divide the Fever and "hijack" the WNBA.

Right before she said, "Everybody else can go to hell."

Too many people are trying to turn every WNBA game into something other than basketball.

Most of those forces aren't coming from outside.

For years the league has embraced political and cultural causes far beyond basketball.

Players have been celebrated for speaking out.

Indiana Fever head coach Stephanie White gives instructions to Sophie Cunningham and Caitlin Clark against the Atlanta Dream at Gainbridge Fieldhouse on June 18, 2026, in Indianapolis, Ind. (Getty Images)

But you don't get to invite politics and cultural activism onto the court when you agree with the

message and then complain that outsiders are hijacking basketball when the questions become

Which is why I've been impressed with Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham.

The WNBA has a courage problem and it’s not Sophie Cunningham

Cunningham doesn't need to attack her coach every time someone sticks a microphone in her

She believes boys shouldn't compete in girls' sports.

And she’s standing by her coach and teammates.

Sometimes it's standing your ground without burning down the locker room around you.

Clark doesn't need another national controversy attached to her name either.

Sophie Cunningham #8 of the Indiana Fever smiles before the game against the Washington Mystics on Sept. 20, 2026, at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Ind. (NBAE via Getty Images)

Maybe the adults running the league could help them out.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

And while we're at it, perhaps the people covering the WNBA could ask it.

Not another question about the political climate.

Not another invitation for a prepared statement.

What objective standard determines who is eligible to play in the Women's National Basketball

The WNBA has a courage problem and it’s not Sophie Cunningham

This is what sports journalists are supposed to do.

The tragedy is that the WNBA is sitting on an extraordinary opportunity.

Caitlin Clark brought millions of new eyeballs to women's basketball.

The league finally had what every professional sports organization spends decades trying to build: Momentum.

And somehow the conversation keeps becoming about everything except the basketball.

They didn't buy a ticket to attend a sociology seminar.

And that's why Engelbert's eligibility discussions matter.

The league has an opportunity to remove at least one enormous source of ambiguity.

This debate does not have to be about inclusion.

Transgender people should be treated with dignity and respect.

The WNBA has a courage problem and it’s not Sophie Cunningham

It’s about protection and fair competition.

Women deserve their own athletic category.

And yes, there are people who vehemently disagree with that.

Sophie Cunningham of the Indiana Fever arrives at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Ind., before a game against the Minnesota Lynx on Sept. 22, 2026. (NBAE via Getty Images)

Then have the courage to have the debate.

But first, the league has to have the courage to define its own rules.

The WNBA keeps saying outside forces are trying to hijack women's basketball.

Tell everybody exactly what the W stands for.

And then do something increasingly novel for the Women's National Basketball Association.

articles.title: TalkTalk races to sell consumer and broadband arms as administration looms
articles.excerpt:
Customers and jobs ‘top priority’ as company closes in on deals with Opus Broadband and investment group Octopus

TalkTalk is scrambling to secure its future amid the threat of administration, closing...
articles.body_text:
Customers and jobs ‘top priority’ as company closes in on deals with Opus Broadband and investment group Octopus

TalkTalk is scrambling to secure its future amid the threat of administration, closing in on deals to sell its consumer and broadband arms as it seeks to save 900 jobs.

The telecoms company said on Friday it was in the final stages of sealing deals to sell its consumer business as well as its wholesale operation, PXC.

“The company expects to conclude both transactions imminently,” TalkTalk said.

The UK’s fourth-largest broadband company was founded in 2003 by Charles Dunstone as a subsidiary of Carphone Warehouse. It has struggled in the highly competitive telecoms market, with its customer numbers shrinking from 4 million in 2019 to about 1.5 million.

The debt-laden business is close to sealing a £100m deal to sell its consumer operation to Opus Broadband, and to sell its wholesale operation PXC to Octopus Investments for an undisclosed sum.

A spokesperson for Opus said: “[Our] top priority is to ensure that every customer stays connected and that all TalkTalk employees’ roles are protected.” Octopus Investments declined to comment.

“I’d be surprised if there is real disruption for TalkTalk customers if the deal with Opus goes ahead,” said Karen Egan, a telecoms analyst at the research and consultancy firm Enders Analysis, told the BBC. “They would take over the running of the operations I would expect.

“They may look to move the customers to their own platform but I’m sure [the industry regulator] Ofcom would be focused on that being a very smooth transition, especially given that around 250,000 of TalkTalk’s customers are deemed to be vulnerable.”

If the cut-price deals go through TalkTalk’s owners, which include Dunstone, will have to write off about £1bn in debt.

PXC works with the Ministry of Defence although the sale process is unlikely to interrupt the services it provides.

It is understood that work with the MoD is through a third-party reseller, not PXC directly, and that regulations mean there is always at least one other telecoms company to prevent disruption.

It has been reported that Dunstone and TalkTalk’s biggest shareholders, including the private credit company Ares Management, could inject more money to take control of the consumer business if a deal cannot be reached. Shareholders have provided £350m in emergency funding over the past two years.

Dunstone established TalkTalk in 2003 as a subsidiary of Carphone Warehouse in an attempt to shake up the UK broadband market. The business was later demerged, and floated on the London Stock Exchange in 2010.

Initially a success story, at its peak in 2015 TalkTalk’s market value hit almost £4.8bn. But the company struggled at the budget end of the market, unable to invest at scale to compete with rivals such as Sky and BT. As customer numbers dwindled, Dunstone engineered a £1.1bn deal with Toscafund Asset Management in 2021 to take the company private, which saddled the business with debt.

He has been seeking a buyer for TalkTalk for a number of years, with Virgin Media O2 and BT reportedly considering deals, but rivals and investors have been wary of the company’s embattled position at the budget end of the broadband market.

Dunstone remains chair of TalkTalk but the business is effectively under control of its lenders, led by Ares.

articles.title: Pow! Man in Batman costume chases down suspected Norwich handbag thief
articles.excerpt:
Superhero, who was joined by others dressed as comic book characters, retrieved stolen bag after scaling wall

A scene from the fictional comic metropolis of Gotham City played out for real in Norwich...
articles.body_text:
Superhero, who was joined by others dressed as comic book characters, retrieved stolen bag after scaling wall

A scene from the fictional comic metropolis of Gotham City played out for real in Norwich last weekend when a man dressed as Batman chased a suspected thief and recovered a woman’s stolen handbag.

Sonni Mason, 25, was attending a friend’s fancy dress party on Saturday night in a Batman costume when he witnessed a handbag being snatched after a row in a queue for a nightclub in the city.

Mason was joined in the chase by others dressed as comic book characters including Mister Fantastic from the Fantastic Four, and Poison Ivy, another character from the Batman franchise.

They flagged down a group of police officers on their way before catching up with the suspected thief. But the suspect no longer had the bag.

After a tip-off the bag was eventually discovered about 300 metres from where it was snatched, on top of a high flint wall on the perimeter of Norwich Cathedral.

Failed attempts were made to get the bag down with a roll of toilet paper, before Mason, still in his Batman costume, scaled the wall and retrieved the bag. He returned the handbag to its grateful owner with all the contents still inside.

Much of the incident was captured on a TikTok video uploaded to Mason’s account.

In a post about the incident he wrote: “On a night out for a friends birthday, someone swiped someone bag over a pack of cigarettes out of spite …. myself as Batman, Poison Ivy, Mr Fantastic and various other heroes chased him down.”

Speaking to SWNS news agency, Mason, who is from London and works in a cafe, said: “I hope I can inspire people to be a little bit more like Batman. Not so much the running around in the dark in a costume but helping others out. I didn’t expect to be scaling up a wall.”

He added: “Everyone needs a little bit of Batman. You have to be brave, bold and kind. I would hope everyone else would do the same, whether or not they are wearing a cape or a cowl.”

Rather than jump off rooftops or beat people up, he just wanted to make sure everybody was all right, Mason said.

“That’s what [Batman] is about. He’s a protector.

“I just hope more people will be inspired to do the same if they see someone being mugged or feeling uncomfortable on a night out. It shouldn’t take a superhero costume to make you want to do that.”

A Norfolk police spokesperson said: “Officers on routine night-time economy patrols in Norwich were approached by a member of the public, on Saturday September 19, who requested help to find a missing bag.

“Following inquiries at the scene, the bag was located with all of its contents intact and subsequently returned to its owner.”

articles.title: Iran pitches seven-day roadmap to end conflict with US
articles.excerpt:
Iran has proposed a seven-day roadmap aimed at ending the war with the United States.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi outlined the plan to reporters in New York on Thursday, according to US media. Th...
articles.body_text:
Iran has proposed a seven-day roadmap aimed at ending the war with the United States.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi outlined the plan to reporters in New York on Thursday, according to US media. The proposal seeks to implement the conditions in the Memorandum of Understanding agreed by Washington and Tehran in June, including a halt to hostilities and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

Reportedly passed to Washington via mediators earlier this week, Iran’s proposal asks the US to meet specific conditions within seven days to restart ceasefire talks and end the blockade choking the strategically important strait.

The restrictions on maritime traffic in Hormuz have become a key issue in the conflict due to the impact on oil and gas exports and the global economy.

The proposal, which was presented to reporters on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, comes as the war, started by US and Israeli strikes, is almost into its seventh month.

The US-Iran MoU deal expired in August as each side accused the other of violations, and there has been little sign since that they could return to the agreement, although Tehran has suggested it could happen.

Under Iran’s proposal, hostilities would end on all fronts, including Gaza and Lebanon, within seven days, The New York Times reported.

Washington would also release Iran’s frozen assets, estimated at no less than $12bn, waive sanctions on Iranian oil and lift its naval blockade.

The Strait of Hormuz would reopen on the final day of the period. Talks on Iran’s nuclear programme, ostensibly the root cause of the conflict according to President Donald Trump, would start immediately.

The proposal closely resembles the MoU, but sets out a hugely ambitious timetable. The Pakistani and Qatari-brokered deal signed on June 17 set a 60-day window for negotiations, but still unravelled within weeks.

Vague wording led to disputes over who controlled shipping through the strait, and the two sides traded attacks before US President Donald Trump declared the deal “over” on July 7 .

Earlier this month, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran would “immediately reciprocate” if the US returned to its commitments under the MoU.

“We have introduced a plan to the United States through the intermediators,” Araghchi told reporters.

An unnamed White House official told CNN that the administration was having “positive and constructive discussions through the mediators”. The New York Times quoted an official as saying that Washington would not rush into a deal.

An Iranian security source told Al Jazeera there could be room for further diplomatic engagement if Washington met Iran’s conditions and commitments.

However, analysts said the proposal suggests that diplomatic efforts between the US and Iran are not advancing significantly.

“Basically nothing has really changed,” Cyrus Schayegh, professor of international history and politics at the Geneva Graduate Institute, told Al Jazeera.

Iran “keeps insisting that it wants to keep the additional power it gained during the war and that the June memorandum still is basically key to the roadmap moving forward,” said the professor, while the US “keeps basically refusing to accept this roadmap debate”.

No significant movement towards ending the conflict is likely before the US mid-term elections in November, he asserted.

Araghchi told reporters that “it would be better” to reach a deal before that vote. Pezeshkian said earlier that any agreements with the US would not be tied to the timing of the midterms, according to CNN.

articles.title: ‘She never accepted no’: Liam Neeson on dogged heroine behind Tuam mass baby grave film
articles.excerpt:
Catherine Corless’s exposure of almost 800 infant deaths at a home led by nuns prompted Neeson to bring the story to screen

Liam Neeson still remembers his shock and shame when he read a New York Tim...
articles.body_text:
Catherine Corless’s exposure of almost 800 infant deaths at a home led by nuns prompted Neeson to bring the story to screen

Liam Neeson still remembers his shock and shame when he read a New York Times article about the mother and baby institution in Tuam, County Galway.

It was 2017 and the article chronicled the campaign by Catherine Corless, an amateur local historian, to expose abuse and neglect by Irish nuns that led to hundreds of children being buried in a mass, unmarked grave.

“I had such a visceral reaction,” Neeson told the Guardian. “I’m obviously Irish, I was raised in the Catholic church, and I had a deep sense of embarrassment and obligation for the truth to come out and for there to be some accountability.”

It prompted the actor – and former altar boy – to use his heft in the film industry to become a producer for the first time. He optioned the article, visited Corless at her home and assembled a team to put the story on screen.

The result, nine years later, is The Lost Children of Tuam, a feature film that is released in Ireland this week and in the UK next month. “This was such an important story for the world to know about and to give a voice to the hundreds of babies and children that died,” said Neeson.

The release coincides with the continuing excavation of a 5,000 sq metre (53,820 sq ft) site where the Bon Secours order is believed have interred 796 infants who died at the St Mary’s mother and baby home between 1925 and 1961.

An international team of forensic archaeologists and other specialists has found skeletal remains of 99 babies and children since starting work last year – the result of Corless’s research, a judicial commission and a promise by the Irish state to seek truth and justice for survivors and relatives of those who died.

It is part of a wider reckoning of the mistreatment of women and children in state- and religious-run institutions across Ireland. Tuam, however, stands out for its macabre details – some infants were buried in a disused subterranean septic tank – and the doggedness of the woman who exposed it.

In her quest for answers, Corless never accepted “no”, said Neeson. “The detective work she did to uncover this atrocity involving the relationship between the state and the church was extraordinary.”

The film, based on the New York Times article by Dan Barry, tells the story of how Corless, a former textile factory secretary with an interest in local history, began researching the site for an essay. Officials and the Bon Secours order fobbed her off but Corless discovered that 796 children had died without burial records before the institution was closed in 1961 and demolished.

Early reviews of the film, which was written by Rebecca Lenkiewicz and directed by Frank Berry, say it is sensitive and stirring, with the English actor Monica Dolan giving a powerful central performance.

“She’s brilliant – so natural, so down to earth,” said Corless. “She portrayed me as I am. She has an English accent so how on earth did she capture the way I speak?”

Andrew Bennett, who plays her husband, Aidan, has also captured his personality and the couple’s relationship, she said.

Corless has watched the film three times – two private viewings for her family and survivors, and the premiere at the Galway film Fleadh in July, where it won best Irish film. “I was so nervous I needed to see it a few times,” she said.

“We’re ordinary people. We have a farm. That a film would be made about us, it was out of this world. It’s done with great respect, with the odd little bit of humour in it too, and it just hits people, it hits you hard.”

Berry, the director, said the film showed Corless’s integrity and persistence. “Her work revealed a lot of very hard truths about Ireland. It’s a way of telling truths but with an inspirational central character. It shows that one person can achieve amazing things.”
