articles.title: Justin Bieber performs surprise acoustic gig in beleaguered Los Angeles park
articles.excerpt:
Small crowd enjoys singer’s free concert in MacArthur Park, which has often drawn headlines for less cheery reasons

With no announcement and little fanfare, Justin Bieber performed a free acoustic se...
articles.body_text:
Small crowd enjoys singer’s free concert in MacArthur Park, which has often drawn headlines for less cheery reasons

With no announcement and little fanfare, Justin Bieber performed a free acoustic set on Monday at a Los Angeles park often in local headlines for less cheery reasons.

In videos that surfaced online, four musicians flanked the global phenom, who wore a plain T-shirt and shorts as he sang hits including Daisies and Yukon. The low-key affair with a small crowd stood in stark contrast to Bieber’s recent blockbuster World Cup and Coachella performances.

Some online users expressed surprise at the venue choice. A spokesperson for Bieber could not be immediately reached for comment about what spurred the show.

MacArthur Park, located west of downtown Los Angeles, is often described in ominous terms. The area has been plagued by gang activity and rampant drug use. Homeless encampments have also cropped up around the park in recent years.

Earlier this year, federal authorities condemned the park as an “open-air drug market” after arresting several individuals who they accused of trafficking meth and fentanyl on to its grounds.

The park also became a flashpoint in the Los Angeles mayoral race, with mayor Karen Bass’s challengers using it as a benchmark for her progress on public safety.

In June, Bass disavowed crime in the park, saying the Los Angeles police were employing every resource to curtail illicit activity. Bass said the state and county had a role to play in the solution. “They must increase funding for treatment facilities and recovery services to stop the revolving door between jail and our parks,” she said.

Bieber’s performance comes after Los Angeles district attorney Nathan Hochman hosted a picnic at the park, following up on an earlier pledge to make the park family-friendly.

“He’s definitely on the invite list for next year’s Labor Day weekend picnic!” Hochman wrote on X of Bieber.

“Bieber in MacArthur park. That’s progress,” first assistant US attorney Bill Essayli posted on X. “Amazing what can happen when criminals and drug dealers are removed from public spaces.”

articles.title: Trump greets Xi Jinping at plane as Chinese leader arrives for state visit
articles.excerpt:
US president to give red-carpet treatment to Chinese counterpart despite tensions over AI development

AI, trade, Taiwan and climate: what will and won’t be on agenda at Trump-Xi summit

Donald Trump ...
articles.body_text:
US president to give red-carpet treatment to Chinese counterpart despite tensions over AI development

AI, trade, Taiwan and climate: what will and won’t be on agenda at Trump-Xi summit

Donald Trump welcomed Xi Jinping on Wednesday evening, taking the unusual step of greeting the Chinese leader on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews to kick off his state visit to Washington.

Xi’s plane was met with a lavish arrival ceremony that included a 100ft long red carpet flanked by US service members, a military flyover by two B-1 bombers and a presentation of the flags and national anthems of both countries. US presidents typically welcome foreign leaders at the White House, but Trump and first lady Melania Trump traveled to the the military base in Maryland, just outside Washington, to personally shake Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan’s hands upon their arrival in the US.

It came as Scott ⁠Bessent, the US Treasury secretary, announced that the US ⁠and ​China agreed on Wednesday to extend the so-called “Busan ⁠agreement” – a temporary trade truce between the world’s two biggest economies.

Bessent, who met Chinese ‌vice-premier He Lifeng earlier on Wednesday, told Fox News the agreement would be extended until 10 January, two months after it was due to expire.

The pageantry will continue with a formal state welcome on the South Lawn of the White House, private tea with the US president and first lady, and a tour of the National Archives, among other special events.

The simmering trade war is one of many thorny issues Trump and Xi must confront during the visit, including the race in artificial intelligence development and geopolitical instability during the two-day visit.

On Thursday, the White House has invited major tech leaders, such as executives from OpenAI, Apple, xAI, Microsoft, Nvidia, Meta and others, to a state dinner being held for Xi.

The US and China have long been competing to develop increasingly powerful technology, but the race to further AI has become a major topic among tech companies – especially after several executives came forward to warn about the dangers of rapid development.

Trump has dismissed concerns that AI development could harm people, instead promoting more investment in the technology so the US can beat China in the race.

“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so,” Trump wrote on Truth Social last week.

The president and members of the administration have insisted that leading AI development also means leading the world militarily and economically – further raising the stakes for the US and China.

Xi’s visit is expected to be filled with ceremonial displays, reciprocating the treatment Trump received when he visited China earlier this year.

Trump’s decision to greet the Chinese leader at his plane, rather than at the White House, shows how far the US president is willing to go to honor Xi.

“He’s coming on our soil,” Melania Trump said of the visit to Fox & Friends on Wednesday morning, “and we need to welcome them with the most respect.”

articles.title: Bessent reveals extension to Busan agreement with China until January
articles.excerpt:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent discuss U.S.-China relations as President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington D.C., as well as artificial intelligence and Iran on ‘Special Report.’

Treasury Secretary S...
articles.body_text:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent discuss U.S.-China relations as President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington D.C., as well as artificial intelligence and Iran on ‘Special Report.’

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that United States and Chinese officials agreed to extend their bilateral trade truce known as the "Busan agreement" Wednesday on Fox News.

"We have agreed today that we will extend what we call the Busan agreement, the economic detente between the two countries that was scheduled to end on Nov. 10 that is going to be extended until Jan. 10 to give us more time to see what we can do on the economic front," Bessent told "Special Report."

As the United States’ war with Iran nears the seventh-month mark, Bessent is outlining three possible ways the conflict could end while warning that the regime is a "cornered animal."

Bessent that the conflict could end in three ways: members of the regime turn on one another, the Iranian people revolt or Tehran finally comes to the negotiating table and reaches an agreement.

"One, the regime turns on each other — not impossible," he told Fox News. "Two, we get some kind of uprising for the Iranian people. They've probably killed 50,000 of their own population, so very difficult. And then three, to get the Iranians to, if they want to make a deal, to stick to the deal."

AFTER 6 MONTHS OF WAR, US MUST PREPARE FOR A FUTURE AFTER IRAN’S GOVERNMENT FALLS

Scott Bessent, U.S. treasury secretary, during a House Ways and Means Committee hearing in Washington, D.C., on June 11, 2025. (Eric Lee/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

The Treasury Department is continuing its sweeping economic pressure campaign against Iran, targeting Iranian assets and financial networks while pressuring foreign governments and businesses to sever economic ties with Tehran — an effort Bessent said the "world has never seen."

"We have an effort never seen before in terms of constricting and cutting off the financial oxygen to them," the Treasury chief said. "And I don't know whether it's gonna be a week, a month or two months, but they're going to yell uncle."

BESSENT WARNS IRAN'S OUTSIDE BACKERS TO 'STAY AWAY' AS TRUMP SEEKS TO 'ASPHYXIATE' TEHRAN'S ECONOMY

The Treasury launched Operation Economic Outcast in August. It is an extension of the economic strangulation campaign aimed at further severing Iran’s financial lifelines sustaining the regime and further isolating Tehran from the global financial system.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian speaks with Fox News Channel's Martha MacCallum during an interview on September 25, 2025 in New York City. (John Lamparski/Getty Images)

"We have made it very clear around the world, whether it's the financiers, the people who are doing business, the people who are supplying the Iranians, we know who you are, you know who you are, and we are going to prosecute and execute your companies and your bank accounts every day and every week," Bessent warned.

The Treasury chief said he is "not sure" how Iranian officials attending the United Nations General Assembly will return home after imposing hefty restrictions on Iranian airlines.

"External flights from Iran, probably more than 80 or 90% of them, got shut down. I'm not sure how the Iranian representatives at the UN are gonna get home," he told Fox News.

WALTZ DELIVERS BLUNT WARNING TO NATIONS DEFYING IRAN SANCTIONS, TOUTS GREENLAND DEAL

Bessent, who dismissed reports suggesting he is Trump’s top pick for AI czar, went on to address his multi-day talks with China’s Vice Premier He Lifeng this week.

Trump, who is pushing the U.S. to beat China in the global AI arms race, has dismissed concerns surrounding the technology as a "hoax." (iStock; Rob Newell - CameraSport via Getty Images)

The secretary proposed an AI "notification mechanism" between the U.S. and China that would allow the two countries to alert each other about AI-related safety incidents that could pose national security risks.

"They're very eager to engage with us on AI because… the U.S. is substantially in the lead, China's behind us," Bessent said.

China's President Xi Jinping (R) and US President Donald Trump visit the Temple of Heaven on May 14, 2026 in Beijing, China. (Brendan Smialowski - Pool/Getty Images)

"It's very important for us to engage on this," he continued. "I think we are working to define with them what we think the most important or the most perilous risk factors are, whether it's uncontrolled AI agents, whether it is non-state actors using AI, either for cyber ops or for biologics."

Nora Moriarty is a Writer at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Anthony Albanese says OpenAI agent hacked Medicare and he expressed ‘extreme concern’ to Sam Altman
articles.excerpt:
Prime minister says he told chief executive he was disappointed it had taken company ‘way too long’ to inform government of breach

Anthony Albanese says an artificial intelligence agent developed by ...
articles.body_text:
Prime minister says he told chief executive he was disappointed it had taken company ‘way too long’ to inform government of breach

Anthony Albanese says an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare in June and the tech giant notified the government earlier this month using an email sent to a public-facing mailbox.

Australia’s prime minister made the comments at the UN summit in New York, saying it appeared no personal information had been accessed in the AI breach.

Investigations assisted by the Australian Signals Directorate were ongoing, however, into how the agent had infiltrated Australia’s government-run universal health care system.

“This situation is obviously unacceptable,” Albanese said.

“Today, I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident.

“And I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred.”

Albanese said both the delay and the manner in which OpenAI notified the government was disappointing.

“It took until 10 September before there was any notification at all. And the notification was an email sent to just the public mailbox,” Albanese said.

Services Australia then reported the notification to the Australian Cyber Security Centre on 15 September.

A taskforce has been launched to explore the “legal situation” of the breach.

Albanese said the OpenAI agent had gained unauthorised access into the public-facing Medicare statistics reporting service portal, which is administered by Services Australia.

The portal contains non-sensitive Medicare information relating to data and statistics, such as spending.

Albanese said the agent had accessed “public and non-public files within the portal” and, in order to do this, “engaged in writing files as well to the internal server.”

“A forensic investigation, aided by the Australian Signals Directorate, is now under way to ascertain more information, including what other government systems were affected,” Albanese said.

He said there appeared to be no broader compromise to the Services Australia network.

The deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, said the government learned of the June breach “a couple of weeks ago” and ministers were informed last week.

Marles said the agent was non-human and called the breach a “very serious incident”.

“What we have seen is unauthorised access in to an Australian government website and that is completely unacceptable and we have made that clear to OpenAI,” he said.

The AI agent had been given “a benign task” of researching health and medical statistics, and in doing so had approached three other Australian websites as well as the Medicare portal: the Victorian Department of Health, the New South Wales government website, the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, Marles told ABC RN on Thursday morning.

“In relation to those three, it interacted in a way that a member of the public might, so it only acted in an authorised way.

“But in relation to the Medical Portal of Services Australia, it sought information, information was not given, and then it effectively hacked into that medical portal and got that information anyway,” Marles said.

“It’s that unauthorised access which we are very concerned about. … The impact is relatively minor, but the incident is very serious.”

Marles said the government had established a taskforce that will be led by the the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet and working with the Australian Signals Directorate and the AI Safety Institute.

“We will look at what is the legal situation in respect of this and what it means to have gained an unauthorised access, albeit in an unintended way.

“This is a warning about the fact that artificial intelligence, which is a technology that has huge opportunity to benefit humanity, has to be developed with enormous care. There have to be guardrails and safety measures in place which are way ahead of the capability which is being developed,” Marles said.

In a statement, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company was conducting an extensive review of “misaligned model activity during training and evaluation” and was “notifying third parties when our review identifies potential impacts to their systems.”

“During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation,” Pusateri said.

“In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend.”

He said the review had found no evidence of patient records being accessed.

“The information accessed included aggregate health statistics and internal file names.”

Pusateri said OpenAI was supporting investigations and that its review was ongoing, adding it was committed “sharing what we learn as that work continues”.

Lizzie O’Shea, spokesperson for Digital Rights Watch, said the fact that it took three months for OpenAI to tell the government about the incident showed the need for “basic rules and standards for tech companies”.

“Artificial intelligence has potential to do some things well, but it also poses huge risks – like hacking systems that store Australians’ sensitive personal data,” O’Shea said.

“The question is whether governments are going to let AI and tech companies run wild or whether they, on behalf of ordinary people, will put rules in place for tech companies that will promote accountability and trust.”

Ed Santo, former human rights commissioner and co-founder of the Human Technology Institute, told ABC Australians ought to “be worried”.

“This is the first time that this has happened in any major way to an Australian database, and it’s one of the most sensitive databases that we have in government.”

OpenAI had “instructed their AI agents to go looking for information about the public health system in Australia. When the AI agents couldn’t easily find that information, they decided to break the law,” said Santo.

Describing this behaviour as “misaligned model activity” was using “a very euphemistic term”, said Santo.

“That’s ‘misaligned’ in the sense that that was not the intention of Open AI, that it would break into the database. That’s the first problem. The second problem is that these AI agents are hugely capable of hacking.

“If we were in the bricks and mortar world, if an employee of a company went and broke the law, particularly if it broke the criminal law, then that individual would suffer serious legal consequences, but so would their company. And so we need to make sure that that is true also in this era of AI,” Santo said.

articles.title: Indians are discovering the thrill of shopping without paying
articles.excerpt:
FoodNeverComes calls itself a 'dopamine kitchen'

You are hungry. Or you are not. It doesn't matter.

You open FoodNeverComes, pick from 22 cuisines and start scrolling. Butter chicken looks good. So ...
articles.body_text:
FoodNeverComes calls itself a 'dopamine kitchen'

You are hungry. Or you are not. It doesn't matter.

You open FoodNeverComes, pick from 22 cuisines and start scrolling. Butter chicken looks good. So does bibimbap. You add a few dishes, watch the total climb and hit checkout. A tracker says a rider is on the way.

Then you get a dummy AI-generated call from inside the site. He is outside your building, he says, but cannot find your street or door. Except there was never any food in the first place. The order exists only on the screen.

"Order the food. Skip the bill," says the site., external Its slogan is blunter: "The food never comes - but the dopamine does."

Built by two 26-year-old software developers - Purvansh Parmar and Anshul Sharma - from Udaipur in India's northern state of Rajasthan, FoodNeverComes says it has attracted more than 2.7m visitors since its launch in June.

It now offers 22 kitchens, 327 dishes and 319 real recipes, complete with fake prices, a simulated checkout and a fictional delivery experience.

The site offers 22 fake kitchens, 327 dishes and 319 real recipes

FoodNeverComes belongs to a new internet genre: "dopamine sites", which recreate the rituals of consumption without the consumption. There are fake shopping sites, fake delivery services and even fake holidays.

The genre took off in South Korea, external and has since travelled well beyond, spawning a growing crop of sites - Dopamine Shop, external or Fakehaul, external, for example - that mimic everything from food delivery and shopping to travel.

What, exactly, are we enjoying when we enjoy buying something?

The idea began with the founders' own shopping habits. Parmar and Sharma met on a computer science diploma course and later started NeuroX AI, which builds software and AI products and makes Instagram content. They noticed it in their own lives: online baskets filling up with things they wanted, but never actually bought.

Sharma would browse electronics, fill an online basket and abandon it. Parmar's mother did much the same. "She would add things to the cart and say, 'I will order this later'," he recalls.

Parmar's own version ended at food delivery checkouts. During a two-month project in Mumbai, he says, he was spending 5,000-10,000 rupees a week on food, sometimes ordering treats he did not necessarily need: Belgian waffles, ice cream and, once, a large jar of sour cream he barely wanted and gave away to friends.

He believes "perhaps the real craving was not always for the food, but for the ritual of ordering it".

Purvansh Parmar says he spent a lot of money on a work trip on food and treats he did not necessarily need

What begins as genuine hunger, the two argue, can become associated with the pleasure of ordering. Over time, boredom, anxiety or habit can trigger the urge even when the hunger has disappeared.

"Sometimes you're not hungry at all. You're bored or busy, and then you realise that ordering food makes you feel good. You start associating the act of ordering with that dopamine hit. Eventually, it's not just the food you want," says Parmar.

Ravi Dhar, director of the Yale Center for Customer Insights, calls this "anticipatory utility" - the pleasure of looking forward to consumption. It is especially strong with things that capture the imagination - a new pair of shoes, a holiday, a restaurant meal - because anticipation becomes part of the experience.

Sometimes, Dhar says, anticipation can be more pleasurable than ownership: "The thrill is in the chase." Once the object is acquired and the tension resolved, psychological arousal falls.

Neuroscience has a name for this gap between the chase and the catch, and it complicates a popular idea. Dopamine is not simply the brain's pleasure chemical, whatever the internet's talk of "dopamine hits" might suggest.

Swiggy, a popular food delivery site in India, alone handled roughly 2.5m consumer orders a day in FY2025

Kent Berridge, a University of Michigan neuroscientist who developed the theory of "wanting" and "liking", says they are separate processes. Wanting is the motivational pull towards something; liking is the pleasure of having it. They often travel together, but not always. Dopamine, in his account, drives the first, not the second.

Tempting food or products online are likely to activate this wanting system, which Berridge calls "incentive salience".

"Some situations can trigger 'wanting' by itself," he says. We can pursue something intensely even when the eventual pleasure is weak - or, in more everyday terms, want something more than we ultimately like it.

Dr Anna Lembke, a Stanford University addiction psychiatrist and author of Dopamine Nation, makes a similar distinction.

"To call dopamine a chemical of pleasure is an oversimplification," she told me. "Dopamine is the molecule that says 'get more of' or 'do more of', but it doesn't necessarily equate to pleasure."

TripNeverLeaves lets users plan a holiday before sending them on a virtual flight that never leaves the runway.

What she adds is the role of ritual. Cues and habits attached to a reward can become reinforcing in their own right, she says: in addiction, the routines leading up to drug use can eventually matter as much as the drug itself. "Anticipation of reward can be as reinforcing as the reward itself," she says.

Can repeatedly ordering imaginary food satisfy a real craving? Berridge says the ritual could produce a "dopamine hit and strong 'wanting', and also evoke faint conditioned 'liking'".

But he would expect the "novelty to soon wear off", and would be "surprised" if many people returned to place more than about 10 imaginary orders.

Dhar is more open to the possibility that simulated consumption could serve as a kind of release valve.

"While we still need more empirical data to know if simulated shopping can satisfy a consumer urge, evidence from simulated consumption in gaming shows it can be highly effective," he says.

A festive sale of of e-commerce site in India featuring Bollywood star Amitabh Bachchan

But there is an equally plausible danger: the ritual may simply rehearse the behaviour it is supposed to replace.

Lembke says the evidence is not in yet, and the effect may depend on the person. But her own bet is that, over time, the sites could "reinforce the same addictive neural networks they are trying to simulate".

"The one up side, though, is that people using these sites have on some level already admitted to themselves they have a problem, and that admission is often the first step in recovery," says Lembke.

Sharma ran an accidental experiment of his own. When his phone screen cracked, he spent a week on Amazon comparing six or seven replacements and adding them to his basket. Then he repaired the handset.

"I enjoyed the process of research and putting the phones in the cart," he says. "Eventually I didn't buy a phone."

He now catches himself doing the same on food delivery sites, particularly when anxious, filling baskets without checking out. "I realised that I suffer from this problem," he says.

TripNeverLeaves lists 260 places 'you won't go'

The site's blog explores the "serious side" of the fake takeaway, from food-delivery addiction and why fake ordering feels good to cravings, guilt and the psychology of the shopping cart.

The founders have since taken the idea beyond food. A second site, TripNeverLeaves, lets users plan a holiday - destination, flight, seat, hotel and activities - then sends them on a virtual flight that never leaves the runway. They say it has attracted more than 100,000 visitors.

Who those visitors are is harder to establish. But Lembke says younger people may be especially vulnerable to reinforcing digital rewards because the "developing brain is a vulnerable brain".

"In childhood and early adolescence, the front lobe, which acts like the brakes on appetite, is not yet fully connected to the emotion centres of the brain. Hence, teens are more likely to take risks without appreciating the negative consequences, and more likely to get addicted to reinforcing substances and behaviours, once exposed," she says.

For now, the founders say the sites are not about making money. They plan to keep them free and eventually share the data with neuroscientists and psychologists.

What looks like a joke about ordering too much food has stumbled into a bigger question about modern consumption: if so much of the thrill comes before we get the thing, do we need the thing at all?

articles.title: Local Virginia GOP chair says Arlington County officials prioritize illegal immigrants over public safety
articles.excerpt: Arlington County Republican Committee Chairman Matthew Hurtt discussed the House Judiciary Committee's recent interim report, accusing local officials of prioritizing undocumented immigrants over publ...
articles.body_text:
Arlington County Republican Committee Chairman Matthew Hurtt discussed the House Judiciary Committee's recent interim report, accusing local officials of prioritizing undocumented immigrants over public safety.

A recently released House Judiciary Committee report on one Virginia county's effort to resist the Trump administration's immigration enforcement agenda clashes with the region's deep blue politics, according to local Republicans.

The 23-page interim staff report from the committee's Subcommittee on Immigration Integrity, Security, and Enforcement heavily criticized Arlington County's sanctuary policies, accusing the county and local Democratic-run jurisdictions of ignoring public safety while advocating for policies that make it harder for federal immigration authorities to detain and arrest undocumented immigrants with criminal records.

"Chairman [Jim] Jordan's Judiciary Committee report about Arlington is spot on," Matthew Hurtt, the chairman of the Arlington County Republican Committee, told Fox News Digital. "Arlington elected officials prioritize illegal aliens over the safety of Arlington residents. And as an Arlington resident, I've seen this play out over the last several months."

LOCAL GOP LEADER SLAMS $50K TAXPAYER 'SLUSH FUND' FOR FAMILIES OF DETAINED, DEPORTED IMMIGRANT BREADWINNERS

Federal immigration authorities make an arrest in Arlington, Va., in February. A House Judiciary Committee report heavily criticized Arlington County officials over their sanctuary city policies. (U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement)

The report noted the limited cooperation between local law enforcement and immigration authorities. It cited Arlington County's official Board "Trust Policy" rules governing local law enforcement.

The updated May 2025 "Trust Policy" prohibits the Arlington County Police Department "from initiating contact with federal immigration authorities" even when identifying an undocumented immigrant as a "violent felon, gang member, human trafficker, or terrorist."

VIRGINIA COUNTY TO PAY UP TO $2K TO FAMILIES WITH PRIMARY WAGE EARNER DETAINED BY ICE

Parisa Dehghani-Tafti, Commonwealths Attorney for Arlington County & City of Falls Church, Virginia, speaks at an event at the Center for American Progress about Virginias Newly Elected Progressive Prosecutors on Tuesday, December 17, 2019. (Sarah L. Voisin/The Washington Post via Getty Images)

In addition, the committee report referred to a July 16, 2026 closed-door deposition in which Parisa Dehghani-Tafti, the Commonwealth’s Attorney for Arlington County and the City of Falls Church, acknowledged that her office considers immigration status when determining case outcomes and admitted that written guidelines do not forbid considering immigration status for any crime.

She also defended a memo asking prosecutors to consider other charges when a Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipient is accused of drunk driving.

SOROS-BACKED DA ACCUSED OF GOING EASY ON ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS GETS SQUEEZED BY HOUSE GOP

Since U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services classifies a DUI conviction as a "significant misdemeanor" — which bars DACA renewal and triggers deportation — the memo instructs prosecutors to consider DACA status to avoid "disproportionate and devastating collateral consequences."

"It's not the job of a prosecutor to decide lenience against illegal aliens who are oftentimes committing violent crimes against individuals or property crimes, but that is exactly what Arlington Commonwealth's Attorney Parisa Dehghani-Tafti has been doing," Hurtt said.

JIM JORDAN SUBPOENAS BLUE STATE DAS ACCUSED OF 'PREFERENTIAL TREATMENT' FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CRIMINALS

Arlington Countuy Board of Supervisors (from left to right): Julius D. "JD" Spain, Sr., Susan Cunningham, Takis Karantonis, Board Chair Matt de Ferranti and Vice Chair Maureen Coffey. (Arlington County)

"[Dehghani-]Tafti sees herself as a left-wing criminal justice activist," added Hurtt, while also criticizing Steve Descano, the Commonwealth's Attorney for nearby Democratic-run Fairfax County, which has made national headlines amid a string of crimes allegedly committed by undocumented immigrants.

In a statement obtained by by ARLNow, Dehghani-Tafti described the committee report as a "political sham."

"The Committee refused to hear my testimony in public because open testimony doesn’t let you distort a record," she said. "This report is the predictable product of that process—a piece of political propaganda timed for the midterms, built on the deliberate misrepresentations of my policies and my testimony."

"Now it’s clear why they wouldn’t hold a public hearing and why they stonewalled my requests for the full deposition transcript," she added. "They didn’t want the public to see it. I demand the Committee release the full, unedited transcript of my deposition immediately."

Fox News Digital has reached out to Dehghani-Tafti's office, as well as the Sheriff's Office and the County Board.

Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

articles.title: Sharp weapon discovered by TSA tucked inside unusual item in passenger's carry-on bag
articles.excerpt:
Travel expert Gary Leff discusses how a pair of passengers intentionally concealed a blade in a toiletry item while passing through airport screening in Texas.

A routine carry-on screening at a Texas...
articles.body_text:
Travel expert Gary Leff discusses how a pair of passengers intentionally concealed a blade in a toiletry item while passing through airport screening in Texas.

A routine carry-on screening at a Texas airport took an unusual turn after TSA officers made a suspicious discovery — and later heard an unexpected explanation from the travelers.

Transportation Security Administration (TSA) officers at Dallas Love Field Airport (DAL) found a pocketknife concealed inside a tube of toothpaste, according to an employee story published on the agency's website.

TSA Officer Jazmine Kramer was screening the carry-on bag with an X-ray machine when she noticed what appeared to be a metal object near the toiletries — and flagged the bag for a closer look.

TSA OFFICER SEES ALARMING SHAPES ON X-RAY BEFORE STOLEN CIVIL WAR MYSTERY UNRAVELS

"Usually when people have prohibited items in their bags, it's by accident," Kramer said in the write-up on the iste. "It's not normally because they intentionally put something there thinking it will make it through."

Wade Brown, Jr., a security training instructor, searched the toiletry bag but initially could not find the object seen on the X-ray.

TSA Officer Jazmine Kramer and Security Training Instructor Wade Brown Jr., shown at right, examine the X-ray image of a suspicious item before Brown searches the passenger's carry-on bag. (TSA DAL photo)

Brown sent the belongings through the X-ray machine again to narrow down its location.

He then picked up the toothpaste tube, noticed it did not feel right — and spotted tape near one end, according to TSA.

A closer inspection revealed the pocketknife hidden inside.

"I was super surprised when they said that."

Fox News Digital reached out to TSA for comment and further details.

The married couple who owned the bag told officers their son had suggested concealing the knife inside the toothpaste tube in an attempt to get it through airport security, TSA said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"I was super surprised when they both said that," Brown said. "This was the first time at DAL I had ever seen someone intentionally hide an item inside something else in an attempt to get it through security."

TSA officers discovered a pocketknife concealed inside a tube of toothpaste, pictured above, during a routine carry-on screening. (TSA DAL photo)

The couple voluntarily surrendered the pocketknife.

They were then allowed to continue on to their flight, according to TSA.

Brown said the incident highlighted the importance of communication between officers when something detected on an X-ray cannot immediately be found during a hands-on bag search.

"If one officer sees something and another officer cannot locate it during the search, work together and communicate until you find it," he said.

TSA Dallas Love Field Federal Security Director Amy Williams said officers must be prepared for unexpected discoveries during screenings.

TSA officials stress the importance of communication and teamwork among officers when tracking down a suspicious item. (Lori Van Buren/Albany Times Union via Getty Images)

"A knife concealed inside a toothpaste tube is not something travelers typically encounter, but it is exactly the type of threat our officers are trained to identify and resolve," Williams said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Fox News Digital previously reported on another unusual knife discovery at an airport checkpoint, this time involving a passenger at Tampa International Airport.

TSA officers recently found a 4-inch, double-edged knife concealed inside a baseball bat-shaped flashlight that had been placed beneath the lining of the passenger's carry-on bag.

The passenger initially said he did not know the item was in his luggage — but later told authorities he had placed it beneath the suitcase lining to save space.

He was arrested and was not allowed to travel, TSA said.

Kelly McGreal is a production assistant with the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Mike Macdonald apologizes to Sean Payton for revealing Spygate-type accusations between Broncos and Seahawks
articles.excerpt: "I worked so hard to get the respect of the coaches and the players, to be able to have meaningful conversation in a production meeting. And when that happened, I was devastated. I was devastated that...
articles.body_text:
"I worked so hard to get the respect of the coaches and the players, to be able to have meaningful conversation in a production meeting. And when that happened, I was devastated. I was devastated that I had to go back to square one."

The rift between the Seattle Seahawks and Denver Broncos, personified by threats of NFL investigations and counter-threats of a lawsuit by coaches Sean Payton and Mike Macdonald, has been put to bed by an apology.

Macdonald said Wednesday he has apologized to Payton.

But the interesting thing about the whole deal is that the apology came for the fact the exchange between the teams and coaches went public. And it got out because the Seahawks' coach shared the saga on a podcast without expecting it to get out.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Seattle Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald watches from the sidelines during the first half of an NFL football game against the Arizona Cardinals Thursday, Sept. 25, 2025, in Glendale, Arizona. (AP Photo/Rick Scuteri)

"It's something that I didn't intend for public use but you know, it just felt like it was the most appropriate thing to reach out to Sean and really just apologize to him for having that end up being public where it wasn't meant to," Macdonald said.

"You're kind of, something that they have to deal with in real time that wasn't really on their end. So that's really where you're like, 'Crap!'"

The reason Macdonald was cursing the situation is because he shared on the "In Depth With Graham Bensigner" podcast the story of Payton and the Broncos wrongfully accusing Macdonald and the Seahawks of cheating in 2024 by using practice video obtained from fans.

Macdonald shared the story not expecting it to be shared.

Denver Broncos head coach Sean Payton looks on as players take part in drills at an NFL football training practice Monday, July 28, 2025, in Centennial, Colo. (AP Photo/David Zalubowski)

SEAN PAYTON TAKES VICIOUS SHOT AT FALCONS HOME CROWD AFTER HUMILIATING FIRST HALF

And because it had Payton threatening to report the Seahawks to the NFL for violating NFL filming rules a la Spygate, and because the Seahawks threatened to sue Payton and the Broncos if he took that step, it went viral.

"It's a lesson learned," Macdonald said. "You know, honestly, I got to be better in that moment for understanding, like, I'm responsible for what I say, really, no matter the circumstance – whether you're mic'd up, whether or not you have some certain type of understanding.

"So I fell short in that moment ... It stings for me, frankly, but it's something that I'm definitely going to learn from."

The lesson Macdonald will learn is not to share interesting stories expecting confidentiality – especially when the story is as juicy as this one.

Seattle Seahawks general manager John Schneider speaks during the Super Bowl LX trophy celebration at Lumen Field on Feb. 11, 2026. (Kirby Lee/Imagn Images)

On the clip, Macdonald tells the story of how in 2024 the Seahawks took video sourced from fans attending Broncos training camp practices in scouting their upcoming opponent.

"We took like 100 plays from their training camp. We were scouting them," Macdonald said.

Payton somehow found out the Seahawks had seen some of Denver's plays, called Seahawks general manager John Schneider and "lost it," according to Macdonald.

"He basically threatened to come out publicly and do a whole Patriot Spygate-type of thing," Macdonald said on the podcast.

"I'm sitting there like, 'Oh my God. We didn't cheat.' They thought it was a Michigan thing where we had a plant and the whole thing. So, we had to counter with him and say, 'If you come out with this, we're going to sue you because it's not true.'"

Payton and the Broncos obviously didn't make good on their threat to report the Seahawks, but things got a little frosty between the coaches.

Denver Broncos head coach Sean Payton works on the sidelines during the first half an NFL football game against the Kansas City Chiefs Sunday, Nov. 16, 2025, in Denver. (AP Photo/Jack Dempsey)

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

That relationship, oddly enough, has warmed in part because of Macdonald making it public and calling Payton to apologize.

"Sean was great," Macdonald said. "I'll say, I respect the heck out of him and his program. Always have. He's a phenomenal football coach. It's been it's been great to get to know him at the owners meetings the last couple years.

"And and he was awesome. So I know we're both looking forward to moving forward from it, but I really appreciate how he handled it."

FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

Armando Salguero is OutKick's Senior NFL Writer.

articles.title: Inside GOP Senate hopeful's financial ties to controversial data center boom
articles.excerpt: FOX Business correspondent Connor Hanson reports on the infrastructure and resource usage of data centers in Northern Virginia ahead of the midterm elections. Hansen tours a facility to detail server ...
articles.body_text:
FOX Business correspondent Connor Hanson reports on the infrastructure and resource usage of data centers in Northern Virginia ahead of the midterm elections. Hansen tours a facility to detail server cooling systems, water conservation metrics and corporate agreements regarding President Donald Trump's ratepayer protection pledge.

Michael Whatley, the former chair of the Republican National Committee and the Republican nominee for U.S. Senate in North Carolina, holds between $246,000 and $690,000 in energy investments with companies fueling the data center growth in the Tar Heel State, according to his federal reporting.

Those holdings raise questions about whether Whatley stands to benefit from his support of data center expansion, an issue that has drawn national attention over community zoning, energy use and state growth.

Most of his reported holdings are with four companies.

FOX NEWS POLL: DEMOCRATIC ENTHUSIASM SHAPES NORTH CAROLINA SENATE RACE

Now-former Republican National Committee chair Michael Whatley is interviewed by Fox News Digital at the RNC headquarters in Washington, D.C., on July 14, 2025 (Paul Steinhauser - Fox News)

Whatley and his family have holdings between $149,000 and $410,000 in Duke Energy, between $1,000 and $15,000 in Arista Networks, from $80,000 to $200,000 with Dominion Energy, and between $16,000 and $65,000 in GE Vernova.

While most of those, like Duke and Vernova, don’t directly build data centers themselves, they offer services or products used by them. Duke is a major utility provider in North Carolina, and Vernova produces on-site gas turbines used by data center facilities operated by companies like Amazon and Microsoft.

In addition to those investments, Whatley reported $361,000 from CAPCVentures LLC, a D.C. for consulting services in 2025, according to his financial disclosure. That firm lists GE Vernova— a major supplier of turbines and grid equipment used to power data centers — as a client, along with Centrus Energy and the Renewable Fuels Association.

Earlier coverage put his pay from the same shop at about $755,000 between 2022 and 2025.

When asked about his holdings and whether he saw them as a potential conflict of interest, Whatley's campaign noted that he supports restrictions on stock trading for members of Congress.

"Whatley supports the Stop Insider Trading Act and urges the U.S. Senate to pass the commonsense legislation, and supports commonsense reforms requiring elected officials to place their assets in qualified blind trusts, ensuring they have no control over how those assets are invested," DJ Griffin, a campaign spokesperson, said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

The campaign also said that Whatley would support letting local communities decide for themselves what kinds of data center projects to accept and which ones to rule out.

"Michael Whatley's standard is simple: data centers pay their own way, families pay nothing and communities decide. That means Big Tech builds or buys every megawatt it needs and covers every dime of the grid upgrades to deliver it, with zero costs shifted onto residential ratepayers. It means no special subsidies and no sweetheart deals cut over the heads of taxpayers," Griffin continued.

"And it means the people of North Carolina's counties and towns, not bureaucrats in Raleigh or Washington, decide what gets built in their communities. North Carolina should win the AI economy, and it should win it on terms that protect the families who live here."

THE DATA CENTER FIGHT COULD DECIDE THE NEXT PRESIDENT AND COST AMERICA THE AI RACE

Michael Whatley, former chair of the Republican National Committee and Republican U.S. Senate candidate for North Carolina, arrives at the Grace Chapel Fire Department polling location during the North Carolina primary election in Granite Falls, N.C., on Tuesday, March 3, 2026. Senate candidates Roy Cooper and Michael Whatley will look for momentum from the primary vote in what looks to be one of the most expensive races of the 2026 midterms. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Whatley's campaign also turned the spotlight on his Democratic opponent, Roy Cooper, the former governor of North Carolina.

"Roy Cooper is the only candidate in this race who has used the powers of his elected office to recruit data centers to NC and to have them subsidized by NC Taxpayers," Griffin added, noting that Cooper also has supported restrictions on congressional stock trading.

Notably, the bulk of North Carolina’s tax breaks already existed by the time Cooper became governor in 2017.

The year before, in 2016, the state had implemented statute G.S.105-164.13. Under that provision, lawmakers had expanded data center tax exemptions on sales, servers, storage and networking for companies investing at least $75 million in projects over five years.

The state did, however, approve several major grants to companies like Apple and Corvid Technologies under Cooper's watch through "Job Development Investment Grants" (JDIGs). Those aimed to further job development in the state, dovetailing with existing development efforts. Among the more high-profile JDIGs, Apple entered into a $845 million grant over a period of 39 years alongside another $112.4 million that would go to an industrial development fund to build out rural infrastructure. The agreement is contingent on Apple creating a certain number of jobs, but the company has yet to meet the JDIG's projected goals since its implementation.

For his own part, Cooper's campaign bashed Whatley for, in their view, not being sensitive enough to local resistance to data center expansion.

"Longtime utility company lobbyist Michael Whatley believes people’s concerns about data centers are fake as he continues to shill for his billionaire buddies in the utility industry instead of standing up against rate hikes that are crushing hardworking families," a spokesperson for the Cooper campaign said in a statement.

Cooper has taken a more critical approach to their expansion, arguing that they are forcing local communities into higher and higher utility bills.

SILICON VALLEY IS LOSING THE DATA CENTER FIGHT, RISKING A REPEAT OF A CLASSIC FAILURE

Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Roy Cooper and Republican U.S. Senate candidate Michael Whatley are the top candidates in North Carolina's Senate race. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Alex Wong/Getty Images)

Like many Democrats on the topic, Cooper has framed his stance in the broader context of championing affordability policies.

"[Cooper] believes local communities must have the final say on new projects coming to their area, which includes local moratoriums, and data centers must pay for all of the energy they use without passing on any of their costs to consumers," Cooper's campaign said.

Having cleared their respective primaries, Cooper and Whatley will face off in North Carolina's general election on Nov. 3.

Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

articles.excerpt:

The prime minister made the co...
articles.body_text:
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Anthony Albanese has revealed an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare in June.

The prime minister made the comments at the UN summit in New York.

double quotation markThis incident occurred in June this year and involved an Open AI agent gaining unauthorised access into the public-facing Medicare statistics reporting service portal, which is administered by Services Australia.

The AI agent accessed both public and non-public files.

A forensic investigation, aided by the Australian Signals Directorate, is now under way to ascertain more information, including what other government systems were affected.

The Medicare statistics reporting portal is a public-facing statistics portal that contains non-sensitive Medicare information relating to data and statistics, such as spending.

No personal information is believed to have been accessed at this stage but investigations are ongoing.

Evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the Services Australia network.

Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable.

Today, I spoke with the CEO of Open AI, Sam Altman, to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident.

And I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred.

Albanese pays tribute to Ukraine’s resistance

Albanese said the bilateral agreement would be in place not only during the war in Ukraine, but during peacetime once the conflict concludes.

The prime minister became emotional as he paid tribute to his “friend” Zelenskyy in his fight against Russian aggression.

“[Zelenskyy’s] leadership has been, I think, quite extraordinary, leading people in circumstances which are extraordinarily difficult,” he said.

“Russia thought it could just steamroll through in a matter of weeks, and what we have found is that the people of Ukraine were underestimated.”

The two leaders hugged when they first met in-person at the summit, with Zelenskyy thanking Australia for its support to Ukraine throughout the conflict.

“[The agreement is] the strongest document between our countries,” he told reporters.

“We really will increase our co-production and trade and, of course, security, which is really important.

“It’s all for our people, for the security.”

As part of the agreement, Australia will also step up training to help Ukrainian forces deter and repel any future Russian attacks.

It will also look to explore cooperation for training centres and jointly produce air-defence measures, missiles and drones.

Australia will join forces with the United Kingdom and Norway-led coalition to help support the development of Ukraine’s navy.

Work will be carried out to strengthen Ukraine’s maritime capability.

Australia and Ukraine will also work together to rebuilding infrastructure such as military healthcare facilities and training centres.

Extra sanctions have also been imposed on Russia, coinciding with the announcement of the agreement.

It brings the total sanctions placed on Russia and its supporters by the federal government to more than 1900.

In a busy day of dipolomacy, Anthony Albanese also announced Australia will provide $60m more in support for Ukraine’s fight against Russia’s invasion as part of a fresh security agreement, Australian Associated Press reports.

The prime minister met Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr ⁠Zelenskyy, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

The 10-year bilateral security agreement, signed by both leaders, will lead to an extra $45m in Australian Defence Force equipment for Ukraine.

A further $10m will go to Ukraine’s energy support fund, while $5m will be spent on humanitarian assistance.

The $60m fund will bring Australia’s total contribution to Ukraine since Russia’s invasion in 2022 to $1.9bn.

The prime minister said the agreement was a proud day for Australians in seeking to uphold international laws.

Albanese told reporters in New York upon signing the agreement.

double quotation markThis is an issue not just for Europe, this is an issue for the world. If a large, more powerful country in Russia is allowed to profit from breaking the international rules of law with its illegal and immoral invasion of Ukraine, then that sets a bad precedent for the entire world.

PM to say Indo-Pacific ‘not a chessboard’ for superpowers

While Australia had ties with the US and China as its key security and trading partners respectively, Albanese will say the competition between the two powers should not be the only lens the Pacific should be dealt with.

“The Indo-Pacific is not a chessboard on which superpowers move the pieces,” he will say.

“Its countries are not spectators, they are shaping its future and writing their own script.”

The prime minister will make the speech after receiving the Atlantic Council’s Global Citizen award, where he is being recognised for his role in deepening alliances and promoting security and stability in the Indo-Pacific.

He will be among four award recipients at the event, including Formula One boss Stefano Domenicali, the president of Finland, Alexander Stubb, and actor Cynthia Erivo.

The speech comes a day after Albanese met briefly with Donald Trump at a gala dinner hosted by the American leader.

The prime minister and Trump have issued divergent calls on whether to rein in the use of AI after safety fears or, in the case of the US leader, accelerate its rollout.

The international world order set up after the second world war is no longer fit for the present-day environment, the prime minister will declare in a major foreign policy speech in New York today, Australian Associated Press reports.

In an address to the Atlantic Council, Anthony Albanese will say many of the institutions that were necessary post-1945 were not enough to meet present-day challenges.

The prime minister will use the speech on the sidelines of the United Nations general assembly in New York to argue partnerships with alliances remain crucial in a rapidly changing global environment.

double quotation markSince the end of the cold war, the prevailing assumptions of international affairs were clear: openness was security, efficiency mattered more than resilience and international rules would be observed.

Those assumptions rested on the expectation that the influence of the major democratic powers would remain largely unchallenged.

The post-1945 world order is no longer fit for purpose. Universal institutions that remain necessary are now not always sufficient for the challenges we face.

The prime minister will say Australia needed to shape a world order that will replace the old one, while preserving diplomatic rules.

Albanese will point to the strategic competition between the United States and China in the Indo-Pacific region as being the most consequential issue facing the region.

OECD says Australia will struggle to get underlying inflation below 3%

The OECD says Australia will struggle to bring underlying inflation back below 3% in 2027, despite sub-par economic growth in this year and the next.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development in its interim economic outlook flagged that the world economy had, once again, proved more resilient than expected to the global energy shock triggered by the ongoing Iran war.

The artificial intelligence boom had papered over many of the cracks, the report said, adding that “global economic prospects remain heavily dependent on whether a durable resolution to the Middle East conflict is achieved”.

With fuel costs here jumping over recent weeks and inflation proving more persistent than hoped, there is a strong consensus that the Reserve Bank will deliver another interest rate hike next Tuesday – the fourth this year.

The OECD projected Australia’s headline inflation would drop from 4.1% this year, to 2.8% in 2027.

But “core” inflation – which removes the effects of big price swings, like for fuel – would prove harder to shift back into the RBA’s 2-3% target range.

The OECD expected the underlying price growth measure to ease from 3.5% in 2026 to 3.1% in 2027.

“Faced with renewed energy price shocks and stronger than expected demand pressures, and at a time when inflation is already above target in many economies, central banks need to ensure that underlying inflation pressures are durably contained,” the OECD said.
